text: The inflationary prefactor e^K K^{X X̄} is engineered to have a minimum in the modulus direction. The authors then analyze post-inflationary scalar stability and the risk of overshooting between the two stabilization minima.

Modulus-induced trajectory shifts are calculated perturbatively in W_mod, its covariant derivative and higher derivatives relative to W_X. The resulting potential is used for slow-roll predictions, with m fixed by the scalar power-spectrum amplitude.

Uses cosmological field evolution with Hubble friction for modulus dynamics, and a Boltzmann equation for production of incoherent gravitational relics. These are recorded as methods presented in the source, without reproducing their calculations.

Uses messenger integration, wave-function renormalization and RG equations with analytic continuation into superspace to describe soft masses; Coleman–Weinberg corrections lift the spurion pseudomodulus.
Studies finite-temperature effective potentials, thermal masses, free-energy preference for light degrees of freedom, and classical transitions versus barrier-suppressed tunneling between vacua.

Decompose dust kinematics into expansion, shear and vorticity, then spatially average the scalar Raychaudhuri, Hamiltonian-constraint and mass-conservation equations. The resulting Buchert equations couple kinematical backreaction to averaged intrinsic curvature.

Review exact spherical and disjoint-region toy models, statistical peak/trough models and volume partitions into overdense and underdense regions. The peak model uses an initial Gaussian power spectrum, spherical regional evolution and a smoothing scale selected by σ(t,R)=1.

Power counts arbitrary 1PI diagrams using k^−4 graviton propagators, k^−2 ghost propagators and two-/four-derivative gravitational vertices. In Landau gauge, each external ghost or antighost contributes two external momenta, strengthening the convergence bounds.

Decomposes the quadratic graviton operator into spin-2, spin-1 and scalar projection operators, adds BRST gauge fixing and Faddeev–Popov ghosts, and inverts the operator to study large-momentum propagator behavior.

Introduces BRST sources Kμν and Lμ, derives Slavnov–Taylor and ghost identities, and uses an induction in loop order to constrain the divergent effective action. Dimensional-regularization poles are separated from finite terms.

Variation gives the nonlinear Maxwell equation d(*F/√ℱ) = 0 and the Einstein equations with the nonlinear electromagnetic stress tensor. The magnetic branch is integrated to a metric function given by quadrature, followed by small- and large-radius expansions.

Uses the charged test-particle Lagrangian, its conserved energy and the trajectory normalization to obtain a radial equation of the form ṙ²+Veff = ℰ². Series expansions test for linear terms; a specially chosen electric example is integrated explicitly.

Invert the extrapolate dictionary using Green's theorem, finite-global-time Green functions with spacelike/null support and perturbative iteration of interacting bulk equations. Ordinary Cauchy evolution and CFT time evolution convert bulk operators into single-time nonlocal boundary precursors.

Use folded real-time path integrals, with forward and backward evolution, to represent precursor insertions. Bulk Hamiltonian boundary terms and canonical constraints supply an alternative argument for dependence only on boundary dynamics near the chosen measurement time.

Interpret fixed-gauge fields through boundary-anchored Wilson lines or geodesically defined positions. Canonically quantize Maxwell theory after imposing generalized Coulomb gauge, solve the elliptic constraint using Fourier/Bessel Green functions and obtain nonlocal equal-time commutators.

Derive leading smearing kernels from normalizable mode expansions and boundary current/stress-tensor dictionaries. For gravity, solve the Hamiltonian constraint in transverse gauge, then obtain source-free metric smearing separately in radial gauge.

Generalized complex geometry expresses supersymmetry through compatible pure-spinor polyforms, twisted exterior derivatives and RR Bianchi identities. A b-transform simplifies the generic AdS flux expressions.

Expand forms in an ISO(3)-invariant basis, impose orientifold parity and algebraic compatibility, eliminate redundant variables, and fix radial reparameterization freedom. The resulting radial equations are investigated perturbatively and numerically.

Expand the action to quadratic order in the graviton fluctuation, add harmonic gauge fixing and gauge ghosts, and invert the kinetic operator using orthogonal spin projectors to isolate physical and gauge-dependent propagator sectors.

Estimate loop divergences from propagator and vertex scaling using I = V + L − 1. A second estimate treats exponential form factors. Static Fourier transformation of the modified propagator supplies the gravitational potential.

Use SU(8) formulas for the scalar equations, all 70 scalar masses and Killing-spinor conditions. At the chosen origin, flux constraints and stationarity become algebraic equations; gauge brackets then identify the gauging.

Decompose the embedding tensor under SL(2) × SO(6,6) into f, ξ, F and Ξ components, solve the linear constraint and derive the quadratic constraints. A T-tensor and vielbein change of basis connect these components to SU(8) fermionic mass tensors.

A charged-fluid analogy separates flux pressure, attraction toward opposite charge, and annihilation. It contrasts a finite-density stationary metastable configuration with increasing clumping that removes the annihilation barrier.

An anti-D6-inspired, T-dual flux relation introduces a clumping parameter λ multiplying the BPS flux-duality relation. For the KS application, the authors require this simplified relation only in an integrated sense, rather than as the complete local flux structure.

The NS5 probe potential is modified through the clumped three-form flux and its B6 coupling, retaining the topologically fixed F3 flux. The potential for the NS5 position ψ is obtained by setting momentum to zero in the higher-derivative Hamiltonian.

The supercovariant derivative expansion counts derivatives, fermion bilinears and auxiliary F terms together. The author requires |F|/M²≪1 as well as small derivatives and fermion bilinears, with M the lowest integrated-out mass scale.

Matter metrics and sectional curvatures are expanded at large volume and inserted into m²_(αβ̄)=(V0+m²_(3/2))K_(αβ̄)−F^iF^(j̄)R_(ij̄αβ̄). Canonical normalization separates flavor-universal and flavor-violating pieces; A-term alignment or suppression is also considered.

The adopted FCNC criterion is Δm²/m²≲10⁻³[m/(500 GeV)]. Bounds on the volume are combined with the independent upper bound on the gravitino mass to assess whether TeV-scale soft masses remain possible.

Determine downstairs spectra by tensoring upstairs cohomology representations with Wilson-line representations and extracting Γ invariants. Graded multiplicities follow from equivariant characters, spectral-sequence methods and character inner products.
Enumerate J-invariant effective operators as singlet expansions and analyze supergravity D/F terms. Extension spaces Ext¹(Ub,Ua)=H¹(X,Ua⊗Ub*) identify candidate deformations away from split bundles.

Compute bundle cohomology using indices, Serre duality, vanishing theorems, Koszul resolutions and Bott–Borel–Weil representations; exceptional unresolved cases require more explicit methods such as Čech cohomology.

Two anomalous matter-field redefinitions move the FN phase into currents and then remove the axion-gluon coupling. Current algebra determines nucleon couplings. Choosing Q_A=M_q⁻¹/(2 tr M_q⁻¹), with tr Q_A=1/2, removes axion–meson mass mixing; kinetic mixing remains suppressed.

Gauge-invariant Yukawa and higher-dimensional FN operators are constructed from closed quiver loops. Quark mass ratios determine ⟨φ⟩/M; dimension-five or dimension-seven neutrino operators then provide an estimate of the high scale M.

An anomaly-free hypercharge direction and two anomalous charge combinations are identified. Green–Schwarz couplings, together with abelian Chern–Simons terms where needed, cancel anomalies; Stückelberg terms determine heavy-vector masses and the surviving scalar combination.

Interpret the overdamped gauge equation through an effective potential, derive the axion trajectory in e-fold time, and estimate scalar fluctuations using δN≈(∂N/∂X₀)δX while neglecting gauge-field fluctuations.

Reduce the action on the homogeneous background, neglect Ẍ, ψ̈ and Ḣ in the slow-roll analysis, and diagonalize the coupled equations. The authors explicitly require diagonalization before substituting the gauge-field minimum and integrating out ψ.

Fix a winding-direction connection by metric compatibility and a prescribed covariant-derivative commutator on scalars. Construct curvature from the commutator on vectors, contract to Ricci quantities, and organize the DFT action using these geometric objects.

Introduce the anholonomic derivative D̃ᶦ=∂̃ᶦ−βᶦʲ∂j. Its commutator is expressed through Q and R fluxes; the strong constraint is used both in establishing this algebra and in showing scalar-derivative covariance.

Four-dimensional supergravity with α′ and string-loop Kähler corrections, racetrack gaugino condensation on T3, and T5-dependent poly-instantons. Stabilization is organized at successive orders V^(−3), V^(−10/3), and V^(−3−p).

Canonical normalization of the Kähler metric order by order in inverse volume; extraction of moduli–gauge-boson couplings from gauge kinetic terms; expansion of Γ(σ) and curvature correlators through the trispectrum.

Thermal and turbulent fits are combined by matching the first two moments of a two-Gaussian mixture, weighted by exp(−AICC/2). Comparable fits with discrepant Δα/α values increase the resulting uncertainty through a between-model variance term.

Simultaneous nonlinear least-squares Voigt-profile fitting uses VPFIT. Velocity components are selected using χ²ν near unity, minimal corrected Akaike criterion AICC=χ²+2p+2p(p+1)/(n−p−1), and absence of substantial residual correlations. Δα/α is introduced only after constructing the velocity model.

Modified least trimmed squares retains k=0.85n points to estimate extra quadrature scatter σrand. Residuals exceeding 3σ are discarded only in full-sample applications, followed by ordinary weighted fitting. Angular dipoles admit linear least squares in Cartesian components; bootstrap resampling estimates amplitude intervals and sightline-randomization significance.

The authors calculate linear spatial Ricci curvature R(3)=4∇²ΦN/a², average it over the last-scattering volume using Gauss's law, and evaluate its ensemble variance through Fourier and spherical-harmonic/Bessel decompositions.

CMB multipoles are calculated using the Sachs–Wolfe approximation δT/T0=−ΦN/3 and spherical Bessel kernels. Small-scale power is calibrated to historical WMAP-seven-year CAMB output with scalar spectral index set to one; C2 and C4 are additionally renormalized by hand to match the large-L* limit.

Bayesian conditioning on C2, C3 and C4 integrates out L*. At fixed L*, curvature is Gaussian and multipole estimators have χ² distributions; the likelihood factorizes under the Gaussian model. Flat and logarithmic L* priors give similar results, with the more conservative logarithmic prior presented.

Minimize first with respect to the geometric small modulus and then the volume, imposing vacuum-energy tuning conditions. Analyze loop corrections and the loop-induced blow-up field redefinition separately, including stability conditions for candidate extrema.

Compute the supergravity F-term potential together with the anomalous-U(1) D-term, expand order by order in inverse volume, and minimize the leading 𝒱⁻² terms before analyzing the 𝒱⁻³ stabilization potential.

Reconstruct scalar fields and potentials parametrically from f, including V(x) = x² + f(x)/2 with x = √ρ. A second construction prescribes H(t) and reconstructs a scalar-tensor action with field-dependent kinetic coefficient and potential.

Classify future evolution through convergence of the dark-energy-dominated time integral and the corresponding scale-factor integral. The classification, credited to earlier work, distinguishes finite-time divergent-density singularities, Little Rip evolution, finite-density de Sitter limits and divergent-pressure Type II events.

Compare luminosity-distance and distance-modulus curves with historical Supernova Cosmology Project data; examine deceleration and jerk parameters. Numerically integrate redshift-time relations to estimate universe ages and remaining lifetimes for example parameter choices.

Diagonalize the slow-roll equations for the axion and gauge-field velocities. Identify an approximate gauge-field trajectory ψ_min = [μ⁴ sin(X/f)/(3g̃λH)]^(1/3), then compare it with numerical background evolution.

Numerically evaluate the approximate e-fold integral and compare it with integration of the full equations across the cases considered. Separately evolve the axion-integrated Gauge-flation action to compare phase-space trajectories with the full axion theory.
Introduce a gauge-dependent source Ξ in the effective axion potential and extremize it. At leading slow-roll order, sin(χ/f) = Ξ ≃ 3gλHψ³/μ⁴, obtained after dropping ψ̇ relative to Hψ.

Expand the resulting nonpolynomial U(Ξ) through quadratic order for Ξ ≪ 1 and match the induced (F F̃)² coefficient to the Gauge-flation action. Compare parameter examples and initial-condition ranges credited to earlier analyses.

Expand χ̃ = χ + δχ around the selected minimum, retain quadratic fluctuations and evaluate a one-loop determinant. Approximate the inflationary Laplacian by its flat-space form for the dominant subhorizon contribution and use the stated MS prescription.

Compare the HJ rewriting of the action as sums and differences of squares with the usual fake-superpotential rewriting. Factorization ℳW=e^(aU)W(φ) reproduces both the standard scalar/warp-factor flows and the defining potential relation for W.

Introduce configuration variables qᵃ=(U,φⁱ), canonical momenta and Hamilton’s characteristic function ℳW. The HJ construction gives S=ℳW−2c²τ and gradient velocities q̇ᵃ=Gᵃᵇ∂ᵦℳW; local existence is invoked as a standard mechanics theorem.

The original analysis transports scale derivatives to obtain spectral running and interprets trends using a slow-roll sum-separable approximation: a cubic radial inflection-point potential plus linear angular slopes. These analytic developments belong to the original flat-metric analysis.

Construct bulk corrections through conifold Laplace/Poisson solutions expanded in angular harmonics and radial powers, then sample unknown Wilson coefficients. The repeated experimental procedure rejects throat ejection, failure to reach the lower radial boundary and insufficient inflation.

The corrected calculation uses covariant perturbations and their momenta, a covariant mass matrix and transport equations for two-point correlators. Quantum transport begins eight e-folds before horizon exit with subhorizon Minkowski initial conditions and continues through superhorizon evolution.

An auxiliary nonrelativistic model treats gravity through a Newtonian potential and the cloud as a time-dependent Gaussian wavepacket. Its radial width, angular width and peak radius become collective coordinates; an effective potential and normal-mode analysis describe equilibria and oscillations.
A small-amplitude Green-function analysis retains the cubic source J=−μ²ϕ₀³/6, imposes initially vanishing nonlinear corrections and examines bound-state poles to explain counterrotating waves.

Three-dimensional evolution uses ZAMO coordinates with repeated coordinate pullbacks, sixth-order spatial differences, fourth-order Runge–Kutta time integration and seventh-order Lagrange interpolation. Pullbacks occur every M/4.
Use an Omnès function built from the elastic phase shift to impose the same strong final-state rescattering in longitudinal gauge-boson and fermion-initiated electroweak amplitudes.

Compare leading Nc and Nf dependence of tree-unitarity violation with a fixed underlying QCD scale; then use elastic rescattering resummation and the inverse amplitude method, incorporating chiral results through order p⁶, to study unitarity and second-sheet scalar poles.

Project gravitational scattering into partial waves, calculate scalar vacuum-polarization corrections, and resum their iterations either in the partial amplitude or dressed propagator. The real loop contribution requires gravitational effective-theory renormalization.
The bits-per-area prescription discretizes the scalar down to a minimum spacing a_min, assigns two independent states per horizon lattice site, and obtains S_horizon = 4π ln(2) a_min^−2/H² per field.

Interior states are approximated by free massless bosons in a box of size H^−1, with mode energies quantized in units of H and total energy below ΔV/H³. Eta-function degeneracy asymptotics estimate their entropy.

The second prescription traces over exterior degrees of freedom and uses the leading entanglement area term S = λΛ²A. Universal constant/logarithmic terms are omitted; an imported Minkowski radial-lattice calculation supplies an illustrative coefficient.

An imported adiabatic-suppression mechanism gives an effective modulus mass correction 3C²H² and exponentially damps oscillations for C ≫ 1. Taking the KK scale as cutoff gives C = M_P/M_KK = V^(2/3); its application here remains a proposed remedy.

ISAJET evolves soft masses, μ and Bμ/μ using two-loop RG equations and computes benchmark spectra and relic abundances. The displayed mass-evolution figure uses one-loop RG equations; the spectrum table specifies ISAJET 7.79 and m_t = 172.6 GeV.

The high-scale gaugino boundary condition is M_i = b_i g_i²m_3/2/(16π²), with b_i = (33/5, 1, −3). This is imported from the super-Weyl anomaly framework; the string construction supplies a proposed sequestered realization.
Gauge helicity modes are solved using Coulomb wave functions and approximated by a late-time growing solution with exponential enhancement e^(πξ).

Previously obtained helicity-resolved tensor spectra are applied to the strong-backreaction background. The background equation and scalar normalization then express the tensor-to-scalar ratio in model parameters.

A retarded Green function solves the sourced scalar perturbation equation, including the gauge-production response to inflaton velocity. Source correlators generate general n-point expressions; polarization contractions and numerical integrals give the power spectrum and equilateral bispectrum.

Sourced scalar perturbations are treated with Green functions. The imported inverse-decay spectrum is Δ_R² = Δ_R,sr²[1 + Δ_R,sr² f₂(ξ)e^(4πξ)], with f₂ evaluated numerically. The massive extension uses a separate-universe δN estimate for conversion of Higgs fluctuations.

Bispectrum bounds are estimated by projecting onto the constrained equilateral template, with shape cosine approximately 0.935 and an adopted volume ratio 5.3. μ-distortion is estimated analytically from dissipated scalar power, rather than a full Boltzmann evolution.

Modified CAMB and COSMOMC compare spectra with WMAP7 and ACT using four MCMC chains and a target Gelman–Rubin R−1 < 0.01. Exact Whittaker gauge solutions extend numerical evaluation to ξ = 0; tensor contributions are included.

Gauge closure and bracket antisymmetry determine quadratic constraints. Polynomial solutions are obtained using the Gianni–Trager–Zacharias primary-decomposition algorithm in Singular, then grouped under duality transformations.

For the D=7 three-form sector, symmetric matrices M and M̃ obey M̃M=(tr M̃M/4)I. A GL(4) transformation puts M into signature form and permits diagonal M̃; ’t Hooft symbols relate these embedding-tensor components to O(3,3) fluxes.

Explicit uplifts use light-cone twist parameterizations involving a vielbein, two-form B and bivector β, or Cartesian O(n,n) twists built from rotations and boosts fibred over doubled base coordinates.

Extend the tagged-particle counting to B equally charged constituents, formulate coupled occupation-number and charge-depletion laws, and examine their small-B/N evolution. Compare these finite-N effects with a double-scaling semiclassical limit; the extracted integrated solution is not reconstructed in this pass.

Estimate rates through constituent scattering and combinatorial counting. Ordinary depletion has approximately N² available graviton pairs; a process involving one specified charged constituent has only approximately N choices. A virtual charged constituent interacts with an external probe and returns to the condensate.

Use an autonomous phase-plane system, analytical instantaneous fixed points, and numerical trajectories to study the poly-instanton plateau and loop-dominated region separately and in the full potential.

Construct the potential from an α′-corrected Kähler potential and a racetrack superpotential corrected by fibre E3 poly-instantons. Expand in inverse volume, stabilize the heavier moduli, canonically normalize kinetic and mass terms, and estimate closed-string loop contributions using Coleman-Weinberg reasoning.

In holographic gauge, reduce zAμ to scalar equations with effective m²R² = 1−d and dimension Δ = d−1; reduce z²hμν to massless scalar equations with Δ = d. Fourier-Bessel mode expansions yield the corresponding smearing distributions.

Smear conformally fixed CFT two-point functions, evaluate integrals using hypergeometric identities, and analytically continue from large spacelike separation. Wightman discontinuities distinguish bulk-lightcone singularities from gauge-dependent boundary-lightcone singularities.

For interactions in AdS3, analyze CFT three-point functions and operator products, adding smeared higher-dimension spin-one operators to cancel nonanalytic terms responsible for spacelike commutators.

Use maximal symmetry and index structure to show that surviving corrections in the combined equation contain positive powers of external curvature, then solve order by order in α′. A separate ten-dimensional argument integrates the traced external equation over compact space and discards the resulting total derivatives.

Separate the dilaton zero mode, transform to four-dimensional Einstein frame, and split the action into Einstein–Hilbert, internal-field contribution V, and external-index contribution W. Combine the zero-mode dilaton equation with the traced external Einstein equation to eliminate V using its uniform τ^(−2) scaling.

Add a two-form worldsheet coupling to examine flux forces; derive FRW evolution equations to distinguish expansion effects on internal and external motion. Model gravitational radiation through decreasing total energy and use energy–length inequalities to discuss confinement.

Vary the zero-width Nambu action in transverse temporal gauge, obtaining coupled nonlinear worldsheet PDEs. Analyse the circular reduction through conserved energy, angular momentum and an effective potential; combine near-tip expansions with numerical integrations of reduced and internally extended loops.

Derive consistency constraints using boundary domains of dependence, deterministic bulk field equations and independent variations of disjoint boundary density matrices. Compare candidate regions against causal upper bounds and explicit geometrical examples.

Use the proposed holographic entropy–area relation to define a union of minimal-area extremal surfaces. A cut-and-paste argument followed by cusp smoothing establishes a restricted static-slice nonintersection result; smooth families of surfaces motivate conditional coverage and upper-bound arguments.

Apply the optical theorem to the imaginary part of the photon polarisation operator in the background. The single-photon pair-creation probability uses an imported constant-crossed-field polarisation operator, expressed through an Airy-function integral and then expanded at small χ.

Relate the thermal average to a two-loop finite-temperature calculation with a thermal photon correction and a zero-temperature electron loop. A Matsubara contour transformation and a proper-time saddle provide an alternative derivation and additional validity conditions; numerical integration tests the asymptotic formula.

Sum over two photon polarisations and integrate the single-photon result against the Bose–Einstein distribution: ρ_th = Σ_a∫d³k/(2π)³ R_a(k,χ_E)/(exp(ω/T)−1). Use η = ω/T and y = 1−cosθ for the asymptotic thermal integral.

Higgs calculations integrate out heavy scalars, match the Higgs quartic including threshold corrections, include superpartner-fermion loop effects, and use RG evolution. The displayed prediction is described as two-loop.

Effective-supergravity potentials specified by K, W and gauge kinetic functions; hidden-sector strong dynamics and instantons generate nonperturbative potentials. The G2 examples admit an expansion about minima in a small hidden gauge coupling.

The mass argument uses a smallest-eigenvalue bound evaluated along sGoldstino directions. For specified stabilization models, homogeneous-volume coordinates separate radial and angular moduli, with an uplift depending only on a negative power of total volume.

Construct walls as ij-trajectories satisfying Im(e^(−iϑ)ẇ^(ij))=0. Grow a mass-truncated network from three walls at each simple branch point; intersections generate descendants with soliton indices fixed by joint rules. A descendant enters the cutoff only at the sum of its parents’ masses.

Organize framed indices into formal path-generating functions F. Composition and twisted homotopy invariance constrain wall data and signs. For general networks, soliton traffic rules determine content inductively by discrete path length, with American/British choices for degenerate networks.

Nonabelianization pushes a twisted rank-one connection to C away from branch points, then cuts and reglues across walls using soliton-controlled transition functions. The modified parallel transport removes branch-point monodromy and defines a twisted rank-K flat connection.

Within the low-energy regime, solve the isocurvature equation algebraically as F=−2θ̇(φ̇₀/H)Ṙ/(p²+M_eff²), neglecting its time derivatives. Substitution into the quadratic action yields a tree-level curvature EFT with momentum-dependent kinetic coefficient.

Analyze the coupled quadratic perturbation equations using coherent low- and high-frequency mode pairs (R₋,F₋) and (R₊,F₊). In the short-wavelength approximation, neglect Hubble friction and treat p=k/a and φ̇₀/H as constant to identify the physical frequency hierarchy.

Solve the toy model’s slow-roll background equations approximately, track adiabatic changes over repeated turns, and numerically compare the resulting curvature power spectrum from the full two-field equations and the single-field EFT.
For QCD axions, use the approximate relations g_sN∼Θ_eff f_π/f_a∼Θ_eff m_a/m_π, g_pe=C_em_e/f_a, and g_pN=C_Nm_N/f_a to express force limits as bounds on Θ_eff, C_eΘ_eff, and C_NΘ_eff.
Translate inverse-square-law and weak-equivalence-principle limits on a Yukawa correction V=−G_Nm₁m₂[1+αe^(−r/λ)]/r into scalar coupling bounds using α=(g_sN)²/(4πG_Nm_u²)=1.37×10³⁷(g_sN)².

Multiply the scalar-coupling upper envelope by nominal stellar bounds on g_pe or g_pN, then juxtapose the resulting product bounds with polarized-electron, nuclear-precession, depolarization, and ultracold-neutron searches. The comparison supplies sensitivity benchmarks for direct experiments.

The authors use toric line-bundle cohomology, rationom representatives, long exact sequences and cohomCalg, together with intersection forms and Kähler-cone constraints, to determine divisor topology and rewrite threefold volumes.

Neutral zero modes are counted using orientifold-even and odd H^{n,0}(E), n=0,1,2. Holomorphic and topological Lefschetz indices determine parity splittings when applicable; the displayed fixed-point formulas assume the fixed locus intersects E in a curve.

The Gaussian effective potential minimizes a Gaussian state's energy over its width at fixed mean field. A gap equation determines the variational mass; derivatives of the potential at zero field define renormalized mass and quartic coupling.
Normalized generating functionals, perturbative Feynman diagrams and the oscillator's Gell-Mann–Low expression expose vacuum-bubble cancellation in nongravitating correlation functions.

Vacuum energy and pressure are calculated separately from the stress tensor. Dimensional regularization in d spacetime dimensions, gamma-function integrals and expansion about d=4 are used to preserve the vacuum equation of state.

The reviewed Hartle–Hawking proposal integrates over compact Euclidean geometries with one prescribed boundary. Semiclassical estimates use Euclidean saddles and minisuperspace restrictions; the quoted hemisphere weights are approximately exp[3π/(2ΛG)] for de Sitter and exp[π/(ΛG)] for Nariai.

Classical methods include constrained Cauchy evolution and a late-time Fefferman–Graham expansion. Boundary data comprise a three-metric g^(0) and a transverse-traceless tensor g^(3), with remaining expansion coefficients determined by these data.

Scalar modes are constructed using Bessel functions and the Klein–Gordon inner product; invariant two-point functions use hypergeometric solutions. Retarded propagators use regular/outgoing solutions and their Wronskian, whose zeros give quasinormal poles.

Strip off known helicity factors and write a finite-subtraction dispersion relation in one energy invariant. Relate low-energy coefficients to moments of discontinuities across cuts; the author uses an asserted square-integrability and basis argument to infer a contradiction if all sufficiently high moments vanish.

Estimate soliton pair production by crossing a current form factor into the timelike region. The semiclassical spatial profile motivates exponential suppression controlled by physical size divided by Compton wavelength; this is then extrapolated to argue against such suppression for small-charge BPS black holes.

Use unitarity cuts and induction from SU(8)-covariant tree amplitudes to characterize finite perturbative constructions. Their final four-dimensional amplitudes are asserted to preserve SU(8), although a footnote notes that dimensional regularization can break its manifest realization during intermediate calculations.

Two-loop QCD thresholds use a Taylor expansion in xht=Mh²/Mt² through xht⁴. In the Yukawa result, Nc² and Nc⁰ pieces are exact, while the Nc piece uses a large-top-mass asymptotic expansion through xht³.

The pole Higgs mass is decomposed into effective-potential curvature, including tadpole cancellation, plus momentum-dependent self-energy corrections. On-shell-to-MS matching includes finite contributions generated by O(ε) parameter shifts multiplying dimensional-regularization poles.

The NNLO analysis combines the two-loop effective potential, three-loop beta functions for relevant couplings and two-loop electroweak-scale matching. The principal new calculation supplies QCD and Yukawa threshold corrections to λ.

Use bosonic thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz densities and free-energy extremization, with E0(R)=R f(1/R). Obtain excited-state equations by deforming integration contours around branch points; select solutions continuously connected to the free theory.

Extract the elastic phase from the large-volume two-particle binding energy. Take R,N→∞ with N/R fixed to retain finite collision energy; the authors describe the initial argument as semi-rigorous and report a wave-packet refinement.

Analyze Gaussian scattering packets through reduced density matrices. Calculate entanglement using analytic continuation of Tr ρ^n, Gaussian integrals, and an auxiliary harmonic-oscillator partition function.
Dimensional reduction of RR fields and D-brane Chern–Simons terms determines axionic kinetic terms, gauge couplings and flux-induced Stückelberg charges.
Diagonalise the Kähler metric, canonically normalise axions, project onto null vectors of gauge–axion mass mixing, and subsequently remove axions made heavy by non-perturbative effects.

Matter couplings follow from supergravity Kähler-metric derivatives. Low-energy matching uses quark chiral rotations; field-theory loop corrections include photon/electron and supersymmetric gaugino/sfermion contributions.

An operational pixel thought experiment localises one representative of every species, estimates the required energy and induced graviton occupation, and compares black-hole hair-extraction time with the intended resolution time.

Count leading two-constituent rescattering and annihilation channels to estimate condensate depletion. Combine self-sustainability with the rate of temperature change, and compare tree-level 2→2 scattering rates with perturbative unitarity.

Compute contact terms through perturbative RG flows and background-field diagrams; use localization results to extract κff=−(1/2π)∂²m Im FS3 and κfr=(1/2π)∂m Re FS3 at m=0 on the unit sphere. Compare relative counterterms across proposed dual descriptions.

Use current conservation and supersymmetry Ward identities to parameterize correlators, identify background Chern-Simons completions, and derive position-space and dispersive sum rules for κUV−κIR. The position-space integral excludes coincident points.

Define background Chern-Simons functionals through extensions to four-manifolds; independence of the extension quantizes admissible counterterms. An alternative discussion uses the APS eta-invariant, whose zero-mode jumps restrict smooth short-distance counterterms.

Toric searches use reflexive polytopes, triangulations, weight matrices, Stanley–Reisner ideals, intersection rings and Mori cones, implemented with PALP/mori.x and Sage. Brane consistency is analysed through charge vectors, tadpoles, Freed–Witten quantisation and the invariant SU(2)-probe criterion for K-theory charge.

A four-dimensional EFT expanded near the quiver singularity combines anomalous-U(1) D-terms, leading α′ corrections and nonperturbative superpotentials. RG equations and scalar-potential extrema are used to outline radiative trinification breaking.

Perturbative ODE expansions near the poles and equator establish limiting warp-function behaviour. Numerical solutions sample initial conditions and explore the extent of the equatorial region with order-one scale ratios.

The separated test-scalar equation becomes a singular Sturm–Liouville problem. The substitution h=g/u with u=1−log(sinθ) produces coefficients satisfying the stated regularity conditions, allowing use of imported large-eigenvalue asymptotics.

Internal and external components of the ten-dimensional Ricci tensor are traced to form curvature ratios. Flux quantisation is imposed on closed modified RR forms through integral homology, cohomology expansions and rational topological periods.

A supplementary global argument rewrites the f,k,F sector using a nonnegative reduced Lagrangian whose zero occurs at vanishing ξ₁,f,k,F⁻. The remaining fields are treated as free functions subject to regularity conditions; the argument is explicitly cautioned because the equations are singular in the infrared.

The principal analytic argument compares admissible leading powers in the infrared equations for ξ₁⁻ and ξ_F⁻, splitting according to their relative leading orders. A separate direct expansion of the second-order equations is carried through order τ¹⁰.

Combinations ξ₁± encode probe forces, and ξ_f±, ξ_k±, ξ_F± encode three-form components and conjugate momenta in the radial effective theory. Their first-order equations isolate the obstruction without solving all eight nonlinear second-order equations.

Numerically evolve covariant linear field perturbations, including the potential Hessian, field-space curvature and background-velocity contributions to the mass matrix. Initialize six independent Bunch-Davies modes six e-folds before crossing and sum their power contributions incoherently.

Compare the full six-field linear calculation with the naive H²/(8π²ε) estimate, an exact-in-time adiabatic-only truncation, and a truncation retaining the adiabatic and first entropic modes. This separates slow-roll errors from multifield and higher-entropic-mode effects.

Compare numerical covariant-Hessian eigenvalue spectra with a simplified random-supergravity matrix model built from three complex symmetric 3×3 matrices. Estimate a weighted number of fluctuating fields using massive de Sitter Hankel-function mode powers.

Use worldsheet vertex operators, picture changing, H-charge conservation and spin-structure sums. Internal barred-field correlators receive classical winding contributions; Riemann theta identities reduce the remaining correlators.
Evaluate winding sums and the cylinder-modulus integral through elliptic functions or derivatives of a torus Green function. Extend the calculation to a Yukawa operator coupled to n hidden scalars.

Compute opposite-boundary cylinder amplitudes tr(AA)tr(φφφ) to extract visible-matter dependence of the hidden gauge kinetic function, and tr(λλ)tr(ψψφ) as a supersymmetry-related consistency check. The double-trace structure excludes a Möbius-strip contribution at this order.

Apply the GSR Green-function iteration around y0=(1+i/ks)e^(iks). The source is G′, with G=−2 ln f+(2/3)(ln f)′; integrals I1 and I2 supply second-order corrections. The quadratic term in G′ preserves constant curvature fluctuations above the sound horizon.

Solve the background field and acceleration equations with initial conditions satisfying the Friedmann equation exactly, then solve the Mukhanov–Sasaki equation with Bunch–Davies initial conditions as the numerical reference spectrum.

For a small sharp step, use energy conservation during crossing, perturb the background field about the smooth solution, and integrate the GSR expression by parts. Window functions describe the feature, while D(y)=y/sinh y accounts approximately for finite tanh-step width.

Yukawa-force sensitivity is estimated using geophysical models ranging from local laboratory topography to regional geology and Earth's structure. The hillside, lake and nearby excavated wall provide horizontal sensitivity to ranges down to approximately 1 m; this is a geometry-dependent interpretation.

Uniform turntable rotation moves the WEP signal to approximately mHz frequencies. After notch-filtering the free torsional oscillation, two-rotation data segments are fitted to harmonics of turntable angle plus a quadratic drift.

Composition reversal and multiple pendulum orientations separate a composition signal from frame-dependent offsets. Tilt, gravity-gradient, magnetic and temperature couplings are measured by deliberately enhancing each disturbance and scaling its response to operating conditions; tilt and gravity-gradient corrections are applied.

The LVS procedure first fixes complex-structure moduli and the axio-dilaton using bulk flux, yielding W₀. No-scale cancellation removes the leading Kähler-modulus potential; α′ corrections and a nonperturbative instanton superpotential then stabilize the small cycle and overall volume, using a_sτ_s ≫ 1.

Loop corrections and the D-term are minimized in two dimensionless cycle ratios, then substituted into an effective volume potential. The leading retained loop terms give y_min = (2B/C)x; balancing the resulting loop energy against V_D ∝ n²x²/V² fixes x. A separate warped-throat contribution supplies the final uplift.

Estimate AD charge by integrating its sourced evolution equation during inflaton matter domination, distinguishing early phase oscillation from radial oscillation. Combine this with modulus entropy dilution and charge-dependent Q-ball surface-decay estimates.

Use supergravity potentials, F-terms, canonical modulus eigenstates and visible-sector couplings to estimate spectra and decay widths. Integrating out heavy chiral/vector multiplets supplies candidate inflaton–AD contact operators; the vector example requires opposite-sign charges for the desired operator sign.

Construct superspace actions, project to bosonic components, eliminate gravity auxiliaries, perform Weyl rescaling, and solve the remaining algebraic chiral-auxiliary equations. Substituting distinct solutions produces distinct on-shell branches.

For one chiral multiplet with nonzero superpotential, reduce the auxiliary problem to a cubic in x=F F̄ and apply Cardano's method. For two restricted chirals, solve coupled equations using the auxiliary norm and an auxiliary-field ratio.

The authors run eight MCMC chains and stop at Gelman–Rubin R − 1 approximately 0.02. They report marginalized means with 1σ errors, best-fit values, and 68%/95% contour regions; this is their convergence criterion, not an independently assessed guarantee.

To illustrate spectral response, one DM equation-of-state coefficient is varied at a time while other parameters are held at their fitted mean values. Matter-power comparisons are evaluated at z = 0; these illustrations do not marginalize over compensating parameter changes.

A modified CosmoMC implementation evolves DM and DE perturbations and fits ten parameters: baryon and dark-matter physical densities, acoustic angular scale, optical depth, four CPL coefficients, primordial spectral index and scalar amplitude. The joint data are SNLS3, BAO and Planck+WMAP9+WiggleZ matter-power measurements.

Trace and integrate warped Einstein equations to obtain cosmological-constant constraints, while retaining stronger pointwise conditions. In massive IIA, examine both the dilaton equation and external Einstein equation together with the localized-source Bianchi identity.

Compute circle-fibration spin connections and curvature forms, reduce Pontryagin couplings along isometries, apply T-dualities, and lift back to M-theory. An invertible metric/flux map expresses the reduced characteristic form in the dual flux variables.

Embedding-space polarization derivatives generate spinning exchange diagrams from scalar diagrams. For a conserved spin-ℓ current of dimension d−2+ℓ, applying the conservation operator collapses the exchanged propagator to a contact contribution.

Use Mellin representations, OPE conformal blocks and factorization to fix poles and residues from CFT data. Subtract the exchange contributions; meromorphy and polynomial boundedness restrict the remaining entire function to a polynomial, represented by local derivative interactions.

Use a previously established R→∞ integral transform relating large Mellin variables to Mandelstam invariants. With appropriately scaled couplings, polynomials map to momentum polynomials, while coalescing Mellin poles generate flat-space loop branch cuts.

Compute the N=1 F-term potential from K=−2 ln(V+Cα′) and the nonperturbative superpotential. Expand in inverse volume and poly-instanton exponentials, solve leading extrema, then analyze the subleading Wilson-line potential analytically and numerically.

Canonically normalize the Kähler kinetic metric and analyze eigenvalues/eigenvectors of one-half the inverse metric times the potential Hessian. Use potential slow-roll derivatives and e-fold integrals, and estimate reheating from inflaton couplings to gauge bosons.

Flux search starts from rational moduli and an approximate prepotential constant, solving W0=DSW0=DU1W0=DU2W0=0 linearly for integer fluxes subject to the tadpole bound. Supersymmetry equations are then solved with instanton corrections and the exact constant; Kähler stabilization is numerical.

Rigidification uses a holomorphic curve C with normal bundle O(-1)⊕O(-1), and gauge-invariant flux C−s trivial in the threefold. Requiring its (2,0) component to vanish fixes both D1 deformation parameters.

Toric weight systems, Stanley–Reisner ideals and intersection theory determine geometry and brane factorizations; PALP and cohomCalg supply topological data. Tate factorizations and toric resolutions provide the F-theory analysis.

Convert hidden branching fractions into ΔNeff using comoving visible-sector entropy conservation: ΔNeff=(43/7)[fhidden/(1−fhidden)][g(Tdec)/g(Treheat)]^(1/3). Decoupled hidden radiation and visible radiation evolve differently during visible entropy release.

Expand K=−3 ln(Tb+T̄b), canonically normalize the volume mode and extract its axion coupling. Extend the Kähler potential by local matter metrics and the Giudice–Masiero Higgs bilinear to calculate leading perturbative decay widths.

Use a Higgs-dependent modulus redefinition and conformal-compensator rescaling to identify unsuppressed GM-mediated scalar decays, no-scale cancellations and suppressed classically scale-invariant channels. Quantum superconformal anomalies generate gauge-boson couplings.

Relate the axion branching fraction to ΔNeff through entropy conservation: ΔNeff≈(43/7)[10.75/g*(Td)]^(1/3) Ba/(1−Ba). Estimate annihilation-limited nonthermal LSP abundance and numerically iterate the temperature-dependent relativistic degrees of freedom.

Estimate stabilization, F-terms, masses and interactions using four-dimensional supergravity, the large-volume expansion, the α′ correction and nonperturbative stabilization. Add an uplifting sector because the initial SUSY-breaking vacuum has negative cosmological constant.
Worldsheet tadpole factorization and Fischler–Susskind background shifts are compared with nonlinear spacetime effective equations and singularity-theorem arguments.
The hypothetical Census Taker framework is reviewed through Markov transition rates, entropy detailed balance and eigenvector perturbation theory about the minimum-total-width vacuum.

CDL boundary-value analysis uses an O(4)-symmetric scalar/metric ansatz, overshoot–undershoot reasoning, an analog FRW cosmology and Lorentzian continuation. Compact dS instantons require regularity at both zeros of the scale factor.

Coset NGB matrices and Yukawa spurions organize gauge and four-fermion contributions to the potential. The appendix estimates leading quark-loop potentials and expands them to identify Higgs and σHuHd interactions.

A Coleman–Weinberg potential built from global-current two-point functions is estimated using the lowest vector resonances. Wilsonian integration from mρ to infinity supplies a quartic matching condition; SM RGE running supplies the lower-energy contribution.
PQ electromagnetic/QCD anomaly ratios distinguish axion models. One-loop gauge β-function coefficients are used to assess unification with incomplete SM multiplets.

Realize higher-spin algebras with associative oscillator star products, Clifford generators and matrices. Impose compatible conjugation, automorphism, graded anti-automorphism and projection conditions, then use Vasiliev curvature constraints or their deformed-oscillator form.

Linearize around a maximally symmetric spin-two connection and use algebraic Cartan integration: background gauge functions transport constant adjoint and twisted-adjoint data into harmonic fields and Killing parameters, with representation-compatible boundary conditions.

Use perturbatively defined master-field redefinitions to simplify the interaction deformation to signature-dependent phase or exponential forms governed by real zero-form invariants θp. This simplification does not establish global equivalence of nonperturbative theories.

Solve the resulting quadratic inequalities for momentum uncertainty, estimate temperature, and use the first law dS=Mp c² dm/T and C=Mp c² dm/dT for thermodynamics. Estimate mass loss with a Stefan–Boltzmann law dominated by four-dimensional brane emission.

Use the photon-gas relation c⟨p⟩=2.821 TH together with the Hawking–uncertainty identification to set μ=[2.821(D−3)/π]², ⟨p⟩=√μ Δp and ⟨p²⟩=(1+μ)Δp². Substitute these moment relations into the GUP inequalities.

Model the position uncertainty of an emitted particle as Δx≈2rs and identify cΔp with its characteristic energy. Multiply the uncertainty-based estimate by the calibration factor (D−3)/π to reproduce the standard D-dimensional Hawking temperature before applying GUP modifications.

Integrate covariant two-field moduli equations coupled to FRW expansion. Sample initial positions near the inflection point in an open universe; the distribution calculation uses random positions rather than explicitly locating every parent minimum.

Construct periods and the flux superpotential from integer three-form fluxes; solve D_I W=D_τ W=0 for complex structure and axion-dilaton, then evaluate W0. Numerically examine approximately 10^9 flux combinations.

Nonabelianization supplies regional decompositions into lines of flat sections. S-wall crossings impose coplanarity; snake moves organize basis changes, and compositions of canonical homs around closed paths produce coordinate holonomies.

Newton-polygon constraints organize perturbations δc_{p,a}z^a(dz)^p, with a≤floor(Np/2) and dimension D[p,a]=(Np−2a)/(N+2)≥0. The criterion ∫Σ|δλ|² distinguishes normalizable deformations D>1, logarithmically divergent mass deformations D=1, and non-normalizable deformations D<1.

For one hypermultiplet, use the local Przanowski–Tod parametrization of four-dimensional quaternionic spaces with an isometry. Geometry is encoded by h(r,u,v), satisfying h_uu+h_vv+(e^h)_rr=0, with f=2−r h_r. Connections, curvatures and truncation conditions are obtained using vielbeins and torsion-free equations.

Study the mass submatrix along supersymmetry-breaking sGoldstino directions. Its averaged mass bounds the lightest scalar mass from above, producing general necessary conditions without solving positivity of the full scalar mass matrix.

Observational methods combine distance and growth probes, supernova χ² fitting with nuisance-H₀ marginalization, and parameter-penalized model comparison: BIC = −2 ln Lmax + k ln N and AIC = −2 ln Lmax + 2k. The χ² identification assumes Gaussian likelihoods.
The vacuum-energy estimate sums bosonic zero-point energies with a UV cutoff λ, giving a leading quartic contribution approximately λ⁴/(16π²); it serves as an EFT naturalness estimate.

Reconstruction is treated as an inverse problem using specified equations-of-state ansätze, redshift bins/PCA, polynomial representations or Gaussian processes. CPL uses w(z) = w₀ + wₐz/(1+z); GP reconstructions specify a mean, covariance and fitted hyperparameters.

The review organizes axion spectra by the corrections used to stabilize Kähler moduli: nonperturbative superpotentials, perturbative and nonperturbative Kähler-potential corrections, and D-terms. It then relates the surviving spectra to dark-matter production and photon-conversion searches.

Kaluza–Klein reduction of the D7-brane action yields axion kinetic mixing, anomalous gauge couplings and Stückelberg masses. Transforming to canonically normalized axion fields allows matching to a multi-axion low-energy Lagrangian and extraction of decay constants and couplings.

Decay widths are converted into a number-to-entropy yield with weights 2 for direct gravitino pairs, 4 for zz† followed by two pair decays, and 2N3/2 for hidden jets. The explicit IYIT realization additionally includes tree-level three-body channels above threshold.

The authors expand the supergravity potential, diagonalize inflaton-sector mixing and estimate inflaton–z mixing. For an inflaton much heavier than the gravitino, the equivalence theorem permits calculating longitudinal-gravitino production through goldstino couplings.

Orthogonal projectors P = ∇□₀⁻¹∇ and Π = 1−P decompose Δa into ΔT+aΔL. Exterior-calculus identities give local operators ΔT = −δ₂d₁ and ΔL = −d₀δ₁, commuting sectors and determinant factorization on nonzero spectra.

Proper-time heat kernels and their small-s expansion evaluate regulated determinants. The longitudinal nonzero spectrum is identified with the scalar Laplacian, reducing nonminimal coefficients to minimal 0-form and 1-form coefficients.
The replica method introduces a deficit δ = 2π(1−α) at Σ. Momentum-space heat kernels supply the surface contribution, with Tr Π = d−1, Tr P = 1 and ghost weight −2 in the entropy.

Choose a future null vector along a NEC-violating ray with n·u=1 and parameterize a future timelike observer as V=αu+ηn, normalized by α²+2αη=1. Taking the observer toward that null direction isolates the negative leading contribution to its measured energy density.

For the heat-flow stress tensor, minimize its null contraction over directions. Then split density, pressure and flow into background and perturbations in comoving gauge. The paper also summarizes stronger WEC and DEC restrictions and their hierarchy, drawing on prior imperfect-fluid analysis.

Schwinger–Keldysh in/in diagrams, self-energy insertions and overlap integrals of Hankel modes extract infrared and secular corrections. The leading-log resummation is approached through a kinetic/Dyson ansatz.
WKB and Bogolyubov matching describe electric pair creation; matching asymptotic plane waves to de Sitter Hankel modes determines gravitational particle production.

Vary Wess–Zumino couplings and use democratic RR field strengths, source-modified Bianchi identities and improved NS5-dependent field strengths to distinguish brane-source currents from conserved Page currents.

Apply S/T dualities and dimensional lifts to masses and supergravity backgrounds. Buscher duality generates the local 5_2^2 solution; holomorphic scalar functions and Killing-spinor conditions analyze supersymmetry and duality patching.

Integrate the algebraic axial torsion field in a constrained path integral, implement torsion-charge conservation with a Lagrange multiplier, and use the axial anomaly after partial integration. Counterterms are invoked to express the anomaly using the torsion-free spin connection.

An alternative geometrical argument promotes the Holst/Nieh–Yan parameter η to a pseudoscalar. For the mass estimate, diagonalize axion kinetic mixing, canonically normalize a, and apply two-loop effective-field-theory power counting; the multi-axion extension uses off-diagonal propagator falloff.

Derive the homogeneous Einstein and scalar equations, impose slow roll and braiding dominance, and express slow-roll parameters through the enhancement parameter τ. Inflationary endpoints are determined by ε=1, and the e-fold integral is evaluated analytically or numerically for the two models.

Use scalar and tensor perturbation formulas imported from the cited G-inflation framework, including PR=3√6 H²/(64π²Mp²ε) and ns=1−6ε+3η+α/2. Numerical examples are selected using roughly 60 e-folds and the paper's historical WMAP normalization.

Analyze quadratic kinetic actions in Newtonian gauge using Fourier-space kinetic determinants, constraints and local field redefinitions. Obtain Newtonian responses by neglecting time derivatives and adding pressureless matter sources.

Choose uniform-scalar time slices, build spatial-diffeomorphism-invariant operators from δg^{00}, extrinsic curvature, curvature tensors and projected derivatives, and organize them by perturbation order. Restore the scalar π and full diffeomorphism invariance through t→t+π.

Vacuum searches combine flux constraints with extremality equations and use the GTZ algebraic method of prime decomposition. Appendix B applies this to geometric IIA backgrounds with and without metric flux.

The embedding tensor specifies gauge generators and covariant derivatives. Linear constraints restrict its representations; quadratic constraints enforce gauge invariance and algebra closure. Dressing it with the scalar vielbein gives the T-tensor and fermionic shifts.

Critical points are searched at the origin of moduli space while retaining flux components closed under the relevant non-compact dualities. The thesis uses this closure to justify exhaustiveness for its half-maximal geometric IIA analysis.

Use S³ localization and a large-N matrix-model saddle with real eigenvalues, scaling exponent β=1/2, and a common even eigenvalue density to calculate the proposed equivalent theory's leading free energy.
Compute five-brane fluxes and D3 Page charges on noncontractible cycles; identify large gauge transformations with brane moves and derive partition inequalities using bounds on f(x)=2 arctan(e^x)/π.

Starting from imported local solutions specified by two harmonic functions, periodically replicate strip five-brane sources and quotient translations. Jacobi theta functions express the resulting annular harmonic functions.

Estimate decay widths, yields and entropy dilution, then use a post-injection Boltzmann equation with ⟨σv⟩=cχ/mχ² to determine whether neutralino annihilation erases dependence on the injected abundance.

Use an O’Raifeartaigh-type effective Kähler potential and superpotential for pseudo-modulus oscillations; investigate messenger-loop and higgsino-threshold corrections to anomaly-mediated gaugino masses.

Write the Euclidean action as vacuum-cap volumes, wall tension times area, and a gravitational kink contribution from delta-function curvature. Introduce independent locations for the matter wall and a geometric junction.

Construct continuous thick-wall field profiles satisfying the gravitational constraint near a vacuum. Compare their action with the ideal geometric-junction term, and estimate the small-field contribution near an equatorial junction.

SO(3,2) representation shortening protects the single-gluon energy near weak coupling. A bulk partition function with boundary gauge-field sources generates formal current correlators and supports a state/operator interpretation.

Supersymmetric analysis uses the rigid-AdS chiral effective action, the vacuum equation ∂W+(∂K)/L=0, and large-ΛL Veneziano–Yankielowicz or Seiberg–Witten descriptions. N=4 examples use S-duality and holographic gravity.

Dimensional reduction and a generalized Gukov–Vafa–Witten expression yield K and W. F- and D-term equations, the Dirac index and Breitenlohner–Freedman stability tests analyze stabilization, chirality and extrema.

Associated bundles are constructed from representations of the isotropy subgroup. HYM equations constrain their geometry, while matching observable-plus-hidden gauge and tangent-bundle characteristic classes supplies the cohomological anomaly constraints.

G-invariant differential forms encode the SU(3) structure and reduce supersymmetry to Hitchin-type flow. Explicit Hull-connection curvature and gauge-curvature calculations reduce the Bianchi identity to an algebraic equation for the flux coefficient C.

Derive nonrelativistic source transformations through a c→∞ limit with chemical potential tuned to cancel particle rest energy. Construct the bulk dictionary through both a shrinking-circle Kaluza–Klein scaling limit and a direct Einstein–Maxwell nonrelativistic limit.

Match asymptotic combinations of bulk fields to source transformation laws, identify radial diffeomorphisms with boundary conformal transformations, and evaluate a chosen scalar's on-shell action for a two-point-function check. Source variations also yield particle-number, momentum and energy conservation identities.

For LVS, the authors use moduli stationary conditions and a large-volume expansion to estimate the tadpole. The appendix also expresses its coefficient through the conformal compensator and moduli F-terms, exposing sensitivity to uplift couplings and to a moduli-dependent linear superpotential.

Integrating out the heavy waterfall fields generates a one-loop Kähler correction and a logarithmic inflaton potential. The authors then isolate the linear term in the supergravity scalar potential and examine how singlet couplings or no-scale identities alter it.

Estimate heavy-field corrections through a Wilsonian path integral and schematic Coleman–Weinberg derivative expansion. Import established P(X,χ) power-spectrum and bispectrum formulae to calculate model observables.

Rescale A=Â/√g and λ=√g λ̂, then take the slow-roll hierarchy scaling limit. The gauge fields become algebraic; solve them in a local Lorentz rest frame of the axion gradient and covariantize the selected solution.

Use the phase-space Yang–Mills action, Gauss constraint, and symmetric spatial gauge matrix to isolate six physical gauge modes. Examine quadratic mass terms and, separately, the leading high-momentum kinetic terms.

The authors construct gauge generators from the embedding tensor, form the scalar potential using the coset matrix M = LLᵀ, and calculate full scalar mass spectra analytically at the identified critical points.

A consistent truncation retains six SO(3) × SO(3) singlets, followed by a discrete Z2 projection. Only the g5 and g6 scalar coordinates enter the resulting potential; the retained g4 direction is gauged. Noncentral extrema are characterized through a cubic equation for x*.
Minimize anchored homologous area on a complete achronal slice Σ containing ∂A, then maximize that minimum over Σ. Subsequent results use the stable maximin choice.

Project extremal surfaces onto another slice using null representatives x̃=N∩Σ. Raychaudhuri focusing, null-expansion comparisons, and the causal-horizon area theorem control the relevant area inequalities.

Existence arguments use compactness, lower/upper semicontinuity, the extreme value theorem, and Ascoli–Arzelà. Entropy inequalities reduce to cutting and reconnecting minimal surfaces on a common slice; the monogamy reconnection details are delegated to an earlier static proof.

They track pre-existing and reproduced modulus yields and optimize over flaton VEVs. The thermal displacement is δφb ∼ cbV0/(mφb²MP). Single-stage dilution gives Ytot = (YBB,0 + YTI,0)/Δ; the double-stage expression is [(YBB,0 + YTI1,0)/Δ1 + YTI2,0]/Δ2.

The authors combine a large-volume supergravity expansion, modulus couplings and decay estimates, and historical BBN, CMB, diffuse X/γ-ray and relic-density constraints to assess permitted modulus yields as functions of mass and lifetime.

Apply previously derived tree-level holographic formulae and trace/diffeomorphism Ward identities. Domain-wall/cosmology continuation reverses κ²V and sends q→−iq; its sign selects the Bunch–Davies vacuum. For adjoint SU(N) theories, the parameter continuation is N²→−N².

Regulate integrated insertions by a minimum separation Λ, extract leading λ-poles using the OPE, and resum infinitely many insertions. Since In scales as λ^(−n) while ϕ^n scales as λ^n, every perturbative order contributes at leading order. The recurrence uses a dilute-gas approximation neglecting simultaneous multiple coincidences.

Express perturbed correlators as sums of CFT correlators with shifted dimensions before Fourier transformation. The appendices use Schwinger parameters, triple-Bessel integrals, Appell functions and analytic continuation to handle coincident-insertion divergences.

Use M-theory lifts and T-dualities to relate flux-induced discrete charges to torsion cycles. The torsion-domain-wall discussion also retains nonclosed forms satisfying dω2=kβ3 in dimensional reduction.
Dimensionally reduce higher-dimensional Chern–Simons terms to BF couplings and dualize two-forms to Stückelberg scalars. In M-theory the relevant coupling matrix is stated as ΘΛΓ=2∫ωΛ∧ωΓ∧G4.

Use Freed–Witten consistency conditions and their dual versions to identify emitted branes, instantons and string junctions; Hanany–Witten creation effects diagnose noncommuting string charges. Bézout identities and electric–magnetic symplectic rotations organize allowed charge violations.

Enumerate S4 choices of residual generators and compatible CP transformations, reduce equivalent choices by group similarity transformations, and examine all row/column permutations. Historical mixing-angle fits are assessed with χ² functions.

Factor the symmetric unitary CP matrix as X=ΩΩT and choose a basis with canonical CP and diagonal Z. The neutrino mass matrix becomes a real block matrix, diagonalized by Uν=ΩR(θ)K, with tan2θ=2m13/(m33−m11).
Determine Ue by simultaneously diagonalizing the charged-lepton residual generators Qi. Their distinct generation charges ensure that the same Ue diagonalizes ml†ml, up to phases and permutations.

Fefferman–Graham radial expansion solves the field equations recursively. In vacuum, γ^(0) and constrained γ^(d) provide free asymptotic data; lower coefficients are locally determined. Even boundary dimension generally requires a z^d log(z²) term.

Counterterm subtraction regulates the Einstein–Hilbert plus Gibbons–Hawking action at z=ε, cancels divergences using local boundary terms, and obtains the boundary stress tensor by varying the renormalized action. Logarithmic counterterms retain conformal-frame dependence in even d.

The covariant Peierls bracket is defined as advanced minus retarded response to an action deformation. A spacetime-dependent symmetry variation establishes the generator property of the boundary charges.

Manipulate equal-time commutators as distributions using Fourier representations of the periodic delta function. A doubled-coordinate O(2,2,Z) formulation translates target-space monodromies into boundary conditions, determined up to constant shifts.

Buscher's gauged-isometry procedure supplies relations between derivatives of dual coordinates. Integrating these relations transfers the twisted-torus classical solution to the Q background, introducing position integration constants.

Expand coordinates through first order in flux; Fourier-expand combinations made periodic by the boundary conditions and solve the resulting wave equations with sources. Promote twisted-torus modes to operators and extract the commutator combinations needed for directions 1 and 2.
Reviewed CMB searches use modified CAMB spectra and COSMOMC sampling. Computational cost restricts exploration to primordial parameters while fixing the other cosmological parameters.

Non-Gaussianity calculations use the cubic perturbation action, field redefinition and an interaction-Hamiltonian commutator integral. In slow roll, integrations by parts combine three dominant vertices.
Modified-dispersion toy models replace k² by a²ωphys²(k/a). WKB analysis tests whether modes initialized in the local Hamiltonian's minimum-energy state track the evolving vacuum.

For the single-T model, solve the supersymmetry condition using the W−1 branch of the Lambert W function, then transform a distribution of c1 into P(Λ) with a delta-function change of variables. Analytical and numerical distributions are presented.

For many Ui, derive semianalytic relations for ui, s and W, first solve the complex-structure/dilaton sector neglecting Ae^(−aT), and then stabilize T using the resulting W0. Numerically sample the parameter distributions and compute Λ quantiles.

Evaluate HIJ=∂ψI∂ψJV at extrema, with ψI=(x,s,ui), taking derivatives before inserting the vacuum solution. Positivity is tested for this real-field Hessian; an invertible canonical normalization preserves its definiteness.
The authors solve consistency equations on group generators, track character-table row and column permutations, and transform explicit invariant contractions to determine coupling-phase restrictions.

Physical checks use weak-basis CP invariants, scalar-potential extrema and supersymmetric F-term alignment equations. These distinguish invariance of an individual VEV from invariance of the full vacuum.

Automorphisms are represented by extending G to G⋊θZn, where the selected automorphism becomes inner. The CP matrix is constructed using the extension representation and the conjugate-exchange matrix W, then restricted to G.

Compute the Hessian and canonically normalize it using a vielbein. Average the three physical hypermultiplet directions and two vector-sector scalar directions into a two-by-two matrix; its eigenvalues constrain the extremal eigenvalues of the full physical scalar matrix.

Parametrize the allowed geometries by Δf=0, ∇×ω=∇f and ∂z∂z̄l=0. At a chosen vacuum point, stationarity fixes first derivatives; remaining values and second derivatives can be scanned subject to harmonicity.

Weierstrass discriminants, Tate vanishing orders and explicit resolutions organize F-theory gauge and matter loci. Chirality is computed by integrating four-form flux over the corresponding matter surfaces.

Four-dimensional N=1 supergravity uses the flux superpotential W=∫G3∧Ω, nonperturbative superpotentials and corrections to the Kähler potential to study stabilization. Moduli F-terms and matter–moduli couplings determine gravity-mediated soft terms.

Local methods use twisted eight-dimensional gauge theory with spatially varying adjoint Higgs backgrounds, spectral covers and matter-curve cohomology. Ultra-local Yukawas arise from overlaps of internal wavefunctions around enhancement points.
Reviews an information-storage argument: localizing N distinguishable species in a box costs energy N/Lbox; requiring the box to exceed its gravitational radius gives the species resolution bound.

Uses boundary effective actions, successively integrating out bulk directions while retaining leading scalar nonlinearities. For the second Vainshtein radius, integrates radial equations for T=−Mδ³(x) and matches short- and long-distance behavior.

Tests ν0∈{3,5} and fluctuation times t_f∈{1,10,100}, scanning initial shifted dilaton and anisotropy. For each parameter choice, 100 integrations sample initial and post-fluctuation velocities and matter populations.

Numerically couples lowest-order dilaton-gravity evolution and the Hamiltonian constraint to Boltzmann equations for winding and KK modes. In particular E=(2π)²e^(−ϕ)[ϕ̇²−d1ν̇²−d2λ̇²] is matter energy, and Ẇ=−Γ_W(W²−〈W〉²).

Uses microcanonical weights proportional to exp S to sample Gaussian expansion rates: S=E/T_H in Hagedorn equilibrium, with a quadratic entropy expansion in radiation. Winding and KK populations after the fluctuation are sampled uniformly within prescribed bounds.

Background methods include slow-roll analytic solutions, exact power-law ansätze, autonomous dynamical systems and linear stability, and numerical trajectory analysis; multi-vector backgrounds also use tetrad variables.

Superhorizon end-of-inflation modulation is treated with the δN expansion. Anisotropic perturbations are reduced to physical variables through quadratic actions and evaluated perturbatively using interaction-picture, time-ordered expectation values.
Canonical quantization of gauge modes with transverse polarizations and a time-dependent kinetic function; temporal or Coulomb gauge is used according to the model.

Matched expansions connect near-horizon hypergeometric and outer confluent-hypergeometric radial solutions. The resulting gamma-function resonance condition supplies ZDM solutions near numerator poles.
Leaver continued-fraction searches determine numerical frequencies and phase boundaries. The illustrated bifurcation search uses complex-frequency contours with the expansion truncated at 800 terms.

Leading eikonal WKB analysis relates damping to potential-peak curvature. An angular Bohr–Sommerfeld condition determines the eikonal transition µc≈0.74398; a transformed real radial potential is used to discuss nonzero-spin perturbations.

CFT reconstruction smears operators over complexified boundary coordinates, expresses three-point functions through hypergeometric functions of an AdS invariant, and uses large-N factorization to evaluate higher-dimension operator corrections.

Constrained Hamiltonian analysis uses primary and Gauss constraints, holographic gauge fixing, inversion of their Poisson-bracket matrix, and equal-time Dirac brackets to identify the permitted nonlocal commutators.

A bulk counterpart solves equations of motion perturbatively in q using boundary smearing and spacelike Green functions. The radial Maxwell equation fixes the boundary-direction divergence of A in terms of the bulk current.

Numerical polynomial homotopy continuation tracks paths from a solvable start system to all isolated polynomial roots. Bertini and Paramotopy implement generic-parameter start solutions and parameter homotopies across flux choices.
The exhaustive scan uses H3=(h1,h2), F3=(−h2,h1), with h1,h2 integer three-vectors, making L=h1²+h2². After fourfold duality identifications it scans 52,329 parameter points with L≤34.

The minimal flux method starts with rational moduli and rationalized ξ, solves integer linear equations including W0=0, then restores transcendental ξ and instanton terms and solves nearby F-term equations. The final W0 need not vanish and is not directly controlled.

Computes a probe D5 DBI-plus-Wess–Zumino potential with n dissolved anti-D3 units. A large-n expansion produces quadratic, cubic and quartic radial terms, whose coefficient inequality is used to exclude finite-radius extrema.

Recasts eight second-order equations as sixteen first-order equations using ξa±=Gab φ̇b−(1/2)∂aW±. The two superpotentials distinguish KS and anti-KS flows; ξ1± determines the corresponding probe-brane force.

Imports a Polchinski–Strassler mean-field argument: treat polarized shells as probes in the other branes' geometry and invoke position independence of the potential to infer collective and localized D5 polarization behavior.

An alternative route uses type IIA duality and the c-map to a type IIB hypermultiplet problem with a trivial F-theory fiber. Schwinger-loop results are then restricted to their auxiliary IIB string-tree-level part to recover the original vector corrections.
Use special Kähler geometry to obtain K from the holomorphic prepotential and its derivatives, then expand its logarithm to organize corrections by powers of the volume modulus.

Translate imported heterotic threshold results through heterotic/type I S-duality and two torus T-dualities to type I′. Explicit corrections use trilogarithms with coefficients generated by Eisenstein series and the Dedekind function.

The authors sample random supersymmetry-breaking parameters and compute scalar mass spectra. They complement this with two-dimensional slices fixing four parameters at a previously known isotropically stable dS point, comparing potential and minimum-mass contours. The initial scan uses 10^7 points; the small dS tail receives ten times that sample.

For geometric IIA, prime ideal decomposition implemented in Singular separates the residual polynomial equations into branches. This is an algebraic classification within the specified isotropic effective theory.

At the origin, replace N flux combinations by N real supersymmetry-breaking parameters through DαW=Aα+iBα. The remaining flux variables enter the stationarity equations linearly, while the breaking parameters can still enter quadratically.

For mass-deformed KS, the authors scan selected parameter families and use quadratic fits or extrapolations to estimate charge minima. This supplements direct horizon-charge evaluation, rather than exhaustively covering the three-dimensional parameter space.

Kaluza–Klein reduction gives five-dimensional effective equations. The KT radial problem has five coupled second-order nonlinear ODEs, total order ten; the mass-deformed KS problem has eight, total order sixteen. The radial metric component is determined algebraically.

Numerical shooting matches horizon and ultraviolet series at x=0.5, requiring continuity of fields and first derivatives. Horizon regularity is imposed in ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates, with expansions in even powers of 1−x.

The authors examine Hessian minors restricted to selected scalar directions. A negative eigenvalue of such a restriction establishes an instability of the full critical point; increasingly large restrictions identify a small subspace sufficient to detect the observed instabilities.

For the isotropic family, the N=1 F-term potential and ten-dimensional supersymmetry conditions identify a degenerate limiting solution. The limiting hierarchy of F-terms then motivates examination of the real z2 direction.

Dimensional-reduction scaling arguments track the dependence of curvature, flux and source energies on the universal moduli and orientifold volumes. Orientifold parity restricts flux legs and allowed group-manifold structure constants.

Uses ADM variables, spatially flat metric gauge, and a scalar–vector–tensor decomposition with wavevector along x³. Non-Abelian Coulomb gauge makes the scalar Gauss constraint algebraic in momentum space; eliminating constrained fields gives a coupled three-scalar action and a reduced magnetic-drift system.

Solves the approximate gauge-tensor equation with Whittaker functions, imposing canonically normalized positive-frequency waves at early times. Inverting the gravitational equation gives integrals expressed through Meijer G-functions. Numerical evolution of the coupled perturbations and a parameter-space exploration support the phenomenological conclusions.

Separate topological flux from globally defined fluctuations: H=dB+Hᵇ and Fext=d−H Cext+eᴮ∧Fᵇ. Internal RR fields are replaced by their spacetime-filling duals at the equation-of-motion level, allowing integrations by parts without discarding gauge-patch contributions.

Differentiate the action under two global scalings, impose the equations of motion, and combine the resulting on-shell identities with the integrated external Einstein equation. Appendix A supplies an alternative manipulation using the Bianchi identities, H equation, Einstein equation, and dilaton equation.

Numerically integrates covariant Einstein–scalar background equations in cosmic time and converts to e-fold time. Fields and their velocities form a first-order phase-space system. Trajectory examples start with specified field positions and zero initial velocities and are followed beyond slow roll.

Imports the δN method of Refs. [68,69] for generic potentials, including evolution beyond slow roll. Computes derivatives through backward and forward transport of N_A, Θᴬ, and Ω_A using twelve first-order ODEs, with final uniform-density boundary data and the stated initial fluctuation covariance.

Generate type II backgrounds from AdS5×S5 through T-duality on the Hopf circle, the shift φ→φ+βϕ+αh f(w/h), and a second T-duality. The derivative f′ is assumed bounded and 2π-periodic; the shift changes asymptotic boundary data.

Use bounded metric functions to analyze curvature invariants and geodesics. Decompose linearized metric/scalar perturbations, choose longitudinal gauge, Fourier transform external directions, and rewrite the tensor and scalar equations using positive Q†Q operators.

Construct explicit warp factors and an axion profile using reparameterized Jacobi elliptic functions. The author states that a first-order formulation generates the solution, but defers that formulation and broader families to future work.

Choose a phenomenological correction K=−2MPl² ln[−i(ρ−ρ̄)+λ exp(−αρρ̄)] and an engineered inflationary prefactor B(ρ). Compute the Kähler metric and scalar potential, then apply canonical normalization and slow-roll formulas; trial-and-error parameter searches select an illustrative inflationary regime.

Estimate gravitational particle production and integrate post-inflationary scalar evolution analytically during kinetic/radiation eras. For X domination, solve the conformally coupled scalar–Friedmann system numerically and identify scaling attractors while neglecting desert potential energy.
