Local parameter-space analysis holds the other SUSY-breaking coordinates fixed and plots normalised-energy and minimum-mass contours in the (AS,BS) plane. The overlap of positive-energy and positive-minimum-mass regions identifies stable dS slices.

The scalar potential is constructed from the Kähler potential and holomorphic superpotential using the N=1 F-term expression. An imported prescription uses 2N flux couplings at the scalar origin to turn the extremum equations into linear conditions, leaving N real SUSY-breaking parameters.

A differential-evolution-inspired search mutates populations of SUSY-breaking parameters and selects candidates using normalised energy and mass eigenvalues. Reported successful inputs include population 16, 50,000 iterations, initial Gaussian mutation width 0.01 and probability 2/3 of mutating each coordinate. Stagnation increases mutation width and eventually triggers replacement.

The construction replaces the single KKLT-type exponential by two exponentials, computes the supersymmetric potential, solves the Kähler-covariant stationary condition approximately, and expands near the AdS minimum to estimate the cosmological chameleon mass.

The potential is analysed through a quadratic neighbourhood of its minimum and a steep-exponential region. The transition σ* is defined approximately by equality of the derivatives of the two exponential contributions. Laboratory bounds, galactic thin-shell screening and a density threshold for accessing the near-minimum region constrain parameters.

Uses toric weight data, Stanley–Reisner ideals, intersection numbers, and Mori/Kähler cones. Computes ordinary and equivariant cohomology using Riemann–Roch, Lefschetz fixed-point formulas, and line-bundle tools; PALP supplies polytope information. These calculations identify suitable divisors and orientifold zero-mode splittings.

Expands the N=1 F-term scalar potential order by order in inverse volume. Analytic large-action relations guide stabilization, but the successful racetrack treatment retains corrections to stationarity and solves numerically. Loop effects are estimated with a Coleman–Weinberg argument using a six-dimensional Kaluza–Klein cutoff.

Integer flux configurations satisfying R-R tadpole, T-dual tadpole and Q·H3=Q·Q=0 Bianchi constraints are generated before numerical minimisation. A genetic algorithm searches the six real moduli with stated convergence criterion 10^-20 and a finite flux cutoff.

Slow-roll diagnostics are projected onto two-dimensional planes while two of the four light real fields are held fixed. E-fold estimates along fixed-field cuts are used to assess single-field trajectories; two-field trajectories are discussed qualitatively.

The authors diagnose stability by diagonalising their matrix Mij²=Di∂jV+(2/3)V0Kij. They also compute F-terms, the gravitino mass and the mixing matrix to identify mass hierarchies and the approximate s-goldstino direction.
Recasts the coupled Friedmann, scalar-field and matter-continuity equations as an autonomous system for Ωφ, γ, z and λ, then evolves initial conditions numerically from decoupling to today.
Adopts longitudinal-gauge perturbations and the Amendola prescription for coupled baryon/dark-matter density fluctuations in the small-scale Newtonian limit, neglecting axion clustering.

Multiplies supernova, BAO/CMB-summary, H(z) and growth likelihoods. Uses the historical Union2.1 sample of 580 supernovae and 18 chronometer H(z) points; propagates fitted parameter errors to wφ bands.

Describe local special geometry through a covariantly holomorphic symplectic section and its derivative identities. Impose stationarity, then express the canonically normalized scalar Hessian using α, the complex third-derivative parameter β, and the relative breaking angle θ.
Use the local Przanowski–Tod parametrization with h satisfying (e^h)_{ρρ}+h_{ϕϕ}+h_{χχ}=0 and f=2−ρh_ρ. The Toda equation constrains the trace of the dimensionless second-derivative matrix α.

Average the three nontrivial hyper directions and two vector directions into a real symmetric 2×2 matrix. Its eigenvalues bound the extreme scalar masses; extremizing over θ gives bounds depending only on ε.
Project the Hermitian scalar Hessian along the Goldstino direction to obtain λ=e^{−G}V_{i j̄}G^iG^{j̄}. Decompose G^i=αK^i+N^i and σ=−2s_is^i+ω, then study normalized N orthogonal to K.
Reformulate constrained extrema of D_NNN=e^K d_ijk N^iN^jN^k using e^K d_ijk v^jv^k=λI_ijk v^jv^k, where I_ijk=(K_i g_jk+K_j g_ki+K_k g_ij)/3. Use discriminants as characteristic polynomials.
For p=3, reduce the relevant stationarity equation D_NNM=0 to a cubic in tanϑ. Combine analytic invariant formulas with numerical classification of randomly generated intersection tensors.
Evaluate the oscillator form of M^{−i} and the spin translations T^i on first-level massless string states using the light-cone constraints and oscillator commutators.
Separate orbital and spin parts of the light-cone Lorentz generators. Introduce SO(d−2) vectors T^i obeying [T^i,T^j]=im²S^{ij}; for m=0 they become commuting little-group translations.
Identify the massless little-group generators at representative momentum p=(E,0,…,E), and test whether the commuting translation generators act trivially on physical states.

Tracks separately conserved visible/dark entropy after thermal decoupling, estimates additional effective neutrino species and applies standard analytic thermal-freezeout calculations to the heavy symmetric relic.
Uses stellar-kinematic surface-density estimates and an exponential-radial, sech²-vertical isothermal disk profile to infer an approximate Oort-limit bound on disk mass.

Compares bremsstrahlung, Compton and Rutherford-equilibration timescales; estimates final disk thickness using a thin-disk Jeans equation and Saha recombination. Indirect signals use line-of-sight density-squared integrals.

MultiNest nested sampling handles narrow, multimodal likelihood structure and computes Bayesian evidence E=∫P(α)L(α)dα with a normalized prior. The comparison model is the purely linear potential V=μ³φ.

Maps the power-spectrum posterior to an approximate resonant non-Gaussianity amplitude using Eq. (4.1). This predicts a three-point signal; the three-point data are not included in parameter estimation because the shape lacks applicable standard constraints.

ModeCode numerically solves inflationary perturbation equations to infer potential parameters directly. Small-f calculations initialize modes further inside the horizon and increase primordial-spectrum sampling and CAMB accuracy.

Sum one-loop contributions over KK towers of six-dimensional chiral fields, using Riemann-zeta regularization of KK-level sums. These imported loop results provide information unavailable from the massless five-dimensional spectrum alone.

Separate Chern-Simons couplings obtainable by classical circle reduction from couplings generated by integrating out massive charged spin-1/2 fields, spin-3/2 fields and two-forms. Compare the resulting five-dimensional coefficients with six-dimensional Green-Schwarz and anomaly data.

Adjunction expresses fourfold Chern classes through base classes. Scaling in the shrinking elliptic-fiber limit selects surviving terms; corrected variables and Legendre duality organize the Kähler potential and no-scale identities.

The weak-coupling interpretation uses divisor intersections, seven-brane tadpole cancellation, Einstein/string-frame conversion, and relative powers of string coupling. Worldsheet Euler characteristics suggest amplitude topologies rather than provide an explicit amplitude calculation.

Classical Kaluza–Klein reduction of J0=t8t8R^4−(1/4!)ε11ε11R^4. The appendix splits external/internal curvature contractions and rewrites internal curvature invariants using Chern classes and the Kähler form.

Use slow-roll background equations and evolution equations for the dissipative ratio and potential slow-roll parameters, calculate spectral indices and their runnings, and eliminate model parameters to obtain observable consistency relations separately for weak and strong dissipation.

Restrict the potential to canonical forms to reduce the number of independent slow-roll parameters. Illustrate allowed regions using the paper's 2013 Planck 68% and 95% contours in the scalar-index/running plane and historical isocurvature bounds.

Match inflation to the radiation era using an effective reheating fluid and Rrad: ln Rrad = ΔNreh(3w̄reh−1)/4. Solve for the observable field value using reheating matching rather than assigning a universal ΔN*. For w̄reh=1/3, Rrad=1 and this background matching cannot distinguish reheating from radiation domination.

Compute the first three potential-based slow-roll parameters, determine the inflationary endpoint, and integrate the trajectory through ∫V/Vφ dφ. Analytic expressions use functions including Lambert W and the dilogarithm; numerical quadrature or root finding is retained where necessary.

Expand scalar and tensor spectra around a pivot, with coefficients expressed in Hubble-flow functions evaluated at crossing. The adopted Planck 2018 + Bicep-Keck inference uses second-order spectra and marginalizes over second-order slow-roll parameters.

ADM expansion in spatially flat gauge isolates scalar field fluctuations. First-order lapse and shift constraints suffice for the cubic action; background equations and removal of total derivatives simplify the result.

Hamilton–Jacobi background evolution is combined with the separate-universe δN formalism. A sum-separable Hubble rate supplies an integral of motion and analytic N derivatives, quoted from the authors' previous work.

A path-integral calculation uses the leading cubic DBI interactions and field propagators to obtain the horizon-exit three-point function. The dominant time-integral contribution is evaluated near sound-horizon crossing.

Homogeneous linear instability analysis compares parallel two-stream, perpendicular filamentation and oblique modes. Appendix A obtains the oblique/filamentation transition from the curvature at zero parallel wave number of the large-transverse-wave-number growth-rate branch.

PIC validation compares growth, saturation and timing, including periodic counterstreams, piston-wall and full two-shock setups. The authors report smaller-cell convergence tests and runs with up to 800 particles per cell.

Three existing saturation estimates compare the growth rate with cyclotron or magnetic-trapping frequencies, or set the particle Larmor radius equal to the inverse selected wave number. Spontaneous magnetic spectra are calculated using linearized Vlasov–Maxwell response and Maxwell–Jüttner distributions.

Bayesian parameter estimation uses CosmoMC or MontePython MCMC, with MultiNest nested sampling for evidence or strongly non-Gaussian likelihoods. Model comparison reports both best-fit effective χ² differences and prior-averaged Bayesian evidence.

Observable-window reconstruction Taylor-expands V(φ) through orders 2–4 and numerically computes spectra. A separate nonparametric reconstruction writes PR=P0(1+f), represents f with cubic B-splines, and penalizes squared second derivatives in ln k, with additional penalties outside the fitted interval.

Inflationary predictions use slow-roll spectral expansions and numerical integration of linear scalar/tensor mode equations with ModeCode or CLASS. The numerical treatment removes the slow-roll approximation, while retaining linear perturbation theory. Appendix A also samples Hubble flow functions using second-order analytic spectra.

Power-spectrum pipelines use an unconnected segment model with one-scale network evolution coupled to CMBACT, or field-simulation unequal-time stress-energy correlators (UETCs), decomposed into scalar/vector/tensor parts, diagonalized and supplied to modified CMBEASY. COSMOMC fits the additional defect fraction.

Blind Planck String Challenges combine simulated post-recombination string maps with Gaussian CMB, masks and progressively realistic noise. Component-separation simulations estimate foreground residuals. Lower-resolution string maps receive anti-aliasing filtering and the HEALPix pixel window before analysis.

Non-Gaussian searches use separable modal bispectrum reconstruction, steerable Gaussian-derivative wavelets measuring signed-intensity kurtosis, and four normalized Minkowski functionals: area, perimeter, genus and cluster number. The MF posterior uses a chi-squared likelihood assuming multivariate Gaussian functional measurements.

Construct collision functionals from leading 2-to-2 processes, including Bose enhancement or Pauli blocking. The displayed collision formula assumes time-reversal-invariant processes and averages squared amplitudes over incoming and outgoing spins.

The C++ implementation uses a generalized predictor-corrector procedure, 2,000 logarithmic time steps and 100 logarithmic momentum points from 10 keV to 10 GeV. Runs typically span SM temperatures of 200 MeV to about 1 MeV; a thermal two-sector variant tracks separate temperatures.

Numerically solve coupled Boltzmann and Friedmann equations, retaining the new species' potentially nonthermal momentum distribution. Infer its recombination energy density from the post-decoupling distribution and convert this to Δg*.

For slow-roll models, calculate potential slow-roll parameters and use ns = 1 + 2ηv − 6εv, r = 16εv and αs = −24εv² + 16εvηv − 2ξv. Normalize the scalar amplitude using the observed primordial power, then compare trajectories with reported observational contours.

For IR DBI, obtain tilt and running from the parametrized scalar spectrum. Use feqNL = −0.35(1 − cs²)/cs², forthNL = 0.032(1 − cs²)/cs² and cs⁻¹ ≈ βNeDBI/3 to compare predicted non-Gaussianity bands with Planck bounds.

Relate horizon-exit e-folds to the observed comoving pivot through subsequent expansion and reheating. Under instantaneous reheating, the stated pivot relations are approximately Ne = 61.2 + ¼ln εv for WMAP9+ and 58.2 + ¼ln εv for Planck+WP; the authors use iteration starting near Ne = 60.

Construct exact fixed-point tensors for the singlet example, then replace spin-½ singlets by entangled pairs carrying suitable projective representations to generalize the construction. For numerical phase identification, propose optimizing symmetric scale-invariant MERA with transitional layers and examining the fixed-point tensor pair.

Impose tensor intertwining identities u = (Vg⊗Vg)u(Vg†⊗Vg†) and w = (Vg⊗Vg)wVg†. Cancellation of representation actions on internal bonds leaves the global symmetry action on open indices, establishing symmetry preservation through coarse-graining.

When only a few SPT phases are available, the authors suggest trying each explicitly constructed fixed-point tensor pair and restricting energy minimization to transitional layers. This is a proposed computational strategy rather than a reported numerical benchmark.

Use Mukai charge vectors and their antisymmetric pairing to compute RR charges and chiral indices. Restrict global flavour-brane charges to the blow-up divisor, match the local quiver charges, and impose tadpole, Freed-Witten and probe-brane K-theory consistency conditions.

Stabilize order by order in inverse CY volume: leading D-terms and flux F-terms scale as V⁻²; subleading effects include the α′³ Kähler correction, SO(8) condensation Wnp=As exp(−πTs/3), and supersymmetry-induced matter potentials.

The displayed superpotential is W=P₀−SP₁+Σm(P₂m−SP₃m)Um, with cubic polynomials in the complex-structure fields and coefficients determined by fluxes. The Kähler potential is K=−Σi=1⁷ln(2ψi). Numerical mass matrices, F-terms and gravitino quantities characterize the candidates.

Use a genetic algorithm to minimize the scalar potential for preselected flux families satisfying tadpole and Bianchi constraints. The authors then refine numerical solutions with a Newton method in Mathematica, reporting 1000-decimal accuracy; the refinement code is not supplied.

For the present spectrum, distribute exponential modulus decays over production times and redshift their energies using a numerical matter-to-radiation transition. Continual matter domination and continual radiation domination supply early- and late-decay analytic approximations.

Compute fermion-pair production amplitudes, integrate final-state phase space, average over incident photon directions with the pair-production threshold, then integrate over the thermal photon distribution to obtain the scattering rate.

Integrate the deposited energy per photon, εa=∫dt Ea(t)|Γaγ→qq̄(t)|ξa(t), and fit each channel's deposition history to a neutral decaying species. Apply imported BBN bounds separately to the fitted channels.

Four-dimensional F- and D-term supergravity is expanded in loop- and volume-suppressed parameters. With Φ = S − βb Tb/2, the leading equations DZ Ŵ = DΦ Ŵ = 0 fix heavy fields; threshold effects, worldsheet instantons and α′²/α′³ Kähler corrections generate the subleading Kähler potential energy.

Hodge decomposition separates harmonic, exact and co-exact H-flux. The Chern–Simons superpotential is expanded in bundle deformations to recover holomorphicity conditions and the coupled bundle/complex-structure moduli space.

For linear matter growth, expand w and the growth index in Ωφ, approximate the index as nearly constant, integrate the density contrast, and express the result as f(z)σ8(z) for comparison with redshift-space distortions.

Rewrite the background equations as an autonomous system in normalized field velocity and potential variables, then classify exponential-potential fixed points through eigenvalues of the linearized system.

Construct tracker solutions by perturbing around constant matter-era w in powers of Ωφ. For thawing, Taylor-expand the potential to second order about the initial field value and solve using an approximately ΛCDM scale factor.

Add and subtract an off-shell rounded-cone configuration. At first order in n−1, the equations of motion cancel the bulk variation with fixed outer boundary data; the remaining localized curvature contribution gives the area term. An equivalent calculation uses the inner boundary variation.

Derive the surface condition from potentially singular normal Einstein equations and 2π-periodic perturbations. The argument uses reduction to two-dimensional dilaton gravity and, separately, a direct D-dimensional calculation.

Evaluate classical on-shell actions for smooth integer replicas, analytically continue in n, and differentiate at n=1. The central object is a relation between replica actions and a surface in the original geometry.

Axionic energy injection is translated into ΔNeff using the axion branching fraction, relativistic degrees of freedom at decay and the visible-sector reheating temperature. Constraints on axion and SM partial widths are then compared with model-specific decay channels.

The authors extract two-body decay interactions from Kähler kinetic terms, Higgs bilinears, gauge kinetic functions and modulus F-terms, applying canonical normalization and equations of motion. Appendix A supplies the interactions underlying the quoted partial widths.

Supersymmetric phase and duality arguments use N=2-to-N=1 mass deformations, monopole/dyon condensation, Higgsing, gaugino condensation and matching the area/perimeter behavior of lines across candidate dual descriptions.

The Euclidean description weights bundles by ordinary instanton phases and discrete terms involving Pontryagin squares and cup products of lifting-obstruction classes. A line insertion on S2×T2 relates these phases to its electric and magnetic charges.

Charges are reduced modulo electric and magnetic root lattices to center-charge classes. Closure, inversion and Dirac mutual locality classify allowed spectra; for C=Zk, locality requires nm′−mn′=0 mod k.
Construct a parameter-induced density using a delta-function integral, change variables to κ = −z/β³, and invert the vacuum-energy relation with the W−1 branch of the Lambert function.

Expand the F-term potential at large volume, dropping quadratic non-perturbative terms and higher powers of ξ/V. Solve extremum equations and constrain both real and axionic Hessian directions, retaining subleading terms when leading curvatures cancel.
Compare numerical stationary points of the full and approximate potentials with analytical large-volume estimates. Numerical histograms are also compared with the derived probability density.

The quoted Wolf theorem states that a Riemannian homogeneous flat space is Rm × Tn. Applied to a compact homogeneous flat quotient, it identifies the vacuum geometry as a torus; the Riemannian homogeneity hypothesis is essential.

The authors use Milnor’s flat-Lie-group criterion to establish exhaustiveness of the Scherk–Schwarz construction and organize the flat algebras through dimension six. Lattice classification uses finite Abelian integral linear actions on torus fibres.

Explicit ISO(2) Maurer–Cartan forms, metric reduction, scalar/vector masses, Lie-algebra cohomology and covariantly constant spinors exhibit which modes the left-invariant truncation retains or misses.

Construct higher-dimensional neutrino operators with either Δ†Δ/MPl² or σ/MPl insertions. Reexpress the type-II contribution using the corrected right-handed mass matrix, exposing corrections associated with unequal left/right operator coefficients.

Fit the tree-level neutrino matrix to the quoted oscillation best fits, add the singlet-induced correction, and evaluate changes in mass-squared differences, mixing angles and the Dirac phase while scanning its overall coupling strength.

Transition sensitivities q are computed from spectra at x=−0.01, 0 and +0.01 using configuration interaction plus many-body perturbation theory. The construction uses a Dirac–Fock VN potential, B-spline orbitals and excitations from 3dn, 3dn−1 4s and 3dn−1 4p, with n=4 for Fe V and n=6 for Ni V.

A linear fit of fractional wavelength shifts against relative sensitivities Qα separates a common redshift intercept from an α-dependent slope. Separate Fe V and Ni V estimates are reported using selected transitions with usable laboratory wavelengths and identifiable calculated levels.

To test sensitivity to gain calibration, the authors fit and subtract a linear dependence of fractional wavelength shift on laboratory wavelength, then refit against Qα. This diagnostic can remove part of a genuine α signal as well as calibration contamination.

Estimate axion decay constants by combining periodicities with canonical normalization from moduli Kähler metrics. Separately estimate endpoint curvature amplification for primordial-black-hole production and derive the tilt/running constraints in a curvaton-dominated regime.

Evaluate potential slow-roll parameters and integrate the slow-roll trajectory to obtain the e-fold count. First place the CMB point at φ0 = πf/2, then move it slightly above that inflection point to obtain the observed red tilt while retaining a relatively large tensor fraction.

Minimize a joint χ² from growth, 580 UNION2.1 supernovae, BAO distance ratios and a CMB shift parameter; eliminate the supernova nuisance parameter μ0. The reported scan varies β from −0.3 to 1 and Ωm0 from 0.2 to 0.35.

Analyze scalar metric perturbations in Newtonian gauge and obtain a linear, subhorizon matter-growth equation with an effective gravitational coupling Geff. Rewrite this equation using the logarithmic growth factor f.

Recast background evolution as an autonomous system in dimensionless variables and study its numerical evolution and phase-plane behavior. For the exponential potential, Γ=1 and the system reduces to four autonomous equations.
Compute QCD mirror-quark pair production with a tree-level Monte Carlo and CTEQ6L PDFs at 8 and 14 TeV. Renormalization and factorization scales equal √ŝ; NLO/NLL rescaling is deliberately omitted.

Use parton-level signal/background simulations, Gaussian jet-energy smearing, and jet cuts pT>100 GeV, |η|<2.5, ΔR>0.7. Select jet–Z mass peaks using five adjacent 20-GeV bins; the ZW channel additionally uses Δφ(lepton, missing pT)<1.
Diagonalize the neutral gauge-boson mass matrix, expand in ε=v²/v̂², and use bi-unitary transformations for charged-fermion mixing. An illustrative neutrino sector combines Dirac and Majorana masses.
Compare full YM–CS and pure CS loop integrals using Wick rotation and contour residues. Examine the order of the g→∞ limit and loop integration to identify finite contributions from a heavy pole.

Study CS-deformed real YM instantons using a radial ansatz invariant under simultaneous spatial rotations and gauge transformations. Solve the radial equations numerically between short-distance YM behavior and the specified large-distance scalar expectation value.

Compute the component-field one-loop two-point function of the branch fluctuation χ3 and expand through p² to extract its kinetic correction. The full calculation includes bosons, fermions and Faddeev–Popov ghosts in arbitrary Rξ gauge.

Approximate gauge tensors by a free equation solved with Whittaker functions, then source metric tensors using a Green’s function. Observational comparisons instead use numerical background and perturbation evolution, initialized to isolate the WKB slow scalar mode.

Analyze scalars through a charged-particle analogy with a harmonic well and an analogue magnetic field. WKB separates fast Larmor and slow magnetic-drift modes; dropping axion kinetic energy and subleading mass terms gives a reduced gauge-scalar action through horizon crossing.

Expand the action to quadratic order in ADM variables, choose spatially flat coordinates, and perform a scalar-vector-tensor decomposition. Non-Abelian Coulomb gauge makes Gauss’s law algebraic; gauge fixing and constraints leave six propagating gauge-field degrees of freedom.

For Abelian production, the review presents helicity mode equations, constant-ξ Coulomb-function solutions and an adiabatic-vacuum approximation. Backreaction is described through a mean-field inflaton equation and an approximate sourced perturbation equation.

The article primarily summarizes and critiques published constructions, usually presenting results without derivations. Its model summaries and imported observational findings are review evidence rather than independent demonstrations.
The four-form construction is explained by treating F4 and A3 independently, imposing F4=dA3 with a Lagrange multiplier, and integrating out F4. The dual scalar q yields V=(q+μφ)²/2.

Uses the coherent-domain axion–photon oscillation probability in equation (5). Magnitude estimates generally use P(a → γ) = (B⊥L/M)²/4 when both θ ≪ 1 and Δ ≪ 1; plots instead use the full expression.

For the diffuse-background illustration, takes B⊥ = 1 nG, L = 10 Mpc, electron density 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm⁻³ and M = 10¹³ GeV. Accumulates coherent-domain conversions over an assumed 10¹⁰ years with orientation averaging.

Computes luminosity by summing conversion over magnetic domains and averaging field orientation for a homogeneous, isotropic axion flux. Figure 2 marginalises a uniform coherence-length distribution over 2–34 kpc, with ΔNeff = 0.57, B⊥ = 1 µG and axion energy 200 eV.

Randomly scans m0,m1/2 ∈ [0.1,10] TeV, A0 ∈ [−30,30] TeV, tanβ ∈ [1,60] and both signs of µ. Varies mt = 173.2 ± 5 GeV and αs(mZ) = 0.1184 ± 0.0021; retains Higgs masses in [123,129] GeV and includes reheating uncertainty through 3.12κ ≤ ΔNeff ≤ 3.48κ.

Explicitly calculates one-loop self-energy and vertex diagrams for the modulus–Higgs interaction in the stated DR subtraction scheme. Uses Wess–Zumino gauge and arbitrary Rξ gauge for vectors; the authors report cancellation of ξ dependence in the summed result.

Resums logarithms by solving dZ/dt = γZ Z jointly with gauge- and Yukawa-coupling RG equations. Numerical evolution uses SoftSusy 3.3.7, relevant one- and two-loop effects, low-energy SM inputs, string-scale MSUGRA boundary conditions and one-loop electroweak-breaking conditions.

Uses boundary time evolution to represent an early simple left operator A′ by a later scrambled operator A″ = exp(−2iHLt)A′exp(2iHLt). Bulk evolution relates A′ to an interior mode A; that relation depends on the bridge and on possible right-side disturbances.

Reviews Euclidean magnetic-field pair-creation instantons and Lorentzian continuation as a preparation of entangled near-extremal black holes. The appendix distinguishes the entropy enhancement obtained by comparison with monopole production from the full tunnelling rate, which remains very small.

Proposes describing the bulk by Wheeler–DeWitt wave functions over the spacetime region spacelike separated from a boundary slice. Overlaps evaluated on different bulk slices would encode interior scattering experiments without selecting one instantaneous bridge geometry.

Galaxy mass modeling compares cored and NFW-like halo rotation curves while including stellar and gas contributions and uncertainties. Dwarf stellar dynamics provides central-mass estimates, whose correspondence to simulated subhalo properties requires care.

The review compares collisionless N-body predictions with hydrodynamic simulations, including matched initial conditions, smoothed particle hydrodynamics and adaptive mesh refinement. An imported analytic model describes orbital heating by rapid baryonic-potential fluctuations.
Proposed substructure tests use gravitational-lens flux anomalies and astrometric perturbations, together with density and dynamical perturbations of cold stellar tidal streams.

Compute toric intersection data and corrected potentials for one-modulus, two-modulus swiss-cheese and fibered examples. Compare corrections with the original stabilization potential; supplement estimates with a numerical uplifted vacuum and a stated leading-order Hessian stability check.

Expand the F-term potential around K0 = −2 log V and flux superpotential W0, retaining terms through second order in δK and contributions from nonperturbative δW. Expand the inverse Kähler metric and use homogeneity identities to identify cancellations and leading volume powers.
For single-field slow-roll models, the review uses n_s−1 = 2η−6ε and r = 16ε to connect effective scalar potentials to observables, then compares prediction ranges with WMAP and Planck constraints.

Imported model analyses also use numerical multifield trajectories: uplifted D3-D7 inflation mixes brane position with a geometric modulus, while racetrack inflation lacks a simple analytically extracted single-field potential.

Large-volume constructions organize the low-energy theory in string coupling and inverse cycle sizes. The tree-level Kähler potential K_tree = −2 ln V and extended no-scale structure explain why some moduli enter the potential only at suppressed orders.

Long-wavelength response uses L=ΘIJ ε^{μνλρ}∂μAIν∂λAJρ/(8π²), with symmetric Θ having diagonal θc, θs and off-diagonal θ0. Flux insertion, exchange statistics and deposition of 2D Hall layers determine allowed responses and angle periodicities.

The Abelian K-matrix approach couples intrinsic statistical fields to symmetry currents, then integrates them out to obtain KG=−q KS^{-1} q^T. Higher-spin response instead uses an SU(2) embedding, representation-dependent traces and large gauge invariance.

A charge-N Higgs condensate is dualized using a (D−2)-form multiplier B. Integrating out the phase-gradient variable produces N B∧dA/(2π) plus a Maxwell term; particle–extended-object braiding is used to motivate the normalization through phase 2π/N.

Construct compatible, torsion-free generalized connections for O(d,d)×R⁺, then preserve O(d−1,1)×O(1,d−1) and use spinorial derivatives to obtain a generalized curvature scalar. Additional connection choices reproduce ordinary and β-dependent covariant derivatives; remaining unfixed pieces are set to zero for simplicity.

Derive field equations using metric compatibility, analogues of Palatini identities, decomposition of the new connection into tensorial and ordinary-connection pieces, and integrations by parts. The β equation retains dependence on the ordinary Ricci tensor.
Use subgroup branching and symmetrized squares of fermion representations to identify family content and allowed fermion-mass operators, including SO10 decompositions under SU5 and SU2×SU2×SU4.

Discuss condensates, renormalization-group scales and generalized nonlinear sigma models as qualitative tools for dynamical symmetry breaking. Linearized sigma models are suggested as a connection to explicit Higgs representation algebra.

Adopt a previously derived scalar bispectrum expression and examine flattened and squeezed/local configurations. Track its excitation and phase dependence after expressing the amplitude through the normalized scalar power spectrum.

Use leading-slow-roll Hankel mode solutions and Bogoliubov coefficients to compute spectra and excitation energy. Compare perturbative energy and pressure evolution with the slow-roll background, then combine the resulting bounds with COBE normalization.

Replace mode-basis descriptions by an infinite BBGKY hierarchy of ghost-renormalized spectral moments coupled to Einstein equations. Seek exact hierarchy solutions and operator/state-vector realizations; use asymptotic expansions and imaginary-time instanton constructions for other regimes.

Start from a Hamilton-gauged Faddeev–Popov path integral; use exponential metric parameterization and factorization of classical and quantum variables. Separate variations and differential identities are used to obtain compatible background and operator equations with conserved averaged EMT.

A Pauli-vector density matrix describes mixing with V = (gaB, 0, (ωp²−ma²)/(2E)). Damping is modeled by D = D0 + ℓB⁻¹, with D0 = σγe ne/2; the two contributions represent scattering and magnetic-domain decoherence.

Analytic conversion estimates over one Hubble time separate off-resonant and resonant evolution. The resulting photon injection is compared with BBN, CMB spectrum and anisotropy, reionization and diffuse-photon constraints.

Spin-projector decomposition and inversion of the gauge-fixed quadratic action produce graviton and scalar propagators. In Landau gauge these are stated to fall as k⁻⁴, while the Faddeev-Popov ghost propagator falls as k⁻².

Nilpotent BRST transformations, sources for BRST variations, the ghost equation and the Slavnov-Taylor identity constrain divergent effective actions. The argument proceeds inductively in loop order using dimensional regularization and a finite/divergent split.

Graph topology and derivative counting determine superficial divergence. Landau-gauge transversality permits integration by parts at ghost vertices, giving each external ghost or antighost two external-momentum factors and improving 1PI power counting.
Quantized boosts of bosonic and fermionic charge lattices determine gauge-boson vertex operators. OPEs with base momentum and winding charges then produce the effective gauging matrices.

Faithful embeddings of orbifold rotations into O(d,d) determine background monodromies through E = G+B and E′ = (AE+B)(CE+D)⁻¹. Complex structure and Kähler moduli give explicit elliptic-fibration expressions.

Explicit partition functions and worldsheet gauging track T-duality at the orbifold point. A total-derivative term contributes nontrivially on the worldsheet torus, producing the phases that identify the dual winding shift.

Identify equal-Hodge-diamond divisors with different GLSM charges, enumerate exchanges involving up to four pairs, impose Stanley–Reisner ideal invariance, and examine the orientifold-invariant Kähler cone and volume.
The scan combines PALP polytope data, maximal triangulations and Kähler-cone generators from SAGE, coordinate-divisor Hodge numbers from cohomCalg, and intersection numbers from SINGULAR.
For non-toric examples, determine parity directly through bundle-valued cohomology and Koszul exact sequences, rather than inferring it solely from the toric volume expression.

Sum integer instanton flux sectors to obtain a holomorphic Jacobi-theta prefactor. With the chosen stabilized axio-dilaton, this supplies the odd-axion dependence used in the effective superpotential.

Construct the N=1 F-term potential from K and W, retaining leading large-volume contributions from the perturbative α′³ correction and nonperturbative instanton terms, then solve selected coupled extremization conditions.
Estimate decay constants from the Kähler metric and masses from the canonically normalized potential Hessian. Analytic volume scalings are supplemented by sampled numerical extrema and spectra.

For nonrotating backgrounds, evolve Gaussian initial data using separate neutral characteristic and charged finite-difference schemes. Extract damped frequencies with Prony fits, checking convergence as the number of exponentials increases and the grid spacing decreases.

Use sixth-order WKB conditions involving derivatives of the effective potential at its peak. Because the potential and angular eigenvalue depend on frequency, solve the resulting implicit frequency equation numerically.

Separate the charged Klein–Gordon equation into angular eigenvalue and radial Schrödinger-type problems. Use a horizon Frobenius expansion, three-term recurrence and Leaver continued fractions; apply Nollert acceleration for nonzero field mass.

Match a comoving mode at k = akHk to its horizon-exit time. Parameterize the intervening expansion by an effective equation of state: ΔN = [(1−3w)/(12(1+w))] ln(ρr/ρend), with ρend = 3Vend/2. Propagate the shift into inflationary observables using slow-roll relations.

Estimate the scalar decay rate as Γσ = c3 mσ³/mp² and the resulting reheating temperature from √(Γσmp), including relativistic-degree factors. Compute the relic abundance from rapid annihilation of the scalar-produced WIMPs at this reheating temperature.

Use DarkSUSY scans and contemporary direct/indirect limits. The general-neutralino scan includes about 100,000 models with bino fraction below 10%, M2 and μ between 100 GeV and 2 TeV, and tan β between 10 and 50; impose collider compatibility and a 126 GeV Higgs.

Use the static Euclidean replica trick: construct smooth integer-n bulk geometries gn, quotient by replica Zn, and continue the quotient geometries with conical opening angle 2π/n. Entropy follows from −∂n(log Zn−n log Z1) at n = 1.

Express the geometry-dependent terms through off-shell Lagrangian variation, a Wald-like boundary contribution, and linearized backreaction sourced by the quantum stress tensor. Add entropy contributions from local counterterms needed to make the bulk calculation finite.

Represent the quantum partition function as Zq,n = Tr(ρ̂n^n), with ρ̂n obtained from path-ordered bulk evolution through angular interval 2π. Differentiation separates entropy in the original n = 1 geometry from terms caused by the n-dependent geometry.

Explicit superpotential constructions include W=M[φ²/2−φ³/(3√3)] with T fixed at 1/2, and W=√3 Mφ(T−1/2) with the matter field fixed at zero. Interchanges and sign changes in the symmetric coordinates generate further examples.

The paper uses a Weyl rescaling and scalar redefinition for higher-curvature gravity, then compares Kähler metrics and scalar potentials. Changing between (T,φ) and (y₁,y₂) also transforms W by the factor (1+y₂/√3)³; transforming coordinates alone is insufficient.

The geometric extraction solves supersymmetric D-term constraints and integrates out vector multiplets in the formal e²→∞ limit, producing the sigma-model one-form K_i and its metric and B-field. Charged logarithms require a quantum-corrected replacement for the conventional quotient.

One-loop Wilsonian supergraphs integrate out massive chiral/Fermi pairs. Calculations in unitary gauge and without fixing that gauge determine local AV₋, logarithmic FI and Higgs kinetic terms; anomaly matching constrains their coefficients.

The loop prescription imposes an infrared cutoff on shifted Euclidean loop momenta after Feynman parametrization. Divergent integrals use dimensional reduction: superspace derivative algebra remains two-dimensional while loop momenta continue to 2−2ε dimensions.

The algorithm assembles compatible partial sums rather than explicitly enumerating every full integer matrix. It determines the fifth summand using c1(V)=0 and removes redundancies from relabelling ambient projective factors.

Fast intersection-theoretic index and anomaly tests precede expensive line-bundle cohomology computations. Cohomology is then used to reject anti-families and models without the required vectorlike Higgs pair.

Stability pruning tests whether matrices (Ma)st=drst c1r(La), and sampled linear combinations with integer coefficients between −5 and 5, have both positive and negative entries. Surviving bundles undergo explicit common slope-zero solution searches, mostly exact and otherwise numerical, especially at h1,1=6.
The relic-yield prescription is YDM=min[Yobs(〈σv〉th_f/〈σv〉f)(Tf/Trh), Yφ BrDM], with Yφ=3Trh/(4mφ). The adopted normalizations are Yobs≈5×10^−10(1 GeV/mDM) and 〈σv〉th_f≈3×10^−26 cm³ s^−1.

Decay-channel estimates distinguish tree-level Higgs production through the Giudice–Masiero coupling, unsuppressed closed-axion channels, loop-induced gauge-boson production, mass-suppressed other visible channels, and suppressed open-axion production.
The analysis parameterizes Γφ=c mφ³/(2πMP²), takes decay at H≈Γφ, and relates reheating to c, mφ and the relativistic degrees of freedom. Earlier dark matter is diluted by at least order (Tf/Trh)³.
For the stabilization example, expand K and the F-term potential in ξ/N̂, solve the leading minimization conditions, and estimate masses and auxiliary F-terms using further large-aτ_s expansions.

The reviewed one-loop formula uses spectral integrals and boundary-dependent determinants for gravitational, vector and chiral loops, with weights (−2,−1,1/2). Its bulk contribution depends on the function Z(d_a·Re T).
Tree-level reduction uses N=1 superfields and norm-derived matrices. The projector P_V removes the graviphoton combination and satisfies N_I(P_V)^I_J=0 and P_V²=P_V.

For the quartic potential, the coupled slow-roll equations reduce to an equation for Q that can be integrated analytically to determine the number of e-folds. The authors additionally report numerical fluctuation evolution supporting their small-Q predictions, with details deferred.
Background evolution uses φ̈+(3H+Υ)φ̇+V′=0 and radiation production ρ̇R+4HρR=Υφ̇². In slow roll the radiation is approximately stationary, with ρR/ρφ≈εQ/[2(1+Q)²].

Scalar perturbations are treated with a Gaussian-white-noise Langevin equation and the fluctuation–dissipation relation. Inflaton occupation numbers enter operator correlation functions, and the power spectrum is expanded in the weak-dissipation limit.
Near-boundary asymptotic analysis of the canonical-field relation, leading large-N predictions, and numerical trajectories for quadratic and quartic choices of F as ξ varies.

Jordan-to-Einstein frame conversion and canonical normalization. The displayed general field relation is dϕ/dφ=√(1+ξφ²+6ξ²φ²)/(1+ξφ²); detailed metric formulas require the extraction checks listed below.
Compare Euclidean actions with Hawking–Moss and solve the gauge-invariant O(4) scalar fluctuation eigenvalue problem −f″+Uf=εf to track negative and zero modes.

Numerically integrate regular north-pole initial data, count scalar passes, and locate jumps by bisection. Instanton diagrams display these discontinuity curves against an initial field value and a potential parameter.

Expand solutions around critical Hawking–Moss backgrounds to study small-field branches and critical masses. Appendix B separately gives a stationary-parameter zero-mode argument under a simplified assumption about reparametrization invariance.

Use Brown–Teitelboim Euclidean brane nucleation for transitions between flux sectors, which correspond to different effective potentials. Use Coleman–De Luccia tunneling for decompactification at fixed flux within one effective potential.

Extremize the large-volume moduli potential, study changes of its extrema under shifts of W0, and expand the BT bubble radius and action in inverse volume. The uplift analysis treats general volume powers rather than selecting one microscopic mechanism.

Decompose geometry and fluxes into SU(2) torsion representations. With left-invariant forms, solve algebraic supersymmetry conditions, Bianchi identities and d²=0 consistency conditions, then determine source terms from the remaining RR Bianchi identities.

Rewrite supersymmetry variations as differential equations for pure-spinor polyforms constructed from internal spinors. Impose flux Bianchi identities in addition to supersymmetry; the stated integrability framework then supplies the equations of motion.

Estimate scale separation using volume/dilaton scaling and ratios of curvature scalars. Compute the internal Ricci scalar by embedding the SU(2) structure into an SU(3) structure and expressing curvature in torsion classes.
Vary the effective potential with respect to u and v to obtain a coupled nonlinear elliptic system. The formulation also includes separate warped-normalization and volume constraints.

Construct solutions using sub- and supersolutions, the maximum principle, the Fredholm alternative and implicit-function arguments in sufficiently regular Sobolev spaces. Positivity and regularity are controlled by choosing small neighborhoods and using Sobolev embedding.

Lemma 3.9 alternatively prescribes u and v near one and algebraically solves for the coefficient combinations a=2R−|F1|² and b=|F3|²−2Tstring. This changes which data are dependent and enables explicit small-function ansätze.
Treat dimension as a continuous external parameter and expand to first order in ε=D−4. Rescaled RG time removes one power of λ when locating preferred fixed values of coupling ratios.

Background expansion g=ḡ+h through quadratic order, with BRST gauge fixing chosen to cancel nonminimal fourth-derivative terms. The calculation includes a fourth-order graviton operator and the Faddeev–Popov and third-ghost operators.
Evaluate the one-loop functional RG traces using heat-kernel coefficients B0, B2 and B4 and Q-functionals. The chosen profile is R_k(z)=(k^p−z)Θ(k^p−z), with p the operator order.

The spectrum uses the square-root field–e-fold relation for φk rather than expanding it into oscillations periodic in log k. The authors say this distinction becomes noticeable across Planck's multipole range, although it was unimportant for WMAP.

A brute-force grid evaluates an imported analytic primordial spectrum, varying scalar amplitude, modulation amplitude, decay constant and phase. Transfer functions are cached because most runs hold the background cosmology fixed; additional runs vary Ωb h².

Significance is calibrated by fitting the modulation parameters to 5,000 simulated Gaussian residual datasets. Bayesian evidence is obtained by integrating the likelihood over the computed grid, with background cosmology held fixed.

The local selection probability is approximated by Pg(Dloc) f(Λ,Q,t0) θ(t0−tC), where f is the fraction of protons in galaxies and tC is a classical collapse time. This connects the quantum probabilities to approximate galaxy-formation calculations.

Regular compact Euclidean saddle points supply the semiclassical wave function. A rapidly varying phase relative to the real action gives a WKB classicality condition. Gaussian perturbation probabilities are used, with tensor perturbations coarse grained out for the scalar observables considered.

Top-down probabilities sum over histories conditioned on at least one occurrence of ultralocal observer data. A smooth threshold weighting approximates the transition between rare observer occurrence in small universes and near-certain occurrence in sufficiently large eternally inflating histories.

Constructs benchmarks by numerically imposing flatness near the CMB point and approximately vanishing vacuum energy and gradient at the final minimum. Evolves the noncanonically normalized modulus using covariant background equations.

Calculates slow-roll observables, including next-order spectral-index terms when running matters, and estimates μ/y distortions through power-spectrum integrals. The authors report comparison with numerical background solutions.

Uses a necessary sectional-curvature condition for inflation/dS and a large-t expansion to study how the two perturbative corrections modify the tree-level obstruction. This condition is necessary, rather than a sufficient existence test.

Uses stationarity conditions, the quaternionic curvature sum rule and special-Kähler curvature identities to cancel curvature dependence from the averaged matrix for one gauged isometry. Linear-algebra arguments relate its eigenvalues to extremal masses of the full system.

Optimizes the averaged eigenvalues over the angle describing relative hyper/vector supersymmetry breaking. Exact optimized functions are numerical; analytic approximations reproduce asymptotic behavior and remain valid bounds but are no longer saturable.

Evaluates covariant Hessians at a stationary point and projects onto normalized sGoldstino directions. For mixed matter and one gauging, separate averaging over the hyper triplet and complex vector direction produces a 2×2 matrix.

Uses T-duality rules for NS fields and RR field strengths, tracks quotient/source transformations, and imposes quotient-dependent flux quantization and integrated tadpole cancellation. Circle-bundle forms and their closure properties diagnose topology change.

Uses a democratic RR formulation, imposing Hodge-duality constraints after varying the action. RR equations then follow from Bianchi identities; the simplest IIB and IIA examples are checked by reducing the remaining equations to a warp-factor Poisson equation.

Classifies parent fluxes through self-dual G4 on T8: 20 real choices have one leg on the distinguished u-torus and admit Lorentz-invariant IIB limits. Imposing primitivity leaves 14 choices; primitivity is not required by the flux equations of motion.

Background evolution is written in e-fold time, making the trajectory φ′≈−∂φ ln V a dynamical attractor. The kinematic quantity Ξ=φ″/φ′ tracks departure from slow roll, including the transition between exponential-potential dynamics and the plateau.

Canonical normalization and a potential expansion through linear order in δ lead to slow-roll estimates. Benchmark trajectories, perturbation behavior and scans over initial field values and the (n,δ) plane illustrate the transition and the available redshifted e-foldings.

Linear curvature perturbations are treated in comoving gauge. The supplied calculation introduces Qk=aRk, outgoing spherical Hankel modes and a varying index ν, then integrates the primordial spectrum against spherical Bessel functions to obtain angular multipoles.

Semiclassical vacuum-energy estimates are reformulated through renormalization and Wilsonian path integrals: integrate out heavy fields and match effective vacuum-energy parameters across physical mass thresholds.

Higher-dimensional examples use rugby-ball compactifications, flux quantization, and integrated Einstein/dilaton equations to relate brane sources to boundary derivatives and on-brane curvature. Brane back-reaction is essential; a probe approximation misses the tension cancellation.

Topological actions are analyzed through the Serre spectral sequence of the classifying-space fibration. Four-dimensional quadratic terms use the Pontryagin square; with nonzero β the text says closure occurs only after applying q*, rather than for PB itself.

Local flat 2-connections are reduced to a Π1-valued 1-cocycle and a Π2-valued twisted 2-cochain. On a triangulation these become edge variables A and face variables B constrained by flat A and dA B=β(A).

An ungauged lattice ground state is constructed by a cocycle-weighted path integral on the cone CM. Matter labels lie on vertices and edges; the cone supplies a nullhomotopy. The state is claimed short-range entangled, and gauging its symmetry returns the 2-group TQFT.

Combine dilaton, Einstein and RR Bianchi equations into sums of squares; integrate over compact space to constrain curvature and obtain BPS relations. Solve the remaining warp-factor equation with localised source terms.

Use Taylor and near-source power expansions, global tadpole cancellation, and the extremum constraint sgn(α″)=sgn(α) where α′=0 away from sources. Compute polarisation potentials from probe D8 DBI and Chern–Simons actions.

Uses mapping tori, extending bordisms, characteristic-element signature congruences and quadratic refinements. The general-loop argument combines curvature matching on contractible loops with horizontal/vertical loop factorization.

Constructs the anomaly bundle as a pulled-back theta line bundle. Its connection differs from the theta connection by a metric-only one-form involving Cheeger half-torsion; its curvature splits into gauge and metric blocks.
Models higher abelian gauge fields by differential cocycles, including torsion and micro gauge transformations. Extensions to bounding manifolds use cocycles shifted by the degree-(2ℓ+2) Wu class.

Use autonomous dynamical systems, critical points, linear perturbations and Jacobian eigenvalues to classify stationary ratios and their stability. Effective interaction pressure Π, defined through Q=−3HΠ, provides another parametrization.

Apply Legendre and conformal transformations to express Jordan-frame f(R) gravity as an Einstein-frame canonical scalar coupled to matter. In that representation the scalar balance equation contains Q=β√κ φ̇ρ_m, while traceless radiation is an exception to the direct coupling.

Integrate modified component conservation equations for specified linear or nonlinear couplings. For Q=Hq(ρ_dm,ρ_de), replacing time differentiation by H d/d ln a removes explicit H dependence from component-density evolution; the review attributes this step to conservation equations rather than a particular gravity theory.
Uses mapping-cone cup products for integral Hopf invariants, differential-form Chern–Simons expressions for rational Hopf invariants, and Sullivan minimal models for the rational four-sphere.
Uses relative characteristic classes and Wu-class quadratic refinements, Wall’s signature non-additivity, and Dirac-index/modular-form descriptions of corner invariants.
Uses Pontryagin–Thom collapse and framed bordism. The reported groups are Ω^fr_3≅Z₂₄ and Ω^fr_6≅Z₂, represented by S³ and S³×S³ with Lie-group framings.

Reduce D6-brane Chern–Simons couplings and identify charged objects through Wilson-line and surface operators. Gauge-invariant instanton and monopole insertions describe annihilation of k AB particles or k AB strings.

Obtain the string-sourced gauge potential from the BF equations and couple it to the particle current. Apply previously calculated moving-solenoid emission formulas, integrate loop power over an assumed network distribution, and compare energy injection with BBN and electromagnetic-cascade bounds.

Solve supersymmetric extrema at leading large-x_1 order using Lambert-W branches W_{−1} and W_0. Substitute extremal conditions into real and imaginary Hessian blocks and apply Sylvester's criterion. For LVS, eliminate the volume and solve coupled equations for the small-cycle variables.

Sample compactification parameters, find extrema, impose supergravity cuts, and count positive Hessians among retained solutions. LVS searches use multiple starting points across three solution domains; increasing each domain's subdivision from six to seven–nine reportedly changes probabilities insignificantly. Selected extrema are also compared with the full potential.

Numerically evolve a damped density matrix from a pure axion state along 30 kpc trajectories ending at the Solar System, 8.5 kpc from the Galactic centre. Photon attenuation uses gas distributions and an energy-dependent absorption cross section per hydrogen atom.

Fold the assumed incident spectrum with directional conversion probabilities, then compare the resulting photon flux with historical ROSAT band fluxes. Pole directions probe diffuse backgrounds; a low-latitude direction near (l,b)=(0,−π/8) probes central emission.

Use a three-state photon–axion mixing system for two photon polarizations and the axion. Its terms include transverse-field mixing Δ_Mi=B_i/(2M), axion mass Δ_m=m²/(2ω), and plasma refraction Δ_p=ω_p²/(2ω), with ω_p²=4παn_e/m_e.

Use potential slow-roll parameters, an integrated e-fold relation, r≈16ε_V and n_s≈1−6ε_V+2η_V. The scalar-amplitude normalization fixes the inflationary scale and c₀ once the geometric parameters, f and pivot-scale e-fold count are specified.

Diagonalize the Higgs–Σ scalar mass matrix and estimate the one-loop Higgs portal generated by seesaw neutrino interactions. Requiring the induced Higgs mass correction to remain near the electroweak scale supplies conditional naturalness bounds on right-handed-neutrino masses and portal mixing.

Dimensionally reduce a five-dimensional Chern–Simons term to obtain the inflaton coupling to two gauge bosons. Estimate the tree-level inflaton width, convert it to a perturbative reheating temperature, and compare the resulting thermal history with the standard e-fold matching estimate.

Write the moduli potential as a sum of exponentials, impose common scaling of its terms, and rotate to a rolling field Φ and transverse fields σ with diagonal kinetic terms. Solve logarithmic scalar evolution and a power-law FRW ansatz, requiring a positive minimum in the transverse potential.

For finite density, rotate canonical scalars into a sourced direction and an orthogonal classical flat direction, then solve the density-dependent FRW equations. The bound K≤2/d_perp motivates codimension-one sources; network consistency is investigated through intersecting-brane supersymmetry and separation.
Dimensionally reduce higher-dimensional Chern–Simons couplings in quantized flux backgrounds. For torsion examples, expand gauge potentials on nonclosed forms whose derivatives contain the integer p.
Use the Stückelberg-type action ∫|dφ−pA_r|², its dual ∫|dV−pB|², and the topological coupling p∫B_(D−r−1)∧F_(r+1), with F=dA. These descriptions expose different charged defects.

Gauge-invariant operators with boundaries describe junction-mediated charge violation, linking numbers determine mutual phases, and Bezout's lemma determines the minimal charge violation when several integer couplings p_k occur.

Linearize the Einstein and Maxwell equations, then simultaneously perform Hodge and Lichnerowicz decompositions separately on each internal factor. Factorwise decomposition is needed to decouple the nonuniform stress tensor.

Fix gauge, identify residual gauge sectors, redefine fields and diagonalize coupled mass matrices. Stability arguments use the matrix determinant lemma and continuous paths from explicitly tractable backgrounds that avoid zero eigenvalues.
Vacuum statistics are estimated by counting annuli in the complex W0 plane and changing variables to vacuum energy using the stated KKLT and LVS stabilization scalings.

Three volume-scaling arguments estimate KK couplings: expansion of the volume-dependent KK mass, holomorphy plus canonical normalization, and dimensional reduction of the ten-dimensional Einstein–Hilbert term.
An O’Raifeartaigh model is used to identify the fractional heavy-multiplet splitting as ΔM/M=g|F|/M², illustrating why a small heavy–light coupling changes the naive F/M² expansion criterion.

The authors numerically evolve all fourteen homogeneous scalars together with a spatially flat FRW scale factor, using the Friedmann constraint and scalar equations. Acceleration duration is measured by log[a(t_final)/a(t_initial)].

A genetic algorithm varies flux parameters to minimize ε_V, |η_V| and |η_proj| while keeping V>0. Four selected backgrounds are tabulated as the best examples found, not as an exhaustive classification.

Organize the effective superpotential by inverse powers of MG and include a soft A-term proportional to the gravitino mass. The discussion assigns the PQ-defining interactions to W^(4), the DE-symmetry-defining interactions to W^(6), and the leading displayed breaking interaction to W^(10).

Classify interactions allowed by an exact discrete symmetry. A few lowest-order interactions define an accidental continuous U(1); higher-order interactions allowed by the discrete symmetry but violating that U(1) generate the small pseudo-Goldstone potential.

Determine late neutralino survival with a Boltzmann annihilation equation in radiation domination. For the quoted typical cross sections, about 10^−7–10^−8 GeV^−2 near the benchmark region, the authors find annihilation ineffective.

Track the inflation-dependent minimum until H≈2m_z/3, then model damped modulus oscillations with matter-like redshifting. Analytic estimates use instantaneous inflaton decay and distinguish modulus decay before and after reheating.

Expand supergravity interactions using G=K+log|W|² and small Λ to estimate scalar, fermion, gauge-sector, and gravitino decay channels. The paper also calculates the gravitino channel in the goldstino description and reports agreement.

Use slow-roll expressions, large-N expansions, and numerical investigations of n_s and r. Explicit finite-parameter formulas and trajectories are developed for tanh^(2n)(ϕ/√(6α)) potentials and for the exponential α−β potential.
Compute the inflaton Kähler metric and curvature, add a quartic S stabilization term controlled by g, and examine masses of scalar fluctuations orthogonal to the inflationary trajectory.
Fix the conformal gauge X^0=X̄^0=√3. The resulting theory has K=−3α log[1−(S S̄+ΦΦ̄)/3] and W=S f(Φ/√3)(3−Φ²)^((3α−1)/2), followed by truncation to S=ImΦ=0 when stable.

Complete the domain-wall energy into Bogomol’nyi squares to obtain correlated-sign equations A′ = ∓√2 g|W| and Σ′i = ±2√2 g K^ij ∂j|W|. Numerically integrate the actual four-field system; two-dimensional slices are used only to display trajectories.

Construct the E7(7)/SU(8) coset representative, dress the embedding tensor into the scalar-dependent T-tensor, and trace it to obtain the fermion tensors A^IJ and A_I^JKL. These determine the potential, superpotentials and full maximal-supergravity mass matrices.

Evaluate the full 70-scalar and physical-vector mass matrices at a critical point, rather than examining only truncation singlets. Scalar perturbative stability in AdS is assessed using the Breitenlohner–Freedman bound.

Derive Einstein-frame radius potentials and iterate the single-sphere compactification. Convolve approximate step-function distributions in successive Hubble scales to estimate the descendant-vacuum density near zero.

First approximate flux-lattice counts by continuous lengths or volumes in flux space, then examine integer quantization. Track the vacuum-dependent lower-dimensional Planck mass when converting Hubble distributions into distributions of Planck-normalized cosmological constants.
Numerically evolve coupled energy-density equations, ρ̇SM + 3H(ρSM + PSM) = −W and ρ̇DS + 3H(ρDS + PDS) = W, with expansion sourced by both sectors. Track neutrino energy separately after decoupling.

Compute collision energy transfer from SM pair annihilation, plasmon decay, Coulomb scattering, Compton conversion and mixed vector fusion. Production channels work with an initially empty sector; scattering becomes important during decoupling when MCPs remain abundant.

Feed calculated thermal histories into an adapted BBN reaction code. Both Neff and the baryon-to-photon ratio can evolve over roughly 100 keV–2 MeV, so a constant-Neff rescaling of standard BBN predictions is insufficient.

Functional RG using the Wetterich equation and background-field splitting. Background volume and curvature terms determine βΛ and βG; momentum-quadratic two-point terms on flat space determine anomalous dimensions.

Analytic expansion near the Gaussian fixed point is followed by nonlinear fixed-point searches. Coupled linear equations for anomalous dimensions are solved for RG improvement and compared with their leading one-loop terms.

The new technical calculations include graviton and matter anomalous dimensions, with the graviton two-point structure projected onto tensor K. Type-II regulators are compared with a type-Ia graviton regulator.

Construct non-primary scalar bilinears from Tρν, scalar operators and derivatives by iterative coefficient matching. At leading order in 1/N, the required three-point functions factorize into products of two-point functions.

Write tensor–scalar three-point functions as differential operators acting on scalar three-point functions. Smearing exposes unwanted nonanalyticity in the spacelike region 0 < χ < 1; appropriately chosen higher-dimension corrections cancel its expansion.

Use ADM Hamiltonian and momentum constraints with holographic gauge fixing. Eliminate nondynamical gravitational variables in principle, then use stress-tensor conservation and symplectic block inversion to establish the matter-sector brackets without computing the complete gravitational bracket algebra.

Solve coupled metric, gauge and scalar linear perturbations with harmonic time dependence and ingoing horizon conditions. Extract conductivity from boundary coefficients, fit its low-frequency Drude form and test intermediate scaling through 1+ω|σ|''/|σ|'.

Linearize around candidate IR geometries to identify relevant, marginal and irrelevant modes. Parameter counting assesses possible UV–IR domain walls, and the scalar IR exponent supplies the expected metallic resistivity exponent.

Use an anisotropic radial metric, A=a(r)dt and φ=e^(ikx1)ϕ(r). The equations reduce to four second-order ODEs and one first-order ODE. Numerically match regular horizon expansions to asymptotically AdS4 boundary data.

Reduce the gaugino and gravitino variations to first-order equations using a Kähler potential, holomorphic superpotential V, and spinor projections. The relevant gravitino eigenvalue is e^(K/2)V; its modulus defines the real superpotential.

For numerical sectors, initialize at A'(0)=0 with prescribed scalar values, obtain remaining initial data from BPS conditions, integrate second-order field equations, and then test the resulting solutions against the BPS equations. The authors use this method to pass through the square-root branches smoothly.

Promote the interaction strength to a spacetime-dependent spurion g(x), split it into region-supported g1 and g2, and use functional Bogoliubov causality. Represent the boundary unitary by the Magnus form ω = exp(iφ), with Hermitian φ, allowing noncommuting operators.

Derive functional evolution iδS = ∫[Hh + ωHω†]S δg[d⁴x], where Hh = i(δω/δg)ω†. The dressed H term retains the original causal restriction; the horizon term is unrestricted by it and contains history dependence.

Use real spinor bilinears and Fierz identities to decompose the geometry into three orthogonal vectors V+, V−, V3 and six-dimensional SU(3)-structure forms J, φ, ρ. Rewrite internal and external Killing-spinor equations as differential and algebraic constraints on these forms.

Project algebraic supersymmetry equations onto a Clifford-generated, generally redundant set of spinors. Analyze probe supersymmetry using the M2 κ-symmetry projector and commutators testing whether individual Majorana-Weyl components also satisfy the Killing-spinor equations. The authors report extensive symbolic tensor and gamma-matrix calculations.

Toric Mori cones, divisor intersections and mirror symmetry determine the polynomial prepotential. Picard–Fuchs equations and the mirror map determine instanton corrections and periods in an integral symplectic frame. Calculations use PALP, Sage and Instanton.

The numerical search first omits instantons, eliminates the dilaton using τ=(f·Π̄)/(h·Π̄), and converts the remaining F-term equations into polynomial systems solved with Paramotopy/Bertini homotopy continuation. Candidate roots are subsequently filtered by instanton sizes.

Tree–loop interference gives mass-dependent CP decay asymmetries. These are weighted by baryon-violating squark branching fractions and converted into an entropy-normalized yield using 3T/(4m). The numerical treatment includes a 28/79 sphaleron conversion factor above the stated thermal threshold.

The supersymmetric modulus minimum and its uplift-induced displacement determine FX. Modulus and anomaly contributions to gaugino masses and trilinears are combined to identify the physical CP phase; low-energy soft parameters also depend on renormalization-group evolution.
Kaluza–Klein tensor reduction, Mathematica/xTensor contractions, Hodge-star identities and Weyl rescaling extract Einstein and vector kinetic terms.
N=2 supersymmetry and scalar–vector Legendre duality determine corrected coordinates; matching circle-reduced four-dimensional supergravity implements the uplift.

Toric Chern-class intersection computations constrain a curve ansatz across bases. Tests cover simple non-Abelian groups of rank ≤10, two or three factors of total rank ≤7, and U(1)-restricted simple groups of rank ≤10; these fits are not proofs.

Bounded dimensionless variables give autonomous evolution equations. Fixed points and linearized eigenvalues characterize asymptotic behavior, supplemented by numerical integration for the quadratic AdS example.
DBI and Wess–Zumino actions determine the scalar and matter couplings; varying a classical particle action yields induced-metric geodesics and the matter stress tensor.

Holomorphy, asymptotic behavior and integral electromagnetic monodromies constrain the special coordinates. Seiberg–Witten curves provide A/B periods; discriminants locate branch-point collisions and Coulomb-branch singularities.

For massless hypermultiplets, construct Higgs branches by imposing three real moment-map conditions per gauge generator and quotienting by G. The alternative holomorphic construction imposes the complex moment map and quotients by the complexified group, with unstable orbits removed. The stated generic quaternionic dimension count is m−dim G for 4m initial real scalars.
The higher-dimensional BPS interpretation uses variable-tension strings: M=∫|λ|≥|∫λ|. Saturation requires constant phase of λ/ds along the string, providing a geometric BPS equation.

Expand the vacuum Maxwell equations and wave amplitudes around a metric background; use an eikonal plane wave exp(ikz−iωt), zeroth-order radiation gauge, and a transverse 2×2 determinant to obtain the leading dispersion relation.

Apply active rotations, cyclic spatial-index permutations and Lorentz covariance to convert conditions for one propagation direction into all-direction constitutive constraints; reconstruct metric, dilaton, axion and antisymmetric deformation variables.

Raychaudhuri evolution of outward future and past null congruences from a codimension-2 extremal surface is used to construct a nonexpanding null barrier, conditional on the paper's null curvature condition. Its printed sign requires review.

A continuous family of extrema crossing Σ would contain a first-contact surface tangent to it. Comparing extrinsic curvatures and contracting with the positive-definite induced metric of the spacelike probe gives KΣμν hμν ≥ 0, contradicting strictly negative curvature.

For totally geodesic barriers, the authors introduce a local separation function and use an elliptic equation, a positive Dirichlet Green function, and continuation to argue that tangential contact without crossing forces the extremal surface to lie on Σ.

Generate a random vector potential with Rayleigh-distributed amplitudes, uniform phases, and power proportional to k^-n; take its Fourier-space curl and transform to a Gaussian tangled magnetic field. Apply infrared/ultraviolet cutoffs and a radial density-dependent modulation.

Integrate conversion probabilities against the adopted CAB spectrum to obtain intrinsic annular luminosities in 0.2–0.4 keV; adjust M to normalize the total excess. Repeated Model 1 realizations varied by at most 9%, usually below 5%; comparisons include an assigned 10% simulation uncertainty.

The simulation uses a 2000^3 lattice with 0.5 kpc cells, approximately 1 Mpc^3. A three-state axion/photon system is propagated by local rotations and exact constant-cell evolution, recursively along 2000^2 sightlines at 14 energies from 25 eV to 2 keV.

Use closed-polygon worldsheet selection rules for three-, four- and five-point superpotential interactions. Build F-, D- and soft-term potentials, then integrate out heavy vector and saxion degrees of freedom using scale separation.

Reduce RR kinetic and D-brane Chern–Simons terms, rotate open/closed CP-odd scalars into eaten and orthogonal directions, and use chiral field redefinitions and anomalous fermion measures to express axion couplings.

Depletion is estimated through two-to-two scattering, with gravitational coupling and occupation-number combinatorics. During inflation, graviton–inflaton scattering has rate Γ_gφ = H α² N Nφ, enhanced relative to graviton–graviton scattering.

AdS applications use homogeneous constituent counting, mean-field criticality, and escape-energy estimates. Large-black-hole properties are inferred from blueshifting soft mass-sourced gravitons through scattering with harder AdS constituents.

The metric dictionary uses weak-field Einstein expansions and transition matrix elements between states of longitudinal gravitons. Single-graviton absorption/emission supplies the leading metric coupling; virtual exchange supplies the first nonlinear correction.

A genetic algorithm searches the six supersymmetry-breaking parameters, requiring positive potential and every modeled scalar mass eigenvalue positive. Five searches optimize the supersymmetry-breaking ratio or hierarchies between RR, NSNS and nonperturbative coefficients.

Homogeneity of the scalar manifold is used to represent solutions at S = T = U = i and x = 1, turning field equations into quadratic flux equations. Couplings are organized into six real supersymmetry-breaking parameters, D_IW = A_I + iB_I, and six complementary supersymmetry-preserving combinations.

Pure EFT fixes the expansion history and Ω, reconstructs c and Λ, and independently specifies perturbation-only coefficients. Mapping EFT solves a chosen model's background and reconstructs its EFT coefficients through matching.
For f(R), use Ω=f_R, c=0 and Λ=m₀²(f−Rf_R)/2. The designer method fixes w_DE(a), solves a second-order equation for f[R(a)], and labels the resulting family by its present boundary parameter B₀.

Restore time diffeomorphisms through τ→τ+π, expand the action to quadratic perturbative order, and evolve the resulting Einstein and scalar equations. Substitute metric equations into the π equation to demix degrees of freedom before evaluating stability.

Hirzebruch–Jung continued fractions identify a chain x₁…x_r with a cyclic quotient: p/q=x₁−1/(x₂−⋯), acting as (z₁,z₂)→(ωz₁,ω^qz₂), ω=exp(2πi/p). The appendix illustrates its resolution using toric data.

Use the imported non-Higgsable-cluster classification, blow up forbidden neighboring intersections, and enforce gluing across −1 curves until a consistent resolution is reached. An automated sweep through ten-curve candidates is extended using the forced −2 interior of longer chains.

Zariski decomposition of −K_B bounds vanishing orders. A negative-part coefficient α_i>5/6 forces f and g to vanish to orders at least 4 and 6 along that curve, excluding a nonsingular F-theory model even after further base blowups.

Uses the imported quarter-BPS massive-IIA ansatz in functions S and K, compares its uniform smearing with the seven-dimensional uplift, and constructs radial Laurent coefficients recursively. Compact solutions instead require torus Fourier modes.

Uses fake-superpotential first-order gradient flows for domain walls, distinguishing the true superpotential appearing in supersymmetry transformations from other functions generating second-order solutions. The linear BPS profiles h₁=2|h|z+ℓ₁² and h₂=2|m|z+ℓ₂² are credited to earlier work.

For nonzero neutrino mass, replaces anomalous currents by effective pseudoscalars, integrates the three-form equations with constants β₁ and β₂, and solves constant-field vacuum equations to estimate the residual QCD four-form.

Uses zero-momentum topological susceptibility to diagnose a massless three-form pole, then anomaly-induced current couplings and equations of motion to describe its removal. This is presented as an imported topological formulation of axion and massless-quark screening.

Dualises the scalar axion to a two-form B using an auxiliary one-form and a Bianchi-identity Lagrange multiplier. Diagonalisation of QCD/gravitational three-form mixing identifies massive and unscreened combinations.

Lattice dualizations use discrete Fourier transforms while retaining original variables and introducing gauge fields and Stueckelberg fields. This keeps global holonomies visible instead of solving flatness only locally.

Triangulated formulations use simplicial cochains, δ, cup products, and higher products ∪₁ and ∪₂. Their correction terms restore gauge invariance lost because the cochain cup product is not supercommutative.

Lagrange multipliers impose flatness or Bianchi identities; dualization produces equivalent BF, Higgs/Stueckelberg, and higher-form gauge descriptions. Global fields are described using patch data, Deligne–Beilinson cocycles, or differential characters rather than ordinary globally defined forms.

Expands the N=1 F-term potential in inverse volume, combining α′ corrections, small-cycle nonperturbative effects, string loops and large-cycle nonperturbative terms. Extended no-scale cancellation makes the loop potential subleading despite its larger correction to the Kähler potential.

Adopts an imported statistical treatment: a random axion mass matrix peaked at the predicted mass scale and Gaussian-distributed decay constants peaked near M_KK. This supplies the approximate collective quadratic inflationary dynamics rather than an explicit compactification-specific spectrum.
Uses homogeneity identities for the Kähler metric, diagonalises axion kinetic mixing and expands the cosine potential about its minima to obtain a nontrivial quadratic mass matrix.

Diagnoses perturbations through L²χ=(Uχ̇²−V(∂iχ)²−Wχ²)/2 and Uω²=Vp²+W. For nondegenerate multiple-field kinetic terms, positive-definite U and V are necessary to exclude high-momentum ghosts and gradient instabilities; low-momentum behavior requires separate analysis.

Uses integration by parts and antisymmetrized products of second derivatives to organize generalized Galileons and cancel higher derivatives in their equations. The review reports D+1 classes in D-dimensional Minkowski space, including K0(π,X); covariantizing higher classes is nontrivial.

The current is obtained from gauge-invariant point-split two-point functions and Pauli–Villars subtraction. The regulator mass is sent to infinity after momentum integration; a heavy-mass WKB expression supplies the subtraction. Mellin–Barnes representations and contour residues evaluate the Whittaker integral.
