The Hadamard obstruction is analyzed through geodesic Wilson-line two-point functions depending on the invariant separation Z. The charged wave equation becomes an ODE, whose Frobenius exponents are examined at coincidence and the antipodal point.

Exact flat-chart modes are Whittaker functions. Their asymptotic behavior selects positive-frequency in modes; for heavy particles, comparison with out modes yields Bogoliubov coefficients and the upward/downward particle distributions.

Use D-flatness and canonically normalised open/closed axion decay constants to identify the axionic combination eaten by an anomalous U(1). Compare geometric brane configurations with branes at singularities.
Relate visible/hidden modulus decay widths to reheating and ΔNeff, then combine the cosmological upper bound on ΔNeff with Fermi dwarf-galaxy annihilation bounds to restrict the (ΔNeff, mDM) plane.
Review superficial-degree-of-divergence counting using propagator momentum powers, vertex derivative orders and the loop–line–vertex topological identity.

Fourier-decompose tensor modes, reduce the fourth-order ODE to four first-order equations, and examine characteristic eigenvalues with a Cardano-based diagnostic. Mathematica integration supplies numerical illustrations and comparisons.

Expand the second variation of the gravitational action in Riemann normal coordinates around a point. The retained general-background equation is linear in curvature and lowest nontrivial order in the coordinate expansion.

Project generalised-metric variations onto physical degrees of freedom. Parameterise scalar variations by an exponential map, evaluate the constrained potential Hessian, and diagonalise its symmetric mass matrix.

Factor the generalised vielbein into external fields and an O(n,n) twist. For the relevant fibrations, construct twists by matrix exponentiation of commuting flux generators and explicitly construct density-preserving generalised Killing vectors.

Encode geometric and non-geometric fluxes in FABC=3Ω[ABC], using the C-bracket and generalised frame. For three internal dimensions, use the SO(3,3)/SL(4) representation and two symmetric matrices to solve the flux constraints.

Define restricted complex-structure moduli spaces preserving specified algebraic divisors and the type of the fixed Kähler form. Replace the scanning-flux lattice sum by integration, imposing F-term conditions through delta functions.

Use K3 Torelli theorems, period domains, lattice isometries and hyperbolic-plane embeddings to classify elliptic fibrations. Flux stabilization is interpreted through jumps of integral Hodge classes at Noether–Lefschetz loci.

The loop analysis eliminates interaction coordinates using conservation-law Jacobians and their inverses, then relates the endpoints through proper-time intervals. Covariance of both endpoint conditions and equations of motion supplies restrictions on admissible boundary terms.

Worldline actions use on-shell Lagrange multipliers and interaction boundary terms −ξ^μK_μ. Variation gives free propagation, vertex momentum conservation and endpoint conditions involving derivatives of K with respect to each particle momentum.

Explains the string consistency method of requiring quantum conformal-anomaly cancellation. The chapter reports that, at lowest perturbative order, this selects Maxwell, Einstein and Dirac field equations; it supplies no detailed anomaly calculation.

Uses an order-of-magnitude action estimate for a Hubble-sized patch: E is estimated from ρ(c/H)^3, the time scale is H^−1, and Einstein equations give ρ∼c²H²/G. Comparing the patch action with h diagnoses failure of the classical description; numerical factors are explicitly omitted.

Generalizes black-hole decay kinematics using charge and energy conservation. Mass-fraction weights give Z=Σσ_i z_i with Σσ_i<1; convex geometry of particle and antiparticle charge-to-mass vectors translates this into a discharge criterion.

Uses cutoff-sensitive scalar mass corrections δm²=Λ²(aq²+bλ)/(16π²), then compares the natural physical scalar mass with the WGC charge-to-mass requirement. The coefficients a,b encode ultraviolet sensitivity.

Reduce the symmetric supergravity ansatz to a one-dimensional system with six radial functions and two superpotential choices. Introduce conjugate ξ modes and use their first-order equations and infrared Taylor expansions to constrain regular solutions.

Apply the imported Polchinski-Strassler/M2 polarization method in an anti-M2-dominated region: expand in incoming self-dual flux MSD, solving flux ξ modes at first order and the warp ξ mode at second order.

Reduce the M5–M2 probe along an M2 world-volume direction to a D4 with anti-F1 charge. Use DBI plus Wess-Zumino terms and a Legendre transform at fixed charge n; reconstruct the localized KP potential using supersymmetric and traceless L=2 mass contributions.

A line-free multitemperature APEC continuum plus individual Gaussians models the 2–10 keV search band, followed by 3–6 keV fitting. Known-line energies may move by 5 eV and widths satisfy 0<ΔE/E<10⁻². Nearby K/Ar lines are bounded using reference S/Ca fluxes and AtomDB; Ar XVII DR initially receives 0.001–0.01 of the 3.12 keV triplet flux.

Bright Fe lines determine observation-specific X-ray redshifts, absorbing small gain offsets and optical/gas redshift differences. Event energies and response files are shifted to the source frame before stacking, aligning cluster lines while smearing detector-frame features and background residuals.

Continuum and thermal-line responses are X-ray-count weighted. For the decay interpretation, the new-line response is instead weighted by expected dark-matter flux, proportional to projected mass ×(1+z)×exposure/D_L². Count-weighted refits give similar detected fluxes.

Import form-field representations from decompositions of the adjoint of G+++ under GL(D,R) and the internal symmetry. The brane analysis first selects representations whose highest weights correspond to Kac–Moody roots of maximum positive squared length, then counts their real longest weights.

For orthogonal groups, apply light-cone rules: antisymmetric indices use distinct lightlike directions; the second column of a two-column mixed tensor must be parallel to indices in the first. Mixed hypersector potentials are obtained by imposing consistency of the truncated gauge algebra.

Use Tits–Satake diagrams with a maximally noncompact Cartan subalgebra to determine the Cartan involution on roots and weights. Project onto restricted roots and test whether a representation's highest weight is real before counting real longest weights.

Analyze asymptotic mode mixing with Bogoliubov coefficients, then solve the pulse mode equation numerically using fourth-order Runge–Kutta with 20,000 time points and initial time −T, T=100. Construct finite-window spectral functions from products of the resulting mode solutions.

Extract the out annihilation operator from the asymptotic field, express its number operator using equal-time derivatives of a two-point function, and rewrite this through Wigner-transformed commutator and anticommutator functions. An equivalent expression uses the Feynman-minus-retarded propagator.

Reduce observations with SAS 13.0.0, apply espfilt, and assess residual soft-proton contamination through an in-FoV/out-FoV count-rate diagnostic. Stack central and off-center M31 spectra separately and bin them at 60 eV.

Perform a joint M31-center/Perseus MOS fit with common rest-frame line energy and independent normalizations. Separately estimate a global false-detection probability from individual detections in three datasets, accounting for about 40 independent resolution elements across the fitting range.

Fit spectra over 2–8 keV. Instrumental backgrounds use an unfolded power law plus narrow Gaussian lines. M31 source emission uses a power law with added Ar/S complexes; Perseus uses vmekal with selected free elemental abundances plus a power law. Test an additional narrow line through improvement in χ².

Separate α into background, direct source, and smooth induced contributions: α=αbg+e4Abg−e4A+δbarα. Track volume scaling of deviations from the BPS bulk cancellation, rather than assigning the entire background flux energy to uplift.

Dimensionally reduce tree-level IIB supergravity and transform to four-dimensional Einstein frame. For self-dual F5, use the imported prescription of discarding its external part and doubling its internal part before reduction.

Use an imported on-shell relation between the cosmological constant and antibrane DBI/CS boundary terms, derived from classical supergravity scaling. Combine it with the volume equation of motion and the assumed potential scaling to determine the uplift coefficient.

Parametrize corrections by Tcorr^{MN}=Σi[Λ(t)]^(αi+1/3)C^{MN,i}, rather than specify their complete action. Split internal-base, torus and external Einstein equations into time-dependent and time-independent parts, then compare with the flux equations.

Trace the external Einstein equations and evaluate individual stress-energy contributions. For a direct product, positive external curvature requires (D−6)Tμ^μ>4Tm^m. In warped cases, integrate a warp-factor Laplacian over the internal manifold, retaining possible boundary contributions.

Equations of motion are rewritten in flat indices both directly and through generalized Ricci quantities. This exposes f and Q, which are connection-like quantities rather than tensors, and supplies an explicit flux formulation of the β equation.

A Spin(D,D) × R+ Dirac operator is represented on polyforms using wedge products and contractions. Squaring it supplies Bianchi identities; trace and dilaton contributions are needed beyond merely adding derivatives to the constant-flux operator.

Transverse smearing averages the nonconstant part of each warp factor. Green functions for Laplacians in successively lower dimensions organize the resulting Poisson equations, while Buscher transformations relate the smeared field configurations.

Stress-energy conservation gives (T^r_r)′ = −[(D−2)/r + f′/(2f)](T^r_r−T^t_t). An integrated form, with its constant fixed by finite horizon pressure, constrains the sign and evolution of radial pressure independently of the gravitational field equations.

The gravitational step combines the radial Lovelock equation, β1gf′/f − β2 = 8πG T^r_r, with the generalized Misner–Sharp mass. Its derivative M′ = −V_(D−2)r^(D−2)T^t_t supplies monotonicity; the horizon mass polynomial supplies a positivity obstruction.

The background-field path integral is expressed through determinants of graviton, ghost and regulator operators. The DTPN prescription assigns determinant weights through a special definition of integration over Pauli–Villars fields.

One-loop determinant expansions are reduced to momentum integrals using Feynman parameters and Lorentz-invariant polynomial decomposition. A cutoff expansion, also written through incomplete beta functions, identifies regulator-mass moments controlling divergent terms.

The flat-background quadratic action is inverted in harmonic gauge using spin projectors. UV propagator and vertex scaling, together with I = V + L−1, give bounds on the superficial degree of divergence.

Use polar matter variables and a generalized unitary gauge to remove vector–scalar derivative mixing. Then canonically normalize the surviving scalar and express gauge-invariant non-derivative interactions as a potential for that field.

Expand the gauge-invariant Lagrangian and derive Euler–Lagrange equations for Aμ, B and φ. The vector equation's divergence and the B equation yield two conserved currents; the latter is associated with constant B shifts.

Reports HAP computer-algebra calculations of restriction maps for the two nonabelian order-27 extensions and for H8 and Q8. These are author-reported computations, not calculations reproduced in this record.

Embeds finite extensions in connected groups such as U(3) or U(2), restricts Chern–Simons actions to the central subgroup, and uses Higgsing to construct discrete gauge theories. Successful connected-group gauging is sufficient; failure of one embedding is only heuristic evidence.
Uses group cohomology to classify central extensions by H²(BG,N), and tests whether a discrete gauge action extends by studying the restriction H³(BĜ,U(1)) → H³(BN,U(1)).

Solve V=0 and V′=0 for a Minkowski stationary point, then tune toward small positive energy. Compute the scalar and fermion spectrum with kinetic normalization and Goldstino elimination; the scalar mass is reported positive on the selected branch.

Construct chiral/tensor duality from a master action with an initially unconstrained real superfield. Eliminate either the chiral field or the real field, use modified linearity conditions, and extend the construction with chiral compensators and a supergravity chiral projection.

Computes slow-roll parameters, sets εend = 1, integrates the remaining e-folds, and evaluates scalar and tensor observables at horizon exit. Both small-γ expansions and formulas retaining full γ dependence within the large-field approximation are used.

Estimates a tree-level inflaton-scattering cutoff by expanding kinetic and potential terms around a homogeneous background, canonically normalizing fluctuations, and identifying suppression scales of higher-order operators.
Transforms Jordan-frame gravity to Einstein form and uses the large-field relation χ ≃ κMp ln(√ξφ/Mp), with κ = √(2/ξ + 6), to express the corrected potential and its derivatives.

Pair-difference mapmaking combines polynomial and scan-synchronous filtering with temperature-template deprojection. Planck 143 GHz temperature derivatives model beam leakage; differential gain and pointing are deprojected, while differential ellipticity is subtracted using measured coefficients.

Uses time-stream signal simulations, sign-flipped data noise pseudosimulations, noise debiasing, and simulated band-power windows. Tensor amplitudes use simulation-based direct likelihoods; the frequency-index analysis uses a joint Hamimeche–Lewis likelihood with band-power marginalization.

Matrix purification models filtering by m̃ = Rm, propagates E/B covariances as RCRᵀ, and selects large-eigenvalue solutions of a regularized generalized eigenproblem. The resulting projector removes E/B-ambiguous modes before spectrum estimation.

Introduce M{i,k} with entries x{i,k}(CijCkl+CilCkj)−Cjl and require positive semidefiniteness. Non-simplicial cones are treated through simplicial covers; appendices use integer curve enumeration, permutation reduction, and Lorentz congruence transformations.

Split D9 stacks by fiber flux into β- and γ-branes, then β-branes into special and mixed sign classes. Bound fiber flux first, auxiliary tadpole coefficients next, D5 wrapping numbers next, and γ-fluxes last.

Combine divisorwise tadpoles nI−TI=ΣαNαK(Fα,Fα,DI), ΣαNα=16, and stackwise central-charge conditions 3K(J,J,Fα)=K(Fα,Fα,Fα), K(J,J,J)>3K(J,Fα,Fα). Their different stackwise and divisorwise structures supply complementary inequalities.

Slow-roll scalar and tensor spectra are evaluated at horizon exit. Scalar-amplitude normalization approximately fixes Λ; model trajectories are compared in the (n_s,r) plane while varying f and the number of e-folds.

COSMOMC marginalizes over seven cosmological parameters with flat priors and Gelman–Rubin convergence assessment. Comparisons use Planck, WMAP polarization, ACT/SPT and BAO, with separate BICEP2 bands and a joint likelihood including lensing.

The appendix summarizes the gauge-invariant Mukhanov–Sasaki equation and its leading slow-roll Hankel-function solutions. Scalar and tensor spectra are obtained by multiplying their BD spectra by initial-state factors γ_S and γ_T.

The coefficients are parameterized as α=coshχ exp(iϕ), β=sinhχ exp(−iϕ), removing an irrelevant overall phase. A crude Gaussian momentum cutoff models excitation when physical momentum reaches the new-physics scale M.

Expand the electromagnetic vertex in Dirac-matrix covariants; impose Hermiticity and electromagnetic current conservation to obtain four Hermitian form-factor matrices: charge, magnetic dipole, electric dipole and anapole.

Construct coherent incoming mass-state amplitudes and sum probabilities over unobserved outgoing mass eigenstates. Matter evolution uses effective Hamiltonians; external-field spin evolution also uses a generalized Bargmann–Michel–Telegdi equation.

Expand K=−ln(T1+T̄1)−2ln(T2+T̄2), canonically normalize the bulk moduli, and rotate to volume and transverse mass eigenstates. Derivative axion couplings then determine the lightest modulus's axionic decay width.

Extract visible interactions from a matter metric scaling as V^(−2/3), including a Giudice–Masiero Higgs bilinear. Compare the explicit axionic width with an assumed parametric loop width, then translate the branching ratio into ΔNeff.

Use ADM scalar perturbations in flat gauge, decompose fields into adiabatic and entropy directions, and evolve their canonically normalized coupled modes. Numerical perturbations start well inside the sound horizon.

Use transfer functions for superhorizon conversion and imported in-in bispectrum formulas. Combine amplitude and equilateral non-Gaussianity requirements with compactification bounds to eliminate λ and obtain a necessary geometric inequality, assessed numerically and asymptotically.

Numerically integrate the coupled radial/angular background equations and Friedmann evolution using dimensionless parameters; vary deformation κ and angular strength C=c2κ⁻⁴ᐟ³, with additional checks varying the inflaton mass.

The authors extract modulus decay widths from the Kähler potential and gauge kinetic functions after canonical normalization and integrating out stabilized directions, then infer dark radiation from the ratio of hidden to visible partial widths.

Vanishing flux-induced FI terms gives linear constraints on two-cycle volumes. Under the specified intersection structure, D-term stabilization leaves a Swiss-cheese volume with two independent four-cycle volumes.

The authors dimensionally reduce DBI and Chern–Simons actions and use holomorphic-cycle geometry to express the brane energy as Γi = sqrt[(Re Zi)² + (Im Zi)²], separating induced-charge and D-term contributions before summing branes and images.

RR kinetic terms are reduced to canonically normalize a single axion in an isotropic-volume approximation. Standard quadratic-potential slow-roll expressions then supply the reported inflationary observables.

The review uses a Goldstone EFT, mode equations and canonical vacuum quantization to obtain primordial correlations. Einstein–Boltzmann transfer functions connect adiabatic primordial spectra to CMB angular spectra.

Wilsonian integration over heavy fields, perturbative matching and a local derivative/operator expansion organize ultraviolet effects. Bottom-up EFT instead includes all operators allowed by assumed ultraviolet symmetries.

Methods include a classical small-spacing expansion through cubic order, Gaussian continuum propagator integrals with a short-distance cutoff, and leading strong-coupling expansions using face-variable integration rules.

Abelian calculations use gauge fixing in two face planes, exact Bessel-function integrals in 3d, and heat-bath Monte Carlo. Random, trivial and mixed initial configurations are used to address equilibration and metastability.

Closed orientable Wilson surfaces are defined by contracting face indices along shared edges with prescribed orientations and adjoints. General nonabelian surfaces are not products of enclosed cubets; gluing can instead integrate over a shared face.
For nonperturbative transitions, use the imported thin-wall flat-space estimate P∼exp[−27π²σ⁴/(2ΔV³)]. Consider both flux-branch discharge and membrane-mediated changes of a modulus controlling μ.

Use single-field slow roll and N=∫V dφ/(mpl²∂φV). Expand to first nontrivial order in a subleading monomial, invert the field–N relation, and calculate scalar/tensor spectra, their ratio, and spectral indices.

Integrate out the four-form, including allowed higher powers of its field strength suppressed by Muv. Express the resulting potential corrections as powers of Vtree/Muv⁴ rather than unrestricted powers of the axion field.

D-brane DBI reduction determines field-dependent kinetic terms and potentials; canonical normalization changes their asymptotic powers. T-duality relates massive Wilson lines to brane positions in flux backgrounds.

Kaluza–Klein reduction on non-harmonic forms satisfying dηp=kωp+1 produces axion-dependent internal field strengths. Reduction of the dual potential exposes a massive three-form coupled to a two-form.

The F-term interpretation uses a three-form supermultiplet and a superspace coupling proportional to ∫d²θ ΦS. Domain-wall tensions and generalized calibrations provide a complementary superpotential description.

Explicit calculations use simplicial cochains, extension constraints δAa=c(A), integral lifts and Bocksteins, and higher cup products correcting cochain noncommutativity. Continuum topological actions are formulated using Deligne–Beilinson cocycles.
The Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence organizes successive obstructions in H^r(BG,H^(d+1−r)(BD,U(1))), r=2,…,d+1. Each preceding obstruction must vanish before the next is defined.

Reheating estimates use axion–gauge couplings on magnetized D7-branes, axion mixing, and the quoted dimension-five decay formula Γ=g²mθ³/(64πMpl²). D7- and D3-tadpole constraints determine the assumed available sectors.

Axion masses and mixing are estimated by diagonalizing the kinetic metric and potential Hessian through K⁻¹V, retaining leading volume dependence and small shift-breaking parameters rather than exact numerical coefficients.

Mirror symmetry relates the large-complex-structure Kähler potential to the axion-independent large-volume potential of the mirror fourfold. F-theory period expansions motivate polynomial brane dependence in the flux superpotential.

Small-α,β expansions determine the brane minimum and canonically normalized mass. Expanding in real and imaginary displacements, eliminating the imaginary displacement perturbatively, and retaining cubic/quartic terms estimates departures from quadratic inflation.

The N=1 F-term potential is analyzed using the block-diagonal Kähler metric and no-scale cancellation. The dominant brane term is e^K K^(c c̄)|DcW|², with leading stabilization imposed through DcW=0 before LVS stabilization and uplift.

A local fiber/base decomposition of the three-form motivates the strong-coupling enhancement. Stabilization is discussed using Wflux=∫Y4 Ω∧G4 and nonperturbative terms with theta-function prefactors on the axion torus.

The paper expands the M-theory three-form in harmonic (2,1)-forms, then uses an integral symplectic basis to express these forms through a symmetric holomorphic matrix hab(z). Their intersection integrals determine the axion metric.

IASD flux perturbations are treated around an ISD background using a Poisson equation and radial harmonic expansions. Anti-D3 uplift density is analyzed through an NS5 DBI-plus-Chern-Simons description.

Hodge decomposition and shifts of complex structure and effective three-form flux are used to identify the tensor structure of the nonperturbative AdS potential. The extension to D3 position moduli repeats this identification.

Dimensional reduction and repeated substitutions into the six-dimensional Einstein equation and stress tensor produce the proposed self-tuning constraint. Internal curvature terms are claimed to cancel without imposing quantum-corrected Ricci flatness.

The authors solve the system in Mathematica and C++, using adaptive Runge–Kutta–Fehlberg integration in C++. They report agreement between implementations and unchanged gauge-invariant R under different residual-gauge initial conditions.

Linear scalar perturbations are evolved in Fourier space with harmonic gauge constraints. The equations are organized as A(t)F′+B(t)F=0; regular coefficients and numerical nonvanishing of det A establish regular evolution for the studied trajectory.

The review organizes stabilization through N=1 supergravity F- and D-term potentials, combining flux superpotentials, nonperturbative W corrections and perturbative/nonperturbative K corrections in a large-volume expansion.

Local quivers encode gauge groups, bifundamental matter and anomaly cancellation. Global embeddings use toric Calabi-Yau classifications and impose local/global tadpoles, Freed-Witten anomaly cancellation and K-theory charge constraints.

Diagonalize the neutral Higgs mass matrix, match the low-energy quartic after removing the heavy Higgs, and use cited RGE running to distinguish a light eigenvalue at Mss from nonzero eigenvalues at the string/unification scale.

Expand the D7 DBI action in dilute fluxes, use the local relation B ≃ H3 Φ and Dirac flux quantization, and estimate the induced scalar mass through isotropic compactification scaling. The toy construction also includes Chern–Simons contributions.
The effective quartic uses two-loop renormalization-group evolution with boundary conditions at μ=m_t, together with anomalous-dimension and one-loop effective-potential contributions.

The stochastic calculation uses ∂_tP=∂_h[(V′/3H)P+(H³/8π²)∂_hP], numerical evolution, and a diffusion-dominated analytic approximation. In the single-transition regime, the imported Hawking–Moss exponent is B_HM=8π²ΔV/(3H⁴).

Use cofactors of the first N − 1 coefficient rows to construct the flat direction. Its primitive closed period is fixed by the gcd of the cofactors; restoring the final cosine determines the number of modulations through the full matrix determinant.

Rotate to heavy and light axion combinations and integrate out heavy modes. The N-axion extension uses a mass-determinant estimate for scale separation and random bounded-integer sampling to study alignment frequencies.

Compute canonical single-field slow-roll observables from potential derivatives. Appendix A discusses covariant target-space derivatives and trajectory proper distance to formulate slow roll and large excursions independently of field coordinates.

Construct invariant coset metrics and symmetry-breaking potentials using chiral-perturbation methods. Timelike, spacelike or null SO(2,1) order parameters provide different potential shapes in the noncompact example.

Dimensionally reduce the higher-dimensional Einstein action and transform to Einstein frame. The radius obeys ρ ∝ exp(λφ/Mp), with λ^2 = 2/[n(n + 2)]; inverse-radius curvature expansions consequently become exponential potentials for the canonical scalar.

Numerical eigenvalue distributions exclude det A = 0. With eigenvalues ai² ordered increasingly, the estimated enhancement is feff/f ≃ ⟨a⟩/a1, where ⟨a⟩ is the square root of the mean eigenvalue. One reported ensemble contains 10^5 matrices with Naxion = 10 and n = 2.

The statistical calculation sets Λi = Λ, fi = f, and phases to zero, samples integer anomaly matrices with −n ≤ aij ≤ n, and uses a quadratic cosine expansion. The reported mass proxy is the Gram matrix Aij = Σk aki akj.

The authors report numerical evolution with canonical kinetic terms and evaluate ns = 1 − 6ε + 2η and r = 16ε along the inflationary direction. They also eliminate the field in favor of r and a deviation parameter to organize slow-roll spectral observables.

An orthogonal normalized rotation defines a trough coordinate X and transverse coordinate Y. For sufficiently heavy Y, the authors integrate it out near Y = 0 and evaluate the remaining cosine along X.

They expand the field transformation and light-direction potential in the alignment parameter, then expand the slow-roll expressions near ξ = 0. The reported observables use ε = (MPl²/2)(V′/V)², η = MPl²V″/V, ns = 1 − 6ε + 2η, and r = 16ε.

The authors diagonalize the potential Hessian at θ = ρ = 0 and construct a normalized transformation from its eigenvectors. ξ corresponds to the smaller eigenvalue and ψ to the orthogonal direction; the transformed kinetic terms are described as canonical.

The topological anomaly models are specified by spectrum maps: the even-oriented model uses w₂(X) and a mod-2 Thom map; the general-target model uses spin bordism, [TX] in ko-theory, the spin Thom isomorphism, and the maps θ and γ.

Picard groupoids of superlines and Picard 2-groupoids of central simple superalgebras model truncated ko-modules. Clifford algebras, complexification, and Morita equivalences provide geometric realizations of the spectrum maps used in the anomaly construction.

The exposition uses the Atiyah–Singer families index theorem and KO/ko pushforwards to identify Pfaffian-line classes. Under the even-oriented hypothesis, the calculation reduces to mod-2 transgression of a Stiefel–Whitney class.

Imported analytic spectrum formulae use ranks of GGSO-dependent binary matrices. The imported top-Yukawa criterion is ℓ_2 through ℓ_7 = 0, ℓ_10 = ℓ_11 = ℓ_47 = 0, ℓ_48 = 1, ℓ_8 = ℓ_12 and ℓ_9 = ℓ_13. These conditions are implemented directly rather than calculating general low-energy couplings.

The search uses selection, crossover and mutation on 51-bit genotypes. The empirical population optimum was 50. Roulette-wheel selection uses quadratic criterion scores of the displayed form f = 10 − γ_i(μ_i − ν_i)^2, with γ_i chosen to balance criteria; moderate changes of these weights reportedly have little effect.

If maximum fitness remains unchanged for more than eight generations, the mutation rate is temporarily raised to 25 times its background value across the population. Baseline repeated searches scramble the entire population after each solution; a separate experiment instead mutates the successful population.

The authors analyze the metric geometry of the periodic domain, using eigenvalues and eigenvectors of K to convert dimensionless lattice displacements into physical lengths. Random-matrix eigenvector delocalization supplies the proposed statistical mechanism for approximate alignment.

Potential compatibility is studied by expanding around a minimum, rotating and rescaling to canonical fields, and diagonalizing the resulting mass matrix. An explicit two-field example and reported numerical tests with Wishart kinetic matrices examine mass-induced misalignment.

For possible string realizations, the authors specify toy Kähler and superpotentials, estimate stabilized moduli and nonperturbative amplitudes, and discuss the canonical normalization needed to translate microscopic choices into an effective field range.

The local mass hierarchy is diagnosed at the origin through the mass matrix and its trace-to-determinant relation. A field-space rotation identifies approximately light and heavy directions, followed by an expansion in small f_r2 and integration of the heavy field.
The anomalous dimension is extracted from logarithmic divergences of the scalar two-point function. Integrals use Feynman parameters and a hard momentum cutoff Λ in the Euclidean 1–2 plane.

An infinite chain of gauge-field self-energy insertions is resummed as G = (1 − DΣ)^−1D. The scalar two-point calculation includes fermion self-energy, vertex and additional two-point diagrams built with the corrected gauge propagator.

The M/N expansion retains genus-zero Feynman diagrams. Small α selects a summable vector-model-like subset; increasing α order enlarges that subset. This differs from a full 1/N expansion because nonplanar diagrams remain excluded.

Gaugino condensation produces W_np=A exp(−2πf_D7/N). Magnetization changes the holomorphic gauge kinetic function through odd moduli and fluxes; multiple wrapping changes its coefficients of Kähler moduli. These ingredients are inserted into the N=1 F-term potential.

The authors use canonical normalization and Hessian determinants to diagnose alignment, employ the no-scale identity and a leading expansion with W_0 large relative to W_np, and tune an uplift contribution to obtain cosine potentials. Numerical toy potentials are evaluated at selected moduli values.

They apply imported two-field slow-roll expressions for scalar and tensor spectra, including dependence on the end-of-inflation hypersurface through R, ū, and v̄, and estimate durations using slow-roll field integrals.

The authors expand the supergravity F-term potential using the inflationary superpotential and minimal Kähler potential, neglect suppressed terms, stabilize the real component of T, and integrate out heavy waterfall fields.

Explicit K3×K3 examples use period vectors, intersection forms, and flux maps between two-form spaces. Positive-norm eigenspaces of GᵃG determine stabilized complex structures, subject to the stated tadpole condition tr(GᵃG)=48.

A Neumann-series expansion of the inverse Kähler metric tests first-order loop cancellations. Parametric LVS estimates, toroidal KK/winding corrections, and slow-roll relations then map phenomenological requirements onto string parameters.

The weak-coupling limit of F-theory periods and the GVW flux superpotential is used to separate Type IIB bulk and brane contributions. Five-chain integrals and partial integration track B2 dependence and logarithmic monodromies.

Compares geometric curvature inequalities, physical stress-energy inequalities, and effective density–pressure inequalities. Geometric and physical formulations are equivalent assuming the Einstein equation; effective formulations additionally depend on stress-energy type.

Uses geodesic deviation to interpret average radial acceleration, stated as A_r=−R_ab ξ^a ξ^b/k, with k=3 for unit timelike geodesics and k=2 for null geodesics. Raychaudhuri’s equation and Frobenius’s theorem are used to examine proposed convergence-based motivations.

The reviewed large-N argument combines color counting at fixed ’t Hooft coupling with the Euclidean vacuum-energy generating functional, giving V(θ)=N²h(θ/N)+… and a fixed-angle expansion around θ/N=0.

The finite-N treatment evaluates the soft mass perturbation in the gaugino-condensate vacua. Metastable decay is estimated through an O(4)-symmetric Euclidean bubble in the thin-wall approximation, using a proposed BPS domain-wall tension.

Determines weak freeze-out from Γ(p→n)=H and subsequently evolves neutron survival by beta decay: X_n=exp[−(t_BBN−t_dec)/τ_n]/[1+exp(Q/T_dec)], with Q=m_n−m_p. The adopted weak conversion rate and inverse neutron lifetime scale as v_h⁻⁴ when the mass-dependent prefactors are fixed.

Uses thermal population integrals and chemical-potential equilibrium to calculate sphaleron conversion of B−L into baryon number. The approximation retains top-quark and W-boson mass effects while neglecting other particle masses; the adopted decoupling temperature is approximately 140 GeV×v_h/(246 GeV).

Numerically integrates coupled proton, helium, scale-factor and radiation equations, including helium decay feeding three residual nucleons into the proton population. Evaluates late radiation at t=20τ_p and fits its dependence on the initial neutron fraction as approximately linear.

For many fields, sums are replaced by distribution moments. Truncated peaked distributions on [0,1], interpolating between delta functions and uniform distributions, are used to explore peak widths, displaced peaks and two-peak examples.

Slow-roll evolution and derivatives of the e-fold number give the curvature spectrum and tilt. Neglecting final field values yields Σ_i φ_i²≈2pN_e; scalar normalization supplies Σ_i μ_iφ_i^p=6π²p P_R/N_e. These two constraints leave other field configurations undetermined.

The tilt maximum is obtained by Lagrange multipliers under the two normalization constraints, then established by expressing departures from the extremum as a non-positive weighted sum of squares. A footnote also gives a Cauchy–Schwarz argument.

Scalar and gauge fluctuations are expanded to quadratic order around the SU(2) trajectory and diagonalized into α_j, β_j and vector towers. Numerical calculations estimate the lightest spectator-mode power spectra.

Slow-roll integration determines N_e, inflation ends at ε=1, and n_s−1=−6ε+2η is used to eliminate the initial field value. Numerical solutions determine μ for a chosen n_s and N_e; scalar-amplitude normalization then determines λ_eff.

Use the supergravity F-term potential eᴷ(Kⁱʲ̄DiW Dʲ̄W̄−3|W|²), minimize the dominant matter-sector terms, and estimate VEV shifts caused by the overall eᴷ factor and the small nonperturbative coupling.

Compute the D term from the gauged Kähler isometry, simplify it using gauge invariance of W, and solve D=0 for Re T. Canonically rescale Im T after stabilization; analyze Abelian anomalies using charge traces and a Green–Schwarz variation of the gauge kinetic term.

Minimize modulus potentials along the axion trajectory, compare kinetic terms with potential forces in slow roll, and canonically normalize after accounting for volume dependence. Different flux orientations and dominant balances produce different final exponents.

Dimensional reduction of generalized gauge-invariant field strengths, supplemented by explicit flux backgrounds and T-duality, generates polynomial axion dependence. Flux quantization organizes the branch structure; mirror symmetry motivates complex-structure analogues.

Finite-angular-potential bounds are improved by iterating between canonical and spectral constraints, including numerical minimization of a quartic problem. Symmetric-product spectra are studied through generating functions, Hecke transforms and a long-string sector that saturates an entropy bound.

Modular invariance and positivity bound heavy-state contributions using the light-state partition sum. For β>2π, the central bound is log Z[L]≤log Z≤log Z[L]−log(1−exp[(β′−β)ε]), with β′=4π²/β; modular transformation gives the high-temperature counterpart.

Legendre transformation relates canonical thermodynamics to entropy, with a separate microscopic counting argument. Appendix A averages states over windows E±δ, where δ scales as c^α with 1/2<α<1 and E/c is fixed; exact level degeneracies are not the object controlled.

Use the scalar energy density, pressure and equation of motion; impose slow roll to obtain background solutions and potential slow-roll parameters. Integrate N=∫H dφ/φ̇ and estimate the endpoint using εV=1.

Use gauge-invariant curvature perturbations and scalar-amplitude normalization from COBE and Planck-2013; a tensor-to-scalar ratio supplies a second parameter constraint. Integrate the scalar trajectory to estimate elapsed inflationary time.

Apply exact Brown–Henneaux-type solution-generating diffeomorphisms, parameterized by G± on the right and H± on the left, in four Eddington–Finkelstein charts. Leave a fifth Kruskal chart unchanged and identify overlapping descriptions through trivial diffeomorphisms.

Compute the holographic stress tensor from extrinsic curvature and compare with the Schwarzian transformation law. Compute same-boundary and opposite-boundary scalar two-point functions using regulated geodesic lengths and conformally transformed CFT operators.

Obtain two-sided half-line entanglement entropy from bulk extremal geodesics and CFT replica twist fields. Separately pull the horizon area one-form to the boundary to define a local entropy current and compare with Cardy counting.

Use the bulk-matter Coleman–Weinberg potential, whose harmonic weights scale as n^−5, and define the decay-constant matrix as (2πR)^−1 times the inverse charge–coupling matrix. The first harmonic dominates the potential; the numerical inflation potential retains the harmonic sum.

Estimate hierarchical charge-matrix eigenvalues, calculate single-field slow-roll observables, fix the initial field through the e-fold integral, and estimate perturbative reheating from the inflaton decay width using H≈Γ.
Track Seiberg-duality sequences to describe both radial RG evolution and axion motion. Estimate branch transitions with a Euclidean thin-wall bubble calculation.

Use toric geometry, (p,q) webs and dimer diagrams to encode complex deformations and quivers. Analyze confinement and meson-induced Higgsing; in dP3, equal strong scales and mesonic constraints det M=det N=Λ^(4M) recover a residual conifold theory.

Reduce ten-dimensional Chern–Simons couplings to MφF4 in four dimensions. The physical RR field strength includes Fp∧B2, producing a lowest-order quadratic axion potential and branches connected by wrapped-brane domain walls.
With an external field, duality instead relates M_d,n to M_d,d−n+1, with tanh(β)=exp(−2h*) and tanh(h)=exp(−2β*). Partition-function normalization factors are again omitted.

The phase argument uses low- and high-temperature expansions imported from Wegner. The special three-dimensional calculation evaluates the dual model at infinite coupling, where only its two aligned ground-state configurations contribute.

Imported zero-field duality relates M_d,n to M_d,d−n on the dual hypercubic lattice, with tanh(β)=exp(−2β*). The stated partition-function relation assumes periodic boundary conditions and suppresses symmetrizing factors.

Analyze radial rescalings ρ=r² and R=r⁴, separate terms interpreted as lower-brane corrections, and apply Weyl scalings λ=r² or λ=1/r². Causal patches are rearranged through 2×2 matrix projections, inverse projections and analytic continuation.

Choose Btφ=−P cosθ and a radial trigonometric electric-potential ansatz with charges Q1,Q2, then specialize to Q1=Q2. Insert the resulting torsion and geometric field strength into a prescribed effective metric to obtain four sign-dependent patches.

Iteratively couple the background NS two-form to a torsion-modified derivative, construct a generalized curvature tensor and a scalar quadratic in geometric torsion, and introduce a symmetric metric fluctuation quadratic in torsion. This formalism is drawn from the authors' earlier work.

The authors calculate the N=1 F-term potential from K and W and organize it as VLVS+Vrest. VLVS begins at order V^−3; stepwise stabilization first sets ρs=b1=0 and solves for the volume and small-cycle modulus.

After freezing the heavier sector and assuming an uplift, they canonically normalize the two RR axions and rotate to ψ1,ψ2. Near alignment and an amplitude hierarchy are used to integrate out ψ1 and obtain a single cosine potential.

Numerical tests solve the two-axion Einstein–Friedmann equations using dN=Hdt. Inflationary comparisons use potential slow-roll parameters and their expressions for the scalar spectrum, spectral index, running and tensor-to-scalar ratio.

Apply background-field splitting, a background-covariant gauge fixing and ghost expansion. Decompose tangent-space gauge components into physical and Nambu–Goldstone scalar modes, and use harmonic orthogonality to show that the Abelian monopole's linear fluctuation term vanishes.

Match the higher-dimensional Higgs potential to its KK-reduced four-dimensional zero-mode potential, track volume and cutoff powers, and use four-dimensional renormalization-group running of the quartic coupling to explain the stability cutoff criterion.

Newman–Penrose eth and eth-bar operators raise and lower spin weight. Complete orthonormal spin-weighted spherical harmonics diagonalize the angular K operator with eigenvalue j(j+1); integrated products expressed through Wigner 3j symbols organize cubic and quartic KK interactions.

The corrected polarization equation is contracted with the polarization tensor to obtain a characteristic equation. The paper then represents its asserted homogeneous momentum dependence by an effective metric and substitutes FLRW matter variables to obtain a speed formula.

Weak-field metric expansion and harmonic coordinate condition establish the uncorrected null propagation baseline. Leading geometric optics separates a slowly varying polarization amplitude from a rapidly varying phase, with derivatives acting on the phase.

Conformal maps to a sphere with holes, the state–operator correspondence, and CFT correlation-function factorization relate wavefunctions and reduced density matrices to puncture and degeneration limits.
Fuchsian quotients of hyperbolic space construct time-symmetric slices; Fenchel–Nielsen length and twist parameters describe sewing pairs of pants into multiboundary geometries.

HRT entropies are calculated from homologous closed geodesics. Imported hashing bounds constrain LOCC distillation; a new entropy-deficit bound tests k-producibility allowing local Hilbert-space isometries.

Analyze the holomorphic–antiholomorphic Hessian block Vab̄ at an extremum, then tune third derivatives of W to make the holomorphic block Vab vanish or sufficiently small. Positive Vab̄ then gives full local stability only under the latter condition.

Expand W locally through third order and solve V = Λ, prescribed F terms, stationarity, and selected Vab conditions. For superpotentials linear in adjustable coefficients, these local derivative conditions can determine explicit global coefficient families.

Reduce positivity of Vab̄ to positivity of a two-dimensional quadratic form for every unit direction L orthogonal to supersymmetry breaking. The no-go argument instead uses the stationarity eigenvalue equation and invertibility of the undeformed superpotential Hessian.

Transform the resulting null-contracted string-frame curvature equation to Einstein frame. For reduction, calculate higher- and lower-dimensional Ricci tensors and compare their contractions with the lifted null vectors.

Use a background-field expansion X = X0 + Y and Riemann normal coordinates around X0. Integrating out Y at one worldsheet loop introduces a divergent counterterm proportional to the spacetime Ricci tensor, together with the dilaton contribution to the constraints.

Vary the worldsheet metric to obtain the Virasoro constraints T++ = T−− = 0. At zeroth order these identify ∂±Xμ as spacetime null vectors, supplying the null contractions needed for the geometric condition.

Estimate conversion semi-analytically by integrating the homogeneous-domain conversion probability per unit length over energy, emitting volume, and a coherence-length distribution inferred from the magnetic spectrum. The domain-length interval is Λmin/2 to Λmax/2.

Use the 4°–6° annulus for contemporaneous RASS background subtraction, normalize the thermal component with R7 counts, and extract an R2 excess using alternative CAB, warm-plasma, or power-law spectra. Xspec/APEC includes plasma emission lines.

Represent the electron density by Coma plus NGC4839 β-models. The Coma parameters are β=0.75, rc=291 kpc, n0=3.44×10⁻³ cm⁻³; the group uses the same central density and β with rc=134 kpc. Thermal-emission normalization supplies a density consistency check.

Rotate the magnetic field to place birefringence at twice the magnet rotation frequency. A photoelastic modulator adds a known ellipticity; demodulation at its fundamental and second harmonic linearizes and normalizes the small ellipticity signal. Cavity enhancement is N=2F/π.

Analyze 210 hours with magnet frequencies 2.4–3 Hz, including 40 hours at unequal frequencies to check individual-magnet artifacts. Divide runs into 8192-point blocks, estimate local Fourier noise using a Rayleigh amplitude distribution, and form weighted vector averages before conversion to unit-field birefringence.

Calibrate using low-pressure oxygen and helium Cotton–Mouton birefringence. Calibration determines the physical signal phase modulo 180°; vacuum Fourier amplitudes are projected onto that axis and its orthogonal diagnostic axis.

Obtain stationary, spherical solitons by reducing Schrödinger–Poisson equations to coupled second-order ordinary differential equations and solving numerically. Compare simulated central profiles with those solutions and provide an approximate analytical density fit.

Use GPU-accelerated octree adaptive mesh refinement in GAMER. Wave evolution uses split kinetic and potential operators, a modified fifth-order kinetic expansion, periodic FFT gravity on the root grid, and SOR or multigrid Poisson solvers on refined levels.

Apply spherical Jeans modeling to Fornax's dominant intermediate-metallicity stellar population, fitting its radial distribution and nearly constant velocity dispersion. Other stellar populations provide enclosed-mass consistency checks at different radii.

Construct the flux-induced N=1 superpotential and map its couplings to electric and magnetic embedding-tensor components. Compare the resulting N=4 and N=8 quadratic constraints with metric-flux Jacobi identities and the G(4) Bianchi identity.

Determine preserved supersymmetry from the gravitino mass matrix, compute scalar/vector spectra, and characterize internal geometry through G2 torsion classes. The paper also reports agreement with an embedding-tensor construction of the N=4 potential.

Move critical points to S=T=U=i using real shifts and rescalings, transforming fluxes simultaneously. Solve stationarity and quadratic consistency equations with Singular's GTZ primary decomposition; the authors interpret prime factors through their source content.

Fully extended invertible theories factor through invertible higher groupoids. Their symmetric monoidal structure gives maps of spectra; homotopy classes of these maps describe deformation classes of effective theories.

Computations use Madsen–Tillmann spectra, twisted Thom isomorphisms, Anderson and Brown–Comenetz duality, and Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequences. Background symmetry bundles enter through a smash factor BG_+.

The Smith isomorphism relates reduced Spin bordism of BZ₂ to Pin⁻ bordism one dimension lower. Domain-wall restriction gives a spin structure on TY⊕A*(ξ⊕σ), yielding bordism maps and a decorated-wall interpretation.

Effective topological actions are treated as U(1)-valued characters of bordism groups. Continuous parameters dual to free bordism summands are discarded for deformation classification, leaving the Pontryagin dual of torsion. The paper uses previously computed Spin and Pin bordism groups.

Construct Kähler-adapted vertex operators by varying the worldsheet action with respect to spacetime moduli, then extract the order-p² term of their two-point function. Supersymmetry removes the purely bosonic contraction; four- and eight-fermion pieces remain, evaluated using theta-function spin-structure identities.

Use the method of images to construct propagators on annulus, Möbius strip and Klein bottle, then lift position integrals to covering tori. Chan–Paton states must already be traced over. Twisted Klein-bottle propagators require additional involution phases.

Express twisted Green functions through Eisenstein–Kronecker functions and analytically continue an auxiliary parameter to evaluate position integrals. Generalized Mellin transforms subtract endpoint power-law tails and identify finite modulus-integral parts; results are expressed through trigamma functions and the second Clausen function.

Compute Kähler derivatives through the chain rule using A=∂t/∂τ, obtained by numerically inverting A^{-1}=κt. Algebraic differentiation of the inverse avoids numerical differentiation. Sample positive cone-generator coefficients uniformly, and logarithmically for part of the dataset, with a finite cutoff.

Assess spectral tails using kurtosis, quantile comparisons, and the paper's function h(x)=-log S(x). Parametric concavity fits and an imported nonparametric concavity test support heavy-tail interpretations; for Y25 the latter gives mean concavity -0.62±0.06.

Extract intersection numbers and ambient Mori-cone data from reflexive polytopes. The triangulation algorithm combines compatible regular facet triangulations into star triangulations; retaining only subsets of intermediate combinations reaches larger h^{1,1}, but may fail to find a completion.

Compare proper times of a central observer and a stationary observer at R>2m, synchronized in the common early and late Minkowski regions. Schwarzschild/Kruskal coordinate transformations give an asymptotic duration difference τ=-8m log v0.

Use a reflecting 'crystal ball' of radius a>2m as an entirely classical diagnostic. Compute the shell's return time, then introduce the dimensional accumulation parameter q=l_P^{2-b}ℛτ^b, with b in [1/2,2], and maximize it over observer radius near a=2m.

Construct the classical patches using spherical symmetry and Birkhoff's theorem. Match their areal radii along the null shell, deriving a junction map between Minkowski and Kruskal null coordinates, then glue to a time-reflected future.

Use the Mukhanov–Sasaki variable u=zR, z=a√(2ε), and rewrite its equation in e-folding time for aH proportional to exp(ξN_e). Solve constant-ξ stages with Hankel functions for ξ≠0 and exponential solutions for ξ=0.

Use small-argument mode asymptotics and Bogoliubov-coefficient combinations to distinguish frozen, decaying, and growing contributions and compare infrared with ultraviolet power. Illustrative angular spectra are compared with Planck 2013 data.

Require continuity of H, u, and its first derivative across instantaneous transitions. Recursive two-component transfer matrices propagate the mode coefficients through multiple stages; the appendix's displayed Hankel matrices apply only when ξ≠0 throughout.

First minimize the dominant matter F terms, then impose both D-flatness conditions to determine real-modulus VEVs. Subsequently retain the nonperturbative axion potential, canonically normalize its kinetic terms and rotate to heavy/light axion combinations.

Determine modulus shifts from gauge invariance of the two condensate terms. Evaluate charge traces and use Green–Schwarz variations of linear gauge kinetic functions to cancel cubic Abelian anomalies; gravitational and mixed cancellations are discussed more briefly.

Use the standard supergravity F-term potential and Killing-vector D terms. Gauge invariance of W reduces Da to iKiXai; moduli-dependent FI contributions then depend on real moduli while charged matter contributes through its squared amplitudes.

Reduce five-dimensional Chern–Simons terms to axionic gauge couplings and estimate ξi=αiσ̇i/(2fiH), the parameter controlling gauge-production effects. Naturalness is assessed qualitatively using expected parameter ranges rather than a Bayesian comparison.
Compactify the gauge theory, sum the charged-matter Kaluza–Klein contribution using ζ-function regularization, and approximate the resulting one-loop Fourier series by its leading harmonic.

Rotate the two axions to heavy/light combinations and integrate out the heavy direction when its curvature exceeds H². Translate slow-roll normalization and the assumed tensor ratio into gauge-coupling, compactification and charge constraints.

Fixes cloud energy using the proposed bosenova saturation amplitude, inserts it into the approximate GW amplitude, and compares with an observational upper limit hUL. A conservative cloud-energy criterion is imposed before interpreting parameter boundaries.

Uses the small-Mµ hydrogenic quasibound-state approximation and an imported perturbative calculation of two-axion-annihilation GWs. The flat-background amplitude's functional form is supplemented by Kerr numerical results giving Cnℓ≈10^−2.

Numerically integrates the visibility-weighted source µ=1.4∫dt J(t)[Q/ργ−(4/3)ṅγ/nγ]. Includes energy exchange in both directions, photon-number changes, and the low-frequency thermalization cutoff; focuses on µ-type distortions.

Computes tree-level pair production φ+γ→f+f̄ and Compton/inverse-Primakoff conversion φ+f↔γ+f. Thermal photons are Planck distributed and plasma fermions approximately stationary. Primakoff collinear divergences are regulated by Debye–Hückel screening rather than the photon plasma mass.

Constructs leading low-energy photon and mass-weighted fermion couplings for ALPs, and dilaton-like photon plus Yukawa couplings for unprotected scalars. Scattering is calculated in flat Minkowski space with plasma effects included where relevant.
Hessian determinants and leading mass eigenvalues identify the flat limit and the light/heavy axion hierarchy. Integrating out the heavy mode produces the effective enhanced decay constant.

Decompose the F-term potential into stabilization and axion-dependent contributions, then minimize using hierarchical and large-volume expansions. KKLT saxion minima away from the tachyonic origin require numerical minimization; LVS admits an analytic b_i=0 stabilization analysis.

Apply Lie derivatives and Noether variation of the effective Lagrangian, together with perturbation Euler–Lagrange equations, to obtain matter equations of motion and an integrability condition for the gravitational equations.

Use metric-density and matter perturbations as independent dynamic variables. Matter Lagrangians can depend implicitly on the metric through thermodynamic quantities, which must be included in metric variations.

Taylor-expand the Lagrangian under the action integral. Mixed variational derivatives are reordered modulo total divergences, producing a recursive expansion; boundary contributions are discarded under the stated variational boundary conditions.

Fourier transform the tree amplitude into impact-parameter space and extract t-channel pole residues as products of on-shell three-point amplitudes. Under locality assumptions, contact interactions and s-channel exchanges do not contribute at nonzero impact parameter.

Recast propagation as signal transmission: causality and non-increasing signal norm require analyticity and |Sgg(ω)|≤1 in the upper half-plane. Apply this constraint to negative delays and finite higher-spin exchanges, including possible inelastic final states.

Use polarization-dependent phase shifts, coherent source states that suppress unwanted spin transitions, and many successive weak scattering events to make an accumulated advance exceed wave-packet uncertainty. Shock waves provide an illustrative realization rather than the sole basis of the argument.
For practical on-shell calculations, import the prescription of treating S as an ordinary chiral multiplet and replacing W by W+if₀S, without explicit three-form boundary terms.

Use superspace F-density/D-density identities and chiral projection. In the Starobinsky duality, the relation R=μS₀S connects the chiral multiplet to higher-derivative supergravity; the added flux term becomes a total derivative in that formulation.

Integrate out the nondynamical four-form while retaining its integration constant and required boundary action. Master actions give scalar/three-form and chiral/massive-three-form dualities by eliminating alternative fields.

Argue for five-dimensional dualities by viewing circle-reduced M5-branes as D4-branes probing ADE singularities. Compare Coulomb-branch dimensions: every six-dimensional tensor gives a five-dimensional vector, so the count is total gauge rank plus tensor number.

Use Weierstrass form y²=x³+fx+g, with f and g sections of O(−4KB) and O(−6KB), and discriminant 4f³+27g². Apply an explicitly imported algorithm of successive base blowups until fibers admit Kodaira–Tate descriptions, then read tensor-branch gauge algebras and matter.

Describe flavor-brane boundary data using the Hitchin system with defects, simple-pole residues and conjugacy classes of flat complexified holonomy. In the M-theory/IIA description, the corresponding data appear as su(2) Nahm poles.

Impose the vanishing FI/D-term condition, eliminate the associated heavy modulus and gauge multiplet, and expand the remaining F-term potential at leading LVS order V^(−3). Vary the second nonperturbative prefactor to follow the vacuum through Minkowski into positive energy.

Analyze Freed-Witten flux quantization, choose a B-field cancelling one stack’s gauge-invariant flux, and derive sufficient intersection/flux conditions for effective triviality of the other. This appendix calculation assumes a restricted intersection pattern rather than a general compactification.

Locate numerical extrema and inspect Hessians, including the remaining small-cycle axion. Compare the truncated uplift potential with one retaining c3² and c2c3 terms. Analytical estimates use a further modulus limit, linearized uplift, and Sylvester’s criterion at Minkowski.

Combine the empirical core–specific-energy relation with the spherical-collapse virial estimate |Eh′|≈3Mh′²/(10xvir′), then use the halo virial-mass definition to obtain the redshift-dependent core–halo scaling.

Conduct 29 controlled merger runs with randomly placed, initially stationary solitons. Repeat fixed total mass and energy using different positions, sizes and initial soliton counts from 4 to 128. Each soliton has at least about 10⁴ cells; reported mass and energy conservation errors are at most a few percent.

Run three cosmological realizations in 2 Mpc comoving boxes, from approximately z=3200 to z=0, reaching 60 pc spatial resolution with adaptive mesh refinement and GPU acceleration. Trace additional halos in a 20 Mpc box at the same resolution and evolve a 40 Mpc box to z=8.

Reduce the operator basis using curvature identities, Gauss–Bonnet relations and tree-level Einstein equations, equivalent at this order to graviton field redefinitions. In 3D, dualize the photon through Fμν=iεμνρ∂ρφ to a canonically normalized shift-symmetric scalar.

For 3D forward scattering, the paper uses M(s)=16A3s², a Cauchy contour integral of M(s)/s³, crossing symmetry and the optical theorem. With the boundary contribution absent, the resulting cross-section integral is nonnegative.

Parameterize ultraviolet intermediate states by spectral representations, decompose their tensor structures, and integrate them out at low momentum. Separately, compute effective photon metrics in background fields and thermal photon gases to diagnose propagation speeds.

Reduce archival MOS pointings with Sgr A* within 0.5 arcminutes of the telescope axis using SAS and soft-proton flare screening. Exclude the MJD 54000–54500 flaring period, combine 14-arcminute spectra with addspec, and subtract rescaled closed-filter backgrounds normalized using energies above 10 keV.

Fit 2.8–6.0 keV using an absorbed thermal-plasma plus power-law model. Set non-Fe elemental abundances to zero in the plasma component and add selected astrophysical lines as Gaussians with adjustable intensities and energies, tying energies across MOS cameras. The baseline explicitly omits K XVIII lines at 3.47 and 3.51 keV.

Jointly fit GC, M31 and Perseus with a shared additional-line energy and independently varying normalizations, adding four parameters for three datasets. Scan the width of the approximately 3.685 keV Gaussian against the candidate-line normalization to explore an important systematic degeneracy.

Define quantum extremality by vanishing generalized-entropy variation in both normal directions. Quantum trapped surfaces have strictly negative variation along every future-directed null generator; marginally trapped surfaces have zero variation. These definitions reduce to their classical counterparts as ħ→0.

Proofs use the imported null-surface comparison Theorem 2.1, the GSL, and first-contact deformation arguments. The comparison requires nested null splitting surfaces, smooth classical geometry near contact, and an ħ expansion; equality requires local coincidence. Time-fold invariance is argued by induction.

Use Euclidean background-field quantization with graviton, gravitino, and ghost determinants. The conformal-factor contour is rotated to imaginary values to replace the negative trace fluctuation operator by a positive one.

Compute the two-derivative action by a gradient expansion and Pauli-Villars regularization. Subtracting the uncompactified momentum integral isolates finite circle-dependent terms; heat-kernel coefficients determine bulk ultraviolet divergences and Gauss-Bonnet running.

In an anti-self-dual background, reduce determinants to chiral Dirac-operator ratios. Integrate regulated indices including anomaly and boundary contributions, match finite terms using Pauli-Villars, and combine collective-coordinate Jacobians with a two-fermion correlator to extract the superpotential.

Impose algebraic chiral-superfield constraints with F-term Lagrange multipliers in a superconformal action. N has Weyl weight 2, the superpotential weight 3, and the multiplier weight 1; varying a term Λ(X^(2))² enforces nilpotency while the unsolved action is manifestly supersymmetric.

Gauge-fix the superconformal compensator to obtain supergravity and the frame-function relation K=−3logΩ. In the brane review, gauge-fix κ-symmetry with θ1=0 and θ2=αλ to identify the surviving VA-type worldvolume fermions.

Rescale the scalar by q = aφ, solve its mode equation using normalized Whittaker functions, and select positive frequency in the asymptotic past. Evaluate the current expectation value directly in that initial vacuum.

Where an adiabatic out-vacuum exists, compute Bogoliubov coefficients. Converting the momentum integral into a production rate uses a rough estimate of the particle-creation time from adiabaticity violation.

Use a WKB adiabatic expansion and subtract through second order. The unregularized momentum integral is evaluated with Mellin–Barnes representations and contour residues; the hard cutoff is a calculational convenience.

Expand the field equations in α, combine the three-form equation with external Einstein equations to obtain self-duality of the internal flux, and use the resulting warp equation to simplify the internal Einstein equation.

Decompose the closed third Chern form as c3^(0) = Hc3^(0) + i∂∂̄F, with F a co-closed (2,2)-form. Express the nonconstant curvature scalar Z through a Laplacian of the contraction of F with two Kähler forms.

Reduce the proposed corrected gravitino variation, construct J and Ω as spinor bilinears, use Fierz identities, and solve their differential and algebraic constraints. Compare Killing spinor integrability with the corrected Einstein equation.

Causal decompositions partition boundary and bulk into two domains of dependence and the causal future/past of their separating surface. Matching these decompositions proves causal compatibility; a compact-acausal-set extension lemma supplies the changed Cauchy slice needed for wedge invariance.

The proof studies null normal congruences using focusing and the Raychaudhuri equation. Infinite physical affine distance to the boundary forces boundary-reaching, nonexpanding generators without conjugate points to have zero expansion and shear; connected families then reach isolated boundary points.

Takagi factorization of the complex symmetric fermion mass matrix; projection of the scalar Hessian along fermion eigenvectors orthogonal to the sGoldstino; first-order eigenvalue perturbation theory for small mixing between sectors.

Altland–Zirnbauer CI ensembles model fermion masses. Marčenko–Pastur densities are transformed into scalar spectra; the Wishart correspondence, Tracy–Widom tails and large-deviation formulas estimate atypical spectra.

Use a Lagrangian treatment that imposes gravitational constraints before expressing the quadratic fluctuation action in manifestly gauge-invariant scalar combinations. Decompose fluctuations into harmonics on the three-sphere.

Numerically explore specified scalar potentials while varying dimensionless gravitational coupling. Study the lowest slowly varying mode using y = χ/√Q where permitted, and diagnose rapidly oscillating modes from negative kinetic coefficients.

Use dilute-gas multibounce sums, finite Euclidean four-volume, and local comparisons with flat-space configurations to estimate which saddle configurations dominate. The generic many-bounce argument extends beyond overall O(4) symmetry heuristically.

Complete the square and impose perfect-square factorization of the fibre polynomial; use SINGULAR prime decomposition and ideal saturation to isolate matter curves, their singularities and codimension-three intersections.
Compute Euler-characteristic changes by adjunction and flux intersections using toric homological relations, ambient complete intersections and normal-bundle Chern classes.

Use toric tops, Stanley–Reisner ideals, Jacobian discriminant expansions and resolved fibre splittings. Intersections with Cartan and section-derived divisors determine representations and charges; fibre degenerations identify Yukawa couplings.

Expand potentials around hilltop or inverse-hilltop benchmarks using coefficients cq. Analyze their effects in large-N and small-μ limits; an n=3 example through fifth order illustrates how endpoint corrections enter at higher powers of μ. Constant-excursion contours are then fitted in the observable plane.
Integrate dφ/dN=√(r/8) to estimate the field excursion, and integrate ε=dlnH/dN to reconstruct asymptotic potentials. Separate the N-dependent contribution to Δφ from the endpoint contribution.
Use vector-meson dominance for low-mass hadronic decays: the isospin-zero B−L vector is treated as ω-like, with suppressed ππ decay and resonance-dependent hadronic branching fractions.

Thermally average ff̄ ↔ νRν̄R using Fermi–Dirac distributions and the full Z′ propagator. Treat resonant production with a narrow-width delta-function approximation; numerical calculations restore lepton mass thresholds.

Recast hidden-photon searches using the relevant visible branching ratios and total lifetimes. Beam-dump production at small coupling and decay inside shielding have different dependence on the invisible width.

For KT, combine the H3 equation and F5 Bianchi identity into a radial equation for α. At stationary points it enforces sgn(α)=sgn(α″); negative horizon charge and positive asymptotic flux charge then constrain the horizon value of α.

For the broader ansatz, integrate a combination of the worldvolume Einstein equation, dilaton equation and flux Bianchi identity, retaining total derivatives as boundary terms. Evaluate the KS boundary expression and compare it with the BPS-subtracted ADM mass using a first-order anti-brane perturbation.

Use the homogeneous axion equation with Hubble friction and the Friedmann equation, distinguishing frozen fields, coherent oscillations and hilltop evolution. The adopted acceleration eligibility criterion is the potential slow-roll condition ε=(MP²/2)(V′/V)²<1.

Estimate onset probabilities with a geometric distribution over successive axions. Track unwanted axion densities through their scale-factor redshifting and compare them with BBN, CMB matter-density and structure-formation requirements.
Expand DBI and Chern–Simons actions in slowly varying brane coordinates, extract kinetic normalization and potentials, and identify the angular decay constant after canonical normalization.

Treat finite-curvature corrections through an iterative Green-function solution of the Poisson equation. Estimate D5 backreaction separately on the warp factor and internal geometry using localized-source equations.
Apply imported exact RC Laplace solutions: spherical harmonics multiply two independent hypergeometric radial functions. The selected invariant-sector expansion remains valid near the tip.

The asymmetric model uses separate particle/antiparticle equations with production asymmetry κ and transfer reactions. The non-Abelian model tracks separate sector temperatures and estimates Sommerfeld-enhanced annihilation.
Numerically evolve coupled modulus, radiation and dark-matter Boltzmann equations with Friedmann expansion. MSSM annihilation rates in the neutralino scan are computed using DarkSUSY.

Confront predicted abundances with gamma-ray fluxes, CMB energy injection and nuclear scattering. Gamma-ray tests vary halo profiles; annihilation constraints account for the squared fractional dark-matter abundance.

Uses Euclidean path integrals for vacuum states and gravitational thermodynamics, including integration over metrics and different topologies. Comparing thermal-AdS and AdS-Schwarzschild saddle actions gives the Hawking-Page exchange of dominance.

Separates scalar modes into angular harmonics and radial effective Schrödinger equations. For collapse, matching modes across the shell mixes positive and negative frequencies; transmission through the exterior potential supplies greybody factors.
States the RT/HRT entropy prescription as a conjectural method: at leading order in 1/N, S_A=A(Σ)/(4G), selecting the least-area codimension-two extremal surface anchored on ∂A and homologous to A.

Compute moduli F-terms and gravity-mediated gaugino, scalar, trilinear and Higgs-bilinear terms, including relevant D-terms and subleading no-scale corrections. The authors developed the Mathematica package LargeVol for potential minimization and soft-term calculations.

Minimize the N=1 supergravity potential in an inverse-volume expansion: fluxes fix S and U supersymmetrically at order V^(−2), while α′ and non-perturbative effects stabilize Kähler moduli at order V^(−3) and shift S,U. The shifts are parameterized where explicit functions are unknown.

Stitch truncated Taylor patches together, transporting lower derivatives deterministically and adding Gaussian perturbations to a higher derivative tensor. For V∈C^k, the Taylor expansion extends through order k+1 and stochastic changes enter that highest derivative tensor.
Match the DBM Hessian-increment mean and raw second moment: E[δv_ab]=−v_ab δs/Λ_h and E[(δv_ab)^2]=(1+δ_ab)σ²δs/Λ_h. Gaussian moment propagation determines corresponding higher-tensor perturbations.

Two C² prescriptions rotate coordinates either to align a basis vector with the displacement or to diagonalize the Hessian. Conditions are imposed in that frame, then tensors are rotated back. The displacement-aligned prescription extends to arbitrary k and leaves unconstrained components unperturbed.

For two-axion alignment, p₂/p₁=q₂/q₁ produces a flat direction; small misalignment lifts it with an effective decay constant increasing as inverse misalignment. Smaller starting decay constants require tighter tuning. Hierarchical decay constants provide another reviewed route.

The EFT discussion uses Wilsonian operator power counting, radiative corrections and loop resummation to assess slow-roll stability. Integrating out a heavy modulus in a two-field toy potential illustrates how an initially quadratic inflaton potential can flatten.

Dimensional reduction of generalized flux kinetic terms gives schematic V∼(N_p+bN_(p−2))². Reduction of wrapped-brane DBI/Chern–Simons actions supplies a complementary monodromy description: the reviewed D5 example is asymptotically linear in b, while D7 constructions can be quadratic.

Estimate the effective b_i range by sorting Mori generators by volume, selecting a minimal-volume independent charge set, retaining additional contributions through a volume-threshold prescription, and imposing |Σ_i a_ji b_i|≤π for retained curves.

Use classical Kähler metrics, straight-line geodesics at fixed Kähler moduli, and a triangle-inequality bound on the metric quadratic form. For simplicial cones, a curve-dual nef basis supplies nonnegative triple intersections and identifies t_i with curve volumes.

Analyze 8,395 simulated spaces with N=h^{1,1}=2–15, using favorable Kreuzer-Skarke polytopes, selected regular star complete triangulations, ambient toric nef cones and hypersurface intersection numbers. Minimize volume subject to ambient generating curves having volume >1; estimate radius through f̃=π√N f, with f the square root of the largest metric eigenvalue.

Uses coupled proton-number, helium-number, Friedmann and radiation-production equations. A previously obtained numerical estimate reduces the final radiation to a factor proportional to (N_B m_p)^(4/3) τ_p^(2/3)(1−cX_n), with additional fixed Planck-scale normalization.
Determines weak freezeout from H=Γ(p→n), then estimates X_n=exp[−(t_BBN−t_dec)/τ_n]/[1+exp(Q/T_dec)]. The neutron lifetime is calculated using Fermi theory and a beta-decay phase-space integral.

Models hadronic inputs phenomenologically: m_p=αΛ_QCD+β(2m_u+m_d), Q=β(m_d−m_u)−M_em, and Γ_p∝m_p⁵G/M_G⁴. An effective proton-decay interaction gives the approximate phase-space factor G∝(1−m_π²/m_p²)².

Regulated scalar-gravity interiors end inflation in a crunch; numerical examples examine accumulation near the maximum of an effective scale factor. Pure dS extremal-surface expressions are analytically continued onto complex Riemann sheets.

Cut-and-paste construction with continuous induced metrics and shell stress tensors obtained from jumps in transverse extrinsic curvature. Parameter choices satisfying the shell NEC, expressed here as μ+p≥0, are exhibited for every d≥2.

Raychaudhuri focusing constrains null congruences orthogonal to extremal surfaces. A complementary maximin argument uses achronal slices approaching IdS, forcing the minimal wormhole-spanning area to grow without bound.

Express the modulus-dominated duration using its lifetime, the equality Hubble scale and initial displacement; combine this with slow-roll relations and observational normalization. Reheating is parameterized by an effective equation of state and its duration rather than a detailed decay model.

Factor the horizon-exit condition k=a_k H_k across successive expansion epochs and separately track the energy density. Combining the resulting expressions eliminates the intervening radiation-era e-fold count and the scale factor at modulus decay.

Express the flux potential through the period matrix and solve e_Λ+N̄_ΛΣ m^Σ=0. Positivity follows from regular negative-definite Im N in the physical domain; the equivalent no-scale F-term formulation supplies the minimum equations.

Use explicit minimum equations, numerical solutions of coupled high-order polynomials, positive-metric checks and mass eigenvalues for the four-modulus example. In the toroidal example, integrate the kinetic metric along the whole flat valley to obtain a global canonical field rather than relying on local fluctuations.

Impose holomorphic independence ∂_ΘW≡0 along an axion direction, translate this into flux constraints, and count remaining stabilization equations. For complex-structure-only directions, classify possibilities using A_ij=κ_Nij and its kernel.

For large coupling, expand the continued-fraction equation in qQ. Near extremality and the charged threshold frequency, match near-horizon hypergeometric and far-region confluent-hypergeometric solutions, imposing outgoing behavior at infinity to obtain a separate frequency condition.

Separate the charged field equations using spin-weighted spherical harmonics and a common radial master equation. A tortoise-coordinate transformation produces a radial wave equation with a frequency-dependent complex potential.

Apply Leaver's horizon-centered series, three-term coefficient recurrence and continued-fraction quantization condition. Root finding uses inversions for overtones and Nollert's asymptotic estimate of the truncated fraction's remainder.

Measure the energy gap and distance between each found local minimum and its nearest adjacent minimum. These statistics motivate the energetic argument for post-tunneling initial conditions along the light valley.

Numerical landscapes usually set Λ_i=Λ, f_α=f and C=0, draw integer coefficients with |n_iα|≤3 and random relative phases, and repeatedly search for minima from random initial positions until the found-minimum distribution converges. Alignment-selected examples require R<10^−2.
