Use the spectrum of the anomaly Gram matrix as an alignment diagnostic, inspect the potential in local mass-eigenstate coordinates, and follow the light direction while integrating out heavier modes. Position-dependent eigenstates motivate a superposition of cosines rather than a fixed single cosine.

Applies the N=1 supergravity F-term potential, supersymmetric stabilization conditions, D-term contributions, and a gauge-singlet SUSY-breaking uplift. Heavy fields are integrated out before canonical normalization of the remaining axion; slow-roll formulas supply the illustrative observables.

Uses dimensional reduction and the one-loop Green-Schwarz term to obtain Stückelberg couplings, moduli-dependent Fayet-Iliopoulos terms, and correlated non-abelian gauge kinetic functions fvis=S+βiTi and fhid=S−βiTi.
Reformulate supersymmetry with a generalized Dolbeault operator. Appendix A uses symplectic cohomology pairings and an explicitly assumed dδ-lemma to recover the bulk period obstruction.
Expand the classical D6 chain superpotential ΔW=∫Σ4(Jc+F)^2 in open deformations and harmonic bulk two-forms. For D7-branes, use W=∫Σ5 Ω∧F and its complex-structure covariant derivatives.

Compare Hodge components of quantized backreacted F2 with bulk supersymmetry, then use four-chain integrals and Poincare duality to express displacement-induced obstructions as periods over D6 two-cycles.

Imposes Killing-spinor conditions in an adapted index basis, reduces the quadratic constraints using SO(3)d singlets, and uses Mathematica to scan real solutions. The inequivalent massive-gravitino decompositions considered are 5, 3+1+1, and 2+2+1.

The going-to-the-origin method uses scalar-manifold homogeneity to move a vacuum to φ=0 while transforming its embedding tensor. Supersymmetry and vacuum equations then become algebraic conditions on the SU(8) tensors Aij and Ai jkl, in representations 36 and 420.

Identifies gauge algebras through Cartan-Killing signatures and compares traces of powers of an E7(7)-covariant quartic tensor to determine deformation parameters. Evaluates bosonic and fermionic mass matrices and matches their eigenvalues to AdS supermultiplets.

Solve the linear density-contrast equation with Hubble damping, pressure and gravitational terms for selected comoving scales and Λ densities. Reaching Δ≈1 before the present is used as a necessary threshold for possible nonlinear structure formation.
Use the component-scaled Friedmann expansion law and integrate t(a)=∫0^a da′/[a′H(a′)] to compare redshift plots with linear cosmic-time plots and to estimate cosmic ages and era durations.

Compute intersection matrices using Euler characteristics of intersections, orientation signs and equivalence classes under projective scaling and quotient actions. The appendix notes that its common rescaling changes numerical intersection values but leaves matrix rank unchanged.

Determine three-manifold topology and fundamental groups, then apply imported Chern-Simons results for Lens spaces, Seifert fibrations and torus decompositions. Contributions from pieces with boundary require gauge choices compatible with the gluing map.

Construct explicit three-cycle representatives as fixed loci of isometric antiholomorphic involutions: A-type uses coordinate conjugation and C-type also exchanges identical projective factors. Track whether quotient generators preserve a representative or merely identify distinct representatives.

Treat Ward identities as linear inhomogeneous differential equations. Solve the homogeneous problem using eigenfunctions f_z(k)=(1+ikz)e^(−ikz), impose OPE limits, and give a formal integral prescription for the sourced solution.

Impose spatial and time reparametrization invariance on the wavefunctional; lapse and shift equations supply the constraints. Translate coefficient-function identities into perturbation correlators using |Ψ|². AdS/CFT techniques organize the calculation without assuming an inflationary holographic dual.

The authors report checks in canonical slow-roll inflation: the scaling identity follows from momentum homogeneity and the soft four-point limit; the special-conformal check uses Mathematica. These are reported checks, not reproduced here.

For heavy strings, applies Israel junction conditions to the discontinuity of shell extrinsic curvature. A large-radius expansion determines a critical-tension condition and mass bound; mixed junction components test the possibility of a rotating exterior.

Uses the asymptotic probe-string action and its Liouville limit, together with imported exact light-string central-charge formulas and ceff=c−24Δmin, to assess whether probe or tensionless strings reproduce the proposed pure-gravity gap.

The gravitino calculation uses an irreducible SO(5) decomposition on a four-dimensional spherical background and local-supersymmetry gauge fixing with alpha'=0. Faddeev-Popov and Nielsen-Kallosh ghosts reduce the stated eight components to two propagating degrees of freedom.

Euclidean functional RG using the Wetterich equation and background split g=bar g+h. Background-Laplacian eigenvalues define the coarse-graining scale. The calculation uses a Litim-type regulator shape and type-II cutoffs.

In the fuller analysis, anomalous dimensions are solved as functions of G and lambda and inserted into their beta functions. The interacting fixed point is followed numerically from vanishing matter content as field multiplicities increase.

The mixed axion kinetic matrix is diagonalized and canonically normalized numerically at selected t_1,t_2. The resulting mass hierarchy is used to eliminate the heavy axion combination and extract an effective light-field decay constant.

An analytic small-misalignment example illustrates inverse-misalignment enhancement of the light-field decay constant. A separate numerical toy example uses explicit superpotential and modulus parameters.

The supergravity F-term potential is simplified using K^ij K_i K_j=3 and fixed complex-structure/dilaton fields. Terms quadratic in W_np are dropped, leaving interference between W_p and derivatives of W_np.

Integrate solutions satisfying the respective endpoint conditions and locate eigenvalues through zeros of their Wronskian, evaluated at theta=pi/2. Scan background initial data to obtain the first positive eigenvalue as a function over the admissible domain.

Numerically integrate the background using a=exp(2A), c=exp(2C), retaining globally bounded nonnegative solutions. Mathematica's Backward Differentiation Formula addresses equatorial instabilities. Alternative initial data near theta=pi/2 use a local expansion with an offset of order 10^-4.

Restrict to modes depending only on theta. Their equation is (p g')'+lambda q g=0, with p=exp[4(A+C)] sin(theta)/f and q=exp[4(A+C)] f sin(theta). The paper maps this singular problem using g_tilde=g/u, u=1-log(sin theta), to what it identifies as a regular Sturm-Liouville problem.

Expand the fixed-point equation about R=0. Algebraic recursion expresses every λ_n for n≥2 as a rational function of λ_0 and λ_1. Numerically select real roots consistent across orders, reject coincident denominator zeros, and compare both coordinates and eigenvalues.

Use the functional Wilsonian RG with a background four-sphere, Landau–De Witt gauge, transverse-traceless decomposition, ghosts and Jacobians, and heat-kernel traces. The optimized scalar cutoff is R_k(y)=(k²−y)θ(k²−y).

Compute the stability matrix as M=(I−V)^(−1)(∂U/∂λ) at the fixed point, retaining flow-dependent terms on the RG equation's right-hand side. Estimate infinite-order quantities by averaging the last eight orders, following the observed approximate eight-fold periodicity.

Identify accidental global symmetries from a restricted superpotential, such as its dimension-three terms, while the full superpotential respects the exact discrete symmetries and contains higher-order global-symmetry violations.
Analyze two axions with two confining cosine potentials through their 2×2 mass matrix. Near alignment, αδ−βγ=Δ≈0, the light direction acquires an enhanced effective decay constant.

Evaluate genus-zero CSFT vertices through cubic order using a truncated string field, BRST operations, normal ordering, reflector identities, and current/ghost Ward identities. Auxiliary fields are subsequently eliminated and fields and gauge parameters redefined.

Represent Lie-algebra generators by differential operators on group-manifold scalar functions. Express two- and three-point coefficients as integrals of these functions and impose compatibility with the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equation; zero-mode substitutions translate amplitudes into target-space expressions.

Numerically vary the flux-superpotential deformation and condensate-prefactor ratio in a phenomenological racetrack potential. Only three real one-parameter paths are explored, including one coordinated deformation.

Estimate the condensate prefactor by matching the gaugino-induced scalar potential to moduli supergravity, tracking reduction, superspace and Einstein frames, Weyl rescalings and the gaugino rescaling anomaly.

Use large-complex-structure period expansions, polynomial truncations and common roots of rational flux polynomials to seek approximately vanishing flux-superpotential vacua and estimate their response to deformation.

Expand flux near the North Pole, extract its designated (1,2) and (3,0) components to determine m′/m, and combine this with the rescaling invariant λ=a_2a_4/a_3² to infer NS5 and oblique quadratic terms.

Transfer the transverse D5 polarization potential from a smeared anti-D3 solution to localized sources, using the closed/co-closed three-form combination and harmonic scalar mode to argue insensitivity to source positions in the chosen regime.

Apply a nonsupersymmetric Polchinski–Strassler expansion of five-brane probe actions, retaining quartic, cubic and quadratic terms. The argument relates the resulting polarization potential to asymptotic mass-deformation data.

Compare two conifold-transition paths from a common resolved geometry. With J=t1 U+t2(S+U), t1,t2>0, the quartic blowdown takes t1→0, whereas the Weierstrass blowdown takes t2→0 and simultaneously shrinks BI and BII.

Interpret the transition through circle reduction of a six-dimensional Higgs model. A first-KK-mode Higgs has a varying phase, equivalently a linear axion profile and fluxed Stückelberg reduction. The linear Higgs, Stückelberg, and M-theory geometric pictures are described as dual descriptions.

Use integral divisor–curve intersections, oriented boundaries of chains after conifold transitions, and the universal coefficient theorem to identify torsion. A local prime-decomposition and base-blowup analysis supplies explicit fibre combinations representing the expected torsional two-cycle.

Insert a flux-clumping parameter λ into the Abelian NS5 DBI plus Chern-Simons action and extract a potential for its polar angle ψ. The B6 coupling supplies the λ-dependent force, while quantized F3 flux fixes the retained KS expression for C2.

Describe decay through Euclidean bubble nucleation, with an energy-density gain competing against wall tension. An appendix evaluates the effective wall tension from Euclidean momentum near the critical clumping value, connecting the internal NS5 polarization profile to the spacetime bubble wall.

Use the S-dual non-Abelian anti-D3 action expanded through quartic order in matrix scalars. Stationary configurations are represented by a fuzzy sphere; the paper compares the expansion's breakdown with the instability inferred from the NS5 description.

Evaluate scalar coset representatives at known critical points, invert the resulting internal metric, calculate the internal four-form, and impose eleven-dimensional Maxwell and Einstein equations. The smaller-symmetry example uses a two-scalar SO(3)×SO(3)-invariant truncation.

Compare four- and eleven-dimensional supersymmetry variations of electric vectors and their dual potentials to identify generalized vielbeins. Appropriate contractions yield the inverse metric and three-form; the authors establish a Clifford property and the antisymmetry needed for the three-form interpretation.

Construct an exceptional generalized frame on TM ⊕ Λ²T*M ⊕ Λ⁵T*M ⊕ (T*M ⊗ Λ⁷T*M). Its generalized Lie derivative encodes the gauging, and the generalized metric obtained from a scalar-dependent frame reproduces the metric and three-form ansatz.

Rewrite internal gauge-flux expansions using structure forms and normalized torsion, calculate the Ricci tensor, and match higher-dimensional gauge, dilaton and Einstein equations to derivatives of the isotropic scalar potentials.

Invert differential relations for invariant G2 or SU(3) forms to obtain moduli-dependent torsion classes linear in metric fluxes. Express internal curvature through torsion and compare its potential contribution with the N=1 F-term potential computed from K and W.

Represent the WZ coupling by a closed superspace form I5=dΩ4. Impose the orientifold-compatible fermion projector and vanishing supersymmetric vector/transverse combinations, then use Γ-matrix identities to integrate the restricted form into the VA volume form. The appendix repeats this construction for general odd p.

Test compatibility of orientifolding and κ gauge fixing through the commutator of their projector matrices. Establish consistency of removing bosons by showing that the transverse fermion bilinear and the fermionic correction to the vector field strength vanish under the projection.

Relate the surviving VA fermion to a constrained chiral multiplet and evaluate the four-dimensional supergravity potential. For the proposed Calabi-Yau extension, decompose the sixteen-component spinor into an SU(3) singlet and triplet and retain only the covariantly constant supersymmetry parameter.

Multiple dispatch selects implementations from argument-type combinations, allowing structure-specific algorithms and generic fallbacks. The same mechanism is illustrated for scalar arithmetic, matrix operations and user-defined matrix structures.
Macros transform symbolic expressions at parse time. Examples generate inline Horner polynomial evaluation and four typed LAPACK Cholesky wrappers using @eval and ccall.

Dataflow type inference abstractly interprets code starting from input types, follows branches and tracks possible expression types. Runtime-type specialization and LLVM JIT compilation then support native-code generation.

Estimate tuned-vacuum populations by replacing a flux sum with an integral, imposing the D3 tadpole bound and small-coefficient conditions through step functions. Small complex disks supply tuning suppression factors, assuming a regular change of variables and approximately constant local density.

Expand the dynamical heavy-field displacements δx, δz and δz̄ around a supersymmetric locus, retaining quadratic order in their potential without expanding in Δy. Write a real quadratic form with Hessian D and linear term b, minimize it, and substitute the displacement solution into the potential.

Population equations combine exponential superradiance, stimulated transitions proportional to NeNg, and annihilations proportional to N². After spin extraction shuts off growth, the adopted single-level solution is N(t)=Nmax/(1+ΓaNmax t).

Observable counts integrate black-hole formation rate, normalized mass/spin/distance distributions, and time above detector threshold. Design-sensitivity projections use 121 segments of 250 coherent hours and trials factor 10.

Uses imported semi-analytic spin-0 Kerr eigenmode rates. GW power is calculated from the Fourier-transformed classical-field stress tensor using hydrogen wavefunctions and a flat-space radiation formula.

Uses holomorphy of supersymmetric Euclidean D3 instanton actions to identify real parts of chiral coordinates from their on-shell DBI actions. This avoids directly reconstructing globally problematic Chern–Simons potentials; vertical M5 instantons provide the dual interpretation.

Uses the Laplacian Green operator, Poincaré–Lelong identity, harmonic representatives and local bundle potentials to express warped divisor volumes. Implicit differentiation employs a tadpole-dependent relation combining background-source and mobile-D3 contributions.

Extracts the conformal Kähler potential from the dimensionally reduced Einstein-term prefactor: N=(4π/ℓs^8)∫e^(-4D)dvolX. Local superconformal symmetry then relates it to scalar kinetic terms after compensator gauge fixing, bypassing explicit compensator-dependent kinetic reduction.

Generate a stochastic magnetic field from a random Fourier-space vector potential with power-law amplitudes and uniform phases; take its Fourier curl and transform to position space. Impose wavelength cutoffs and a radial envelope B ∝ ne^η. Electron densities follow β profiles, with a double β profile for the cool-core cluster A2199.

Numerically propagate the coupled ALP and two photon amplitudes through cells of constant magnetic field and density using successive matrix exponentials and local diagonalization. Start with a pure ALP state, sum the squared outgoing photon amplitudes, and average conversion probabilities over annuli for energies between 25 eV and 1 keV.

Integrate P(r,E) against the CAB energy spectrum over projected annuli and 0.1–0.28 keV. Use PIMMS to convert luminosities into ROSAT PSPC R1R2 count rates, then scan inverse coupling M and mean CAB energy to match observed excess magnitudes or constrain an unobserved excess.

Expand the eta-function to include a subleading exponential, calculate slow-roll parameters and the e-fold integral, and evaluate ns, r, and running. Higher-order terms in ns are retained when the third-derivative slow-roll combination is appreciable. The scalar amplitude is adjusted through gaugino-condensation parameters.

Use imported holomorphic one-loop thresholds involving ln η(iU), with η the Dedekind eta-function. Its large-complex-structure asymptotic ln η(iU) → −πU/12 yields a gauge kinetic function with tree-level Kähler dependence and loop-suppressed linear complex-structure dependence.

Choose an integer-flux ansatz and redefine U⁴ = U¹−U². Solve supersymmetric flux conditions, then racetrack equations for the remaining dilaton direction and shifted Kähler modulus. Use Kähler extremization for Re U² and examine canonically normalized mass matrices to assess the proposed hierarchy.

Vary independently with respect to the connection, B and tetrad. Decompose ω into a torsionless connection plus contortion, use the connection and B equations, and express the tetrad equation through the torsionless curvature to recover the Giddings–Strominger equations.

Evaluate the on-shell half-wormhole action and resum a dilute gas of unit-charge instantons and anti-instantons. A Fourier representation of the constraint on charge change yields the η-dependent transition amplitude.

Express the Nieh–Yan density as a total divergence and reduce its integral to boundary contortion flux. Relate that flux to the axion charge, and invoke the relation to SO(5) and SO(4) Pontryagin numbers and their integer homotopy indices.

Obtain a complex Kaloper–Sorbo description by dualizing the D7 gauge field and reducing its magnetic potential; integrating out the four-form recovers the small-field potential. A separate no-scale N=1 supergravity description reproduces the leading bilinear potential under Kähler-modulus-dominated SUSY breaking.

Evaluate and dimensionally reduce the D7 DBI+CS action, retaining all powers of the induced internal B-field while truncating to two spacetime derivatives. For the relevant internal two-form, the DBI determinant becomes a perfect square; DBI and CS contribute equally to the scalar potential after tension subtraction.

Solve multifield slow-roll equations using the curved field-space metric Gab=diag(4f,σ²f). Scan flux parameters and initial conditions subject to 50–60 efolds; compute adiabatic spectral quantities using the paper's multifield slow-roll prescription.

Identify the goldstino through gravitino–spinor mixing and impose a local supersymmetry unitary gauge at the vacuum. Construct uplifts by shifting f or g by a constant, or rescaling f; subtracting linear terms from arbitrary functions enforces f′(0)=g′(0)=0.

For the bosonic sector, compute the ordinary supergravity potential and then set the scalar component s to zero. Evaluate the potential on a=0 and calculate scalar Hessian masses. The partner a must still be checked separately in each model.

The explicit construction uses a Kaluza–Klein vielbein ansatz and field redefinitions, assembles a formally O(d,d+K)-covariant action, then solves block generalized-metric constraints to obtain proper O(d,d) variables.

The string argument factorizes sphere correlators into internal holomorphic, internal antiholomorphic, gauge-current, and remaining sectors. Independent internal rotations give O(d)×O(d); combining these with coordinate transformations and two-form shifts supplies the O(d,d) generators.

Weyl transformation gives V=(f′R−f)/(2f′²). Reconstruction substitutes f′=exp(κφ), differentiates the resulting equation to solve for f′, and integrates; the original undifferentiated equation fixes the lost integration constant.

Approximate reconstruction iterates with f′ of order R at large R and expands fractional powers into logarithmic series. A direct Weyl map to another Jordan frame uses f′=ϕ^Δ(1+ξϕ²), relating fractional-curvature corrections to logarithmically corrected quartic potentials.

Takagi factorisation of the complex symmetric supersymmetric mass tensor Z diagonalises the unperturbed X-sector Hessian. Its rescaled eigenvalues are (λi±|W|)², where λi are nonnegative singular values; large holomorphic Hessian entries therefore need not cause instability.

The authors expand critical-point equations and the Hessian in ε, treating the three initially massless real modes as a degenerate sector and estimating mixing corrections perturbatively. Explicit STU families are constructed by solving inversely for fluxes at prescribed moduli values.

Domain-wall supersymmetry is expressed through generalized Hitchin flows. Half-flat mirror reduction supplies a four-dimensional description; Calabi–Yau flows use harmonic symplectic expansions and the complex-structure prepotential.

Atiyah deformation theory and long exact cohomology sequences for nested extensions: 0→End(TX)⊕End(V)→E→TX→0 and 0→T*X→Q→E→0. Connecting maps encode bundle holomorphicity and the heterotic Bianchi identity.

Boundary smearing constructs bulk solutions perturbatively; a Bogoliubov transformation relates global and Rindler reconstructions. The Rindler kernel is used distributionally against suitable CFT correlators rather than as an ordinary function.

Appendix B supplies a matrix proof of the operator-algebra correction criterion, using a reference state and an inverse restricted to the support of a reduced density matrix. Bulk localization additionally uses boundary-anchored spacelike geodesic dressings.

Erasure correction is analyzed by entangling the code with a reference R. Exact correction requires factorization of the reference–erased density matrix; approximate correction uses a small trace-norm deviation. Connected correlations provide a lower-bound diagnostic for that deviation.

Use the exact functional RG equation and split-symmetry Ward identity. Numerical tests integrate imported beta-functions from one single-metric and two differently gauged bi-metric calculations; the latter solve the dynamical sector before the background sector.
Construct the EAA by a cutoff-subtracted Legendre transform. Define C_k=Γ_k[0;Φ̄_k^sc]=−W_k[0;Φ̄_k^sc], where the self-consistent background solves the zero-source tadpole equation δΓ_k/δφ=0 at φ=0.

Represent boundary points by rank-one matrices or vector pairs and quotient elements by 2 × 2 matrices. Regulated lengths follow from traces or vector contractions; the Euclidean boundary formula is log|u⊥ · gv|². Closed Lorentzian lengths use inverse hyperbolic cosines of the left and right traces.

Boundary-anchored geodesics are labeled by quotient-group elements and closed geodesics by conjugacy classes. In orientable cases, homology is computed by abelianizing group words, counting signed generator occurrences and selecting admissible combinations of open and closed curves.

The three-boundary investigation enumerates words of up to eight letters and samples over one million parameter sets. Analytic trace expressions are converted to C-compiled Mathematica functions to identify candidate dominant geodesics efficiently.

Analyze the supergravity Hessian in saxion/axion variables. At a θ=0 supersymmetric minimum with real W and Z, the authors find leading-order axion–saxion decoupling; their stability discussion remains local to the expansion.
Apply φ=Qθ using a square full-rank charge submatrix, obtaining Ξ=Q^(-T)KQ^(-1); diagonalize Ξ and canonically normalize. Additional rows impose linear cuts on the cube.

Rescale selected directions until a domain constraint is saturated, producing directional lower bounds on the maximal diameter. Estimate typical bounds using Wishart smallest-eigenvalue statistics and eigenvector delocalization, with numerical simulations.

Compare canonical kinetic coordinates with lattice coordinates that simplify the potential. Parameterize the potential vectors by their lengths and relative angle; study the kinetic eigenvectors/eigenvalues and the potential Hessian, including the small-angle mass hierarchy.

Use reflection-supported truncations when available, then expand the effective potential either near its minimum or along an exponential plateau. Nonsymmetric examples require an effective description along a curved trough instead of a coordinate-axis truncation.
MultiNest nested sampling searches the multimodal likelihood. Featureless-spectrum simulations estimate look-elsewhere improvements, while injected oscillatory spectra test signal recovery.

An inverse-variance-weighted template inner product estimates detection losses: the expected template signal-to-noise equals the correct-template signal-to-noise multiplied by their normalized overlap.

Taylor expansions of the decay function and expansions of the oscillatory phase in ln(k/k*) motivate templates. Analytic spectra are compared with numerical spectra; Coleman-Weinberg estimates and interaction power counting assess strong-drift radiative corrections.

A magnetic-soliton argument compares the Maxwell self-energy outside a cutoff-sized core with its gravitational radius, motivating a cutoff of order gMpl. The derivation assumes elementary magnetic constituents should avoid already being black holes.

Charged higher-dimensional matter generates a Wilson-line potential through Casimir/Aharonov-Bohm effects. Contributions from mass m5 are exponentially suppressed by winding factors involving exp(-2πRm5).
The bi-axion potential has terms depending on A/fA and NA/fA+B/fB. For large N, integrating out the heavy mode imposes NA/fA+B/fB≈0 and gives a light mode approximately equal to B.

Conserved momenta associated with bulk Killing vectors give variations of geodesic length under endpoint changes. For spatial intervals, the derivative with respect to interval size measures the minimum spatial scale factor reached by the RT surface.

Thermal reference states are optimized by matching stress-tensor expectation values. Small-interval expansions, obtained by inverting geodesic relations in Fefferman-Graham coordinates, translate entanglement inequalities into asymptotic metric-coefficient constraints.

RT/HRT maps boundary entropies to bulk extremal-surface areas. Strong subadditivity is reduced to endpoint derivative inequalities; relative entropy is rewritten as S(ρ||σ)=Δ⟨Hσ⟩−ΔS using computable reference-state modular Hamiltonians.

Field redefinitions relate the α-attractor variables through φ/√6 = (1 − ρ)/(1 + ρ), remove subleading kinetic terms, and produce a canonical potential of the form αf²(tanh(ϕ/√(6α))). Special ξ models use an exponential Ω variable.
For Ω > 0, a conformal transformation gives KE = KJ/Ω + (3/2)(Ω′/Ω)² and VE = VJ/Ω². Choosing Ω or its inverse as field variable exposes the second-order pole.

Expand the kinetic coefficient as a Laurent series and the potential as a Taylor series, retain the leading pole at large e-fold number N, invert the resulting e-fold relation and obtain leading 1/N predictions.

Insert the perturbed ansatz into the eleven-dimensional action, reduce using internal total derivatives, Schouten and Bianchi identities, and perform an external Weyl rescaling to Einstein frame. The authors report computer-assisted tensor manipulations using xAct.

Expand the background and perturbation forms order by order in α. Use the Bianchi identity, harmonic projection and the ∂∂̄ lemma to separate leading harmonic (1,1)-forms from exact corrections parameterized by scalar functions ρ.
Solve the heavy-field F-flatness conditions, neglecting K_YW and K_ZW near Y=Z≈0. Substitute the solutions into both W and K, rather than into W alone, to obtain the effective inflationary theory.

Analyze radial minima and physical masses from the scalar potential and kinetic metric. To connect with the KYY model, use Φ=e^T, expand the transformed Kähler potential, and apply a holomorphic Kähler transformation with the corresponding transformation of W.

Define S by a discrete Fourier transform of partition functions over flat backgrounds, with normalization left arbitrary. Define T by multiplication by a quadratic Pontryagin-square background term. A five-dimensional topological two-form theory on an interval realizes these operations for four-dimensional one-form symmetries.

Use linking and intersection relations between symmetry defects and charged operators to define the symmetry action. Čech cocycles and networks with topological junctions encode background fields; charge-operator networks on a spatial slice are classified by H^q(M_(d−1),G).

Use cohomology of iterated classifying spaces and, when geometric dependence is included, cobordism to describe topological actions and inflow anomalies. Pontryagin-square operations encode quadratic responses to discrete two-form backgrounds, including torsion.

Analyze Jordan forms and conditions (T^p−I)^m=0 to relate monodromy eigenvalue degeneracies to logarithmic powers. Compute K and W from the resulting periods and evaluate leading scalar-potential terms.

Fix an integral symplectic period basis by mirror matching to large-volume D-brane central charges, then use integral combinations selected by the antisymmetric brane pairing. The stated Γ-class correction supplies the ζ(3)χ contribution that is added to the D6 central charge.

Solve fourth-order Picard–Fuchs equations for one-parameter periods using Meijer G functions and Mellin–Barnes integrals. Closing contours on opposite sides gives expansions near large and small complex structure; repeated poles generate logarithmic periods.

Use a local derivative expansion, retain operators to the desired inverse-cutoff accuracy, absorb classical and quantum divergences into brane couplings, and match amplitudes to the UV theory. For D-branes, disk and annulus amplitudes determine successive string-coupling orders. The toy scattering series can be geometrically resummed.

Estimate flux backreaction and counterterms by scaling dimensions and string-coupling power counting. Integrate Bianchi identities and apply flux quantization to constrain decays; distinguish Maxwell flux from conserved Page charge and its behavior under large gauge transformations.

The zero mode, fluctuation modes and scale factor are evolved together, with ⟨Tμν⟩ sourcing semiclassical Einstein equations. A power-spectrum prescription attributed to earlier work is evaluated at first horizon crossing k=aH and used to extract n_s and r.

Hartree closure replaces higher fluctuation powers by expressions involving their two-point function, producing a self-consistent Gaussian theory. The coefficients reproduce perturbative zero-, one- and two-point functions; diagrammatically this sums cactus diagrams. The cosine interaction acquires exponential suppression involving ⟨ψ²⟩/(2f²).

One-loop supergravity determinants are expressed through proper-time heat kernels. The logarithmic term uses the combination a₀M⁴/2−a₂M²+a₄, including gauge-fixing ghosts and the prescribed finite part of the AdS₄ volume.
Scalar and modulino masses are obtained from the effective Kähler potential and superpotential with canonical normalization. Bulk scalar masses are related to boundary dimensions by m²R_AdS²=Δ(Δ−3).

External fermion wavefunctions are treated nonperturbatively in the constant background. Plane-wave solutions give E_r²=m²+(B₀+λ_r|p|)²; helicity-dependent decay kinematics enforce conservation of total energy and momentum.

In the lowest-derivative truncation, integrating out nonpropagating torsion produces repulsive axial-current four-fermion interactions. A Hartree–Fock replacement of the total axial bilinear by an isotropic temporal condensate linearizes the resulting Hehl–Datta equations.

A Seiberg–Witten curve with meromorphic differential λ represents central charges as periods, charge pairing as cycle intersection and masses through pole residues. The review invokes the Riemann bilinear identity to relate UV couplings and Coulomb operators.
Seiberg–Witten special geometry packages local Abelian couplings in a holomorphic prepotential: τIJ=∂I∂JF and aD_I=∂IF. Electric, magnetic and flavor charges enter Zγ=a·γe+aD·γm+m·γf.

Protected quantities are approached through localization with the Ω-deformation and through string dualities. Nonrenormalization theorems permit classical computations in suitable M-theory or IIB descriptions; extension of localization to every Lagrangian N=2 theory is presented as a hope.

Special geometry encodes local low-energy couplings through τkl=∂ak∂alF. In curve realizations, λSW=ydx has periods ar and aD_r on canonical cycles with αr◦βs=δrs, and aD_r=∂arF. Changing the cycle basis gives a dual effective description.

Localization deforms the action by tQV. Under the stated supersymmetry conditions, Q-closed observables are formally t independent; positivity of the bosonic deformation localizes the large-t integral to a solution space that may have finite-dimensional components.

The review describes partial Ω-deformation as leading to an effective two-dimensional (2,2) theory. Its twisted superpotential comes from an instanton-partition-function limit; an argument identifies supersymmetric vacua with eigenstates of the corresponding quantized integrable model.

Group averaging projects the tensor-product Hilbert space onto invariants. Pólya enumeration expresses the untwisted partition function through the cycle index, substituting Z(iτ) for the variable associated with cycles of length i.

For symmetric products, a grand canonical generating function and its vacuum-adjusted p→1 limit give the infinite-N untwisted partition function. An inverse Laplace transform with a saddle estimate extracts its high-dimension growth.

Twisted-sector counting sums over commuting group elements and projects with centralizers. Modified torus moduli encode permutation orbits; seed Cardy asymptotics and convolution estimates supply the long-cycle growth argument.

An occupation-enhanced graviton rescattering estimate considers |N⟩→|N−2,1_k,1_k′⟩ with k,k′∼H. The outgoing pair is taken to lie outside the coherent background; the squared matrix element scales as α²N².

The estimated loss per Hubble time is accumulated until coherence changes by order one. The resulting service time is compared with Euclidean-action-suppressed fluctuation times and the proposed recurrence time.

Search using polynomial expansions, numerical integration and spike plots, Padé approximants and large-field asymptotics. Linearized eigenperturbations are treated analytically where possible and numerically using Chebyshev spectral methods.
Introduce the cutoff by replacing the background Laplacian with Pk after Hessian diagonalization. Extract V and F using a heat-kernel expansion through terms linear in curvature.
Functional renormalization group supertrace equation; exponential metric split g=ḡ exp(h); York decomposition, physical gauge fixing and diagonalization of the coupled scalar Hessian.

Impose unitary equivalence of density matrices on overlapping causal diamonds. Copy appropriate inside-horizon dynamics into another trajectory's outside factor, then match coarse-grained quantum dynamics to FRW hydrodynamics.

Estimate fluctuations using finite-entropy thermodynamics and reheating using semiclassical black-hole evaporation, matter-era dilution and the energy-density–temperature relation. These are model calculations rather than independently checked derivations here.
Construct Hamiltonians as traces of finite-order polynomials in fermion bilinears M. Count vanishing off-diagonal elements as localization constraints and relate entropy deficits to localized energy.

The paper specializes imported three-loop beta functions for products of simple gauge groups, searches for nonzero fixed points, and diagonalizes the matrix ∂iβj at those points to obtain gauge-kinetic operator anomalous dimensions and infrared stability information.

The mass-deformation analysis compares positive kinetic bilinears for real scalars and three-dimensional Majorana fermions with Hermitian kinetic bilinears for four-dimensional Weyl fermions. Gauge consistency is imposed through the summed cubic gauge-anomaly cancellation condition.

A modified CLASS Boltzmann code supplies the background solutions, linear cosmological perturbations, CMB angular spectra, and matter power spectra. Analytic interpretation uses a characteristic coupling function, an apparent dark-energy equation of state, and approximate total-matter growth equations.

Jordan–Einstein frame transformations are derived for background and first-order fluid variables. Conservation in the dark-matter frame permits exact integration of the background density when the Jordan-frame equation of state is constant. Perturbation transformations justify retaining vanishing pressure perturbation and shear for cold dark matter.

The inflation analysis uses second-order slow-roll expressions for ns and r at horizon exit, a numerical Hubble-slow-roll endpoint determination, and integration of the inflationary e-fold count. Horizon matching includes the curvature amplitude, potential-energy evolution, and expansion during reheating.

The superfield treatment diagonalizes scalar and fermion KK spectra, sums their one-loop contribution to the inflaton potential, and integrates out heavy states to obtain inflaton-linear effective operators. Perturbative four-body phase space then supplies the decay width; field-dependent KK masses are used to assess preheating.

Use quadratic constraints for embedding tensors in the SL(8) representations 36 and 36′, and compare the STU scalar potential with the maximal-supergravity potential. This also distinguishes the stated semisimple and non-semisimple branches.

For S^4 × T^3, use the branching through SL(3)_a × SL(5), then SL(4) and SL(3)_i. Require the same physical derivatives as in the toroidal dictionary; the authors identify this choice with a solution of the exceptional-field-theory section condition.

Branch representations of E7(7): the 56 identifies seven physical derivative operators, while the 912 embedding tensor supplies deformation components. Matching group-theoretical scaling weights to STU weights gives flux–superpotential dictionaries.

A background-field expansion X=X_0+Y uses Riemann normal coordinates around the classical embedding. Integrating fluctuations at one worldsheet loop introduces curvature counterterms in the effective action.

The FRW argument examines a local Taylor minimum a(t)=a_*+ct^(2n)+…, c>0, including n>1. A complementary geometric argument contracts the FRW Ricci tensor with a null vector, obtaining a factor proportional to −Ḣ+k/a².

A test string is chosen with tangent equal to an arbitrary spacetime null vector. Separating orders in α′ in its Virasoro constraint gives a null contraction of R_μν+2∇_μ∇_νΦ; conversion from string frame to Einstein frame produces a nonnegative dilaton-gradient square.
Combine analytic small-parameter expansions with numerical minimization in the modulus directions. Compute horizon-exit observables using slow-roll expressions ns=1−6ε+2η and r=16ε.

Expand the scalar potential about the vacuum in moduli displacements, minimize using the inverse scalar mass matrix, and substitute the shifts back to obtain the effective potential through quartic inflaton order.

Solve the extremal perturbation equations analytically and classify their near-throat modes. The paper checks numerics against analytic β=0 hypergeometric solutions and reports vanishing horizon energy flux Tab k^a k^b.

A duality chain maps the unperturbed toy background to an exact plane wave. The author uses regularity and exact string quantization in that frame to argue that strings remain well behaved at the original background's H=0 locus.

Use angular flux ansätze with radial functions; the Bianchi identities reduce these to a second-order ODE for g4. Numerically impose g4(x=0)=1 and horizon regularity, using x=(r+/r)^4 for D3 and x=(r+/r)^6 for M2.
Batalin–Vilkovisky formalism tracks gauge invariance through the master equation. The anomaly functional is A=(Γ,Γ)=〈(S,S)〉; the antibracket Jacobi identity supplies Wess–Zumino consistency.

Subtract divergences using parameter redefinitions and local canonical transformations. After transformations, re-renormalization and renewed finite counterterm tuning invoke an imported theorem preserving anomaly cancellation under convergent canonical transformations.

Chiral-dimensional/higher-derivative regularization combines physical d-dimensional field components and Dirac algebra with evanescent kinetic terms and gauge-invariant higher derivatives placed beyond the chosen truncation.

Planck maps are resmoothed to the BICEP2/Keck beam and passed through its observing/filtering matrix before comparison. Matrix-based purification suppresses E-to-B mixing; Planck single-frequency spectra use independent data-split cross-spectra.

The analysis extends the Hamimeche–Lewis likelihood approximation to correlated single- and cross-frequency spectra. Covariances include simulated signal–signal, noise–noise, and signal–noise contributions; parameter grids and COSMOMC explore the model space.

Validation uses tensor-free lensed-ΛCDM+noise+dust simulations, Gaussian and Planck Sky Model dust patterns, and an alternative compressed spectrum (BK×BK − α BK×P)/(1−α), with α_fid = 0.04 and residual dust uncertainty marginalized.
Compare the homogeneous energy E0=L V(p,ψmin) with two-region configurations, L=L1+L2, p1<p<p2, and p1L1+p2L2=pL. Choose the NS5 position to minimize the local potential separately in each region.
Use the imported NS5 worldvolume action, including its determinant tension term and B6 coupling, and generalize the static KPV potential to spatially varying ψ(s) and charge parameter p(s).

Estimate interface energy from the induced NS5 metric and additional worldvolume field-strength components. In the sharp-step limit, the author estimates a finite cost of order R rather than a cost growing with the external length L.

The FORTRAN95 implementation uses an openMPI master–worker scheme. Workers generate candidates that remain usable only if they satisfy the current likelihood threshold. Ordering parameters from slow to fast permits the triangular transformation and extra fast-direction updates to exploit cached likelihood calculations.

Recognize modes using mutual k-nearest-neighbor connectivity, increasing k from 2 until clustering stabilizes and recursively examining subclusters. Check approximately every O(n_live) iterations. Use cluster-specific covariance and estimated volume fractions to control replacement-point spawning.

Estimate covariance from live and inter-chain points, then use an inverse Cholesky transformation to whiten the constrained region. Starting from a random live point, perform one-dimensional slice updates along randomly oriented orthonormal directions, using initial width w = 1 in the transformed space.

Three primordial-spectrum reconstructions: penalized B-splines with roughness and endpoint penalties; movable log-log linear knots with Bayesian model averaging; and cubic splines with fixed, logarithmically spaced knots.
Bayesian posterior sampling and nested-sampling evidence using MultiNest/PolyChord, supplemented by maximum-likelihood χ² comparisons and simulation-calibrated frequentist feature tests.
Phenomenological spectral parameterization and second-order Hubble-flow slow-roll spectra; numerical mode evolution also reconstructs Taylor-expanded V(φ) or H(φ) without a slow-roll approximation.

Vacuum energies are modular integrals of the one-loop partition function. Theta-function modular transformations resum momentum sums for large-radius asymptotics. The authors report checking their models through partition functions, Poisson-resummed expansions, and explicit low-lying spectra.

Free-fermionic model building specifies boundary-condition vectors and generalized GSO phases k_ij. The construction uplifts existing four-dimensional models, recompacts with a CDC, and adjusts the CDC twist and prior projections to obtain massless boson–fermion balance.

Use integer Higgs-charge matrices and Smith normal form with unimodular basis changes to determine surviving continuous charges and finite factors. Redundancy reduction uses computer scanning with some analytic checks.

Extend the adjoint-derived charge lattice by singlets with charges ti + tj − tk − tl for four distinct indices, then enumerate theories obtained by Higgsing combinations of original and additional singlets.
Use Tate-fibration deformations to exhibit geometric Higgsing, Weierstrass coefficient expansions to examine heterotic dual data, and section-class effectiveness restrictions to remove non-flat loci.
Classify local stability using Jacobian eigenvalues. Numerical phase portraits and equation-of-state trajectories illustrate selected positive λ values and curvature signs, with wM = 0.
Rewrite Friedmann and Klein–Gordon evolution using dimensionless variables and N = ln a; eliminate the fluid density with the Friedmann constraint and solve for critical points.

For Model B, derive linear scalar perturbation equations in Newtonian gauge and Fourier space. This supplies equations and qualitative comments rather than a complete perturbation evolution or stability analysis.

Construct Hubble-normalized dynamical systems, solve for critical points, classify their eigenvalues, and integrate illustrative trajectories. The closure function A = −κn²fn/H yields a two-dimensional Model A or a three-dimensional Model B.

Vary the metric, scalar field, and fluid variables in the action. Project conservation equations parallel and perpendicular to the fluid flow to identify the energy-exchange vector and the modified fluid equation.

Vacuum-loop perturbation theory and dimensional regularisation illustrate the problem using a massive scalar with quartic self-coupling. Wilsonian integration of heavy modes provides an alternative description of sensitivity to the effective cutoff.

Sequestering varies the spacetime metric locally and two spacetime-constant variables, Λ and λ, globally. A function σ(Λ/(λ⁴μ⁴)) sits outside the spacetime integral; its variations generate integral constraints.

Quasi-static equilibrium balances production against depletion; efficient annihilation requires the QSE abundance to exceed the critical abundance set by H divided by the annihilation cross section. Freezeout matching and inverse-annihilation integrals supply the other approximations.

Coupled Boltzmann equations track modulus energy, two radiation densities and X/X' number densities in dimensionless comoving variables. Numerical solutions are compared with semi-analytic approximations, including reduction to a single X' evolution equation.

A Monte Carlo scan evolves soft terms from the GUT scale, enforces electroweak breaking and Higgs-mass constraints, and calculates spectra and DM observables using SPheno v3.3.3 linked to micrOMEGAS v3.

The analysis applies collider, flavor and relic-density cuts followed by direct and indirect searches, treating positive and negative μ separately. Approximate neutralino annihilation and Higgs-exchange amplitudes explain numerical correlations and cancellation regions.

The natural system is solved analytically through a function β and maps from the AdS5 construction discussed by the authors. Endpoint classification uses a simple zero of β for regularity, a double zero for D6 charge, and square-root behavior for an O6 singularity.

Numerical integrations begin with local endpoint expansions: analytic corrections in r^(4/3) near D6, in r^(4/5) near O6, and even/odd regular expansions. These supply boundary data for integrating the five-function system.

Generalized complex geometry packages supersymmetry into pure-spinor equations. An SU(2)-structure ansatz is transformed to vanishing intrinsic b-field, with auxiliary H′ = H − db and F′ = e^(−b)F; the spinor norm is then fixed using e^(3A−φ).

Compare two small-resolution phases related by a non-toric flop: a toric blow-up u → e1u, v → e1v, and a determinantal complete-intersection resolution introducing an auxiliary P¹ with coordinates λ1, λ2.

Compute Higgs charges through intersections of fiber curves with S1−S0 for U(1)6d and with the zero section for U(1)KK. Primary decomposition and prime-ideal methods identify the complete-intersection fiber components and their homology classes.

Use the nonperturbative topological-string prepotential to extract the quantities termed genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariants. The explicit enumerative survey constructs dP1-fibered Calabi–Yau models over P² and computes invariants through a suitable, unspecified degree.

Start from κ-symmetric superspace DBI and WZ actions, impose the orientifold-compatible fermion projection and bosonic truncation, and evaluate the curved-background action through quadratic order in fermions using type-IIB gravitino and dilatino supersymmetry variations.

Reduce ten-dimensional spinor bilinears with a 4+6 gamma-matrix decomposition and SU(3) singlet/triplet projectors. Classify mass terms by Hodge type and primitivity of the three-form flux; an explicit toroidal example illustrates the mass pattern.

Construct Kähler-potential/superpotential pairs with both S-linear and S-independent terms, analyze the real inflationary trajectory and transverse stabilization, and expand selected potentials in small SUSY-breaking and uplifting parameters.

Canonical field redefinition exposes plateau potentials; slow-roll predictions are organized in inverse powers of the e-fold number N. The authors discuss interpolation toward quadratic inflation and compare model curves with the historical Planck 2015 contours.
Boltzmann evolution for WIMPs, classical axion oscillator equations, and number-to-entropy yields organize production, annihilation and dilution during modulus domination and reheating.

Effective supergravity potentials specified by Kähler potential and superpotential; stationary, stable, nearly zero-energy vacua and canonical normalization are used to estimate modulus–gravitino mass relations.
Effective-equation-of-state matching relates observed scales to inflationary horizon exit. Separate visible/hidden entropy evolution and modulus partial widths relate dark radiation to ΔNeff.

Use nef and effective divisor cones, nonnegative triple intersections in a nef basis, divisor volumes and the classical axion metric to bound the cosine-defined domain. Integral intersections and competing divisor contributions provide additional, generally qualitative constraints on alignment.

For two axions, impose the convex-hull condition through (|z1|²−1)(|z2|²−1)≥(1+|z1·z2|)² and maximize the displacement using Lagrange multipliers. The paper reports a numerical maximization check of its result.

Eliminate ζ in unitary gauge using anomaly cancellation, then integrate out the massive vector through its equation of motion. The latter induces Stückelberg-mass-suppressed four-fermion interactions. Analyze the effective decay constant in limiting parameter regions and contour plots.

Use SO(2) rotations and rescalings to diagonalize the axion kinetic terms, rotate the Stückelberg charges and identify eaten and uneaten directions. The metric eigenvalues and charge components determine the Stückelberg mass and ξ's anomalous coupling.

Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the correlator on thermal-strip edges and in its interior. Approximate time-ordered factorization supplies the physical bound; the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle extends boundary control into the strip.
Map a complex-time half strip to the unit disk and apply Schwarz–Pick contraction in the hyperbolic metric to bound the derivative of a bounded analytic function.
The Rindler example uses analytic continuation of vacuum CFT four-point functions, operator-product expansion, spatial separation and smearing to establish uniform factorization control.

Canonical quantization and Fourier-mode traces produce regularized partition functions. Ground-state energies, momenta and fermion number are regularized; products are organized using chiral (1+1)d partition functions and massive theta functions.

CP or parity is enforced through orientifold projection and symmetry-twisted traces. The authors test large flux shifts and modular generators, and seek invariant weighted sums over spin structures and parity-twisted sectors.

For f=λφ² in the Ricci-free model, the authors reduce the system to a Hubble evolution equation and integrate it for k=0. The relation φ²ȧ⁵=C0 is used to determine the scalar evolution, and a recursive Hubble-parameter hierarchy characterizes departure from inflation.

For f=λφ, the scalar equation is integrated once and the integration constant D is set to zero to select the GB-associated contribution. Eliminating the scalar gives an integrated scale-factor constraint and, for k=0, an implicit hypergeometric solution whose early-time limit is compared with the Ricci-free equations.

Construct the supergravity F-term potential from K and W, solve stationary-point equations, and use the kinetic-metric-weighted Hessian for canonically normalized mass eigenvalues. The paper defines V_ij = (1/2)∂i∂jV in this mass calculation.

Solve ∂sV = ∂τV = 0 at fixed rolling θ, substitute the resulting saxion trajectory into the potential, uplift the minimum, and include saxionic as well as axionic motion when determining the effective kinetic term and canonical field.
Numerically evaluate slow roll using L = (1/2)f(θ)(∂θ)² + V(θ), including ε = (V′/V)²/(2f), η = V″/(fV) − f′V′/(2f²V), and the e-fold integral of fV/V′. Comparisons fix ns = 0.967.

The authors form heavy and light linear combinations of moduli, set stabilizers and the heavy combination to their minima, and study the resulting axion–saxion potential. Canonical normalization of the light axion determines its effective decay constant.

Model predictions for ns and r are compared with the observational contours used in 2015. The discussion also imports a leading heavy-spectator correction expanded in V0/M² and considers its flattening of the inflationary potential.

Diagonalize kinetic metrics through orthogonal rotations and rescalings, transform charges and anomalous couplings consistently, identify eaten and surviving axions, and diagonalize the instanton-generated mass matrix before interpreting effective decay constants.

Use dimensional reduction of R–R, DBI and D-brane Chern–Simons terms, followed by two-form/zero-form dualization, to obtain Stückelberg couplings. The low-energy potential is extracted through unitary gauge and elimination of heavy gauge and matter sectors.

They diagonalize G, canonically normalize the fields, and examine integer charges in the dual lattice to identify small-action harmonics. Instanton–string linking phases supply additional charge-selection constraints.

The authors solve spherically symmetric Euclidean Einstein–axion equations with specified asymptotic charge, re-deriving the Giddings–Strominger wormhole. They evaluate a half-wormhole action and use a dilute-instanton-gas treatment to infer harmonic contributions.

Specify a charged wall and two branches, calculate their energy difference at fixed scalar value, and insert tension and energy difference into the cited exponent. Applicability to non-metastable monodromy backgrounds remains unresolved.

Normalize each species' charge by its mass, add antiparticles, and test whether the resulting hull contains the extremality ball. An uncovered direction identifies black holes not discharged by that spectrum.

Transfer a support-function bound into a sum-of-squares bound. This avoids unique convex decompositions and avoids normalizing eigenvector projections into coefficients that may have mixed signs or zero total.

Turn instantons into particles using an external circle, fix gauge normalization from integral brane couplings, and transfer an endpoint particle constraint. The strong-coupling limit requires an M-theory lift before selecting extremality.

Five-dimensional necklace-quiver interfaces and anomaly matching test the geometric interpretation. Proposed orbifold Nahm poles use SU(2) embeddings in SU(kN), with t3 invariant and t+ of charge one under the specified Z_k action.

The protected S3×S1 index is evaluated using elliptic-Gamma contributions and contour integrals projecting onto gauge invariants. Elliptic Fourier inversion extracts a proposed strongly coupled trinion index from a Lagrangian index.

Baryonic and mesonic vevs implement puncture closure through Higgsing and integrating out massive fields. Index poles encode these flows; the prescribed residue removes a Goldstone contribution. Flipping an operator O introduces a singlet φ with W=φO.

The greedy algorithm repeatedly absorbs a perfect tensor with at least half its legs on the current cut. Its output is independent of inclusion order, but its locally minimal cut need not be globally minimal.

The RT argument uses strengthened max-flow/min-cut reasoning and unitary circuit interpretations. Greedy moves also construct local unitaries that distill boundary entanglement into EPR pairs and residual multipartite states.
Compose tensor isometries to construct encoders and push operators using TO = (TOT†)T. Different pushing choices give boundary representatives with the same action on the code subspace.

One-loop gauge kinetic thresholds and integration of heavy charged matter determine the gaugino-condensate superpotential. Requiring modular weight −1 constrains its η dependence, which is then compared with world-sheet instanton coefficients.

Modular covariance determines nonperturbative couplings from matter modular weights and Dedekind η functions. World-sheet terms contain η(T_i)^(2r_i), with r_i=−1−Σ_αm_α^i, yielding exponential moduli dependence in the adopted η approximation.

The benchmarks use supergravity F- and D-term potentials, mass-matrix eigenvectors, and numerical solutions of coupled field equations to assess stabilization during inflation and obtain slow-roll observables.

Construct and extremize the N=1 F-term potential using the tree-level, large-volume Kähler potential. Determine physical masses through the inverse Kähler metric times the half-Hessian, and evaluate F-terms and the gravitino mass.

Engineer common flux scaling by selecting a subset of superpotential terms, typically n+1 flux parameters for n complex moduli. Equal scaling of these terms predicts vev scaling; explicit extrema supply model evidence.

Use a twisted differential with nilpotency constraints for flux Bianchi identities, flux-induced tadpoles, and gauge invariance of the superpotential under D7-induced axion shifts to derive generalized Freed–Witten constraints.

Map the dominant classical instanton to a shortest-vector problem in the charge lattice with metric K^−1. Apply Minkowski's theorem and Stirling's approximation, then use LLL lattice reduction for numerical ensemble estimates.

Transform fields by a full-rank square charge submatrix: φ=Qθ and Ξ=(Q^−1)ᵀKQ^−1. The domain becomes an N-cube cut by additional charge constraints; its extent along the largest-Ξ eigenvector gives a diameter lower bound.

Use a spherically symmetric Euclidean wormhole solution, infer integer axion charge through the fluctuation coupling and Stokes' theorem, and evaluate half the wormhole action as the instanton action.

Evaluate the scalar potential and transverse scalar mass for monomial superpotentials, combine the two zero-potential branches to obtain a positive plateau, and introduce a function F to deform that plateau.

Use holomorphic field redefinitions and Kähler transformations, followed by asymptotic expansions in the canonical real field and large e-fold number N, to relate curved/flat formulations and extract inflationary predictions.

Uses large-complex-structure expansions of the Kähler potential and period vector, together with the Gukov–Vafa–Witten flux superpotential. Selected flux components suppress unwanted polynomial dependence; geometric exponential corrections supply the eventual axion potential.

Expands δK and δW at order ε, rewrites the F-term potential as real squares, and linearly shifts the heavy fields. The authors eliminate 2n+1 heavy-field contributions from 2n+2 squares, retaining one inflaton-dependent square at order ε².

Uses the null Raychaudhuri equation to connect Ricci convergence with focusing. Applied to event-horizon generators, finite-affine-time focusing and cosmic censorship support the classical area law and its thermodynamic interpretation.

Reviews a background-field expansion in Riemann normal coordinates, integration of worldsheet fluctuations at one loop, counterterm-dependent Virasoro constraints and a conformal transformation from string to Einstein frame.

Momentum-space conformal Ward identities reduce three-point functions to differential equations with hypergeometric solutions. Physical folded-triangle regularity selects solutions; analytically continued high-energy singularities fix normalizations.

In-in contour integrals and long-distance propagator expansions isolate nonanalytic exchange terms. Differential operators map conformally coupled to massless correlators; spinning exchange factorizes through three-point functions and inverse two-point functions with a helicity sum.

Solve auxiliary equations on each cosmological background and interpret the resulting Weyl-squared coefficient as local running. Use the factorized TT perturbation equations and previously studied numerical evolution; finally test the logarithmic form factor directly in de Sitter.

Integrate the conformal trace anomaly using a covariant fourth-order operator Δ4, two auxiliary scalar fields and an undetermined conformally invariant functional Sc[g]. Auxiliary-field boundary conditions encode those of the nonlocal Green functions.

Equal-time endpoints separated along one Kasner direction reduce the geodesic problem to ds²=z⁻²(−dt²+dz²+t^(2p)dx²), independently of spacetime dimension. The authors integrate using u=(dt/dx)² and v=z′z, hypergeometric identities, and smoothness at the turning point.

Heavy-operator correlators are approximated by exp(−mL_reg). Lengths are computed in z coordinates but regulated at constant z/t, corresponding to fixed proper boundary resolution, with the pure-AdS divergence subtracted.
Computes the two-axion mass matrix and its eigenvalues, then expands near αδ−βγ=0 to identify the light inflationary direction and its enhanced effective decay constant.

Represents a pseudoscalar as Φ=(f+ρ)e^(ia/f)/√2 and studies explicit breaking by cutoff-suppressed powers Φⁿ with n starting at five. These generate periodic phase potentials; non-Abelian anomalies provide the PQ-breaking mechanism relevant to QCD.
Uses a unit-determinant CKM convention, determinant expansion and repeated unitarity identities to express the CP measure J through the imaginary part of a three-element product.
Apply linear Einstein constraint equations, then expand a point-particle action to second order in the metric potential using the observer's proper time and average over high-frequency oscillations.
Use the Källén–Lehmann representation, conservation projectors, spatial Fourier transformation and an expansion in k²/µ to isolate the leading infrared stress correlations.

Estimate the scalar/vector ISW signal using a past-light-cone integral and the Limber approximation. Separately estimate gravitationally induced entropy and compare it with the Bekenstein–Hawking area bound.
Classify invariant differential forms by extending them to an ambient flat space, applying Lorentz representation theory and pulling the resulting forms back to the (A)dS hypersurface.

Decompose the left central charge into super Kac–Moody and unitary coset contributions. Combine nonnegative integer bosonic level, the central-charge budget and N=1 minimal-model restrictions to constrain candidate levels.

Translate spacetime isometries into physical world-sheet current charges, Wick rotate, and use compactness, unitarity and current two-point functions to show that left- and right-moving currents are separately conserved.

Dimensionally reduce the ten-dimensional action, including conformal rescalings and gaugino normalization. Leading-order equations, positivity and integration by parts imply internally constant scalar fields and vanishing H at zeroth order.

Use the internal gaugino equation to eliminate the condensate-induced terms in the dilaton equation, impose maximal symmetry in the Einstein equation, and integrate the internal divergence to obtain an algebraic equation for Λ.

Expand the density constraint and Lagrange multiplier perturbatively in the displacement a or squashing parameter σ. Integrate the density, evaluate the P-wave potential at its minimizing radius, and examine the D-wave quadratic-form eigenvalues.

Construct a Born-Infeld shell potential from the five-brane excess mass, coupling to the polarizing six-form, and the tachyonic D3 potential. Determine the charge density variationally using a global Lagrange multiplier enforcing fixed total D3 charge.

Compare the classical actions of spectator and dominant instanton families in the same kinetic metric. Examine whether all spectator contributions along the inflationary direction, and higher-charge contributions of the dominant family, remain suppressed.

Define a line through field space by a unit vector c0 and constrain every cosine argument to [−π,π]. Maximize the resulting line diameter over directions. Apply the convex-hull condition to z_k=Q_k/m_k and derive a contradiction for a diameter exceeding the stated bound.

The effective action uses off-shell dimensional reduction in four-dimensional N=1 superspace. Canonical normalization of localized wavefunctions generates physical Yukawa hierarchies, while Kähler four-point couplings determine scalar soft masses.

A perturbative reference-point method estimates vacuum shifts and F-terms. Full one-loop MSSM RG evolution connects GUT and electroweak scales; the Higgs calculation includes effects of unequal stop masses rather than imposing near degeneracy.
Uses the separate-universes approximation for long inflaton perturbations, and Gaussian field contractions to obtain the density power spectrum as a convolution of field spectra.

Integrates out the nondynamical time component, Fourier-decomposes transverse and longitudinal modes, and uses field redefinitions to identify scalar-equivalent limits. In the relativistic limit, π=(m/k)A_L has a free massless-scalar action.

Propagates Gaussian inflationary initial conditions with the classical longitudinal equation of motion, combining analytic regime-dependent scalings with numerical evolution. The late-time abundance integral is reported to approach a mass-independent factor approximately 1.2.

Use toric web splittings to identify complex deformations, and dimer diagrams with zig-zag homology classes to construct quivers, fractional-brane ranks, Higgsings, and the surviving two-cycle charges.

Use S/T dualities and Hanany-Witten configurations to identify axion monodromy with suspended D4-brane winding. Match dynamical scales along a fractional-brane Coulomb branch to extract logarithmic gauge-coupling dependence and estimate twisted-field backreaction.

Translate flux throats into Seiberg-duality cascades, infrared confinement and quantum deformations. Partial resolution corresponds to FI terms and bifundamental vevs splitting the gauge theory into two sectors.

Numerically evolves the exact two-field model and computes n_s and r along the trajectories using slow-roll relations. Appendix B also evolves the coupled canonical perturbation modes from a deep-subhorizon adiabatic vacuum to evaluate adiabatic and entropy spectra.

Rotates into the near-origin mass eigenstates, solves ∂V/∂ψ=0 for the trajectory ψ_s(φ), checks positive transverse curvature, and substitutes the trajectory into the potential to obtain an effective one-field theory.

Expands the effective potential near a saddle as a quadratic maximum, integrates slow roll, and estimates the trajectory endpoint by the vanishing transverse curvature. This yields approximate analytic relations between r, n_s, model parameters and the number of e-folds.

Combines imported random-sphere angle statistics, known face counts and the lower bound theorem for simple polytopes with the recurrence. Estimates use the smallest pairwise angles as candidate dihedral angles and sample a typical vertex, without constructing each complete polytope.

Derives vertex distances recursively using facet-normal lengths and mutual angles. The equal-distance, equal-angle model is treated explicitly; Appendix A extends the construction through successive three-dimensional subspaces to unequal distances and angles.

Numerical shooting starts at small positive η using endpoint Taylor expansions. Eigenvalues are selected by suppressing the singular endpoint branch. The implementation uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta, adaptive steps for backgrounds and fixed steps for modes.

Uses the imported KLT Hamiltonian treatment of constrained dynamical systems to obtain an unconstrained quadratic action. The paper contrasts this reduction with Lagrangian gauge fixing, which produces a different background factor.

Local asymptotic analysis separates simple and higher-order zeros of Q. Background equations cancel the dangerous x² ln|x| coefficient at a simple zero; a related expansion treats finite integer-order zeros.

Assesses BBN through extra radiation, estimates kinetic decoupling by equating dark Compton scattering and Hubble rates, and compares radiative cooling times with astrophysical times. A Landau-pole condition supplies an additional ultraviolet-dependent bound.

Uses separate entropy conservation to evolve the dark/visible temperature ratio after thermal decoupling, and a Boltzmann freeze-out estimate for annihilation into dark photons. Sommerfeld enhancement is imported as negligible for the relic abundance and omitted.

Estimates Debye shielding, the number of particles per Debye sphere, plasma frequency and Coulomb mean free path. Linear instability growth rates are then used to estimate shock formation, rather than deriving nonlinear shock saturation.

Combines normal-bundle splitting on P1, normal-bundle exact sequences and divisor intersections. The central relation is D·C=−2−deg(N_C/D) for a smooth rational curve inside a smooth divisor of a smooth Calabi–Yau. Fiber adjacency and preserved intersection sums then restrict wrapping configurations.

Imports the box-graph description of classical Coulomb phases, relative effective-curve cones and crepant resolutions. Weight-sign assignments determine fiber splittings, Cartan intersections and elementary flops; the paper extends the analysis beyond the U(1) inherited from U(5).

Uses algebraic stationary-point analysis with STRINGVACUA for a simple example and numerical continuation from aligned D-terms to deformed configurations. Uplift searches examine the effective dilaton potential, loop corrections and nonperturbative superpotential terms.

Uses the lower-index ansatz t_i=α ei and very special geometry identities to reduce stationarity equations and evaluate the Hessian. Alignment makes the T-modulus derivatives of the F- and D-term potentials vanish separately.

Tunes racetrack coefficients to obtain a sufficiently flat inflection region, then numerically follows the full field equations using canonical momenta and forward e-fold time. This formulation avoids directly computing Christoffel symbols in the evolution equations.

Uses the noncanonical field metric for ε and the most negative eigenvalue of the covariant potential Hessian divided by V for η. Estimates scalar power, ns and r with slow-roll expressions and examines real and axionic stability.

Treats g as a shift-symmetry-breaking spurion and expands the effective potential in gφ/M² to assess technical naturalness. Hubble-damped slow roll scans the Higgs mass; stopping is estimated by matching the periodic-potential slope to the scanning slope. QCD barriers depend on the Higgs vev through quark masses.

Uses parametric inflationary inequalities, estimates of quantum diffusion and tunneling, and reheating evolution. The non-QCD analysis uses naive dimensional analysis, Λ⁴≈4πfπ′³mN, together with radiative lower estimates for mN and its Higgs-induced contribution.

Use F-theory/M-theory/type-IIA duality followed by mirror symmetry to obtain type-IIB vacuum geometry. Abelian orbifold mirrors are assembled from torus and C² LG sectors, retaining allowed twisted-sector deformations of total weight one.

Locate conformal limits by tuning deformation coefficients to quasi-homogeneous singularities; organize deformations using the Jacobian-ring relations ∂f/∂zi=0. Identify emergent class-S punctures through differential pole structures, explicitly illustrated for E6.

Scalar expectation values are estimated by balancing tachyonic Hubble-induced or soft masses against Planck-suppressed stabilizing interactions. The explicit construction follows the thermal singlet potential and Higgs–slepton flat-direction potential.

One-loop QCD running with heavy-particle thresholds estimates the early confinement scale. In the light-gluino regime, the axion potential is obtained from gluino condensation with one SUSY-breaking spurion insertion.

Linear eigenvalues use Leaver continued fractions, Newton–Raphson iteration, 10⁴ recurrence terms, and a sixth-order small-ak angular-eigenvalue expansion. Selected overtone results are compared with time-domain evolution.

Scalar evolution uses either 3D finite differences in periodically reset ZAMO coordinates or angular pseudospectral decomposition, sixth-order radial differences and fourth-order Runge–Kutta evolution. The sine nonlinearity is evaluated through a truncated Taylor expansion.
Gravitational perturbations are computed with a time-domain Teukolsky equation sourced by the simulated scalar stress tensor, using angular spectral decomposition and finite differences.

Reduce ten-dimensional α′³R⁴ terms for one Kähler deformation, match their four-derivative terms to a supersymmetric off-shell operator, and infer its potential correction. Homogeneity identities and the intersection-form signature support the subsequent volume-Hessian analysis.

Solve the one-field auxiliary cubic exactly and compare small-T branches; use a one-loop Wess–Zumino effective auxiliary-field potential to study truncation artifacts. For multiple fields, eliminate auxiliaries perturbatively to linear order in T.
Thermal relic abundance uses tree-level effective annihilation and coannihilation of the full weak triplet, including dark-color averaging and Dirac versus Majorana multiplicity.
Dark-radiation temperature is estimated with instantaneous decoupling and separately conserved comoving entropy: T_d/Tγ=(g*ᶠ/g*ⁱ)^(1/3). Its energy density is then expressed as ΔN_eff.

DM–gluon scattering retains the dominant forward t-channel contribution, regulates its logarithmic divergence with Debye screening, and supplies drag terms for numerically integrated linear fluid perturbation equations.

Treat W and its derivatives through third order at the chosen point as independent complex variables. First derivatives fix SUSY breaking, second derivatives solve stationarity linearly, and third derivatives adjust the scalar mass matrix.

For the near-supersymmetric construction, impose Vαβ=0 to pair scalar masses and combine stationarity with the geometric sGoldstino bound. Near no-scale points, the authors also construct examples without this pairing restriction.

Auxiliary-field linearisation of four-gravitino interactions, followed by Euclidean integration over graviton and massive-gravitino fluctuations. The one-loop expansion through Λ² is interpreted as Einstein-Hilbert and curvature-square corrections; stationary conditions are imposed on Λ and the condensate.

Match SUGRA and running-vacuum beta functions dρΛ/dln H² with cosmic RG scale μc=H; integrate the Friedmann and energy-exchange equations. An effective scalar description is reconstructed from total energy density and pressure.

Functional RG equations are constructed using the background field method, exponential metric parametrization g=ḡ exp(h), York decomposition, and a physical gauge suppressing vector and trace fluctuations. A scalar field redefinition diagonalizes radial–metric mixing.

The main calculation uses a type-I cutoff replacing background Laplacians by regulated operators, with profile Rk(z)=(k²−z)θ(k²−z). Its gravitational prefactor depends on running F and the background scalar. A scalar-free cutoff provides a scheme comparison.

The authors use analytic fixed-function ansätze, linearized eigenperturbation equations, large-N reduction with hypergeometric solutions, and numerical shooting with Taylor and asymptotic matching for the dressed Wilson–Fisher candidate.

Compare local and spatially averaged Raychaudhuri equations using expansion invariants and the noncommutation of averaging with time evolution. Expansion variance supplies a contribution absent from the corresponding local equation.

Appendix B examines weak and distributional derivatives, integration by parts and nonlinear products using local Sobolev spaces. The proposed regularity setting includes γ in W_loc^{1,2} intersected with L_loc^∞.

Analyze the polyhedral-sphere analogy using intrinsic versus extrinsic geometry and Gauss–Bonnet. Appendix A discusses constructive conformal mappings through circle packing or polyhedral uniformization rather than assuming metric closeness.

Use the four-dimensional N=1 F-term potential V=e^K(K^{αβ̄}DαW Dβ̄W̄−3|W|²), the tree-level Kähler potential and a two-step moduli-stabilization expansion around an approximately supersymmetric vacuum.
