Dimensionally reduce the D6-brane DBI action to obtain the large-field potential, described as summing α′ corrections to that potential. Apply single-field slow-roll analysis and compare predictions for 50 and 60 e-folds with the observational bounds used in 2015.

Evaluate critical-point spectra with the inverse scalar kinetic metric rather than the raw Hessian. Fermion shift matrices provide the supersymmetry conditions and an alternative expression for the scalar potential.

Solve the embedding-tensor linear and quadratic consistency constraints, then identify inequivalent solutions under the global duality group. The classification includes the unimodular ξ deformations and the independent massive deformation.

Use the going-to-the-origin approach: noncompact dualities place scalar extrema at the origin, and residual SO(4) transformations diagonalize Q. In the ξ=0 branch the constraints then imply diagonal Q̃, automatically satisfying the axion equations.

The authors expand independent real-holomorphic functions f and g in a small variable x, extract the constant and linear terms of the potential, and expand the transverse scalar mass. These expansions identify which coefficients affect the inflationary plateau and fall-off.

Canonical field redefinitions and Kähler transformations relate flat and logarithmic constructions. An explicitly proportional f–g choice cancels the negative potential contribution and supplies a separate arbitrary-potential construction.

Magnetic monopole self-energy estimates and naturalness bound the abelian EFT cutoff. Convex-hull black-hole discharge conditions, integral charge quantization and kinetic-matrix diagonalization then relate the cutoff to multi-axion field ranges.

Adiabatic tracking of KK masses across Wilson-line backgrounds diagnoses spectral flow through the cutoff. A lattice regulator and a Pauli–Villars regulator illustrate sensitivity of individual-mode evolution to ultraviolet physics.

The extended-WGC analysis includes the KK U(1) and uses the full charge-to-mass convex hull. A separate lattice-WGC argument estimates the collective contribution of exponentially many subleading instantons.

Represent Σ as H²/Γ and construct the corresponding Euclidean AdS3 quotient; interpret the CFT path integral on Σ as state preparation. Thin causal-shadow annuli are conformally mapped to cylinders whose evolution operators approach the identity away from sewing vertices.

Compare the sewing picture with RT/HRT mutual information. Finite-temperature calculations use geodesic lengths encoded by SL(2,R) matrix products and traces, truncated series expansions in Mathematica, and numerical evaluation.
Use planar BTZ coordinates, orthogonally intersecting hyperbolic geodesics, and large-length asymptotics to locate nearby horizons. Apply Gauss–Bonnet to the geodesically bounded causal shadow.

Use constant-domain analytic mixing and a small-conversion phase-integral representation to interpret simulations. Test smooth versus cloudy plasma profiles through the trajectory of the complex photon amplitude, and convolve conversion maps with a CAB spectrum for observational bands.

Propagate a three-component vector containing two photon polarizations and one ALP. Include absorption with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and density-matrix evolution ρk=exp(−iHkδz)ρk−1 exp(iHk†δz), using environmental quantities at each domain centre.

Integrate out the heavy quark sector to inspect the effective light-quark mixing matrix. Classify dangerous renormalizable and higher-dimension operators by symmetries, and estimate threshold phases through Δθ̄≈Im Tr(y^−1Δy), including one- and two-loop contributions.

Analyze supersymmetric superpotentials, holomorphy, flat directions and soft terms. A single-modulus superpotential/Kähler-potential example illustrates CP-conserving heavy-axion stabilization; schematic flux-landscape counting motivates a separate ultraviolet genericity critique.

Vacuum reconstruction uses spectrum-condition tube analyticity and continuation from spacelike-separated configurations. The trivial-current example additionally uses Reeh–Schlieder, the Källén–Lehmann representation and a cited free-field characterization.

Start from a group of abstract unitaries V(a,g), impose one-parameter-group, restricted additivity/locality and central-commutator relations, take its complex linear span, and complete in the supremum of all GNS operator norms.

Local and causal Poincaré lemmas control supports of co-primitives. Their proofs use de Rham cohomology, homotopy invariance and Alexander duality; translation of test functions then establishes centrality of spacelike potential commutators.

Promote ten-dimensional R4 contractions to curvature invariants of a block metric whose torus complex structure is τ. Hold the auxiliary torus volume fixed, allow only ten-dimensional derivatives, and retain the ten-dimensional integration measure.

Expand around flat space to fourth order in hmn, φ and C0; compare momentum-space expressions using Mandelstam variables, permutations, total derivatives and lowest-order equations. Field redefinitions identify actions differing by terms proportional to those equations.

Extract terms linear in the external Ricci scalar, express internal curvature through the third Chern form, and use adjunction and double-cover relations to obtain the weak-coupling orientifold expression.

Null tests compare equivalently processed observations and FFP8 simulations, typically using 1000 realizations. Methods include variance, skewness, kurtosis, and a low-resolution multivariate-Gaussian quadratic-form test; poorly conditioned covariance matrices are treated by removing degenerate eigenmodes.

Real-space N-point functions use correlated χ² statistics, a connected four-point function, and an inverse-covariance bias correction. Morphology is tested with classical and normalized Minkowski functionals, including needlet components. Filtered-map peak distributions are compared with simulations using KS statistics.

BipoSH estimators probe off-diagonal harmonic covariance, subtract simulation-estimated mask mean fields, and account for mask-modified shape functions. Directional clustering uses local half-mission cross-spectra and a Rayleigh statistic that discards amplitudes. Polarization stacking is assessed with integrated profile deviations.

The authors inspect the lattice dispersion relation near zero momentum and the Brillouin-zone edges. A local charge-density interaction is written in momentum space to illustrate how interactions can populate low-frequency modes near the lattice edges.

For superposed spacings, the displayed interaction integrates over Δ and Δ′ as well as momenta. The substitutions l → kΔ and l′ → −π + k′Δ′ isolate a displayed phase exp(−ixπ/Δ′). Its oscillatory integration is the proposed mechanism for removing low-momentum coupling to edge modes.

Constructs SU(3) or orthogonal SU(2) forms from complex one-form bases, derives diagonal metrics and fluxes, and imposes radius equalities to remove unwanted Bianchi-identity terms. Computes Ricci tensors and studies the fluxless smeared limit.

Studies Buscher duality through generalized vielbeins and O(N,N) transformations. Whether compensating O(N)×O(N) transformations are globally defined is central to distinguishing torus metrics from nontrivial solvmanifold quotients.

Uses generalized complex geometry and pure-spinor supersymmetry equations, together with orientifold compatibility, structure-form compatibility, RR/NSNS Bianchi identities and calibrated sources. The sufficiency of these conditions for the equations of motion is imported background material.

Uses the Goldstone boson equivalence theorem for heavy-quark decay ratios. Estimates collider exclusions by combining existing search cross-section limits with NLO heavy-quark pair-production cross sections, including HATHOR in the stable-particle reinterpretation.

Estimates the strong-CP contribution of dimension-five gravitational operators and translates the neutron-EDM constraint into a parity-breaking scale and mirror-mass bound. Perturbatively diagonalizes mixed quark mass matrices to derive Higgs-mediated flavor violation and decay couplings.

Matches vector-multiplet kinetic terms to three-dimensional N=2 supergravity and uses a Legendre transform to chiral coordinates Ti. Proposes divisor integrals, rewrites them with delta-currents and uses moduli derivatives of the warp equation to relate their variations to the reduced metric.

Dimensionally reduces the Einstein term and higher-curvature terms on the corrected background, adding the flux contribution and compactness/tadpole constraint. Much of the kinetic action is reviewed from Part I; the scalar-potential cancellation is developed here.

Ensemble-average the anomaly equations to obtain five coupled Boltzmann equations with helicity sourcing and sphaleron conversion. Numerically evolve in x = Dmp/T from reheating to about 10 TeV, using Γw ≈ 25αw⁵T and Γs ≈ 100αs⁵T.
Apply finite-conductivity magnetohydrodynamics, neglecting ∂tE, to obtain E·B = B·(∇×B)/σ. With the assumed field evolution, derive ḣ = −2I exp(2πξ)(Hinf/a)⁵/(σξ⁶), where I = 6.8×10⁻⁴ and ainf = 1.

Quantize the transverse gauge field in circular polarizations and solve A±″ + (k² ± αkΦ′/f)A± = 0. Use the amplified mode approximation and a cutoff kc ≈ 2ξaHinf to estimate gauge-field energy and current helicity, retaining the amplified polarization.

Compare local metric/dilaton scaling and flux-leg orientations using e⁻φ|H3|² = e^(φ−8A−2f)|αF3+X3|². Evaluate horizon potentials and charges to obtain MADM = Vol4(αH Q3 + bH Q5 Vol2), then combine this with the polarized-cycle volume and anti-D3 mass scaling.

Adapt the inherited conserved boundary-integral formalism relating IR data to generalized ADM mass. For NS5 sources use B = −C4∧F5 − B6∧H3 + ⋆10d(φ−4A−f), avoiding the patching problem of the magnetic B2 potential. The relation is derived from Einstein and form-field equations.

Fix T(x)=τ before quantization to obtain a physical square-root Hamiltonian. Separate Cgrav=−Λ det(E)+CEinst and expand in inverse bare Λ; then use a Born–Oppenheimer product state, neglect the background state's time derivative at first order, and subtract the constant Emin.

The appendix reviews a topological lattice argument: generic two-level crossings yield Weyl Hamiltonians, helicity is associated with the sign of a velocity-matrix determinant, and phase-oriented curves in compact momentum space balance left- and right-handed crossings.

Use a state-dependent, graph-preserving regulator built from gravitational fluxes and SU(2)/Yang–Mills edge holonomies. A degravitating map removes gravitational labels, while a dressing map adds gravitational amplitudes; their required composition is GΓFΓ=I on the lattice-theory space.

Branch the embedding tensor fα[MNP] in (2,220) of SL(2)×SO(6,6), identify SO(3) singlets, and match representation weights to physical derivatives, geometric moduli, and fluxes. The 40 invariant components organize a duality-covariant set of superpotential couplings.

Use quadratic constraints to distinguish consistency from maximal uplift: QC4=0 ensures closure of the N=4 gauge algebra; additional QC8=0 permits an N=8 lift. For orientifold backgrounds, nonzero QC8 expressions are interpreted as tadpoles supported by allowed BPS sources.

Evaluate the imported leading slow-roll bispectrum formula for the excited state and compute the perturbation energy-density difference from Bunch–Davies. The bispectrum state functions use F(k)=|βk|²+αk*βk; energy-density differences are finite for states of at least fourth adiabatic order.

Condition the short-mode covariance on a long Bardeen-potential mode, using G=(5/3)BR/[ΔR(k)ΔR(kl)]. Expand G in Legendre polynomials and powers (k*/k)^αL, then use the induced CMB covariance and Wigner-3j couplings to calculate typical modulation amplitudes ⟨AL(ell)⟩ averaged over M.

Numerically evolve perturbations through the bounce and encode their state at slow-roll onset in Bogoliubov coefficients αk,βk relative to Bunch–Davies modes. This supplies a physically evolved excited state instead of postulating its coefficients directly.
Generalized unitarity sews physical, gauge-invariant tree amplitudes with D-dimensional physical-state projectors, avoiding explicit treatment of the p-form ghost structure.

The calculation combines bare two-loop diagrams, one-loop single-counterterm insertions, and tree-level double insertions, with infrared singularities subtracted. The authors also report a direct ultraviolet extraction using masses as an infrared regulator.

Dimensionally reduce the democratic ten-dimensional Type II actions, expanding RR/NS fields in internal harmonic forms and keeping their external four-form components. Impose higher-dimensional Hodge dualities at the equations-of-motion level to avoid double counting.

Organize the action into quadratic four-form terms and linear couplings to flux-weighted axion polynomials. Integrate out the nondynamical forms, using equations of motion or Lagrange multipliers, and compare with standard supergravity potentials and auxiliary-field relations.

Track toroidal T-dualities that exchange four-forms and their moduli-dependent kinetic coefficients. For the proposed corrected potential V = f(V0), apply the chain rule at stationary points to relate corrected and uncorrected Hessians.
Open-string Chan–Paton orientifold projections determine the spectrum. Annulus/Möbius open–closed duality explains the extra Ramond-sector sign through the antibrane's reversed RR charge.
SO(6) representation selection rules and decomposition under SU(3) identify flux-induced fermion masses; scalar-mass statements are taken from earlier analyses summarized in the text.
Toric web diagrams, orientifolded dimers, Seiberg-duality cascades, and infrared confinement track complex deformations and the appearance of an O3-plane at the throat tip.

The component analysis solves the auxiliary-field constraint using nilpotent goldstino bilinears. At quadratic fermion order, gamma traces and divergences of the modified Rarita-Schwinger equation identify constraints; gauging away the composite goldstino recovers the conventional massive-gravitino equation.

Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations, superspace density identities, and a chiral Lagrange multiplier convert the constrained gravitational formulation to two-derivative supergravity. The multiplier imposes X²=0; nilpotent expansion and a Kähler transformation simplify the minimal dual action.

Solve geodesic/axial-gauge conditions for gravitational Wilson lines, average line directions to obtain Coulomb dressing, and combine an initial Coulomb-defined frame with timelike geodesics for worldline dressing.
Construct a metric-dependent displacement V with Φ(x)=φ(x+V)=φ+Vμ∂μφ+… and δVμ=κξμ. A linear metric kernel must satisfy the displayed differential constraint 2∂′νfμνλ=δ⁴(x−x′)ημλ.

Use a neutral-particle mixing Hamiltonian with dispersive and absorptive off-diagonal terms, time-dependent oscillation functions, and integrated decay-rate differences to estimate CP asymmetry. The calculation considers one singlet generation and neglects direct CP violation.

Weak associativity is encoded by associator isomorphisms satisfying coherence identities. For finite G, a group-cohomology 3-cocycle with trivial coefficient action supplies the associator and obeys the pentagon identity.

CMB constraints use decay-induced ionization and heating, redshift-averaged deposition efficiencies and CosmoRec modifications of the ionization history. Quark and gauge-boson limits are obtained by efficiency rescaling of existing bounds.

An imported perturbative relation expresses Δ=(e−3p)/T⁴ as A+B⟨φ†φ⟩/T. The lattice condensate supplies the nonperturbative input; integrating Δ gives pressure, and susceptibility information stabilizes temperature derivatives needed for heat capacity and sound speed.

Monte Carlo updates combine overrelaxation and heat bath sweeps. The gauge-invariant Higgs condensate is renormalized and extrapolated linearly in a; partial O(a) improvement is deliberately not implemented.

Operator ordering is specified by analytic-continuation contours around lightcone branch points. A clockwise circuit z → e^(−2πi)z defines the shockwave second sheet; positive OPE expansions bound its magnitude by first-sheet data, whose t-channel identity behavior controls possible singularities.

Classify exponential terms by coefficient signs, arrange one higher-derivative term to dominate the observable inflationary interval, and complete a square with the relevant positive loop term. Shift the canonical field to express left- and right-rolling potentials around their uplifted minima.

Calculate slow-roll observables through a large-e-fold expansion, then perturb the plateau by a rising exponential. Estimate spectral-index corrections, running and integrated scalar-power changes, and provide numerical parameter examples at 55 e-folds.

Construct a supersymmetric light-quark effective theory, integrate out squarks and the srelaxion at leading order in the quark mass, and represent nonperturbative QCD through the chiral condensate to obtain relaxion and relaxino interactions.
Track electroweak breaking using D(a)=(mHu²+|µ|²)(mHd²+|µ|²)−|Bµ|². Analyze its sign changes as soft terms scan, then balance the sliding-potential slope against Higgs-dependent QCD barriers.

Expand the superspace Lagrangian around an auxiliary-field background, canonically normalize matter superfields, and extract soft terms. The appendix includes anomaly contributions and Higgs-sector threshold contributions to gaugino masses.

Map polarization dependence to linear algebra. With H+={ε1,ε2}/2 and H−=i[ε1,ε2]/2, define x=(Tr H+)², y=Tr H+², z=Tr H−². The quartic bound is (2c6+c7)+(32c1+4c2+2c6)x+(8c2+16c3+8c4+2c6+2c7)y+(−16c3+8c4−2c6+2c7)z>0 for every physical polarization pair.

Compute the cylinder correlator with a visible φψψ insertion on the D3 boundary and two universal fermionic zero modes θθ on the instanton boundary. Extract the momentum-independent contact term; opposite-boundary insertion positions prevent the collision poles discussed in the paper.

Express winding correlators as derivatives of the classical partition function with respect to complex brane separation. Poisson resummation and Kronecker's second limit formula give a torus Green function after removing the zero closed-string term responsible for the tadpole divergence.

Picture-change the three matter vertices, factorize bosonic, spinor and ghost correlators, sum spin structures using theta identities, and integrate vertex positions after an open/closed-channel modular transformation. The bosonic derivative correlator receives only classical winding contributions.
The radial potential is expanded to second order about |Φ|=Φ₀ and minimized. During slow roll, superpotential derivatives are neglected in an approximate potential proportional to (Φ₀²−3)|W|².

After freezing the radial mode, the phase is canonically normalized and the resulting potentials and masses are evaluated. Superpotential parameters are adjusted to cancel the vacuum cosmological constant in the examples.

Test candidate bounds using protected chiral spectra and central charges in supersymmetric AdS/CFT examples, free-field spectra, and supersymmetric anomaly formulas in Veneziano-limit SQCD. The SQCD test uses the lightest protected baryon with qB=Nc and Δ=(3/2)Nc(1-Nc/Nf).

Translate extremal-black-hole decay or scalar-hair instability conditions through the AdS/CFT relations between bulk kinetic terms and current/stress-tensor central charges. Monotonicity of the small extremal black hole mass-to-charge ratio makes the smallest semiclassical-hole limit determine the simple kinematic bound.

Reduce the problem to a universal partially off-shell action with auxiliary field F, scalar composite X=Ω²/(2F), and symbolic coefficients FG0,A,B,C. Apply the non-Gaussian elimination procedure previously used for pure de Sitter supergravity; alternatively identify these entries directly in a partially off-shell Poincaré-supergravity action.

Impose the multiplier equations to obtain X1=(Ω1)²/(2F1), integrate the ordinary auxiliary fields Gaussianly, and use nilpotent spinor identities to remove or shift specified X1-dependent terms. A rescaling absorbs the nilpotent-direction metric into the remaining auxiliary variable.

Heatbath ensembles permit large volumes and short autocorrelation times in pure glue. Susceptibility is obtained from the volume-normalized connected variance of topological charge, with an infinite-volume limit in its definition.

Four treatments of the noninteger discretized charge are compared. The subsequent analysis selects the prescription showing little spacing/volume dependence, uses the largest volume at Nτ = 6, and fits a DIGM-inspired power law with both normalization and exponent free.

The abundance estimate combines approximate oscillation onset, 3H(T1) ≈ ma(T1), with adiabatic conservation of ρR³/ma and a spatial average of the initial misalignment. The present susceptibility is approximated by its zero-temperature chiral-perturbation-theory value.

Steepest-descent approximations are applied to background and fluctuation path integrals, retaining the perturbation action through quadratic order. Scalar and transverse traceless tensor harmonics on S³ reduce the calculation to complex mode solutions and on-shell boundary actions.

Slow-roll and superhorizon asymptotics are matched to numerical mode evolution along the straight contour τ=iy. Growing/constant and decaying coefficients are fitted as functions of mode number, initial field magnitude and phase; bending of the actual AdS contour is then estimated.

BPS equations yield the supersymmetric KT solution; second-order equations yield a two-parameter nonsupersymmetric asymptotic family through order z⁴, parameterized by S and varphi. This rederives backgrounds previously obtained in ten dimensions.

Gauge-preserving bulk supersymmetry and diffeomorphisms generate boundary Ward identities. Differentiating source-dependent identities produces contact terms. Bosonic VEVs are evaluated using radial canonical momenta and, for flat domain walls, superpotential counterterms Sct = −2∫√−γ W.

Holographic renormalization defines one-point functions by differentiating the renormalized action with respect to composite induced fields at a finite radial cutoff. The cutoff is removed only after evaluating correlators, accommodating the cascading logarithmic divergences and operator mixing.

Radial OPE expansions track phases of double-trace dimensions after Lorentzian continuation. For the exact two-dimensional bound, quantization on the pillow T²/Z₂ gives a positive elliptic-nome expansion; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the Lorentzian answer by a finite Euclidean correlator.

Contour pinches and Farkas' lemma yield position-space Landau conditions: α_ij d_ij²=0, nonnegative α_ij not all zero, and a weighted-gradient sum vanishing for every integration coordinate. The latter becomes momentum conservation at internal vertices.

Near a bulk collision, a contact Witten diagram is approximated by flat-space plane waves. Momentum conservation leaves an overall-energy integral involving the fixed-angle amplitude A(ωp_a), relating short cross-ratio distances to high-energy bulk scattering.

For global dS₂ the substitution z=exp(Ht) exposes poles at z=±i and infinity; four distinct winding-one contours are summed with branch-cut-dependent residues. The black-hole leading exponent uses a counterclockwise figure-eight contour enclosing ρ=±B.

The reviewed functional Schrödinger, in-in construction transports vacua through complex time or space. Winding-number-one contours of the frequency or momentum determine the mean pair number; contours of all winding numbers enter vacuum persistence.

Assess proposed decay paths subject to Gauss-law and Bianchi constraints. The author's electrostatic example distinguishes varying an energy expression from imposing the physical constraint through the action, warning that an unconstrained ansatz can spuriously lower the apparent energy.

Construct successive descriptions retaining supergravity, Kähler moduli, and throat-bottom modes; replace the throat sector by its dual KS gauge theory; then use a nilpotent goldstino multiplet at very low energy. Gaugino condensation, when responsible for the exponential term, admits a higher-energy description retaining that sector.

Interpret the brane action as a low-energy EFT and organize classical self-field divergences by scale, including renormalization-group reasoning. For small gp, regulate at the string scale and determine finite coefficients by matching to perturbative string theory, rather than treating divergent supergravity fields as the ultraviolet completion.

Generate charged black branes from the Horowitz–Strominger solutions by lifting and dimensional reduction; rotate scalar combinations into coupled and decoupled fields. Lift charged black holes to strings, boost along the compact direction, and reduce to obtain mixed KK charges and ADM extremality bounds.

Evaluate Euclidean instanton actions with Gibbons–Hawking–York boundary terms, reduce the on-shell action to boundary contributions, and minimize over the core parameter. Compare the resulting boundary expression with the higher-dimensional ADM mass.

Expand the four-dimensional scalar potential at large volume, impose D-flatness, and examine extrema and Hessians. Charged matter and instanton modes are counted or bounded through Ext groups, Riemann–Roch, Serre duality, exact sequences and monomial counting.

Use reflexive-polytope triangulations, combinatorial divisor Hodge numbers, intersection-ring linear algebra and Kähler-cone tests in Sage; then scan quantized D7 fluxes and B-fields subject to Freed–Witten and D3-tadpole constraints.

Estimate probe backreaction by comparing local stress-energy contributions of the wrapped D5-brane and source D3-branes. For the resolved conifold, approximate the warped volume using the smeared, l=0 warp-factor mode.

Dimensionally reduce the D-brane DBI action to obtain the four-dimensional gauge coupling and axion kinetic term. Combine them with the assumed WGC and stretched-string mass estimate m∼Ms²ℓΦ to bound the decay constant.

Use Fefferman–Graham asymptotics to argue that finite boundary curvature contributes only subleading bulk curvature: the displayed scalar curvature is R = −d(d+1) + z²R0. Together with localization of quantum effects, this supports a fixed boundary metric away from the singular time.

Apply the No Transmission Principle by contradiction: a bulk causal path between regions dual to independent boundary theories would transmit a forbidden boundary signal. The argument does not invoke a particular N or coupling.

Start from the supergravity F-term potential and tree-level no-scale identity. Since the flux superpotential is independent of Kähler moduli, S and U can be stabilized supersymmetrically while the Kähler directions remain unstabilized at this order.

Assemble volume-dependent corrections: universal α′³ scaling V^(−3), loops V^(−10/3), leading F⁴ correction V^(−11/3), anti-D3 uplift V^(−2), and hidden matter V^(−8/3). In the two-modulus case, nonperturbative effects add a negative logarithm-dependent contribution after eliminating τs.

Determine five parameters using an inflection condition, a slope–third-derivative relation targeting the spectral tilt, stationarity and zero energy at the minimum, and scalar-amplitude normalization. Numerically study both the resulting single-field potentials and two-field background trajectories.

Test the proposal using null shocks, including multiple shocks and locations, and static surrounding shells. Compare action changes with circuit-complexity expectations, scrambling-time cancellations, and gravitational redshift.

Evaluate the regulated on-shell action of the WDW patch and its time derivative. Neutral and rotating examples require cancellations between Einstein–Hilbert and surface terms; charged examples also involve the Maxwell term. The reported asymptotic divergences are time independent.

Analyze logarithms and contact terms in marginal-operator and stress-tensor correlators. In d=2 this imposes constraints beyond Wess–Zumino consistency: the extra parity-odd two-form is closed and the candidate connection curvatures vanish locally.

Construct superspace anomaly sigma models, expand components and integrate the anomaly on spheres. The d=4 construction uses a target-covariant FTPR-type operator; consistency fixes its connection to be Levi-Civita.

Classify local Weyl variations using spacetime and target-space covariance, Wess–Zumino consistency, and equivalence under variations of local counterterms. Nonremovable terms are universal anomalies.

Apply the imported proposal C(t)∝Vol(Σt)/(Gℓ), with Σt a spacelike codimension-one extremal, maximal-volume surface anchored at boundary time t. The estimates primarily concern bare complexity with a time-independent UV cutoff in the selected boundary frame.

Use the Kasner volume Euler–Lagrange equation and null asymptotics, exact initial/final topological-crunch slices, and approximate UV/IR surface decompositions for thin- and thick-wall dS/crunch geometries.

Nonperturbative superpotentials and leading α′ corrections are combined to construct extrema. Modulus F-terms determine the displayed soft terms, which are then discussed after running from the string scale to the electroweak scale.

Exploit the absence of propagating bulk gravitational degrees of freedom: after fixing identifications, hair is generated by nontrivial boundary diffeomorphisms. A time-symmetric solution is encoded by a circle map φ↦ϕ(φ), and its stress tensor follows from a Schwarzian transformation law.

Construct the vacuum region through dilations and AdS translations, then minimize the integrated energy over extensions into the hairy region. C1 matching is imposed; an auxiliary angle satisfies an implicit transcendental equation, with energies also displayed numerically.

Expand Einstein equations in perturbation amplitude ε, with higher-order sources built from lower orders. Analytically continue positive-frequency perturbations around η=0 and diagnose particle production through positive/negative frequency mixing.

Canonical phase-space path integration, Dirac constraint treatment, and gauge fixing Ṅ=0 reduce lapse integration to proper time. Radiation conservation follows from integrating its canonical variables; the remaining isotropic path integrals are Gaussian.

For anisotropies, transform to conserved momenta on H^M × R^(D−2), solve the radial Wheeler–DeWitt equation, and construct the propagator by the Wronskian method using Hankel-function modes selected by complex-plane regularity.

Taylor-expand the determinant around constant curvature in the Weyl–traceless-Ricci–Ricci basis, where background Weyl and traceless-Ricci tensors vanish. Match quadratic coefficients to Einstein or Einstein–Gauss–Bonnet forms.

An equivalent linear action determines maximally symmetric vacua. An equivalent quadratic curvature action determines the free spectrum; it agrees with the full action through O(h²), while generally differing at O(h³).

For the preferred family, introduce y=1+λ/(n−2) and count roots of y^n−2y^(n−1)+(1+λ0)=0. Appendix C combines Sturm chains and monotonicity within the positivity interval, separately for even and odd dimensions.

Large-deviation probabilities distinguish typical gapped spectra from atypical dangerous light modes or unusually heavy sectors. The authors also propose combining direct stability checks of retained fields with RMT assessment of truncated fields.

The fermion mass matrix is modeled statistically using the Altland–Zirnbauer CI ensemble. The imported tree-level scalar–fermion mass relation maps its spectrum to a large-N scalar spectral density; light-field counts follow by integrating below a correction-sized mass threshold.

The numerical inflation treatment re-solves heavy-field extremum conditions as the axion varies and evaluates single-field slow-roll quantities with the induced kinetic metric. The pivot is chosen to match the quoted spectral index; the reported scalar amplitude is used to infer Hinf.

A twisted differential encodes H, geometric, Q and R fluxes; D²=0 generates Bianchi identities. The orientifold separates flux contributions to F- and D-term potentials, with additional mixed identities constraining the D-term model.

Stationary points and canonically normalized scalar mass matrices are evaluated analytically or numerically. Small-vacuum-energy expansions characterize the brane branch; a large-λ expansion integrates out heavy moduli after adding a P-flux deformation.

Use approximate vacuum-realignment relic densities and inflationary isocurvature amplitudes. Add the two dark-matter densities and the uncorrelated isocurvature powers, applying misalignment-angle priors to sketch viable parameter regions.

Compute color and electromagnetic anomalies from charges; convert derivative fermion couplings using equations of motion. Nucleon couplings use imported hadronic matching formulas and specified F,D,S inputs.

Higher-spin Ward identities, conformal properties, permutation symmetry and cluster decomposition fix their correlators; OPE expansions then reconstruct current correlators.

Fourier transformation in the minus coordinates turns charge-conservation identities into polynomial relations involving hypergeometric form factors. Uniqueness is established by subtracting solutions, dividing by powers of 1+z and evaluating at z=−1, where z=p⁺1/p⁺2.

Ordered lightcone limits first take x⁺12→0 and then transverse separation to zero, with different scaling factors isolating bosonic, fermionic and tensor behaviors. These limits convert selected symmetric-current three-point functions into free-field expressions.
Minimize the softly broken supersymmetric Higgs potential to leading order in msoft/M, track phases in Higgs bilinears and soft parameters, and examine axion stabilization when mirror QCD dominates.
Analyze renormalizable scalar potentials and quark mass matrices, estimate phase-generating loop corrections, and constrain symmetry-breaking scales using higher-dimension operators.

Classify extrema and mass spectra, extract their flux scaling, and seek new Minkowski minima by solving stationarity and zero-vacuum-energy conditions with an uplift contribution included from the outset.

Coupled Fredholm equations determine anomalous dimensions. Inside loop integrals η(q²) is approximated by η(k²), motivated by the integrals' peak near q = k; external momentum dependence and the distinction between η(0) and η(k²) remain.

Functional RG vertex flows for two-point functions and the graviton three-point function, using dressed classical tensor structures. Closing the three-point flow requires vertices containing up to five fields.

Transverse-traceless tensor projections separate momentum-dependent and cosmological terms. The three-point function uses equal momentum magnitudes with angle 2π/3; bilocal evaluations at p = k and p = 0 extract G and Λ3.
Insert the flux-imposed relations between fermion masses and scalar trilinears into previously computed one- and two-loop beta functions, including nonstandard soft terms.

Expand the D3 potential V = e^(4α) − C around a minimum and identify its Hessian with scalar mass terms. A combination of bulk equations fixes the Hessian trace in terms of the IASD flux that also determines fermion masses.

Decompose four-point functions into group-invariant tensor structures and solve representation-valued crossing relations. For tensor external representations, Young projectors with traces removed construct the relevant structures.

In u ≪ v ≪ 1, matching the crossed-channel identity fixes leading large-spin OPE coefficients. Matching minimal-twist log(v) terms gives anomalous dimensions proportional to ℓ^(−τm), with coefficients determined by the exchanged operator's OPE data.

The large-group argument uses positivity of a twist-density integral. A leading isolated log(v) would require a derivative of a delta function in that density, violating positivity; a finite number of higher-spin currents does not remove the obstruction.
Background Klein–Gordon evolution is treated with exact Bessel-function solutions for power-law expansion, numerical integration when components compete, and a late-time WKB approximation.

Nonlinear clustering is described through a Schrödinger–Poisson approximation and its density/velocity representation, with a quantum-potential force encoding scalar gradient energy. Simulations must distinguish suppressed initial power from modified wave dynamics.

Linear field perturbations are rewritten as fluid equations and implemented in Boltzmann calculations. After oscillations begin, time averaging gives c_s,eff² = [k²/(4m_a²a²)]/[1+k²/(4m_a²a²)] in the time-averaged axion-comoving gauge.

Hamiltonian Gauss constraints and spatial operator algebras diagnose nonfactorization. In ordinary lattice scalar electrodynamics, left and right gauge-invariant algebras still omit a Wilson-line degree of freedom; shared central electric-flux operators obstruct tensor factors.

Introduce auxiliary Aμ and a constraint multiplier σ, integrate out Gaussian z fields, solve the large-N gap equation, and extract the induced Maxwell term from the quadratic effective action using Feynman parameters. An induced Einstein-Hilbert estimate supplies the species correction in the gravity comparison.

A gauge-covariant OPE relates φ†(x)φ(y) to a straight Wilson line times a c-number propagator plus less singular terms. The argument uses conformal state-operator reasoning and a leading nontrivial scalar-QED diagram calculation, with separation much smaller than the inverse charged-particle mass.

Construct nonlinear RN-Ψ and boson-star families as coupled radial ODE boundary-value problems, using asymptotic expansions at the AdS boundary and regular horizon or origin. The author reports thermodynamic first-law agreement better than 10^{-6} for hairy black holes.

Determine scalar-condensation onset by linearizing η=y^{3/2}η1 around charged global-AdS RN black holes. At fixed charge, normalizability at the boundary and regularity at the horizon determine the threshold solution and its mass.

Use small-scalar-amplitude expansions, hypergeometric leading toy-model profiles, and fully nonlinear numerics. The GHPT ground-state series is calculated through l^{30}; inversion of its charge series and fits to coefficient growth estimate a convergence radius.
Studies inflation with potential slow-roll parameters, n_s = 1 − 6ε + 2η and r = 16ε, numerical benchmarks over 50–60 e-folds, and reheating estimates from decay widths using Γ ≈ H(T_R).

Uses imported mirror-symmetry and N = 2 special-geometry results for quantum-corrected periods. The prepotential contains polylogarithms weighted by genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariants; these determine corrections to K and the flux superpotential.
Evaluates the supergravity F-term potential after fixing heavy fields, treating KKLT and LVS stabilization separately and introducing an uplifting sector to obtain a Minkowski minimum.

Map processing includes detector-pair differencing, atmospheric and scan-synchronous filtering, and deprojection of temperature-to-polarization beam leakage. External maps are beam-matched and passed through the observing matrix. Separate matrix purification operators suppress E-to-B mixing for the two BK bands.

An extended Hamimeche–Lewis likelihood uses simulation-derived covariance of auto- and cross-spectral bandpowers, with terms of zero expectation set to zero. COSMOMC explores a lensed-ΛCDM+dust+synchrotron+r model; separate per-bandpower fits provide a presentation-level component decomposition.

The UV construction uses N−1 hidden SU(ki) sectors with one flavor coupled to Xi and ni flavors coupled to Xi+1. Integrating out these charged fields produces anomalous axion couplings; hidden gaugino condensation generates the dominant mixing potential.

A Higgs superpotential involving XN−1² and XN², together with a mixed Kähler term, generates the driving potential and relaxion-dependent μeff and Bμeff. The Higgs scan is analyzed through the determinant of the MSSM Higgs mass matrix.

The authors first identify canonically normalized heavy and light combinations in a two-axion example, then generalize to N axions and integrate out N−1 heavy modes to obtain the relaxion effective potential.

Start from a supergravity action off shell only in the chiral auxiliary fields. Integrate out spectator Fi first, leaving F1 with coefficient g1bar1 − g1barj(gbarji)−1gibar1, the relevant Schur complement of the Kähler metric.

Substitute the auxiliary solution back into the action. The authors identify cancellations of terms involving the nonconstant Schur-complement coefficients, leaving the standard component action with a composite scalar substitution plus explicit fermionic corrections, summarized in equation (38).

Expand the remaining coefficients in nilpotent z1 and zbar1, redefine F1 to absorb selected z1-dependent pieces, and solve its field equation using a finite Grassmann expansion. Nilpotency makes the inverse-auxiliary Taylor expansions exact rather than an infinite perturbative series.

Couple endpoint scalars to fermions charged under confining gauge groups. Their induced axion couplings sample the exponentially different zero-mode overlaps at sites 0 and N, producing two periodic potential terms.

In the Wilson-line UV sketch, charged bulk link matter generates Casimir potentials depending on Aharonov-Bohm phases (πj−qπj+1)/f. Endpoint five-dimensional Chern-Simons couplings then couple the surviving axion to two nonabelian gauge sectors.

Expand about the symmetry-breaking vacuum, retain angular modes, and diagonalize their nearest-neighbor quadratic matrix. Infinite-chain Fourier modes give mθ²=εf²(1+q²−2q cosθ); finite-chain boundary conditions additionally allow a normalizable zero mode.

Track auxiliary-field dependence through the vielbein expansion. After integration by parts, the brane action contains auxiliaries only linearly or quadratically without derivatives, permitting linear algebraic equations and standard Gaussian elimination.

Vary constrained superspace vielbeins to obtain the curvature-superfield equation. Express the brane source through a superspace delta function and the chiral projector D̄D̄−R, then use the source's nilpotency.

Impose Wess-Zumino gauge and brane static gauge, integrate the bulk Grassmann coordinates, and obtain the vielbein expansion recursively by rescaling the fermionic coordinates ϑ→tϑ and using superspace torsion constraints. The vector-supervielbein series terminates at fifth fermionic order when dϑ is counted.

A finite scan of toric B2 bundles over P1 restricts twists through monomial inequalities excluding forbidden singularities, then estimates h3,1 using monomial counts and dual-polytope face corrections.

Toric lattice-point enumeration determines Weierstrass monomials, divisor vanishing orders and generic non-Higgsable factors. Counting monomials with an automorphism correction reproduces the stated complex-structure Hodge number.

The imported Ashok–Denef–Douglas estimation framework is implemented through lattice points in a b4-dimensional sphere of radius √(2Q), using a Jacobi-theta generating function, contour integral and large-dimension saddle point.

Modular transformations and theta-function series evaluate the new theta4 logarithmic-derivative integrals from D9–D5 annuli and twisted Klein bottles. Finite terms are expressed through trigamma and Clausen functions; stated domains include 0<γ<1, or 0<γ<1/2 for the Möbius integral.

For N=2 sectors, introduce momentum/winding lattice sums, separate their zero-mode divergence and evaluate the finite part using Poisson resummation and non-holomorphic Eisenstein series Es(U)=Σ′(Im U)^s/|m1+m2U|^(2s).

Extract the order-p² coefficient of a two-graviton one-loop amplitude, summing torus, annulus, Möbius and Klein-bottle surfaces. For the latter three, perform the even-spin-structure sum early and transform to the tree channel only at the end.

Numerical BAE solutions motivate a continuum eigenvalue ansatz. The authors extremize a dilogarithmic Bethe potential, balance large-N terms to obtain imaginary eigenvalues scaling as √N, and evaluate the residue expression on the resulting density and tail solutions.

On the gravity side, BPS equations become algebraic near the horizon. Constrained attractor extremization fixes horizon scalars, allowing comparison of both the entropy and the R-symmetry with the field-theory extremum.

Supersymmetric localization expresses the index as a meromorphic contour integral summed over gauge magnetic fluxes. Jeffrey–Kirwan residues select the contour; resumming fluxes relocates the calculation to Bethe Ansatz Equation solutions, with a Jacobian for the residues.

Regulate each scalar using five Pauli-Villars fields and impose the stated sums over statistics and regulator masses. Use the same regularization scheme for the gravitational effective action and the entropy so their divergent contributions can be compared.

Illustrate scale separation with two axions coupled in nonorthogonal combinations to three gauge sectors. Rotate to canonically normalized heavy and light modes and integrate out the heavy combination to identify the actual cutoff of the single-field theory.

Impose a Dirichlet brick wall at r=r_H−ε, count near-horizon modes using WKB and large-angular-momentum approximations, obtain the thermal free energy, and calculate S=β²∂F/∂β before evaluating it at the de Sitter temperature.

Use the N=1 supergravity effective action, inverse-volume moduli stabilization and soft-term formulas to compare scalar masses with the volume-modulus mass separately for each matter-metric and uplift case.

Canonically normalize modulus, axion and visible fields; expand kinetic and volume-dependent mass terms to cubic order; integrate by parts and use leading equations of motion to extract two-body decay rates, including Higgs, scalar and Higgsino thresholds.

Numerically run Yukawa couplings and soft terms at one loop using SusyHD and SARAH, with illustrative GUT boundary conditions, then evaluate decay widths at m_Φ rather than directly using high-scale masses.

Numerically evolve the multifield background with its field-space metric and fit the potential along the inflationary valley. Compute scalar and tensor spectra through Mukhanov–Sasaki mode equations with Bunch–Davies initial conditions, rather than relying entirely on slow-roll estimates.

Apply the multi-axion convex-hull prescription to charge/action vectors. Subleading η terms shift n_i to n_i+12k_i, with analogous shifts for the second instanton family, enlarging the hull beyond that of the two leading instantons.
Expand η(T)=exp(−πT/12)∏ₖ[1−exp(−2kπT)] to identify leading and subleading instantons, then integrate out the heavy axionic combination to estimate the light-field potential and its modulations.

Differentiate S=A/4 along the congruence and combine the resulting entropy derivatives with the optical Raychaudhuri equation. With twist absent and shear negligible, the authors obtain R_μνv^μv^ν=−S̈/S+(1/2)(Ṡ/S)².

Construct locally stationary or near-equilibrium congruences by treating C=R_μν(p)v^μv^ν as constant near p and solving the shear-free Raychaudhuri equation. Select an integration constant for which θ vanishes at λ=0 and examine a sufficiently small open patch excluding that point.

The appendix reproduces a statistical-mechanical argument using a quadratic entropy expansion about a maximizing density ρ₀, linear Onsager evolution δρ̇=Lδρ, and an eigenfunction expansion of the assumed symmetric operator. The generator L is additionally presumed time independent over the relevant interval when differentiating the entropy.
Late decay is parametrized by Γτ = mτ3/(2πM*2), TRH ∼ g*−1/4√(ΓτMp), and dilution factor Yτ = 3TRH/(4mτ). Net yields are ηB = Yτ BrN εB and ηd = Yτ Brφ εd.

Separate entropy conservation relates post-decoupling temperatures through g*s. For relativistic dimension-six contact scattering, the authors estimate Γ ≈ 0.039T5/Λ4 and set Γ ≈ H to find decoupling, then match quark operators onto nucleon scattering amplitudes.

Decay asymmetries come from tree–one-loop interference with both CP-odd coupling phases and an absorptive CP-even phase. Cutkosky cuts identify on-shell intermediate states; vertex and self-energy loop functions are evaluated for scalar decays to fermions.

Rotate the two scalar fields, reduce to the inflationary valley, and use single-field slow-roll formulas for ε, η, the e-fold integral, n_s, and r. Compare trajectories with N*=50 or 60 against the historical Planck 2015 constraints.

Dimensionally reduce the DBI action, identify its Taylor convergence radius after field stretching, and compare its square-root potential with a quartic description. The displayed comparison fits the quartic phenomenologically rather than treating it solely as a literal Taylor truncation.

Compute the zero-mode one-loop potential through Kaluza–Klein expansion and ζ-function regularization, including gauge, Stueckelberg, ghost, and fermion contributions. Retain the leading fermionic harmonic for the main Dante's Inferno potential and estimate the omitted gauge-loop contribution.

Fit the oscillatory spectrum to the paper's Planck temperature-anisotropy and low-multipole polarization data using CosmoMC with the PolyChord nested sampler. Translate likelihood constraints on oscillations into bounds on the potential modulation.

Expand the background inflaton, Hubble slow-roll parameters and comoving curvature perturbation to first order in a small modulation parameter b. Parameterize the resulting spectrum as PR(k)=PR⁽⁰⁾(k)[1+δns cos(φk/fmod+β)].

Apply the convex hull condition to the light-direction projection of axion couplings. Compare couplings producing alignment with instanton couplings required by the WGC, then integrate out the heavy directions.

Correlation functions are calculated perturbatively with the in-in formalism, treating quadratic π–σ mixing as insertions and combining it with cubic interactions for bispectra. Free scalar mode functions use the Bunch–Davies choice.

The Stückelberg construction introduces π and σⁱ to restore diffeomorphism invariance, then interprets them as Goldstones in a gravitational decoupling limit. Quadratic and selected cubic operators organize the calculation in derivatives, slow roll and α.

Euclidean spacelike results are analytically continued using Q=iq, ϕ=iχ and b=−iβ. A background-field expectation value and Schwinger–Keldysh interpretation supply Lorentzian effective dynamics with retarded Green functions.

The momentum tensor is obtained by metric variation, including variation of the nonlocal Green function, and alternatively reconstructed from Ward identities. A local auxiliary-field formulation reproduces the nonlocal expression after eliminating its auxiliary fields.

Covariant heat-kernel regularization and dimensional regularization determine the coincident Green function and metric dependence of renormalized exponential operators. The calculation relies on the imported result that free-field normal ordering removes short-distance divergences of the interacting spacelike Liouville exponential.
Match the expected asymptotic anti-D3 ADM mass to near-source flux behavior through the Smarr relation. This constrains backreaction without solving all local equations of motion.

For the polarized anti-brane system, evaluate an infinitesimal ten-dimensional inner boundary with B=−C4∧F5−B6∧H3. Magnetic dipoles require gauge-field patches; overlap contributions are essential to the mass formula.

Use the five-dimensional Komar mass at spatial infinity and Stokes' theorem to express mass through an inner-boundary contribution and a bulk integral H∧F. H is described as the harmonic part of the dual field contracted with the timelike Killing vector.

Use formal rescalings of ranks, fields and fluxes to rescale the potential and explore mass-scale ratios. The rank rescalings must leave λNc and λNf positive integers; choosing β=1 preserves the stated D3 tadpole under the formal transformation.

Directly minimize the coupled four-complex-field potential VF=e^K(K^(ΦΦ̄)DΦW DΦ̄W̄−3|W|²). Local stability is evaluated with a mass matrix using the inverse real kinetic metric and the potential Hessian.

Express VF as h+hc cosϕnp+hs sinϕnp. The phase extremum obeys ϕnp=arctan(hs/hc)+nπ; the displayed dS extrema select even or odd branches. This reduces the phase analysis while retaining the coupled moduli dynamics.

Embedding-space polarization vectors encode symmetric traceless tensors. Differential operators acting on scalar three-point functions and partial waves construct spinning conformal blocks; conservation and Ward identities constrain their coefficients.

Match direct-channel identity exchange to infinite crossed-channel spin sums, using large-spin Bessel-block asymptotics and replacing sums by integrals. Match subleading log(v) terms from J/T exchange to anomalous dimensions; use an OPE-coefficient ansatz Aℓ^B 2^(−2ℓ).
Match the X-induced uplift, proportional to |ρ|²/(βV^(4/3)), to warped antibrane tension. Allowing ρ(φ)=ρ0+ρ1φ+… reproduces the Coulomb expansion, with |ρ0|∼e^(−2ϱ) and |ρ1|∼e^(−6ϱ).

Evaluate the supergravity F-term potential, minimize it with approximately vanishing cosmological constant, and extract soft terms from matter-metric derivatives. Include nonperturbative effects, the extracted text's “α0” corrections, mixed matter–X couplings and anomaly mediation.

Dimensional reduction of D6 DBI and Chern–Simons actions, retaining two four-dimensional derivatives and quadratic open-string fluctuations. A reduced axion–four-form coupling gives a Kaloper–Sorbo description and integer potential branches.

Two-step moduli stabilization followed by an effective N=1 F-term potential; transverse Hessians estimate stability. The simplified DBI potential is then analyzed using single-field slow-roll parameters.

Split the fluctuation Hessian into local and nonlocal terms. The matrix determinant lemma isolates the nonlocal correction; Gel’fand–Yaglom initial-value problems determine the local determinant, and a Dirichlet Green function evaluates the remaining term.

Morse theory relates negative fluctuation modes to focal points on the trajectory caustic. A separate proper-time saddle calculation formally reproduces the short-path contribution, rather than independently evaluating the full finite-temperature decay problem.

Rewrite the scalar determinant as a proper-time integral over worldlines. Evaluate proper time by a saddle approximation, then solve the worldline equations by steepest descents. Temperature is implemented by endpoint shifts x→x+nβê4 in the heat kernel.

Construct the string toy potential from D5-brane DBI dynamics, magnetic worldvolume flux, and adjoint position scalars containing Higgs doublets; canonically normalize the Higgs before interpreting its scanned mass.

Estimate branch-changing membrane nucleation using thin-wall Coleman–De Luccia tunneling, retaining gravitational backreaction. The bubble appendix expands in small p = κT/H while allowing q to remain finite.

Integrate out the four-form to obtain a branched scalar potential. The reviewed Kaloper–Sorbo example gives VKS = (f0 + gφ)²/2. An alternative formulation dualizes the scalar into a two-form eaten by the three-form.

Replace a direct calculation of the lowest nonzero internal Laplacian eigenvalue by the estimate MKK^(2−d) ∼ ∫√gd e^(4A)Rd. Dimensional analysis and a quoted Lichnerowicz result motivate this proxy; the actual KK spectrum is not computed.

Repeat the integrated argument with an e^(2φ) weight. This weight is selected using a classical scaling symmetry; integrating the weighted dilaton equation by parts introduces a dilaton-gradient term into the denominator of the curvature-ratio diagnostic.

Use traced external and internal Einstein equations to express curvature integrals through flux energies, dilaton gradients, and source tensions. In ten dimensions, the integrated dilaton equation eliminates the NS-flux contribution and exposes positivity bounds.

Derive the bosonic potential from the off-shell auxiliary-field action, imposing that Fφ has no bosonic component before integrating out Fs. Separately use holomorphic field redefinitions and Kähler transformations to simplify the general constrained Kähler potential.

Solve the global superspace component constraints, replacing the sgoldstino by S = (χs)²/(2Fs) and expressing the sinflaton, inflatino, and inflaton auxiliary field through the goldstino, Fs, inflaton, and derivatives.

Implement S² = 0 through a chiral superconformal Lagrange multiplier and SB = 0 through a complex vector multiplier in a D-term. Use local tensor calculus and supercovariant derivatives, then simplify the component constraints in χs = 0 gauge.

The note advocates searches using theoretically motivated correlator templates with few parameters, since unrestricted time-dependent EFT functions are unsuitable for significant detection. Deriving production-induced oscillations without continuum averaging in a slow-roll regime is proposed future work.

Classical adjustment of heavy fields in V({φ_H},φ) illustrates flattening. A schematic two-term stabilization potential is f₁(φ)x^γ₁+f₂(φ)x^(−γ₂), with f₁,f₂,γ₁,γ₂>0 and x a ratio of internal length scales; flux–axion dependence changes the preferred x as φ evolves.

Constraints containing the unknown fermion and its derivatives on both sides are inverted iteratively. Goldstino nilpotency terminates the substitutions; the new fermion-only constraint is also expressed through a composite vector field and a chiral field-strength constraint.

Superspace actions specified by Kähler potentials and superpotentials are reduced to components using G_α=0. Field redefinitions and Kähler transformations simplify allowed couplings; auxiliary-field elimination requires care because composite constrained components can make their dependence nonquadratic.

The authors use standard two-component superspace methods. Applying the highest relevant covariant spinor derivatives and then taking lowest-component projections isolates equations for the removed components; lower projections are assessed as consistency conditions.

Matched asymptotic expansions use an inner region x≪1, an outer region x≫σ and overlap σ≪x≪1. Hypergeometric inner and confluent-hypergeometric outer solutions are matched with physical QNM boundary conditions; proximity to Gamma-function poles selects frequencies.

Eikonal WKB combines angular Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization with a radial-potential extremum and its curvature. A secondary approximation for the angular eigenvalue gives algebraic frequency and peak-location conditions, interpreted through unstable photon orbits.

Numerical evidence uses Leaver continued fractions, root searches and contour maps distinguishing zeros from poles. The DF implementation uses 500+ terms; RN's four-term recurrence is reduced by Gaussian elimination to a three-term recurrence and radial continued fraction.

Reviews dimensional analysis and the path-integral quantization of Einstein gravity as diagnostics of the short-distance problem. Graviton scattering and quantum corrections to Einstein solutions are offered as representative quantities affected by ultraviolet divergences.

Uses an explicitly quasi-Bayesian illustration: a 50% multiverse prior, followed by three discretionary reductions of the no-multiverse probability by approximately a factor of two. This produces the author's rounded 94% estimate rather than a fitted statistical posterior.

Uses compact regular semiclassical NBWF saddles, WKB classical histories and probabilities proportional to exp(-2IR). Bottom-up history probabilities are conditioned on at least one occurrence of ultralocal observer data to obtain top-down probabilities for local observables.

Explains the numerical trends with a single-field cubic inflection-point potential V0 + λ1φ + λ3φ³/6, with positive coefficients. Fitted scaling λ3 = V0^α gives α approximately 0.8175 from two observable slopes; this is a phenomenological fit rather than a compactification derivation.

Monte Carlo integration of the curved six-field background equations. Wilson coefficients are independent Gaussian draws with zero mean and width Q; Q is sampled uniformly over [0, 0.3], and log10 a0 uniformly over [-5, -2]. Fixed choices include rUV = 1, T3 = 10^-2, initial x = 0.9, angular coordinates equal to 1 and zero initial velocities.

Fifth-force limits are converted from Yukawa-potential strengths using material lepton charges. Stellar bounds use emission and trapping recasts; BBN bounds use expansion and neutrino-annihilation rates for selected extra-radiation limits ΔNν = 0.5, 1, 1.5.

Published dark-photon searches are recast using production couplings and channel branching fractions. For visible searches the stated relation is gL² Br(Z′→ℓℓ̄) = ε²e² Br(A′→ℓℓ̄); invisible searches instead use the neutrino branching fraction.

Neutrino–electron scattering includes pure Z′ exchange and interference with SM amplitudes. Solar rates integrate the flux and recoil cross section, with flavor oscillations incorporated through Pee dσe/dT + (1−Pee)dσμ/τ/dT.

Derives cosmological equations in both F-flat and R-flat reference gauges. Their variations agree on the Minkowski fiducial background, yielding identical equations in the cosmological setting considered; a general-background equivalence is not demonstrated here.

Introduces a Weyl compensator and fiducial metric, varies the action before specializing to a flat fiducial background, and rewrites the result as Einstein equations sourced by a vacuum fluid and a geometric gravifluid. Homogeneity reduces the nonlocal equations to a Friedmann-type ordinary differential equation.

The appendix evaluates the Minkowski quartic retarded Green function by Fourier integration and contour residues, obtaining θ(t-t'-|x-x'|)/(8π). Its support includes the interior of the light cone as well as its boundary.

An arbitrary target-space null vector is represented locally by ∂+X0 of a test string. The next-order constraint is then transformed from string frame to Einstein frame, converting a dilaton-Hessian equality into a nonnegative squared derivative.

The string argument uses a background-field expansion X = X0+Y, integrates out fluctuations, and retains the one-loop curvature/dilaton counterterms. Varying the worldsheet metric supplies the Virasoro constraints order by order in α′.

The thermodynamic argument differentiates S = A/4, relates area change to null expansion, and applies the optical Raychaudhuri equation. Entropy concavity near equilibrium supplies the sign needed for Ricci convergence.

Coarse-graining the local minima produces integer-labeled vacua described by a nondynamical four-form flux. Matching vacuum energies gives e = 2πmf, and a barrier estimate gives wall tension TDW ∼ α^1/2 f. Vacuum transitions are discussed using bubble nucleation.

Dimensional analysis compares magnetic-brane field energy with black-brane tension, giving Λ^[2(p+1)] ≲ ep,d² Md^(d−2). Its use for four-dimensional domain walls is explicitly proposed by analytical continuation rather than derived from an actual magnetic object.

Dimensional reduction uses a symplectic harmonic-form basis, Kij = ∫wi∧⋆wj, and charge norm |qΣ|² = K^ij qiΣqjΣ. The F5 self-duality condition is imposed after handling electric and dual sources; the resulting normalization enters the particle/domain-wall comparison.

Treat the radial throat as a Randall–Sundrum strip. Convert the KK equation into a one-dimensional Schrödinger problem with delta-function boundary potentials; use Bessel solutions and small-argument expansions to separate the bound mode from excited modes.

Construct a symmetry-preserving nonlinear KS ansatz for metric, forms and axio-dilaton, with regular IR and prescribed UV boundary conditions. Appendix A supplies the coupled equations intended for a future numerical boundary-value solution.

Reduce the C₂ kinetic term to five dimensions using C₂=φ(x,y)ω₂. Stokes' theorem on the closing cap converts the boundary value into F₃ flux, yielding an IR-localized quadratic mass term with Λ of order R⁻¹.

GRChombo supplies adaptive mesh refinement, fourth-order spatial finite differences and RK4 time integration, using 8–13 refinement levels. The horizon interior has at least 50 grid points after gauge adjustment; periodic boundaries are placed sufficiently far away to avoid boundary contamination during the runs.

Linear waveforms are fitted to two exponentially growing sinusoids. Rescaled sliding-window fits estimate frequencies, growth rates and their scatter. Nonlinear deformation is monitored through geodesic S1 radii and areal S2 radii.

Numerical evolution uses Cartesian CCZ4 equations, lapse-rescaled constraint damping with κ1 = 0.1 and κ2 = 0, and the modified cartoon method to reduce the symmetry-preserving problem to 3+1 dimensions.

Use the twisted eight-dimensional supersymmetry equations: holomorphic Φ, vanishing (0,2) and (2,0) gauge curvature, and J(h)∧F=[Φ,Φ†]. A nilpotent upper-triangular Φ implements cancellation of the nonprimitive Cartan flux.

In four-dimensional supergravity, minimize VD+VF with respect to hidden matter, substitute its VEV, and then analyze the small-cycle and volume extrema. The LVS calculation retains leading α′ and nonperturbative effects and tracks subleading inverse-volume corrections.

Expand D7 DBI and Chern–Simons couplings locally around z³=(2πα′)Φ to quadratic order. Promote the couplings to non-Abelian traces, insert the T-brane background, and use flux quantization and metric scaling to infer the four-dimensional volume dependence.

Dimensional reduction with Weyl rescalings compares Einstein frame with a 'keinstein' frame where the volume modulus propagates through mixing with gravity. Pairing its real component with a p-form axion constrains possible higher-dimensional origins.
Dimensional estimates of gravitational loop divergences, large-volume expansions, and a preliminary quadratically divergent one-loop effective Kähler potential test the proposed power counting.

Conformal-compensator superspace and the Cheung–D’Eramo–Thaler gauge disentangle kinetic mixing while keeping supersymmetry manifest; auxiliary equations and superspace operators expose the parametric suppression of soft terms.

Solve the photon initial-value problem using the retarded vacuum-polarization tensor, scalar proper-time propagators, and an eikonal resummation into the phase. The formalism is imported from the authors' earlier work and applied here to shockwaves.

Use the Penrose plane-wave limit and Van Vleck–Morette matrix to encode geodesic deviation. Proper-time integrals with prescribed contours around conjugate-point singularities yield analytic asymptotics and numerically evaluated frequency-dependent phases.
SU(2) characters, a plethystic exponential and residue evaluation count singlets and triplets in symmetric cubic products, identifying potentially destabilizing scalar operators.

Primary decay spectra are convolved with secondary-particle spectra, including prompt and inverse-Compton photons. Fermi continuum limits use signal-only and signal-plus-background prescriptions; H.E.S.S. line comparisons use 15% Gaussian energy resolution.

Decay calculations use spin-averaged matrix elements, the high-energy Equivalence Theorem and massless four-body phase-space factorization. The authors also use the Equivalent gauge to assess their dipole-channel calculation.

The instanton calculation extremizes I_E = m × perimeter − e|E| × area. The zero-temperature saddle is circular; above the thermal threshold it becomes a lens bounded by circular arcs of unchanged curvature radius. Analytic continuation supplies the post-nucleation trajectories.

Relativistic WKB integrates imaginary momentum across the nucleation barrier. At finite temperature, the calculation balances Boltzmann suppression for absorbed energy against reduced tunneling suppression, followed by classical acceleration after tunneling.

A parent Hanany–Witten construction uses NS, NS′ and suspended D4-branes. T-duality along x6 gives D3-branes at xy = z²w⁵; brane crossings and conserved linking numbers motivate the host's simultaneous column dualities.

Balanced sub-web splitting describes complex deformation. Its gauge-theory counterpart is partial confinement; ADS superpotentials and meson F-terms determine nonzero meson vevs and the surviving low-energy theory.

Bipartite dimer tilings of T² encode gauge factors as faces, chiral matter as edges and superpotential terms as nodes. Orientifold quotients translate geometric identifications and signs into gauge and matter projections.

Supercharge phase counting combines rk phases e^(−πi/k) on three supercharges and e^(3πi/k) on the fourth with the common sk phase e^(πi/k). Protected scalar-primary branching is then used to test possible N = 4 enhancement.

Induced charges are obtained from the curvature coupling −∫C3 ∧ I8 and sums over singular-fiber fixed points. The cited local formulas used are Q0 = −(k−1/k)/24 and Qp−Q0 = p(k−p)/(2k), with p = 0,…,k−1 discrete torsion.

The construction takes an F-theory limit of the M-theory orbifold. Torus automorphisms encode SL(2,Z) actions, while rotations of the three transverse complex coordinates encode the field-theory R-symmetry action.

Expands the Einstein–Hilbert functional under Weyl rescalings after subtracting its Euler-characteristic pole. The finite Weyl variation is related to a Liouville/Wess–Zumino functional; Diff×Weyl invariance restricts the remaining ambiguity to moduli dependence.

Constructs a functional-integral representation through bare-action reconstruction, then combines matter, ghosts and measure Jacobians in conformal gauge. Applies imported DDK–KPZ dressing formulae to that reconstructed theory.

Uses the functional renormalization group equation for the EAA, projected onto the Einstein–Hilbert truncation. Self-consistent backgrounds obey a tadpole equation, reinterpreted as vanishing total stress tensor of matter and metric fluctuations.

Global constructions use toric GLSMs, hypersurfaces or complete intersections, Weierstrass fibrations and the Sen limit. Adjunction computes divisor Euler characteristics and induced D3 charge; repeated Lefschetz arguments establish H³(O7,Z)=0 in the first example.

T-duality along the conifold U(1) isometry gives an NS5/D4/O4 description. Independently, orientifolded O(Q)×USp(2P) probe theories, projected superpotentials, mesonic F-terms and gauge-enhancement loci diagnose the deformation and O3 signs.

Canonically normalizes fields around their vevs, diagonalizes kinetic and mass matrices, and extracts modulus–axion and visible-sector cubic interactions. Partial widths scale as m_s³/M_pl² times squared coupling/mixing combinations; axion widths sum over accessible species.

Uses the imported conversion ΔN_eff=(43/7)(Γ_axions/Γ_visible)(g*/g*_reheat)^(1/3). Some illustrative calculations set its numerical factors to one, and the general multi-field estimates explicitly drop numerical coefficients.

Explicit block-matrix factorizations, requiring an invertible leading or trailing diagonal block, relate alternative field parametrizations. Antisymmetrized products induce metrics on wedge powers; their determinant identities support the geometric treatment.

Leibniz algebroids organize anchors, brackets and induced Lie derivatives. Lie algebroids additionally admit a square-zero exterior differential and Cartan calculus; the text explicitly warns that the analogous construction fails for a general Leibniz algebroid.

Compute K=−log(−i Π†ΣΠ) from symplectic periods and a prepotential containing cubic intersection terms, the Euler-number ζ(3) correction and polylogarithmic worldsheet-instanton contributions; differentiate K to obtain the Kähler metric.

Use mirror maps, Picard-Fuchs information and singular loci to delimit the large-complex-structure description. Determine one-axion period lengths or diagonalize the multi-axion metric and integrate square roots of eigenvalues over unit axionic intervals.

Match different Schottky descriptions of the same boundary moduli by numerically integrating e^φ along symmetry-fixed geodesic cycles. Three reflections reduce the computational domain to one eighth; action formulas account for nontrivial inversion transformations. Integration by parts removes numerical derivatives from the final action integrals.

Use Schottky uniformization X = G\Ω(G), extending G into H3 to construct handlebodies distinguished by contractible boundary cycles. Import the reduction of the gravity action to the Takhtajan–Zograf Liouville action. Solve ∇²φ = e^(2φ), with φ(L(w)) = φ(w) − ½ log|L′(w)|², to obtain the constant-curvature boundary metric.

Linearize the Liouville equation by Newton–Raphson iteration. Discretize its weak integral form using quadratic finite elements on triangular meshes, allowing curved boundary edges; solve the resulting sparse linear systems. Integrals use Gaussian quadrature.

Higher moments produce ferromagnetic Symn permutation-spin models with cyclic boundary pinning on A and identity elsewhere. The uniqueness argument uses the transposition-distance metric, edge-disjoint integral flows, and max-flow/min-cut.

Boundary correlations are studied through singular values of the correlation matrix in Hilbert–Schmidt orthonormal operator bases. Moments C2n=tr[(M†M)^n] become permutation contractions and Sym2n partition functions.

The swap trick and Haar second moment, E[(|Vx⟩⟨Vx|)⊗2]=(I+F)/[Dx(Dx+1)], convert averaged purity numerators and denominators into Ising partition functions. Edge and boundary mismatch costs are proportional to log D; the bulk contributes its second Rényi entropy on the spin-down region.

Evidence is surveyed from matter-only numerical evolution, linear joint matter–metric perturbations, and nonlinear numerical relativity in one and three spatial dimensions. These are reports of earlier studies, rather than new simulations performed in this review.

The review summarizes classical phase-space analyses of field value and momentum, together with a redshifting argument comparing excess kinetic or inhomogeneous energy against a slowly rolling homogeneous mode.

Explicit-breaking models are studied through their induced axial and radial masses, residual strong CP violation, and corrections ΔV to inflaton slow-roll parameters. Illustrative scans cover S^N, IS^N, and multiple PQ fields; SUSY-breaking spurions test whether dangerous operators return.

The analysis combines misalignment abundance estimates with isocurvature bounds. For the normalization mechanism it uses δa=(HI/2π)(fa/fI), then compares the required hierarchy with energy-density and post-inflationary resonance constraints.

Particle horizons are estimated by integrating da/(Ha²) through expansion phases. A large-T field redefinition to σ permits a first-order-in-λ scalar expansion used to estimate contraction e-folds up to the onset of deflation.

During vacuum-dominated locking, H is approximated as constant and φ is treated as a damped oscillator with amplitude proportional to a^−3/2. The critical value ⟨φc²⟩=V0/(4λMs²) determines the end of locking and enters the locked-era e-fold estimate.

The background analysis uses the closed-universe Friedmann equation and coupled tachyon/scalar equations of motion. The tachyon has a square-root kinetic action, while φ has a canonical kinetic term; the string mass is suppressed in some displayed evolution equations.

For indefinite polarizations, f is a real biquadratic form in α and β. A random-start ten-variable gradient flow dXI/dt=−∂f/∂XI searches for negative values, with df/dt=−ΣI(∂f/∂XI)²≤0; a negative result supplies an excluding polarization witness.

A contour integral f=(1/2πi)∮ds M(s,0)/(s−μ²)³ is deformed onto crossed production cuts. Crossing, Schwarz reflection, the optical theorem, and a vanishing boundary contribution yield positivity; low-energy evaluation uses pole residues or an EFT residue at infinity.

Tree-level four-graviton amplitudes are constructed from transverse-traceless polarization tensors and Feynman rules for the canonically normalized action. High-energy behavior and the scalar Goldstone-equivalence limit provide author-reported consistency checks.
Covariant phase-space methods use Lee–Wald presymplectic ambiguities, a boundary counterterm, Iyer–Wald surface forms and the on-shell relation between presymplectic currents and surface charges.

Exponentiation and resummation of asymptotic BMS generators produce closed-form bulk metrics. Static coordinates and advanced/retarded BMS expansions are used to examine their geometry and connect past and future null infinity.

The argument combines relative entropy, its positivity and equality condition, the first law of entanglement, and a generalized-entropy formula to relate boundary modular Hamiltonians and distinguishability to bulk quantities.

The reconstruction proof studies states related by exp(iλO), derives vanishing commutator expectation values with erased-region operators, and invokes an imported operator-algebra quantum-error-correction theorem. The appendix sketches a reference-system and Schmidt-decomposition construction.

Combine that minimum eigenvalue with an imported supergravity directional-Hessian bound along the normalized G-gradient f^i. This direction removes second-superpotential-derivative dependence and introduces the projected Kähler curvature R(f).

Project background equations and the potential Hessian onto tangent and normal directions. In the two-real-field system, minimize the Hessian contraction over a rotated unit vector to obtain its minimum eigenvalue η_V in terms of bending, masses and slow-roll quantities.

The new negative-energy construction uses vacuum-plus-two-particle vectors with smooth compact momentum support, yielding Hadamard states. Summing the resulting sampled-energy estimates over independent species links finite QEI bounds to restrictions on the mass spectrum.

Curved-spacetime arguments interpolate globally hyperbolic metrics between spacetimes with oriented-diffeomorphic Cauchy surfaces. Regular Cauchy pairs, inheritance under their preorder, and chains of Cauchy morphisms transport the desired state property using the timeslice axiom.

Nuclearity is formulated for ΞO,β(A)=exp(−βH)AΩ. Its nuclear norm is estimated through decompositions into bounded linear functionals and Hilbert-space vectors, orthogonal local excitations, and products of single-species estimates.

Appendices construct a fermionic matching model and discretize a gauge theory on an AdS5 slice. Boundary symmetry breaking and gauge fixing produce a Goldstone mass matrix matching the few-site matrix at quadratic order.
