Expand the nonlinear sigma model to quadratic order, identify the zero eigenvector of the site mass matrix, and integrate out heavier pNGBs to obtain a light-mode potential containing oscillations with hierarchical periods. Spurion power counting is used to assess radiative stability.

The authors describe the field using a Langevin equation and approximate its escape from a finite interval by a random walk. They combine an estimated inflating fraction ΓI∝exp(−t/⟨t⟩) with volume growth exp(3Ht), testing whether the resulting inflating-volume exponent is positive.

Slow-roll formulas for ε,η, the e-fold count N and the horizon-exit spectrum P=H²/(8π²MP²ε) relate the quantum-dominated width to potential parameters. The observed amplitude and spectral tilt are then used to assess the width-to-kick condition.

The authors solve the radial background equations analytically, choosing C(r)=r² and B=D⁻¹. Homogeneous vector perturbations of the gauge field, metric and scalars determine transport; the Donos–Gauntlett horizon-data method gives DC conductivity.

At zero density the charge fluctuation decouples. A tortoise coordinate and field redefinition produce a Schrödinger equation with energy ω²; negative wells and a WKB bound-state estimate diagnose possible instabilities associated with poles entering the upper frequency half-plane.

Ultraviolet power counting uses I=V+L−1. Feynman parametrization, Lorentz-invariant momentum reduction, and dimensional regularization organize one-loop divergences; selected curvature operators are used to cancel beta functions.

Expand gμν=ημν+κD hμν, fix harmonic gauge, invert the quadratic operator with spin projectors, and partially fraction the propagator into massless and complex-conjugate contributions. Conserved-source saturation is used for the tree-level optical-theorem argument.

Fourier transforms of the propagator give coordinate-space two-point functions and the linearized gravitational response to a static point source. The Newtonian potential is extracted from h00 and evaluated for selected polynomial form factors.

Numerically solve the Friedmann and Klein–Gordon equations, or the equivalent Hamilton–Jacobi equations when φ is a single-valued time variable. Compare smooth and modulated potentials under matched initial conditions and integrate the expansion to obtain e-fold counts.

Evaluate CMB observables using the first four Hamilton–Jacobi slow-roll parameters during a suitably tuned horizon-crossing window. Potential normalizations are adjusted to Ps≈2.1×10^−9; benchmark pivot exits are approximately 54–55 e-folds before inflation ends.

An appendix chooses an explicit H(φ), reconstructs V=3H²−2H′² in Planck units, and solves the field evolution through an arctangent substitution. This separate illustrative model supplies analytic support for the plateau mechanism.

The gIMR null test replaces phase coefficients p_i by p_i(1+δp̂_i), with GR at all δp̂_i=0. Analyses vary either one deformation or all deformations in one waveform stage, alongside physical parameters. Amplitudes remain unperturbed.

Bayesian parameter estimation uses LALInference, including nested sampling for the frequency-split consistency test. Numerical-relativity relations map inferred component masses and spins to remnant properties; EOBNR and IMRPhenom posteriors are averaged.

Subtract the maximum-a-posteriori GR waveform and analyze residuals with BayesWave, comparing Gaussian noise, glitches and a coherent elliptically polarized signal. Compare with 100 nearby four-second noise segments. Ringdown is separately modeled by a damped sinusoid with fixed start time varied between analyses.

Estimate magnetic transport as a random walk with mean free path approximately the gyroradius. For v≈10³ km/s, the stated cluster estimate is R_g=3×10⁻¹⁵ ε⁻¹(m/GeV) Mpc. Impose R_g≳1 Mpc to avoid smearing the cluster density profile.

An alternative order-of-magnitude argument compares Lorentz and gravitational force magnitudes: F_L/F_G=εeBv/[GM(R)m/R²]. Combining F_L/F_G<1 with v²/R≈GM(R)/R² is said to reproduce the same charge bound.

Radial quantization on R × S² determines monopole quantum numbers. The Callias index theorem and quantization of fermion zero modes organize vortex states; Clifford-algebra transformations describe their braiding.

The analysis uses η-regularized fermion determinants, APS index-theorem anomaly inflow, BF/Chern-Simons effective actions, and gauging a common Z₂ one-form symmetry to couple Abelian and Ising sectors.
Expand the non-Abelian DBI and Wess-Zumino actions near the tip, use the five-form Bianchi identity to relate warp-factor derivatives to flux, and canonically normalize the scalar kinetic terms.

Fix the relative bosonic/fermionic normalization using the D5 polarization potential: halving its quadratic coefficient produces a supersymmetric perfect square. Apply imported Parkes-West finiteness results to the resulting mass-deformed gauge theory.

Solve the asymptotic Yamabe problem to restore R=−n(n−1). Boundary expansions and maximum-principle barriers establish a strict mass decrease when the initial scalar curvature is nonconstant, contradicting the assumed minimum.

Use normal-form/Fefferman-Graham expansions, parity under changes of special defining function, and static lapse asymptotics to analyze mass aspects. The n=3 rigidity conclusion then invokes imported static spacetime classification results.

Use Corvino's compactly supported scalar-curvature deformation. When the relevant kernel is trivial, the metric can be perturbed to increase scalar curvature locally while preserving the asymptotics and Wang mass.

Use flux/field rescalings, axion shifts and factorisation of stationary-point equations into branches; supplement these with numerical solutions, interpolating fits, flux scans and Hessian stability analysis. Alignment is analysed through the full F-term stabilisation conditions.

For monodromy, displace the massive axion by hand and solve the remaining fields' stationary-point equations as functions of that displacement. These fields remain in the theory; this procedure is distinguished from integrating them out to obtain a single-field effective theory.
Evaluate a metric-dependent proper distance. For the selected axionic combination ρ = Σ hiνi, the paper uses Δφ = ∫(hi gⁱʲ hj)^(−1/2)dρ, allowing the metric to vary through the backreacted moduli.

Photon–ALP mixing is treated with a three-state propagation matrix including photon absorption and magnetic-field-dependent off-diagonal mixing. Homogeneous nonabsorbing media admit analytic oscillation probabilities; inhomogeneous fields are treated using coherence cells or turbulent-field Fourier representations.

Canonical transport uses τγγ = ∫ds/λγγ and attenuation exp(−τγγ), with the inverse mean free path obtained from the background spectrum and angle-averaged pair-production cross section. EBL inference jointly fits intrinsic source spectra and a fiducial EBL shape scaled by nγ = ζnfid; alternative analyses allow more spectral freedom.

LIV analyses reconstruct energy-dependent light curves and search for arrival-time dispersion, incorporating cosmological expansion for linear or quadratic energy dependence. The review emphasises likelihood methods, statistical calibration, independent analysis cross-checks and propagation of systematic uncertainties.

Compares semiclassical evaluations of −ln Z(Q+q) using either a deformed background or an undeformed background plus a minimal-action probe. The general equivalence of these descriptions is assumed rather than rigorously established.
Uses Stokes’ theorem, Fefferman–Graham cutoffs, holographic counterterms and an imported isoperimetric inequality to reduce the AdS probe minimum to a renormalized bulk volume.

The string-correction test compares an R4 integral on the undeformed geometry with a five-form integral on the deformed geometry. An unknown metric function is handled through its differential equation and asymptotic falloff.

Uses the imported shock-shell matching method: a small null perturbation produces ṽ=v+α in Kruskal coordinates. At late injection parameter tw, α is proportional to (Eβ/SBH)exp[2π(tw−r*(Λ))/β], with geometry-dependent coefficients.

Relates interior turning points to α through conserved quantities and segmented extremal-surface integrals, then obtains mutual information numerically. An analytic D5 half-plane calculation is used to calibrate the numerics.

Computes strip entropies and connected two-sided surfaces, subtracting ultraviolet divergences. Dp and Lifshitz examples use area prescriptions; Gauss–Bonnet entropy extremizes a functional containing intrinsic surface curvature and a boundary term.
Estimates plasma delay with H2(z)=∫0^z (1+z′)dz′/√[Ωm(1+z′)³+ΩΛ] and Δtplasma=[νp²(0)/(2H0)](νl^−2−νh^−2)H2(z), then assigns the residual delay to a possible photon mass.
The mass-delay kernel is H1(z)=∫0^z (1+z′)^−2 dz′/√[Ωm(1+z′)³+ΩΛ]. The reported inversion is mγ=hc^−2√{2H0Δtmγ/[(νl^−2−νh^−2)H1(z)]}.
Starts from E=hν=√(p²c²+mγ²c⁴) and the leading vacuum-speed expansion v≈c[1−mγ²c⁴/(2h²ν²)]. Equal comoving travel distances give Δtmγ=[mγ²c⁴/(2h²H0)](νl^−2−νh^−2)H1(z).

Stress-tensor Ward identities and integrated topological surface charges establish symmetry actions. Radial quantization and the Weyl map to R × S^(d−1) translate operator statements into Hilbert-space statements.

Conformal blocks are obtained from OPE differential operators, projectors onto conformal multiplets, or a quadratic-Casimir differential equation with OPE boundary conditions. Radial expansions organize descendants using Gegenbauer polynomials.

Numerical searches use derivatives at z = z̄ = 1/2 through order Λ. Continuous dimension constraints are treated by discretized linear programming, continuous simplex methods, or positive-times-polynomial approximations and semidefinite programming.
Three-state photon-polarization/ALP propagation includes plasma and CMB dispersion plus photon damping. Expansion is implemented with E ∝ (1+z), B ∝ (1+z)^2 and physical domain size l ∝ (1+z)^(−1).

The converted spectrum is folded with scattering probability, a fitted ionization-energy fraction and E/13.6 eV to estimate extra free electrons. Their Thomson optical depth is compared with the adopted observational allowance.
Coupled Boltzmann and Friedmann equations determine moduli decay and the ALP spectrum through a dimensionless numerical evolution. A quasi-thermal fit uses α = 1.434, β = 1.980 and K = 0.445.
Computes twisted cohomology H³(S⁵/Zk,(Z⊕Z)ρ) using alternating differentials 1−ρ and 1+ρ+⋯+ρ^(k−1). Pullbacks of torsion classes to wrapped D3-brane worldvolumes test generalized Pfaffian operators.

Uses a Leray–Serre filtration to distinguish circle shifts, three-form torsion and C4 holonomy, then compares summed orbifold M2 charges with D3 charges. Appendix A uses Borel equivariant cohomology, Gysin and Mayer–Vietoris sequences, and equivariant push-forwards to establish the required cohomology maps.

Classifies candidate parent moduli-space quotients using complex reflection groups G(k,p,N) and polynomial invariant rings. Their invariant degrees supply candidate Coulomb spectra, followed by anomaly and large-N charge matching.

Solves the separated Klein–Gordon equation with hypergeometric functions, analytically continues logarithmic branch points into straddling modes, and computes transmission through conserved-current flux ratios.

Defines the singular horizon integral by a complex semicircular contour and evaluates its imaginary part using a fractional residue theorem. A gauge transformation first makes the electromagnetic potential regular at the relevant horizon.

Uses WKB Hamilton–Jacobi tunneling and a gauge-covariant action integral along a horizon-crossing null path. The chosen implementation includes the temporal contribution needed in the canonical-invariant null-geodesic formulation.

Parametrize the observed lag as mγ² F(E1,E2) Hγ(z)/(2H0) + ΔtDM + bsf(1+z), where F = E1^-2 − E2^-2 for E2 > E1 and bsf is an unknown source-frame lag. The mass propagation kernel is Hγ(z) = ∫0^z dz'/[(1+z')² sqrt(ΩΛ + Ωm(1+z')³)].

Model plasma dispersion through the electron column density and DMIGM = 3cH0 ΩIGM He(z)/(8πGmp), with He(z) = ∫0^z (1+z') dz'/sqrt(ΩΛ + Ωm(1+z')³). Compare the remaining lag after selected plasma subtraction with the photon-mass contribution.

For a future redshift sample, propose optimizing reconstructed intrinsic source lags against mass and plasma parameters, for example by minimizing their RMS. This suggested estimator assumes identical FRB origins; it is not an analysis performed on an observed population here.
Combines the standard supergravity F-term potential with VD=g²D²/(2h), where D=iKiXi. Uses no-scale cancellation and derivative combinations ∂±=s∂S±t∂T to impose ∂SV=∂TV=0 and V=ε≥0.

Inverts the extremum problem: chooses a moduli-space point (s,t) and target ε, then solves for paper-defined superpotential quantities A,B,a. Positivity of A,a,B, physically meaningful parameters and numerical potential analysis select candidate minima.

From W = W0 + Σ Aα exp(−2πqα_i T^i), the potential charge matrix includes both 2πqα_i and pairwise differences. Dominant instantons are selected by decreasing amplitude, retaining linearly independent rows until a square full-rank matrix is obtained.

For −π ≤ Qθ ≤ π, enumerate polytope vertices and maximize their K-norm. Numerically maximize this radius over the stretched Kähler cone, checking whether the dominant instanton set changes. Omitting further constraints preserves an upper bound.

Toric intersection and cone data determine the classical metric. Toric divisor cohomology comes from polytope combinatorics; Koszul sequences implemented in cohomcalg treat combinations. The small-h1,1 search includes nonnegative sums of at most three toric divisors.

Electroweak gauge-field rotation and generator traces determine the photon anomaly coefficient. With the stated representation conditions, sin²θW = Tr(T3²)/Tr(Qem²), while the color-normalized coefficient is c0aγγ = Tr(Qem²)/Tr(F3²).

A DFSZ charge-accounting method starts from HuHdσ² with Γ(σ) = +1, assigns several field charges to zero, and computes the Γ–Qem–Qem anomaly from the remaining right-handed fermions. The electron's Higgs coupling distinguishes the assignments.

The author follows the ten-dimensional B-field gauge transformation into four dimensions and examines matter kinetic terms after the anomalous gauge boson becomes massive, identifying the same matter charge Γ as a residual global charge.

Construct the compact geometry through lattice identifications and globally defined Maurer–Cartan forms. Parametrize the left-invariant metric using representatives of Aut\GL(3,R), where Aut is the Heisenberg-algebra automorphism group.

Adapt a wave-evolution spectral algorithm: discretize the fundamental domain with twisted boundary conditions, evolve ∂t²φ = Δφ using centered spatial differences and leapfrog stepping, and extract eigenfrequencies from temporal Fourier peaks. Tests use localized Gaussian initial data and truncated analytic eigenmodes.

Separate fiber-independent Fourier modes from fiber-dependent Weil–Brezin–Zak transforms. Changes of variables reduce the fiber eigenvalue problem to the Hermite equation. The appendices integrate mode overlaps and argue completeness using boundary conditions, invertibility of the Zak transform and exclusion of divergent non-polynomial solutions.

Construct Jacobian fibrations, which the paper states share singular-fiber locations and types with the original genus-one fibrations. Use discriminants and Weierstrass vanishing orders to identify Kodaira fibers and gauge enhancements; check them using monodromies and associated Euler numbers. Mordell–Weil rank and torsion constrain Abelian factors and global quotients.

Use generic Néron–Severi lattices and intersections with the fiber to exclude sections: double covers have matrix [[0,2],[2,0]], while the complete intersections have [[0,4],[4,4]]. Divisor–fiber intersections are consequently divisible by two or four, respectively.

For flux backgrounds impose ½∫G∧G + N3 = χ(K3×K3)/24 = 24 and the stated quantization G ∈ H4(K3×K3,Z). Use an imported classification of attractive-K3 pairs for tadpole compatibility, and adjoint branching under rank-one singularity enhancements to identify potential matter representations.

Add supersymmetry-breaking mass operators, take their coefficients formally large, and require divergent parts of the superspace equations of motion to vanish. For example, −(m_y²/f²)∫d⁴θ |X|²|Y|² generates scalar decoupling; combinations of operators implement multiple component removals.

Apply superspace derivatives to the constraint and project to components. The highest derivative projection determines the eliminated lowest component recursively; lower projections are treated as consistency conditions. The appendix establishes derivative identities supporting this component count.

Compute curvature-correction phases from one-loop KK diagrams with a specified iε prescription. Independently study bosonic Euclidean-worldsheet quantization, T-duality, one-loop modular invariance through Poisson resummation, and analytic continuation of sigma-model couplings.

Lift negative D0 backreaction to an eleven-dimensional pp-wave, then use spacelike/timelike T-duality, S-duality and KK reduction to infer other signature-changing backgrounds and effective actions. Analytic continuation around H=0 provides a complementary, initially heuristic singularity-crossing prescription.

Obtain the N=2 Seiberg–Witten geometry through three approaches: D4/NS5 brane manipulations, Taub–NUT geometric engineering and mirror symmetry, and analytically continued Nekrasov calculus for a two-node quiver restricted to opposite couplings, q₁q₂=1.

A Noether/Komar construction, with dimensional reduction along brane spatial directions, extends the ADM energy prescription beyond asymptotically flat transverse spaces. A counterterm with ξ = d log H subtracts CGLP energy; supergravity equations move the energy surface integral from infinity to the horizon.

For extremal sourced configurations, delta-function form equations give the Smarr relation as a sum of on-shell brane couplings. This alternative derivation assumes that source delta functions account for singularities and that the remaining total derivative is nonsingular.
Regular Killing-horizon identities imply constant C0 and closure of C3 − C0H3 on the horizon. Harmonic decomposition and Poincaré duality identify the dipole potential–charge contribution.

For string gas fluctuations, compute thermal stress-energy correlations on sub-Hubble scales and apply Einstein constraints at Hubble exit; density variance is related to heat capacity by ⟨δρ²⟩=T²C_V/R⁶.
Expand the matter-plus-gravity action to quadratic order and evolve canonical Fourier modes: v_k''+(k²−z''/z)v_k=0, with ζ=v/z. Tensor modes use μ=ah and the squeezing function a''/a.

Restrict the Kähler metric to fixed overall volume, canonically normalize two-cycle coordinates, and examine general two-field cubic volumes and their large-volume asymptotics. The generalized analysis addresses the inflationary regime rather than the full stabilized potential.

Use toroidal string-loop results, homogeneity and low-energy Coleman–Weinberg matching to estimate CY corrections. Degree −2 KK corrections exhibit extended no-scale cancellation at leading order; surviving one-loop and estimated two-loop KK terms can compete.

Background attractor analysis, modified Layzer–Irvine energy balance, Raychaudhuri spherical collapse and Press–Schechter halo counting connect coupling to coincidence, virialization and structure abundance.

Covariant energy-momentum transfer, scalar metric perturbations and gauge-invariant density/velocity variables provide the linear analysis; numerical applications adopt conformal Newtonian gauge and adiabatic initial conditions.
Modified CMBEASY/CAMB and CosmoMC calculations fit background and perturbation observables with MCMC. AIC/BIC are reviewed to distinguish improved fits from support for additional parameters.
The authors use V = e^K(K^{I J̄}D_IW D_J̄W̄ − 3|W|²), solve supersymmetric reference extrema, and expand the uplifted potential to obtain shifts, canonical masses and F-terms.

Homogeneous scalar oscillations are analyzed with Hubble-induced displacement terms, the rescaling a^{3/2}(T − T_0), and the virial theorem. Matter-like modulus energy and redshifting radiation determine the entropy enhancement.

Decay widths into gauge particles and gravitinos are combined with a Boltzmann-yield expression for gravitino-produced LSPs. Neutralino illustrations distinguish ineffective annihilation from annihilation-limited abundance.

Dimensionally reduce to four-dimensional Einstein frame, retaining dilaton and selected metric rescalings; match the resulting potentials to F-term potentials obtained from stated Kähler potentials and superpotentials.

Solve the IIA ten-dimensional equations perturbatively in the small parameter defined by a³/v²; compare truncated analytic expansions with numerical solutions. No all-order analytic solution is obtained.

Detect instabilities through negative one-dimensional principal minors and Sylvester's criterion. Compare these directions with the sgoldstino using canonically normalized fields and, in IIB, a basis diagonalizing the orthogonal mass submatrix.

Construct linear combinations of temperature and chemical-potential derivatives at τ=i, z=0. Positivity on neutral states and sufficiently heavy charged states forces a charged contribution below the functional's gap threshold.

An alternative argument forms W4=Z∂z⁴Z−3(∂z²Z)² and divides by a modular discriminant power. The supersymmetric argument instead uses holomorphic elliptic genera and the weight-four modular-form space for Γ0(2).

Use universal modular covariance of the flavored partition function. The argument invokes current algebra order by order in chemical potential; a compact free boson supplies an explicit transformation through Poisson resummation.

Dualize the four-dimensional antisymmetric-tensor field strength to the MI axion, normalize its gluon anomaly coupling using the unit Pontryagin index, and infer its physical periodicity. The paper also presents a pure-gauge string construction with a Gauss-theorem integral.

Analyze the two axion directions and their gluon couplings, separating the QCD-potential direction from the orthogonal Goldstone direction eaten by the anomalous vector. Use continuous motion along that gauge direction to identify apparently distinct vacua.

Fit Cepheids and calibrator SNe simultaneously by minimizing one χ². Generalized least squares propagates parameter covariance, including shared anchor-distance and ground-to-HST zeropoint uncertainties.

SALT-II v2.4 standardizes SN light curves. The additional analysis-systematic error is estimated from alternative fits: 207 NIR variants include anchor combinations, with primary-anchor variants having dispersion 0.71 km s−1 Mpc−1.

Crowded-field NIR PSF scene fitting fixes Cepheid positions from optical images. Local artificial-star tests estimate blending bias and errors; artificial input fluxes and the period–luminosity relation are iterated to convergence.

Use the blow-up inflation potential to calculate slow-roll quantities and numerically impose approximately 60 e-folds and the paper's density-perturbation normalization. Estimate the final baryon yield by combining condensate asymmetry with the entropy yield of χ decay.

Compute supergravity soft masses and A-terms from moduli F-terms and the matter metric, retaining subleading α′ and nonperturbative contributions. Scalar-mass formulae assume a diagonal matter metric and distinguish local from ultra-local behaviour.
Use approximately hydrogenic bound states, the superradiance saturation condition, level-growth times and companion-induced level mixing to identify which black holes should lose spin before merging.

Update blind-search annihilation rates using cited numerical results; the illustrated blind search uses two-day coherent integrations over one year. Targeted strain estimates instead use a cited leading-order annihilation formula and estimates of remnant spin.

Model detector selection and mass/spin errors, then test separability of the mass–spin distribution. The statistic is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance between spins inside and outside a mass interval, maximized over the interval; reported thresholds reject separability at 2σ.

Apply the DeTurck method with a planar Schwarzschild–AdS reference metric. Metric and gauge functions depend on two compact coordinates, with prescribed asymptotic data and regularity at the axis and horizon.
Extrapolate with β=1/T and R_min=c_1 β^b_1 exp(c_2 β^b_2). Logarithmic derivatives estimate b_2, followed by a two-parameter fit; an analogous analysis is applied to total charge.

Use Newton–Raphson iteration with Chebyshev discretization, at least 200 points in each direction for steep gradients. Linear solves use a Krylov method with finite-difference preconditioning; extremely low temperatures require octuple-precision LU decomposition.

Model invertible theories by spectrum maps from Σ^n MT H_n, where MT H_n=Thom(BH_n;−V_n). Character-dual targets track discrete theories, Anderson-dual targets track deformation information, and Borel Z/2-equivariant homotopy theory implements reflection.

Computations use Adams spectral sequences, Ext charts and A_1-modules with A_1 generated by Sq^1 and Sq^2; twisted Atiyah–Bott–Shapiro maps connect to KO-theory. Margolis homology supplies additional spectral-sequence information.

Numerically solve the quadratic warp-factor correction and evaluate the renormalized action using the compact radial coordinate u=tanh w. The reported sign of the free-energy change is extracted as a function of operator dimension.

Compute the finite on-shell action using covariant holographic counterterms. For alternative quantization, obtain the generating functional by a Legendre transformation rather than by changing the counterterm prescription.

Solve the homogeneous scalar equation on the AdS background analytically, imposing bulk regularity; derive asymptotic source/response coefficients and include metric backreaction through quadratic order.

Sum leading large-N diagrams through Schwinger–Dyson equations G(ω)^−1=−iω−Σ(ω), Σ(τ)=J²G(τ)^(q−1). A disorder-averaged bilocal functional integral supplies the saddle action and fluctuation expansion.

Extract chaos using a retarded ladder kernel and the ansatz F(t1,t2)=exp[λL(t1+t2)/2]f(t12), requiring kernel eigenvalue one. Numerical real-time Schwinger–Dyson iteration and binary search implement this condition at finite coupling.

Sum connected ladders as F=(1−K)^−1F0. In the conformal limit, diagonalize K using the SL(2) Casimir, hypergeometric eigenfunctions, and contour deformation; the complete spectral basis includes h=1/2+is and h=2,4,6,… .

Apply horizon matching, Ne+(Nmod1+Nmod2)/4≈57+(ln r)/4+ln(ρ*/ρend)/4, then evaluate single-field slow-roll predictions and scalar-amplitude normalization. The latter retains the explicit gs e^{Kcs}/(8π) potential-normalization factor.

Minimize the LVS potential after eliminating small-cycle moduli, and tune a positive uplift D/V^γ to impose a post-inflationary Minkowski minimum. The detailed displacement calculation sets γ=2; the authors state that its results depend only mildly on γ.

Expand the inflationary volume potential perturbatively in R, using δφ=−δV′(φ*)/V″(φ*). Track matter and radiation redshifting with imported widths Γτn≈0.1mτn³/Ms² and ΓV≈mV³/(16πMpl²) to estimate both matter-epoch durations.

Estimate dissipation from high-temperature on-shell fermion contributions, using their finite-temperature decay widths and thermal masses. The approximate numerical coefficient is obtained by evaluating the width near the momentum p≈3.24T that dominates the integral.

Integrate coupled inflaton–radiation dynamics and evaluate curvature perturbations including occupation numbers, dissipative noise and radiation coupling. The updated numerical growth fit is G(Q*)≈1+0.0185Q*^2.315+0.335Q*^1.364.

Expand the one-loop finite-temperature fermion potential and compute the zero-momentum inflaton self-energy. Separate local contributions, which cancel at leading order, from the retarded nonlocal self-energy responsible for adiabatic dissipation.

Regular skyrmions are obtained through hedgehog energy minimization with F(0)=Bπ and F(∞)=0. Gravitating configurations use coupled Einstein–Skyrme boundary-value equations for the profile, mass function and lapse, with asymptotic normalization.

Three evaporation thought experiments progress from possible charge recovery to monitored recovery. Monitoring uses either a proposed topological surface integral measured through string interference or the Gauss-law flux of an arbitrarily weak spectator baryon gauge field.

Separate the Klein–Gordon equation into a radial scattering problem; impose ingoing horizon conditions and extract partial-wave phase shifts and absorption. Reduced-series summation handles scattering, while null geodesics provide a high-frequency backward-glory approximation.
Covariant phase-space methods use δL=dθ plus equations of motion, the symplectic form W=∫ω, and δH_ξ=W(δg,L_ξg). Boundary integrability permits H_ξ=∫∂Σ(Q_ξ−ξ·K).

An alternative Euclidean replica derivation for time-independent states assumes AdS/CFT, bulk equations of motion, analytic continuation near n=1 and bulk replica symmetry. It derives the relative-energy relation without assuming the RT formula.

For time-reflection-symmetric geometries, parameterize extremal surfaces by f=R, construct a radius-dependent ξ, and differentiate Noether-current expressions with respect to R. Reflection parity and scalar boundary terms simplify the resulting surface integral.

Represent fluctuations by a Gaussian ensemble with spectrum P(k), and estimate position-space variance growth through momentum integration. The authors numerically find the variance difference finite even where the initial variance diverges; its late-time growth is dominated by the largest exponent.

Numerically evolve the homogeneous field, then insert that background into linear Fourier-mode equations and extract momentum-dependent exponential growth rates. The numerical examples take vanishing initial background velocity.

Use Floquet theory and Hill's determinant as a second method for growth exponents. Approximate the infinite determinant by progressively larger central finite matrices; the authors report agreement with direct mode evolution.

Apply the O3 fermion projection and static gauge. The DBI and Wess-Zumino contributions become equal, giving a Volkov-Akulov-type action −2∫Ẽ⁰∧Ẽ¹∧Ẽ²∧Ẽ³ with Ẽ built from all four worldvolume spinors.

Solve S²=SYⁱ=0 in components: s=(ψ⁰)²/(2F_s) and yⁱ=ψ⁰ψⁱ/F_s−(ψ⁰)²Fⁱ/(2F_s²). Implicit coordinate-dependent fermion redefinitions then map superfield components to fields with the brane's nonlinear transformations.

Use K=cS S̄+δᵢⱼ̄YⁱȲʲ̄ and W=fS+gᵢYⁱ+hᵢⱼYⁱYʲ. Substitute the component constraints, solve auxiliary-field equations iteratively in fermions, and compare kinetic, mass and symmetry-related interaction terms.

Solve fourth-order Picard-Fuchs equations recursively with power-series and logarithmic ansätze around the conifold, LCS, orbifold and regular points. Match overlapping solutions to an integral symplectic basis; some transition coefficients are numerical, reported at forty-digit precision.

Numerically minimize the multifield potential slow-roll parameter ε over moduli and flux choices, then inspect minimum η-eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Canonical field displacements are estimated locally with other moduli frozen.

Search for Minkowski roots using the numerator of τ_τ(z)−τ_z(z), obtained separately from DτW=0 and DzW=0. Apply conifold monodromies and compare roots across coordinate patches to test convergence and reject apparent vacua.

Harmonic-gauge propagator inversion and conserved-source residues test the Minkowski spectrum. Entire-function field redefinitions and unchanged Landau singularities/Cutkosky rules support the authors’ perturbative unitarity argument.

Background-field functional determinants, Faddeev–Popov gauge fixing, dimensional regularization and Barvinsky–Vilkovisky traces organize one-loop divergences. Fixing the compensator fluctuation to a constant makes its conformal determinant trivial in DIMREG.

Classical analysis constructs conformally rescaled exact solutions, evaluates curvature scalars, and integrates radial particle equations to examine proper-time access to the putative singular boundary.

Translate weak-gravity bounds into instanton-action constraints, CFT charge/dimension conditions, and wrapped-brane requirements on effective curve classes. These are sketches of applications rather than reproduced derivations.

Motivate strengthening the WGC through Kaluza–Klein reduction: satisfying the higher-dimensional WGC need not prevent lower-dimensional violations. Report spectrum checks in perturbative heterotic compactifications, orbifolds, and selected Higgs branches.

Construct a near-horizon limit around a double root f(rh) = f′(rh) = 0, with f(rh + ρ) = −λρ² + O(ρ³). For the stated real dS2 Nariai identification, the source's R1 = λ^(−1/2) requires λ = −f″(rh)/2 > 0, equivalently f″(rh) < 0; this is an inferred necessary local condition. On this branch, transform coordinates to recover the generalized Nariai metric.

Substitute a constant-radius product metric and an electromagnetic two-form aligned with each factor's volume form into the field equations. The resulting algebraic relations determine charges from radii or, in eligible cases, radii from charges.

Integrate a static black-hole ansatz under restrictions on radial sphere sizes; use null alignment and optical properties for Weyl classification, and curvature contractions for the universality argument.

Analytically continues pure-state density matrices contracted with amputated correlators. CPT and polarization relations make forward crossing act as s↔u, with charge conjugation and helicity reversal; fermionic statistics signs are compensated by polarization behavior.

Classifies low-dimensional fermion operators using field redefinitions and Fierz identities, and uses dispersive matching of calculable low-energy cross sections to estimate where new thresholds must appear.

Uses Cauchy extraction of the second Taylor coefficient, contour deformation, Schwarz reflection, crossing and the optical theorem. Physical direct and crossed discontinuities become nonnegative total-cross-section contributions.

Expand Picard–Fuchs periods near the conifold, transform to symplectic and local coordinates, and obtain Kähler potentials from the symplectic period pairing. The two-modulus numerical sums extend to approximately n = 20000 and quadratic order.

Solve F-term conditions near Z = 0, integrate out the heavy conic modulus, and evaluate canonically normalized Hessian masses. For the aligned potential, include order-|Z| shifts of the stabilized saxions before evaluating the light axion potential.
Combine flux stabilization with the α′-corrected large-volume scenario and nonperturbative Kähler superpotential. Because the Pfaffian is unknown, assume a prefactor As Z^N multiplying exp(−as Ts).

An interpolating ten-dimensional metric is used to extract string scales from the world-sheet action and KK scales from internal harmonic expansions, distinguishing unwarped bulk modes from modes supported in a strongly warped throat.

Uplift balances are combined with gravitino/KK hierarchies. For LVS, extremization with respect to the small modulus and total volume is combined with the inflationary energy bound to obtain an upper restriction on the volume.

Soft-mass estimates use the quadratically cutoff-dependent Coleman–Weinberg supertrace, including an additional field-dependent contribution associated with the incomplete Goldstino multiplet; matter derivatives then determine mass corrections.

Embeds an Einstein-Maxwell field strength into the supergravity fields with constant X, Aμ=0 and T± aligned with the Maxwell field. Separately checks the two- and four-derivative Einstein equations using four-dimensional self-duality identities.

Uses off-shell superconformal multiplet calculus, gauge fixing and consistent auxiliary-field truncations. Derives the full bosonic equations rather than relying on BPS equations, since the intended solutions generally break supersymmetry.

Rewrites the correction as Gauss-Bonnet plus quadratic expressions vanishing on Einstein-Maxwell backgrounds. Applies the Wald entropy variation and, in the BPS limit, attractor equations and a Legendre transform.

Use anomaly cancellation to screen a proposed algebra and matter assignment, then calculate its dimension-weighted H_u shift. Submit surviving candidates to independent geometric tests, because anomaly compatibility can coexist with forbidden non-minimal intersections.

Local toric monomial counting constructs Weierstrass or Tate tunings. Monodromy may require polynomial factorization or perfect-square conditions rather than simply deleting coefficients; the e6 tuning on a −3 curve explicitly illustrates this distinction.
Green–Schwarz anomaly equations, divisor intersections, and adjunction constrain matter spectra. The geometry–spectrum correspondence then converts gauge and matter changes into Hodge-number shifts.

First determine the coefficient family realizing the proposed algebra and count its lost parameters. Then independently evaluate vanishing at intersections. This final check distinguishes genuine local enhancements from anomaly-compatible coefficient counts that require changing the base.
The previously used convexity condition on −2 curves gives k≥(∑ki)/2 for section vanishing orders, implying 2N≥∑Mi when su(N) neighbors carry su(Mi).

Uses reviewed generalized-geometry backreaction results: internal spinors define even and odd polyforms, and supersymmetry conditions source a one-form component of the domain-wall calibration Z that was absent in the CY geometry.

Tests the construction with toroidal/orbifold examples and a local mirror transformation using three T-dualities. D3 and D6 probe superpotential variations are related to integrals of generalized calibrations over chains.

Recasts the sourced forms as dα₁=β₂ and uses them as non-harmonic KK profiles for C₄. The self-dual F₅ expansion determines the Stückelberg combination; manipulating its kinetic term gives the leading axion–four-form coupling.

Local fake superpotentials are expanded around critical points. Hessian square-root choices label branches, followed by order-by-order algebraic equations; the six-scalar numerical construction uses expansion through order 15.

Single-field crossing rules, asymptotic behavior and small-curvature deformations are used to distinguish globally bounding branches, interpolating extremal walls and possible finite-radius decay channels.

Hamilton–Jacobi reformulation replaces the second-order wall equations with first-order flows. For flat static walls, F(a,φ)=2e³ᵃf(φ) separates the constraint and identifies f as a fake superpotential.

Dimensional reduction of democratic type IIA supergravity and D6 Chern–Simons couplings; integration of Minkowski four-form field strengths generates the scalar potential. Appendix B uses a mother action imposing Bianchi identities and implementing dualization.

Chain-integral descriptions of open coordinates and superpotentials, relative homology, and discrete transformations guide the holomorphic-field redefinitions. Homogeneous-function identities and inverse-metric relations then organize the N=1 supergravity calculation.

The equivalent-action algorithm drops products of at least three differentiated-curvature factors, expands composite derivatives, integrates by parts, evaluates suitable curvature coefficients on the background, and uses Bianchi identities to reduce the quadratic curvature basis.

Canonical tensor/scalar quadratic actions are analyzed through additional propagator poles, equivalently zeros of kinetic multipliers. Exponentials of entire functions are used to prevent unwanted finite-complex-plane zeros.

Second variation is followed by decomposition into transverse-traceless tensor, transverse vector and two scalar components. Covariant-derivative recursion relations convert the resulting operators into curvature-shifted functions of the background d'Alembertian.

The author uses dimensional regularization and MS renormalization, the one-loop Coleman–Weinberg potential, and examples of higher-loop mass cross-terms. Terms involving n distinct masses are assigned their first appearance at n loops in the model considered.

Fine-tuning is estimated by expanding the effective potential in field-dependent parameter variations and multiplying the cancellation accuracies required for relevant Taylor coefficients. The multifield calculation counts mixed monomials over the full field domain; Eq. (20) is identified as the main result.

The imported scalar/tensor normalization gives Minf ≈ 1.8 × 10^16 GeV (r/0.1)^(1/4). The essay also uses the Lyth estimate Δφ/MPl ≳ 2(r/0.01)^(1/2), under its stated approximate-constant-r assumption.

Dimensional reduction of the ten-dimensional Einstein–Hilbert term relates string and Planck scales. Combining that relation with the inflationary normalization, scale hierarchies and a geometric volume estimate yields bounds expressed through small expansion parameters.

At the critical endpoint, first-order BPS equations are used to identify the limiting vortex. Separately, a KK mode expansion checks that Wilson-line shifts cancel the half-integer contributions associated with antiperiodic fermions, leaving the light modes needed for supermultiplets.

Smooth solutions are obtained from coupled matter and Einstein ODEs using multiple shooting and Newton's method. Near-core Taylor expansions determine regular initial data; linearized WKB matter tails and vacuum matching provide finite-radius approximations to asymptotic boundary conditions.

A double Wick rotation of Schwarzschild supplies the vacuum bubble geometry. Dressing its tip with a Nambu–Goto string gives the thin-wall estimate 2H0^-1 = R/(1 − 4Gμ), at fixed asymptotic R. The vacuum relation B′ = H0C/R serves as a geometric diagnostic.

Slow-roll estimates use ε=(Vφ/V)²/2, η=Vφφ/V, ns=1+2η−6ε and r=16ε. Numerical field trajectories and e-fold evolution illustrate selected plateaus; local derivative estimates explain the approximate dependence on f.

Perturbative inflaton-decay widths into gauge bosons or matter fields are translated into reheating temperatures. For reheating below dark-matter freeze-out, the paper estimates the direct inflaton-decay contribution to the relic yield.

Dimensional reduction and Weyl rescaling give a four-dimensional Einstein-frame description. Illustrative potentials are analyzed by algebraically integrating out heavy fields and balancing positive, negative and positive contributions for metastabilization.

In-in perturbation theory computes primordial correlators. Time-dependent particle production is described with mode functions, WKB evolution between production events and Bogoliubov transformations, with produced occupation number |βk|².

Fix the dilaton profile and diagonalize the metric gauge, linearize bulk fields, and evaluate tree-level scalar four-point diagrams with graviton exchange in all three channels. Integrating out other perturbations isolates the metric mode coupled to matter; its instantaneous propagator mediates backreaction without representing a propagating gravitational degree of freedom.

For general reduced dilaton gravity, use a Weyl transformation to remove the dilaton kinetic term and eliminate Maxwell fields through their equations of motion. Expand the potential near an extremal root, compute entropy with the Wald formula, and apply the fixed-charge first law to obtain the energy above extremality.

Estimate autocorrelation times with the Madras–Sokal algorithm, bin measurements in widths 3τcorr, and use jackknife uncertainties with bin-size stability checks. Discard 1000 trajectories per ensemble for thermalization. Inflating the less lengthy T=0.4 ensembles' errors by 50% reportedly changes subsequent analyses very little.

At each temperature, fit E/N²≈e00+e01/L+e02/L²+e10/N² simultaneously in lattice extent and matrix size. Here e00 is the continuum, large-N energy and e10 its leading continuum finite-N correction. Sequential extrapolation provides a reported compatibility check.

Discretize Euclidean time and sample configurations with rational hybrid Monte Carlo. Main results use an improved covariant derivative whose unnormalized difference approximates aDt with O(a³) errors, compared with O(a²) for the unimproved definition. Internal energy is measured through the bosonic action.

An inverse search fixes moduli expectation values and vacuum energy, then solves stationarity conditions for superpotential parameters, with one parameter fixed separately. Authors subsequently minimize the resulting potential and evaluate canonically normalized bosonic Hessians and fermion mass matrices.

Dimensional reduction and dualization of the four-dimensional tensor identify axions, kinetic terms and gauged shifts. Matching to N=1 supergravity determines the Kähler potential and motivates the supersymmetric gauge kinetic function.

ADM decomposition identifies lapse and shift constraints; substituting their linear solutions gives quadratic actions. Hamiltonian analysis tests gauge fixing through the nonvanishing determinant of Poisson brackets between gauge conditions and constraints.

Time-dependent orthonormal vielbeins organize fluctuations into useful bases. Their rotation produces an antisymmetric connection Z_IJ, absorbed into a covariant conformal-time derivative. Two-field examples use kinematic and potential-Hessian mass bases.

Canonical quantization and Hankel functions supply free modes. Weak quadratic mixing is treated through in-in expectation values or iterative Green-function solutions. Cubic actions and the large-scale δN expansion organize nonlinear correlation functions.

A quadratic approximation near the final wells estimates curvature M²≈Λ⁴/f² and frictional energy loss Δρ∼Λ⁴f/M_P. Comparing this loss with fluctuation-induced uncertainty δρ supplies the parametric phase-decomposition criterion.

Classical linearized mode equations are solved numerically in an expanding, approximately matter-dominated background, neglecting metric perturbations. Without friction the mode equation is of Hill type; the numerical study searches for resonance before trapping.

Gravitational-wave estimates adapt the envelope approximation, retaining uncollided wall regions, and redshift the resulting radiation through assumed postcollision and reheating histories using entropy conservation.

Introduce chemical potentials for worldsheet currents; combine charge periodicity with modular covariance to obtain spectral flow. Flow the graviton and add noncompact oscillators to construct level-matched charged states.

Fourier-expand KK fields, impose orbifold projections and identify surviving zero-internal-mode towers. Compare their masses with black-hole extremality bounds obtained through consistent truncations and toroidal reduction.
Combine chemical-potential periodicity z → z + 1 with modular S transformations to obtain z → z + τ quasi-periodicity and spectral-flow invariance of the spectrum.
Use Sugawara decomposition and the required Chern–Simons boundary term to separate geometric and current contributions to the stress tensor. Compare fixed-charge Cardy entropy with bulk BTZ entropy.
Project charge-mod-N sectors by finite Fourier transforms, derive their modular mixing matrix, and study derivatives at τ = i through a first-order linear-programming bootstrap.

Fix κ symmetry and worldvolume diffeomorphisms, expand the field-dependent matrix β, and simplify the broken-supersymmetry transformations using ten-dimensional Fierz identities, nonlinear field redefinitions, and an action-trivial fermionic symmetry.

Gather evidence from Goldstino-plus-vector, Goldstino-plus-fermion, and Goldstino-plus-scalar truncations. The scalar argument dualizes a real linear multiplet G to a chiral H. The appendix maps constrained components to standard nonlinear fields using Goldstino-dependent redefinitions.

Use O3 and intersecting O7 projections to select supercharges and truncate worldvolume fields. The O7 calculation explicitly imposes compatible κ fixing and compensating transformations that preserve static gauge.
Far-zone linearization around the prescribed background, replacement by equivalent localized sources, and gravitational/gauge Bianchi identities determine forced stress-energy and current equations.

Euclidean on-shell gravitational actions supply hydrostatic partition functions. Gauge and diffeomorphism Ward identities generate current conservation and intrinsic/extrinsic force equations; Legendre transformations select appropriate charge ensembles.

Near-zone derivative expansions promote seed parameters and embeddings to slowly varying fields. Intrinsic monopole and extrinsic dipole perturbations decouple at first order; selected constraint equations are extracted without solving all radial corrections.

Maps string soft-term hierarchies into reheating temperatures and evaluates one-loop contributions from heavy gauginos to the higgsino mass. In sequestered LVS, fixing the compactification volume correlates reheating and gaugino masses, enabling direct-detection projections.

Uses established entropy-dilution and non-thermal yield prescriptions, distinguishing annihilation-limited production from a branching yield. In the annihilation regime, the quoted abundance enhancement is Ωnt = Ωth sqrt[g*(Tf)/g*(Tr)] Tf/Tr.

Computes higgsino annihilation and spin-independent scattering cross sections with micrOMEGAs and applies published indirect-detection limits and projected sensitivities. SUSYHD is used to obtain a 125 GeV Higgs when evaluating heavy-gaugino loop effects.

Integrating out C_3 produces a step-function branch change. The bounce is constructed as φ_b=φ_i+φ_s, with (∇²−μ²)φ_s=−neμθ and asymptotically decaying φ_s, using Green functions or matched modified-Bessel solutions.

The Euclidean action difference includes bulk, membrane-tension and exterior boundary contributions. Bubble radius extremizes this difference; its general extremum is unavailable in closed form, motivating asymptotic expansions.

Reports in-in calculations of scalar one- and two-point functions. The decoherence discussion couples curvature fluctuations ζ to an environment G and traces over environmental states to discuss suppression of interference.

Uses Hankel mode functions for constant or slowly varying mass ratios and approximate WKB modes for more general profiles. Computes Bogoliubov mixing through two prescriptions, including instantaneous Hamiltonian diagonalization, and uses a one-dimensional scattering analogy. Initial conditions include Bunch–Davies, α and a special equal-coefficient choice.

Higher-order homogeneous fermion integration constants are absorbed into the zeroth-order source and expectation value and then set to zero. The paper interprets the resulting α and β as renormalized source and vev.

Eliminates torsion through its algebraic field equation and solves the resulting Riemannian Einstein and nonlinear Dirac equations perturbatively. Torsion contributes through spin-density terms and a four-fermion interaction.

Computes S(ρ||σ) = Δ〈HA〉 − ΔSA using the vacuum ball modular Hamiltonian, the holographic boundary stress tensor and Ryu–Takayanagi areas. The second-order area is evaluated on a surface obtained perturbatively in the first-order static geometry.

Explicit constructions use gravitational line dressings and angular averaging to obtain Coulomb dressings. Bilocal observables are examined through free-field mode expansion, normal ordering, and a Lorentz-invariant prescription for removing a redundant mass-shell divergence.

The dressing proof rewrites integrated diffeomorphism constraints as a Poincaré boundary generator plus a bulk integral of matter and effective gravitational stress tensors. Gauge invariance then relates the operator's transformation to its dependence on the asymptotic metric.

Represents nonperturbative, α′ and string-loop effects as potential shifts in the two traced constraints. Primed and unprimed corrections are distinguished because their contributions depend on their ten-dimensional origin and need not coincide.

Separates traces of the external and internal components of the ten-dimensional Einstein equations. Integrating the external trace yields the GMN condition; the external trace minus three times the internal trace yields the generalized four-dimensional trace equation.

Tracks the different localized-source combinations: T4loc = Σp[(7−p)/4]NpTpδ(Σp−3) − T3ρ3loc, whereas Tloc = ΣpNpTpδ(Σp−3) − T3ρ3loc. Their responses to added uplift sources drive the comparison of the two constraints.

The author applies the generalized tension bound T_p ≤ M_Pl^(p+1) Q, with Q described as a sum of D-brane charges, to E2 instantons. The resulting geometric bounds are combined with semiclassical and proposed quantum-gravity calculability bounds.

Mixed disk amplitudes couple physical fields to fermionic zero modes localized at E2–D6 intersections. Integrating these modulini generates superpotential terms; intersection numbers determine their charged-field content and gauge transformation.

For inflation, the fibre modulus is canonically normalized through τ1 = exp(2φ/√3). The authors evaluate slow-roll parameters, integrate the e-fold count and impose the density-perturbation normalization, with n_s = 1 + 2η* − 6ε* and r = 16ε*.

The analysis uses the imported correction V_F4 = −(g_s/8π)^2 λ|W0|^4 Σ_i Π_i t_i/(g_s^(3/2) V^4), with Π_i = ∫c2 ∧ D_i. Blow-ups are integrated out first; extremization in two-cycle variables and a Hessian decomposition involving the inverse Kähler metric test stabilization.

The authors expand around inflaton-dependent heavy-modulus displacements and minimize with respect to those fluctuations. They compare the resulting effective potential with a shortcut that replaces heavy multiplets by their vacuum values in K and W before computing the light-field potential.

Type IIB shift breaking is analyzed through period-vector/prepotential expansions and complex-structure-dependent functions in D7 Wilson-line kinetic terms. Canonical normalization and volume power counting then estimate the inflaton mass relative to KK and moduli scales.

The SUSY toy construction uses W=S²(Φ₁²−Φ₂²)/(2m), combines F- and chosen D-term potentials, aligns Φ₁ and Φ₂, and minimizes along S. The local-SUSY extension introduces a minimal Kähler potential and approximates S as sub-Planckian.

Potential slow-roll parameters are expanded with a first correction in (m/ϕ)^n, then expressed through remaining e-folds N. Predictions use r=16ε and n_s=1+2η−6ε, dropping the ε contribution to n_s as negligible. Parameter scans and scalar-amplitude normalization constrain examples.
Construct unitary-gauge operators invariant under spatial diffeomorphisms, restore the Goldstone through the Stückelberg transformation, and use the decoupling limit to obtain mixing interactions.
Use de Sitter representation theory for free equations, helicity decomposition and recursive Hankel-function modes, with normalization fixed through a conserved inner product and orthonormality.
Compute correlators with the in-in formalism; factorize nonlocal soft-limit contributions analytically and evaluate general momentum-dependent shapes numerically.

Numerically solve background evolution, construct Z=aφ̇/H, and solve U″k+[k²−Z″/Z]Uk=0. Evaluate modes after freeze-out and fit the resulting spectrum to extract ns and nrun; the illustrated spectra use 15 k-modes.

Draw selected potential coefficients uniformly within manually chosen ranges. Relate a4 to a5 using the endpoint condition, then refine a5 iteratively through background solutions to obtain the requested e-fold count.

Compare numerical spectra with Stewart–Lyth and alternative approximation schemes. Diagnose discrepancies by separating potential-to-Hubble slow-roll substitutions, the effective Hankel index ν, and its scale derivative.

Develops conventional, subsystem, and operator-algebra erasure correction through equivalent decoding, logical-operator reconstruction, compressed-operator, and reference-system conditions. Proof techniques include purification uniqueness, Schmidt decomposition, commutants, and Schur’s lemma.

Uses block-diagonal reduced states to derive entropy and modular-Hamiltonian relations. An algebraic entanglement first-law argument yields relative-entropy equality from RT; vanishing relative entropy then supplies the reconstruction implication.

Extracts the scalar spectrum from the trace stress-tensor two-point function. The expansion f=f₀[1−f₁g_eff² ln g_eff²+f₂g_eff²+O(g_eff⁴)] uses one-loop f₀ and two-loop f₁,f₂. The appendix summarizes a reported two-loop computation, including UV subtraction and IR regulation.

Uses CosmoMC with matching datasets and a minimizer for best-fit likelihoods. Bayesian evidence integrates the likelihood over normalized flat priors. Microscopic model selection additionally matches the scalar amplitude and β and imposes the tensor bound and theoretical control requirements.

Numerically integrate the third-order fixed-point equation using f, f′ and f″ from the highest polynomial approximation at R = ±0.1. Compare with an infinite-series resummation and Padé approximants, and search for zeros of the stationarity equation.

Functional renormalisation group calculations employ background fields, gauge fixing and ghosts, a linear metric split, York decomposition, optimised cutoffs and an early-time heat-kernel expansion on constant-curvature spherical backgrounds.

Infer complex singularities using a four-parameter oscillatory fit to λ5…λ26 at N = 35. Generalised ratio tests with separation m ≥ 8 estimate convergence radii; the Mercer–Roberts test supports the singularity angle but does not give a stable radius.

Effective-operator power counting and a proposed higher-form Goldstone-equivalence argument constrain mass dependence. A charged particle on a torus, with quantised Landau levels, makes the discrete gauge symmetry and its action on phase space explicit.

Stückelberg fields and Rξ-style gauges expose high-energy propagators. Current conservation, Poincaré invariance and self-energy tensor structures are used to argue that divergences require wavefunction renormalisation rather than independent mass counterterms.

Path-integral dualities introduce independent field strengths and Lagrange multipliers, then perform Gaussian integrations. These connect the massive three-form, axion–four-form action and scalar action with a constant flux variable Q; winding sectors matter for global flux quantisation.

Euclidean path-integral dualization with Lagrange multipliers and flux boundary conditions; dilute instanton–anti-instanton sums, Bessel-function resummation and a quantum-mechanical partition-function comparison.

On-shell bulk actions plus Gibbons–Hawking–York boundary terms, estimates of untrusted core contributions, dimensional reduction of a five-dimensional RN toy model, and cutoff estimates from a self-dual torus compactification.
Numerically evolve one-loop scalar, gauge and third-family Yukawa couplings; impose the tree-level boundedness relations on running quartics and compare with perturbative-unitarity restrictions.

Bilinear gauge-orbit variables and SO(1,3) reparameterization put the potential on the future light cone. Imported stationarity, Morse-theory and discriminant methods are used to study boundedness and neutral minima.

Scan mixing-angle benchmarks and mass splittings; use Lilith diphoton likelihood contours and S,T fits. The stated two-parameter likelihood thresholds are 2.3, 5.99 and 11.83 for 68%, 95% and 99.7% confidence. These are historical fits using the paper's inputs.

Uses boundary expansions, canonical field redefinition, and leading slow-roll expressions to extract predictions. Selected scalar-field simulations illustrate damping of modulus displacement and waterfall evolution; they supply examples rather than an initial-condition probability measure.

Analyzes DTW = 0 trajectories and branches solving ∂TV = 0, their intersections, and real and imaginary scalar masses. Product separability preserves sector supersymmetric critical points, but does not by itself establish their stability.

Expands Fermi occupation numbers, plasma energy, and total entropy through O(Q²), solves the neutrality constraint for the scaled chemical potential, and expresses the results using radial integrals In and mass-dependent momentum integrals A through E.

Imposes energy conservation while differentiating with respect to charge, allowing β = β(Q²). With E = E0+Q²E2 and S = S0+Q²S2, obtains SQQ at Q = 0 as 2(S2−XβE2), where X = β⁻¹(∂βS0)/(∂βE0). Entropy curvature determines the reported stability and fluctuation expression.

T-duality maps the gauge connection to a third D6 scalar. An su(2) matrix ansatz solves Nahm equations. The non-Abelian symmetrized-trace DBI energy and the Abelian D8 DBI determinant are organized into perfect squares to obtain minimum-energy equations.

A diagonal gauge-field/nilpotent-Higgs ansatz reduces the real Hitchin equation to Toda-like equations. Imposing independence of a compact worldvolume coordinate reduces these to ODEs and, with a further ansatz, to (log g)″=4g².

Returns to IIB by approximately T-dualizing the D8 near its equator, then combines two real embedding equations into a holomorphic curve. The appendix also integrates tri-axial funnel equations using Jacobi elliptic functions and studies their degeneration limits.

Hodge decomposition and the ∂∂̄ lemma express c3 as its harmonic part plus i∂∂̄F, with F a co-closed (2,2)-form. The internal metric correction is expressed through a mixed complex Hessian of the scalar obtained from the Hodge dual of J∧F.

Explicit Kaluza–Klein reduction on the corrected background, with spacetime-dependent Kähler fluctuations retained through quadratic order and two external derivatives. Internal total derivatives eliminate contributions involving the metric-deformation functions λi; topological expressions are then promoted to full moduli dependence.

After a four-dimensional Einstein-frame Weyl rescaling, the kinetic terms are matched to N=2 special geometry and N=1 Kähler geometry. A Legendre transform to linear multiplets is used to expose the correction's physical effect.

CLASS is modified by adding the exotic energy density and pressure to the background Friedmann sector. Resulting TT spectra are used to estimate how other cosmological parameters can compensate for the added component.

A Fisher analysis approximates the log likelihood quadratically. Cosmological derivatives use centered 1% finite differences; the exotic-energy derivative uses a one-sided displacement from Ωee=0 chosen to move the sound-horizon angular scale by 1%.

The analysis first refits a no-EE TT baseline, then introduces Ωee and marginalizes over five cosmological parameters for each zc. It uses multipoles 2≤ℓ≤2508, with bins of width 30 above ℓ=30 except for the last bin, to reduce inter-bin error correlations.

Matches the off-shell graviton two-point function at low momentum instead of computing full graviton scattering. This avoids dependence on interactions nonlinear in χ. The Weyl tensors are linearized in gravitons, and integrating out χ yields a spectral expression for λ.

Constructs a Källén–Lehmann representation for the heavy-field two-point function. Weyl index symmetries, on-shell transversality and tracelessness determine the propagator numerator up to normalization, which is fixed by polarization completeness and its physical-state trace.

Uses leading Einstein equations and field redefinitions to remove Ricci-scalar and Ricci-tensor operators. Integration by parts and derivative counting classify linear heavy-field couplings: tadpoles are removed about the proper vacuum, while curvature tensors provide the relevant two-derivative sources.

Holomorphic-block methods organize compact-manifold partition functions through geometric decomposition and corresponding factorization of the partition function. The volume reviews this idea across dimensions and relates it to a five-dimensional AGT correspondence.

Advertised computational tools include Coulomb- and Higgs-branch localization, Jeffrey–Kirwan residues for elliptic genera, matrix-integral analysis, and index-theorem evaluation of one-loop determinants on S⁴. These are chapter summaries, without the calculations themselves in this packet.

The foundational chapters review equivariant cohomology, its Weyl and Cartan models, equivariant characteristic classes, the Berline–Vergne–Atiyah–Bott integration formula, and Atiyah–Singer index theory. The introduction describes a supergeometric finite-dimensional derivation and its formal extension to gauge-theory functional integrals.

Numerical background and linear mode evolution retain time-dependent spectator quantities. Scalar contamination is estimated through gravitationally induced inflaton fluctuations and direct axion density perturbations; amplified-tensor integrals estimate background backreaction.

Analytic tensor estimates use a Whittaker-function gauge-mode solution with subhorizon WKB initial conditions, followed by Green-function integration of the sourced metric mode. These estimates hold mQ and ξ constant.

Expand Z in qᵣ=e^(−2πτ₂) and qᵢ=e^(2πiτ₁). Split the fundamental domain into rectangular τ₂>1 and curved τ₂<1 regions; only the latter retains non-level-matched terms. Equation (5.15) expresses fermionic-point positivity as a weighted sum of spectral coefficients and model-independent integrals.

Computer-aided GGSO scan uses analytic chirality, tachyon-counting and partition-function coefficients. A random sample of 10⁶ from approximately 6.7×10⁷ models produced 1,135 satisfying the stated tachyon, chirality and spontaneous-breaking criteria.

Translate free-fermionic models into orbifold partition functions, introduce marginal current-current deformations, perform spin-structure sums with the Riemann–Jacobi identity, and evaluate the modular integral numerically. Narain-lattice unfolding supplies large-volume asymptotics involving Bessel functions.

Fast backgrounds are reverse-engineered: prescribe θ(t), H(t), the Galileon coefficient, and potential; solve the two Friedmann equations for kinetic functions F1,2, then invert t(θ). Diffeomorphism invariance makes the scalar background equation redundant.

Quadratic scalar perturbations are assessed through kinetic and gradient coefficients A and B. The stated conditions are A>0, B>0, and c_s²=B/A≤1. Canonical normalization estimates the evolving interaction cutoff.
Track gauge-boson mass eigenstates and the surviving charge lattice after Higgsing, then iterate the construction through a chain of Abelian gauge groups.

Estimate composite-monopole size by balancing flux-tube tension against magnetic repulsion and compare it with the Schwarzschild radius. Separately count black-hole charge sectors to motivate an entropy constraint.

Reviews the imported multifield electric criterion that the convex hull of charge-to-mass vectors encloses the unit sphere. For N identical U(1)s with one separately charged particle each, the stated bound is m≤q/√N.
The no-section arguments use Künneth and Lefschetz results to constrain cohomology and Picard groups, then argue that every divisor has fiber intersection divisible by a degree greater than one.

Pull back an ambient hyperplane divisor under q to obtain a multisection, and pull back a base point under p to obtain fiber class F. The divisor–fiber intersection number determines the multisection degree.

For special two-quadric intersections, a determinant of the quadric pencil produces a Jacobian equation. Discriminant multiplicities and extended Weierstrass forms determine fibers; tangent/normal bundle Chern classes yield topological and tadpole data.

Reviews supersymmetric effective-field-theory constructions using W=I(κφ²−μ²), logarithmic quantum corrections along the classically flat inflaton direction, and higher-dimension Kähler and superpotential operators to assess slow roll and tuning.

Uses axion periodicity to organize exponential superpotential terms, examines Kähler-driven saxion stabilization and logarithmic moduli-space distances, and expands an illustrative exponential inflationary potential to compare coefficients with monomial models.

Hamiltonian first-order gravity with lapse/shift constraints and thin-shell junction conditions determines wall dynamics. A rescaled wall radius converts the single-wall equation into motion in an effective potential with bound and unbound trajectories.

Dirac quantization imposes Wheeler–DeWitt constraints; leading WKB action differences estimate tunneling probabilities. An explicit momentum ansatz satisfying the constraints constructs continuous tunneling geometries.

Solve V=0 and ∂V=0 for parameter relations, then perturb the tuning to positive vacuum energy. Extract soft terms and use numerical renormalization-group evolution to obtain illustrative low-energy spectra.

Reformulate supergravity anomaly conditions as fermionic charge traces plus Green–Schwarz and local counterterms. Gravitino contributions carry weights +3 for the cubic anomaly and −21 for the mixed gravitational anomaly.

Provided scripts scan wavenumbers and bispectrum configurations, optionally with MPI. For n_s the guide recommends differentiating a spline through multiple power-spectrum samples rather than relying on the initial example's arbitrary two-point difference.

Integrates coupled background, two-point and three-point transport systems using a variable-step Runge–Kutta–Fehlberg integrator with error control. Field-space correlations are converted into curvature correlations using N_a and N_ab tensors.

SymPy generates potential derivatives and model-specific C++ headers; curved models additionally generate metric, Christoffel, Riemann and covariant-derivative quantities. Noncanonical compilation requires selecting the corresponding C++ implementation.

Combine the dilaton equation, ten- and four-dimensional Einstein traces, and the sourced RR Bianchi identity to eliminate source terms and isolate four-dimensional curvature. Complete flux/warp expressions into squares whose signs constrain R̃4.

Use the internal parallel Einstein trace and decompose fluxes by their number n of parallel flat indices. The erratum restores contributions weighted by n, including terms missed when n ≥ 2. Integrating the corrected curvature identity removes a total derivative under the stated geometric conditions.

Feynman diagrams and power counting organize electron-induced corrections and massless loops. A Newtonian two-body collapse calculation bounds the ladder's lifetime and integrates the photon velocity enhancement.

Geometric optics expands a rapidly varying phase with slowly varying amplitude. Characteristics define a polarization-dependent optical metric, whose null geodesics determine photon or galileon trajectories.
The authors obtain the electron EFT from a one-loop functional determinant and report amplitude matching and direct determinant expansion as checks on coefficient signs.

Combinations of the dilaton equation, Einstein traces, and sourced RR Bianchi identity rewrite the four-dimensional Ricci scalar as negative squares, a total derivative, and initially an indefinite-sign remainder. Geometric and flux restrictions remove that remainder.

Integration over the compact internal space enforces vanishing squares for Minkowski vacua. Sufficiency is then established through flux equations, trace-reversed Einstein equations, explicit Ricci tensors, and identities obtained from the full sourced Bianchi identity.

Use the scalar radial Klein–Gordon equation in the tortoise coordinate r* = r + r0 ln(r/r0−1). In the limit r → r0, the displayed equation reduces to a massless wave equation. This example motivates treating near-horizon species as ultrarelativistic.

Import the statistical-mechanics relation S = (4/3)βU for massless bosonic and fermionic gases, then sum species entropies and energies at a common inverse temperature. Match the resulting total entropy to the Schwarzschild area law.

An inverse method chooses H, φ̇, γ, Ah, Bh, and V to control background and linear perturbations, then reconstructs f1,f2,b,k,q. Couplings as functions of φ follow through t(φ). Specifying only H and φ is explicitly insufficient to characterize the linear theory.

The ADM action is expanded to quadratic order in unitary gauge, δφ = 0. Lapse and shift constraints are eliminated to obtain the scalar kinetic/gradient coefficients A,B and tensor coefficients Ah,Bh; their signs diagnose linear ghosts and gradient instabilities.

Decay estimates match the hidden field-strength bilinear onto φΛ³ and use dimension-six modulus and dimension-eight derivative axion operators. Separate entropy bookkeeping translates gluon or axion radiation into BBN and CMB constraints.

The authors review the scalar glueball treatment and 3→2 freezeout calculation of Carlson et al. They express abundance through Λ and the conserved entropy ratio, using Lambert W solutions for radiation- and matter-dominated decoupling.

Confinement scales are estimated from supersymmetric Yang–Mills running and the group's dual Coxeter number. Extending supersymmetric running to the infrared deliberately gives lower confinement scales than introducing nonsupersymmetric running below a supersymmetry threshold.

Generalized calibration functionals are extended using covariant pullbacks and symmetrization over gauge indices. An alternative derivation extracts Stückelberg couplings and Fayet–Iliopoulos terms from the non-Abelian Chern–Simons action.

The authors specify holomorphic data with A^(0,1)=0, then solve the D-term condition through a complexified gauge transformation. Initially Cartan-valued transformations are enlarged to include identity or non-Cartan generators when required.

Radial SU(2) equations reduce to Painlevé III type. Solutions are expanded near the origin; more involved flux backgrounds use perturbation in λρ, and non-Cartan corrections are constructed by infinitesimal transformations of order λ². Block-diagonal systems are analyzed block by block.

Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac distributions are integrated over phase space to obtain n, e and P, followed by s=(e+P−Σμj nj)/T. Angular integration and dimensionless variables u=E/(kBT), z=mc²/(kBT) facilitate evaluation.

Massless integrals are evaluated analytically using ζ(3) and π⁴ factors; massive-species integrals are evaluated numerically. Contributions are normalized and summed by species, producing temperature-dependent plots and tables.

Separate ideal-gas sums for quark–gluon plasma and the listed hadrons are matched through their energy-density degrees of freedom. Entropy conservation treats decoupled temperatures, while a radiation-dominated Friedmann relation supplies the approximate time–temperature mapping.
Numerically solve inflaton equations of motion for selected two-cosine and polynomial-plus-cosine potentials, reporting observables for 50 and 60 e-folds and comparing them with analytic estimates.

Map inflaton mass to reheating using instantaneous gauge-boson decay: Treh ≈ 6.4×10^6 c (mφ/10^13 GeV)^(3/2) GeV, with g* = 106.75. Estimate additional nonthermal dark matter from the inflaton branching fraction.
Use slow-roll observables, the approximate Lyth relation, and Vφφ ∼ Vφφφ Δφ near a tuned flat region to estimate powers of decay constants. The analysis takes ε small and |η| approximately 10^−2.

T-duality along a worldvolume circle maps the KK5/anti-KK5 decay channel to an NS5/anti-NS5 pair. The authors calculate DBI and Wess-Zumino contributions and include the pair interaction using a near-tip cylindrical geometry and a harmonic function.

Dimensional analysis estimates how flux clumping changes when lower-dimensional antibrane charge spreads over a spherical NS5 brane, distinguishing this from the effectively unchanged dimensionality of the D6-to-KK5 channel.

A small subset n≪p is treated as probes in the backreacted p-antibrane background. Imported Smarr-like energy relations determine near-source gauge data, and the singular flux clumping is evaluated at a string-scale cutoff.

Dressing Θ with scalar-dependent matrices produces the T-tensor, whose components determine fermion shifts. The review relates these shifts through differential gradient-flow identities, including D_s S_AB=(1/2)P_s^{I(A}N_I^{B)}, and uses them to express derivatives of the scalar potential.

Rank factorization Θ_M^α=ξ_M^I ξ_I^α separates the r=rank(Θ) gauged isometries from their symplectic embedding. Locality makes the ξ^I mutually symplectically orthogonal; extending them to a symplectic basis constructs an electric frame and identifies the vectors entering minimal couplings.

Coset and solvable-group parametrizations organize homogeneous scalar geometry. The decomposition S=C⊕N separates dilatonic directions from nilpotent axionic directions; symmetry weights also organize vectors and embedding-tensor flux components.

Topological cycle intersections determine net chirality. Explicit CFT states with Chan–Paton labels determine chirality and localization; beta-function contributions extracted from one-loop amplitudes count massless representations without assigning chirality.

Probe complex-structure deformations using hypersurface parameterizations and periods ∫ΠΩ₃. Developing an imaginary period diagnoses loss of the calibrated sLag condition; changes of cycle volume also change the associated gauge coupling.

Combine dimensional reduction of ten-dimensional SUGRA, DBI and Chern–Simons actions with CFT. Magnetically gauged annulus/Möbius vacuum amplitudes yield thresholds; matching to four-dimensional SUGRA separates holomorphic gauge kinetic functions and leading matter Kähler metrics.

For strong curvature, the authors rewrite the metric and scalar using H1 and H2 and analyze the trace of Einstein's equation. Restricting these functions to Laplacian eigenfunctions leads to logarithmic behavior near relevant poles.

The decomposition g(r)=γ(r)√ρ(r)=γ(r)γ̃(r)/r separates coupling-to-energy tracking from departures of the scalar profile from logarithmic behavior. Equations of motion near the free-field radius estimate the permitted growth of γ.

Newtonian-potential bounds constrain scalar-gradient energy. Power-law profile families approach logarithmic radial behavior at large field variation; a maximal-variation argument also favors logarithmic profiles at fixed gravitational potential.

Original and canonical gauge-field bases are related explicitly. One-loop equations explain why running of gY' is independent of gH and χ; two-loop integrations test the residual dependence and variations in vector-like multiplicities and masses.
